ARTICLE

The Rev. Adam Hamilton Knows What’s the Matter With Kansas
This campaign could be a compelling model for Democrats.
By E.J. Dionne Jr.
Published 2026-09-29 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/adam-hamilton-kansas-senate.html

Political challengers tend to their day jobs when they can, but the Rev. Adam Hamilton has an unusual professional calling. So on a recent Friday afternoon, the Democratic candidate for the United States Senate from Kansas took time out from the campaign trail to perform a wedding. Two days later, he baptized a baby on the vast campus of Resurrection, a United Methodist Church he founded and leads.

Not a word of politics was spoken amid the prayers to Jesus and wonder at the mightiness of God. Instead, it was the insistent calls for selfless love and neighborly service echoing through Resurrection’s hallways and chapels that offered a quiet rebuke to the angry battles raging outside the sanctuary.

It may go too far to speak of the miraculous in an election, but it is a source of wonder and some amazement, for Democrats especially, that Kansas’ Senate race has joined the growing list of 2026 contests in which Republicans are vulnerable.

In a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, at least one recent poll, from Emerson College/Nexstar, gave Mr. Hamilton a two-point lead over the incumbent Republican senator, Roger Marshall. Those who rate Senate races have moved Kansas from a G.O.P. slam dunk to competitive status.

His campaign is important because it wraps together several trends visible across this year’s political map. They include a revolt against the Republicans in a farm belt hit hard by tariffs and rising diesel and fertilizer costs. The rebellion has affected Senate races in Iowa and Nebraska as well as Kansas, and some polls suggest it may be spreading to South Dakota. Mr. Hamilton is also part of a cadre of Democrats whose politics are rooted in their Christian commitments — James Talarico in Texas is prominent among them — defying longstanding G.O.P. claims that their foes are hostile to people of faith.

A former Republican himself, Mr. Hamilton embodies a nationwide shift in the allegiances of moderate Republicans toward the Democrats. And like many other candidates in the middle of the country, Mr. Hamilton is trying to balance blunt criticisms of Mr. Trump — on high prices, tariffs, the war in Iran, cuts in health care and nutrition programs and his handling of immigration — with promises of a less partisan, less angry, more cooperative politics on the other side of the Trump experience. Implicit is the idea that the opposite of Trumpism is not an equally in-your-face politics from the other side but a return to a degree of mutual respect.

This is why the often heated debate among Democratic factions that plays so prominently on the coasts and in the media seems so distant in places like Kansas that local Democrats are determined to make competitive.

“I don’t really pay much attention to the national debate” among Democrats, Mr. Hamilton said in an interview. “My focus is here in Kansas.” But if he prevails, the merits of his middle-of-the-road, values-based approach will become part of that debate. He speaks in fiercely moral terms of how much damage Mr. Trump’s cuts in safety net programs have done to Kansans living on the edge and how tariffs have hurt farmers and small businesses. But he is also running an ad calling out “socialism” and describes himself as “a moderate or independent-minded Democrat.”

The point, he told me, is “to differentiate who I am as a Democrat in Kansas,” noting that is “very different than, maybe, a mayor in Washington or New York City.”

Addressing a living room gathering in Overland Park in the suburbs of Kansas City that account for nearly a third of the state’s voters, Mr. Hamilton devoted considerable energy to detailing the costs of Mr. Trump’s policies and Mr. Marshall’s failure to challenge them. “Senator,” he said, “your job is to be a champion for the people of Kansas, not to be spokesperson for the White House to the people of Kansas.”

His stump speech always returns to a friendlier kind of politics. “I’m pretty sure in this room we have Republicans and we have Democrats and independents,” he told those gathered in Overland Park. “It’s not about that. It’s about decency. It’s about humanity. And what’s happening in Washington, D.C., is not normal. It’s not how things work. I’ve never seen it before.”

If you listen to Mr. Hamilton long enough, you learn that “normal” is both a very good thing and the counterpoint to all the country is experiencing now.

One other thing about Mr. Hamilton, and it may be the most important thing: He has built the largest Methodist congregation in the United States (24,000 members across nine sites in the Kansas City area and 22 services every Sunday) by preaching a Gospel that combines a thoroughly traditional promise of salvation through Jesus Christ with a call for community engagement and a dedication to those in need. He regularly notes that his congregation is divided roughly equally among Democrats, Republicans and independents.

In a state where 70 percent of adult Kansans identify as Christians, Mr. Marshall has taken to calling Mr. Hamilton “a megachurch C.E.O.” Mr. Marshall means it as a negative, even though a lot of Republicans frequent megachurches and respect executives. At the least, Mr. Hamilton can counter a favorite conservative talking point against Democrats “who never met a payroll": Resurrection has 461 employees.

To sharpen the attack, Mr. Marshall and ads on his behalf have added politically loaded adjectives, labeling Mr. Hamilton a “woke megachurch C.E.O.” or a “millionaire megachurch C.E.O.”

If “woke” is just an all-purpose right-wing epithet these days for anyone who believes in equal rights for Black and L.G.B.T.Q. people and for women, well, sure. But “woke” is a strange word for Mr. Hamilton, who has written dozens of books defending the Christian faith and urging readers to embrace it. The title and message of one of them, “Seeing Gray in a World of Black and White,” may best capture Mr. Hamilton’s disposition and his efforts to define what he calls a Christian “middle way.”

In his book, he argues that the use of Christianity in the culture wars has turned it into “a wedge that drives people away from Christ, rather than drawing them to him.” He also insists on “holding on to what is good in the past” and “retaining the historic doctrines of the Christian faith as articulated in the creeds.”

To walk Resurrection’s campus on a Sunday, attend a service and watch hundreds of families take advantage of its meeting rooms and coffee bars is to experience what you might call Heartland Homeyness. The Lord’s Prayer and — this being what Kansas City Chiefs’ fans call their kingdom — a whole lot of bright red Patrick Mahomes shirts take precedence over any kind of politics.

Republicans are finding it awkward this year to confront opponents such as Mr. Hamilton and Mr. Talarico whose faith defines them. The G.O.P.’s backup plan? To insist that their foes embrace defective or heretical brands of Christianity.

Campaigning for Mr. Marshall in mid-September, Vice President JD Vance accused Mr. Hamilton’s church of supporting a “devil-worshiping” drag group. The attack was false in just about all its specifics. The only actual fact Mr. Vance had to work with is that Resurrection joined dozens of other local sponsors of Kansas City PrideFest. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas on X accused Mr. Hamilton of being “heretical” for insisting that Muslims, Hindus and Jews are not condemned to an “eternity in hell.” Presumably, Mr. Cruz is prepared to explain to his non-Christian constituents that they face eternal damnation.

The attacks on Mr. Hamilton’s faith drew reproaches from his Methodist bishop and 120 Methodist ministers in Kansas, and Mr. Hamilton sees the onslaught as a sign of Republicans alarm: “We’ve got a real race on our hands, or they wouldn’t be here,” he told the Overland Park crowd.

Republicans should be worried. In a state Mr. Trump carried with 57 percent of the vote in 2024, his approval rating was down to 40 percent in the Emerson survey. It also found that 48 percent of voters had an unfavorable view of Mr. Marshall; just 41 percent saw him positively. Compounding his troubles, Mr. Marshall has come under scrutiny after The Times reported that he sued more than 700 patients for unpaid bills, the subject of a tough Hamilton ad that went up last week.

As for what Mr. Hamilton’s called his “inclusivist” view of salvation, he said in an interview that it is thoroughly orthodox, shared by, among others, the Roman Catholic Church and widely revered Christian thinkers such as C.S. Lewis and the early church father Justin Martyr. “God can give that salvation to anyone He chooses,” Mr. Hamilton said.

If this theological controversy seems strange in an election that for most voters is about economics, war and Mr. Trump, it reflects back on what makes Mr. Hamilton’s campaign a potentially compelling model: Because of who he is and what he believes, he is constantly linking values to policy.

This is where Democrats have historically fallen short, said Ashley All, a Kansas-based Democratic strategist. A veteran of two decades in Kansas politics who is not part of Mr. Hamilton’s campaign, Ms. All said Democratic campaigns and candidates did not ask often enough, “What are the things that connect people?” Mr. Hamilton does this regularly, she told me, “because building bridges has been his entire job for 40 years.”

He’s trying to prove that’s possible even in a fraught political moment. Recently he posted a video responding to a question he says he gets a lot — are you liberal or conservative? His answer was “Yes, of course!” He continued, “I think we can be both. To be a liberal means to be generous of spirit, open to seeing things with new eyes and open to reforming. And to be conservative means holding on to values or beliefs that are really important. We can be both of those things at the same time. … We need each other, we really do. We’re better together. And that’s how our system’s meant to work.”

A pastor who insists on seeing the grays in debates over politics and religion is making Kansas a laboratory for testing whether that’s still true.

E.J. Dionne Jr., a Times contributing Opinion writer, is the author of “Why Americans Hate Politics,” “Our Divided Political Heart,” “Why the Right Went Wrong” and, most recently, “100% Democracy,” with Miles Rapoport.

ARTICLE

Republicans Are Struggling Everywhere. This State Is the Epicenter.
The problems of technology were there before Trump and will be there after.
By Christopher Caldwell
Published 2026-09-29 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/data-centers-democrats-republicans.html

At the start of this year, the largest underlying trend in national politics still seemed to be the transformation of longtime swing states into Republican bastions. Florida, Iowa, Ohio: The closer you looked, the more invulnerable President Trump’s party seemed.

The situation in Ohio was stark. In 2022, the governor, Mike DeWine, had beaten his Democratic opponent by 25 points. A year ago, the Trump-allied biotech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor, held nearly a double-digit lead over his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

Ohio’s high-tech industry was a big factor. A bipartisan enthusiasm spurred by President Joe Biden’s CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, it nonetheless played to the strengths of Republican incumbents. Intel was building a huge chip plant near Columbus. Mr. Ramaswamy was promising to turn the Ohio River Valley into the next Silicon Valley. “People talk about the Rust Belt,” he said in March of last year. “I don’t want to talk about the Rust Belt. I want to lead us to the platinum belt — the sectors of the future, from semiconductors to nuclear energy to even A.I.”

But times have changed. This month, a YouGov poll for Bowling Green State University found Ms. Acton leading Mr. Ramaswamy by three points. The incumbent Republican senator Jon Husted has fared similarly. Mr. Husted appeared likely at the start of the year to keep his seat. But since June, polls have shown him trailing the former senator Sherrod Brown, who was soundly defeated by the Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024.

A lot has happened to sour the public on Mr. Trump’s party, including the war with Iran and rising prices, but much of the discontent involves high-tech industries (like cryptocurrencies) and their needs (like H-1B visas for tech workers). Above all, Republicans are paying a political cost for the buildout of data centers for artificial intelligence.

Last month, Axios published a leaked memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee that expressed alarm about the devastating effectiveness of video spots Mr. Brown had begun airing. These tied Mr. Husted to the arrival of data centers in Ohio. “More than any other thing in this race,” the memo said, “data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck. If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one.”

It’s not just Ohio. Mr. Trump has been dangerously dim on the subject of data centers. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers,” he wrote on Truth Social, “is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” He will probably hurt his party on Election Day, five weeks from now.

But it will not be easy for Democrats to lay a permanent claim to the moral high ground. The problems of high-tech industries were there before Mr. Trump arrived and will be there after he leaves. At present, the A.I. buildout is driving a large share of American economic growth. There are strong incentives for both parties not to restrain or regulate it. Neither Republicans nor Democrats have come up with a trustworthy set of policies for managing artificial intelligence, the multitrillion-dollar projects required to expand its use or the newfound political power this gives the tech industry.

Thousands of data centers have been built or are under construction in the United States. With 166 in operation, according to the Pew Research Center, Ohio has more than any state besides Virginia, Texas and California. Voters appear to think that’s enough. Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York has declared a moratorium on new construction. Other states are mulling outright bans.

What made Ohio so hospitable to tech expansion — and so vulnerable to a political backlash — is a long story. The state has lots of people, cheap open land, abundant water and weak zoning laws. Most important, it was devastated by deindustrialization like few other places, and has spent decades pursuing an industrial revival. Starting in 2011, Gov. John Kasich, a Republican, signed into law tax reforms and exemptions that would lure Amazon, Meta and Google to build new facilities in the state. In 2022, Intel committed to a $20 billion plant investment and the Biden administration bet heavily on tech in its CHIPS Act.

Last year, Ohio passed a bill that promised to fast-track data centers. In the New Albany International Business Park outside Columbus, there are already 40 data centers serving Amazon Data Services, Google, Meta and Microsoft, with 28 more planned. Last month Nvidia and partners announced an estimated $500 billion building project that will include a facility in Pike County, two hours east of Cincinnati, envisioned as one of the largest data-center complexes in the world.

All of this has costs. These vast installations are wrecking the landscape in unspoiled parts of Ohio, as they have done over the past two decades in Northern Virginia. And this is happening in a national real-estate market transformed by the Covid-19 pandemic, which led millions of Americans to move to more tranquil, nonurban surroundings. Ohio’s peak electricity demand is projected to rise by 56 percent over the next two decades.

Cheery projections made by Ohio politicians have not panned out. Tax exemptions intended to lure tech firms wound up costing $1.4 billion more than anticipated in 2025. Above all, the jobs have not come. Data centers are basically rows of computers sitting on racks — like a supersize version of that mysterious closet full of tangled wires and blinking lights at your workplace. Once construction is finished, no one but a couple of tech guys ever has any reason to go in there. Last year, The Wall Street Journal found that a large data center in Abilene, Texas, would employ about 100 people — a fraction of the jobs created by a cheese-packaging plant nearby. And cheese packaging doesn’t threaten to send residents’ utility bills through the roof.

Most data centers have been built near cities. But two-thirds of those projected for the coming years are being built in the sticks. The voters most up in arms now include a lot of Trump supporters. Ohio Republicans are trying to mitigate the political fallout of data centers while protecting their continued construction. In August, Mr. Ramaswamy called for free electricity for people living near data centers. Mr. Husted has sponsored a Senate bill urging big electricity users to cover their own electricity costs — legislation Senate Democrats criticized as toothless.

Outside of Ohio, Republican politicians appear even more worried. In August, Mike Rogers, a Senate candidate in Michigan who is not just a defender of data centers but an investor in them, called for a one-year statewide moratorium on new construction until better “guardrails” were in place. Last week, Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas, until recently an unflagging tech enthusiast, halted all permits for new data centers. Two new polls have shown the long-serving and perennially popular Mr. Abbott trailing his Democratic challenger, State Representative Gina Hinojosa.

Mr. Husted has cast the argument over data centers as one in which progress is at stake. “I mean, you can go back to the bunny-ear antenna on your TV,” he said on a recent podcast. “You don’t need a data center. But if you’re connected to a wire, you’re using the data center.”

That was true of the data centers that Amazon was building in 2006, but serving customers is less and less what data centers do now. Many of today’s monolithic structures exist only to train A.I.s — making models more powerful by carrying out operations that number in the trillions of trillions annually.

The result is a strange partisan landscape. It’s easy to think that data centers will become the Democrats’ issue, tying in to the party’s environmentalist commitments. But that is not what’s going on. The climate journalist Robinson Meyer told David Wallace-Wells of The Times recently that environmental arguments against data centers are sometimes overblown. The main reason people say they oppose them is water use, followed by electricity prices; but when a data center gets canceled, it is most often because of noise. In this respect the uprising against data centers resembles that against wind farms, a Republican movement if ever there was one.

Mr. Trump’s simple-minded online attacks on those who oppose data centers have led many partisan Democrats to deduce that the tech industry is “allying” itself with him. But the tech industry is merely taking pains, as it always does, to stay on the good side of its regulators. That effort has caused a good deal of quiet corruption through the years, and Mr. Trump’s demand for public avowals of fealty has made the corruption overt.

But all the Democrats have to do is win a presidential election, and they will rediscover that there is nothing — nothing at all — inherently Trumpian about the tech industry. They will inherit all the complexities that come with trying to push back against sector that is, for now, vilified and unpopular but vital to the economy.

Could they push back? Yes: If large numbers of Americans come to accept the argument of many A.I. experts that the technology itself threatens humanity with extinction, then Democrats might be emboldened to take extreme steps to rein in the industry, even on pain of economic upheaval. But in that case the party would be likely to lose its political advantage in another way: through an effort to stop A.I. that becomes bipartisan.

Seventy percent of Americans now oppose having a data center near them. That’s a problem for Big Tech — one that will persist even if Republicans are routed and better policies put in place. The costs of data centers are local, the benefits national. So entrenched has inequality become on the cutting edge of our economy that any promise of eventual top-down redistribution of those benefits will be met with skepticism.

This is especially true as voters grow more savvy about who gets what and from whom in the tech industry itself. There is a reason Mark Zuckerberg had to promise at least $12 billion to settle claims that his business fostered internet addiction: He is now dealing with parents who belong to his own generation — a less gullible bunch, when it comes to tech, than the analog-age parents who raised them.

As the baby boomers’ presence in the electorate wanes, the millennials and their successors will be called upon to weigh A.I.’s promises against the likelihood of human extinction. You can get a sense of how they are leaning by looking at the polls: The problem of data centers is not just the inconvenience they pose; it’s also the project they serve.

These rising fuel costs are going to make their way into your purchases until the world’s supply of diesel increases, which doesn’t seem likely anytime soon, given the Iran and Ukraine conflicts. ARTICLE

$6 Diesel Is Hurting Small Truckers. It Could Hurt Trump, Too.
When fuel costs rise, the price of everything rises.
By Adam Wingfield
Published 2026-09-29 15:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/diesel-prices-truckers.html

Every week seems to bring a record high for diesel prices — and more trouble for the nation’s truckers. They’re hurting. Since January, diesel has increased more than 80 percent, to $6.53 a gallon.

Nearly everything that you buy rides on a big, diesel-burning truck at some point. Farmers are heavy users of diesel for their machinery, too, so diesel figures in twice at the supermarket. These rising fuel costs are going to make their way into your purchases until the world’s supply of diesel increases, which doesn’t seem likely anytime soon, given the Iran and Ukraine conflicts.

President Trump is reportedly considering banning diesel exports. It won’t help. Sure, some regions in the United States, such as the Southeast, would see prices subside for a short time, but prices elsewhere would increase.

For small truckers, the pain at the pump is threatening their businesses. About 92 percent of America’s trucking companies are small operations, with 10 or fewer trucks. If we lose too many of them, freight costs — and then your costs — will go even higher. I’ve been in this industry for more than two decades, as both a truck owner and now as a logistics consultant helping smaller operators. A lot of them were struggling even before we saw a $3 per gallon increase in diesel costs. It’s their largest variable expense.

We’re advising our truckers to be careful about the lanes they choose—as in, what destinations will yield the best outcomes. With truckers now spending as much as $1,400 per tank, you have to tightly control fuel burn. In California, the price is literally off the charts — the pumps were at their limit of $9.999 a gallon. We tell truckers going west to east to buy only enough fuel to get out of California. It’s worth it to add a stop in Nevada and fill up there. My clients generally buy fuel at the pump, often at a discount using a fuel card. But they can’t add a line item called a fuel surcharge.

In trucking, there are two different paths for moving cargo: One is by contract and the other is by the spot market. Contracted freight loads made by big fleets include a fuel surcharge that changes from week to week and is tied to the average diesel price. The spot market moves general freight through brokerages. Small carriers do most of their business this way; they generally don’t haul specialty items or perishables like pharmaceuticals. Truckers bid against one another on each load the brokers offer.

The spot market isn’t working well for a lot of them. This year, overall spot rates are up roughly 66 cents per mile to $3.41 per mile. But fuel costs are up 90 cents per mile. For a small trucking company, that can often become a losing proposition — they can’t hedge the cost of diesel prices as UPS and other large outfits can.

With diesel prices spiking, too often it means running a truckload at a loss, once you include costs such as maintenance, truck payments, insurance, registration and permits and disability coverage. You’ve got to worry about cash management, too. A small carrier running spot negotiates load by load but has to pay the fuel card bill in seven days whether that load is paid for or not.

To make matters worse, the trucking industry has dealt with a prolonged, post-pandemic freight recession that drove down rates and forced out thousands of trucking outfits. The current price spike could be a similar catalyst. That’s how exits happen in this business. Not a sudden collapse, but an owner-operator parking the truck, letting their interstate trucking authority lapse, and walking away because the next load won’t cover his bills.

Small trucking companies tend to drive in the right lane when it comes to politics. And they want immediate relief. Simple as that. If diesel rates keep rising, truckers will show up at the polls and let their complaints be known. They have been posting videos from truck stops and gas stations of their astonishingly high fuel bills, just in case the message isn’t getting across.

There’s been a lot of talk about banning exports of diesel fuel, at least temporarily. One Republican senator, Dan Sullivan of Alaska, said it out loud: “The cost of diesel is just too damn high.” Agreed. We need to get lower fuel prices for the sake of the entire economy. But a ban on diesel exports isn’t necessarily the right solution. We live in a global market. A ban will ultimately raise the cost of imports. It may provide temporary price relief to truckers in states such as Mississippi and Louisiana, close to the refineries that supply diesel, but it will raise prices in the Northeast, which imports diesel. Mid- to long term it could make things worse.

We all pay when there’s a sustained fuel price run-up like one we’ve experienced this year. It will probably push the next wave of small truckers out faster than many of us expect. Fewer trucks on the road means less capacity, and less capacity means higher rates. Those costs pass to the shipper, then the retailer, then to the register — where you will wonder why prices are going up again.

Everything on that shelf got there on a truck. And every one of those miles costs more to run today than it did in January.

Adam Wingfield is a former trucking company owner and founder of Innovative Logistics Group, a consultancy focused on small trucking firms.

That one thing that happens when people get wealthier, and you’d probably know about this, is that they all of a sudden get a lot more human help. ARTICLE

Bill Gates’s Blunt Warning on A.I.
As A.I. capabilities accelerate, the technologist is shocked by the “complete lack of engagement” with the question of how to manage its risks.
By Ezra Klein and Jack McCordick
Published 2026-09-29 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-bill-gates.html

This is an edited transcript of “The Ezra Klein Show.” You can listen to the episode wherever you get your podcasts.

Bill Gates is a fascinating person in the artificial intelligence debate right now. He is somebody with experience in several of the different perspectives that most people can only hold one of: He was a revolutionary technologist who built some of the foundations of the future that we’re now living in. When he was chief executive of Microsoft, he was a corporate leader. He has felt the momentum of corporate competition — Microsoft, of course, is still in some of the race dynamics present in A.I. And then, as chair of the Gates Foundation, he has been working with governments around the world on regulatory issues, poverty alleviation and equity for many years.

Very few people combine technological experience, corporate experience and governmental experience in quite the way he does.

So his recent essay on A.I., in which he says that he is staking his reputation on trying to get people to see how bad what is coming might be and trying to get them to see that we are not ready for what is about to happen, was something.

It was a real departure from what I’ve read from Gates previously.

When I sat and talked to him, I was really struck by how emphatic he was — how afraid even he seemed to be of what we are building, and how so many of the people in positions of authority are denying what is about to happen.

It’s really quite a call to arms.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft claiming copyright infringement. The companies have denied those claims.)

Ezra Klein: Bill Gates, welcome to the show.

Bill Gates: Great to see you.

So I wanted to begin with a clip we found of you on “Late Show With David Letterman” from 1995. I’m going to hand it over to you to play.

Archival clip of “Late Show With David Letterman”: David Letterman: Is there something now, beyond what we understand about computers, that 20 years ago we didn’t fully understand about computers — is there now another level of something, maybe we haven’t even thought of it, maybe it’s not even possible, maybe a whole different mechanism, a whole different software and hardware? Or is this going to be it now through the end of time? Bill Gates: Well, mostly what we’re working on now is the computer being a tool — a tool to help us learn or find other people with the same interests. Eventually, we may figure out how to make the computer think, but that turns out to be a very tough problem. In fact, there’s been almost no progress made on it. So nobody knows when that’ll happen. Some people think it’ll never happen. Letterman: Yeah, we don’t want them to think, do we? Not really, I don’t think. Gates: Well, it’s a scary thought.

So that was 30 years ago. Narrate for me how we went from that being a scary thought that might never happen to arguably the reality we’re sitting here discussing today.

Well, the notion that computation could provide thinking at a human level — you have Alan Turing talking about that before I’m born, and even proposing a test of: If you could be fooled in a conversation, that was called passing the Turing test.

And so the whole time I’m learning software, this idea of: Can we make software see or listen or read or write? That’s the holy grail.

And when I did drop out of Harvard, I said to my co-founder, Paul Allen: Gosh, if there’s a breakthrough in artificial intelligence while we’re off selling basic interpreters and word processors, we’ll feel bad. I might wish I would have stayed in academia.

So that’s 1975. Progress on A.I. is mostly going down dead ends, like Prolog expert systems. And there’s a small group, including Geoffrey Hinton and a few others, who are working on neural nets. And eventually, there’s enough power — actually coming from the graphics processor — that that idea, these highly statistical approaches, start to show promise.

And I was going down to see OpenAI on a regular basis to see the work they were doing, and I challenged them, saying: Hey, if you can read a biology textbook and pass the advanced placement exam — getting a perfect grade, which is a 5 — then you will have proven that you are reading. That is, encoding knowledge in an accessible form.

And so it’s six months before the public release that Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever come to my house and demonstrate to me getting a 5 on the A.P. exam, even on questions that I had made up that it couldn’t possibly have seen — very complex biology problems. It was nearly perfect. So that was shock No. 1.

And then late last year, when Anthropic’s Claude coding models got super good, I could see that they are as good as I am — it’s significantly my most developed talent, because I was obsessed from age 13 to 24 as to whether I could write code as good or better than anyone.

That’s another moment where I went: This is incredible. That the capability of doing long-running, complex tasks has now gotten to the point that they are superhuman at writing code and in finding flaws in code.

So what they’re not superhuman at yet is deciding what to do — that kind of higher-level strategizing. Do you think that’s far from being a capability for them?

Well, definitely, if you’re — our foundation does these strategy reviews. We spend two weeks in October to set how we’re going to spend our $10 billion next year, for 2027.

A year ago somebody said: Well, we should ask the A.I. what it thinks. And that was actually a pretty good joke back then, because it wasn’t coherent enough to see these things.

This year, among the inputs we’ll have to that discussion is taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other.

And in a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage.

So we’ve gone from it being a joke to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution.

So in that “Letterman” interview, you said it would be a scary thought. Why, back then, would you have said it would be a scary thought to have computers that think?

Well, no one who’s ever been fascinated by, nor wanted to develop A.I., doesn’t realize that it’s incredibly scary that it will be better.

Biological minds — it’s amazing how general purpose they are in that the optimization was in staying alive, breeding, socializing with each other for survival and fertility.

And yet, we can write symphonies and play chess and even write some pretty cool software. And the idea that when you move the template away from biology to silicon, you don’t have these boundaries between individuals — you don’t have a limited memory.

The size of the brain is limited by the birth canal — it’s why humans, at first, are very limited. We’re very unusual in how helpless we are at birth, because we’re so optimized for having a large brain. But the silicon intelligence doesn’t have these limitations. The idea of: Read every medical journal and see if there’s anything that we didn’t spot? The A.I.s do that today.

That’s why, particularly for less common diseases, they are so superhuman at seeing a set of symptoms and being able to diagnose them. They can just keep more in their mind and see what things relate to each other — no human will ever be able to do that. So if you don’t retain control over it, you’ve evolved a species that will be to us as we are to, say, dogs or cats — just in a very different realm.

And so the major A.I. companies, whether it’s DeepMind or OpenAI, they all say: OK, whatever goes on here, it can’t just be driven by profit maximization. We have to have a charter that if we get to dangerous thresholds, we can exercise judgment that would be against profit maximization. Sadly, those mechanisms only work if there’s only one company.

And so say OpenAI invented post-artificial general intelligence, and then they said: No, no, we’re going to bury this. If no one else ever did it, then fine, that Pandora’s box stayed closed. But of course, many companies work on this, and even OpenAI spawned Anthropic because Anthropic’s founders thought that some of these safety issues weren’t getting enough attention.

So no one involved with this takes lightly the idea of: OK, what world does superpowerful A.I. create?

I want to hold on that race dynamic for a minute. One of the reasons I was excited to talk to you about this is you’ve both been on the technologist side, and you’ve run a major company in competition with other companies. You’ve worked with a lot of governments.

I spoke last week with Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, and he said that his perspective is that safety is a real concern, but the race dynamic is fake. If the product isn’t safe, don’t release it.

Archival clip of Jensen Huang: If I believe that I’m about to launch a product that is unsafe, it is completely in my ability, my power and my responsibility — and I’m incentivized to do so — to not launch the product.

That we don’t need new laws — and this is the role of individual chief executives to not release a product that is not ready to release.

How do you see that question?

Well, there’s never been a product that’s less understood in terms of what its capabilities are than A.I. And A.I. has crossed the threshold that its ability to empower a bioterrorist to kill hundreds of millions — that exists today. The ability to do a cyberattack that scrambles all of the bank accounts, shuts down the electric grid — that exists today, and we know that’s the case.

And the reason that exists is because somebody with ill intent can take the A.I. and cause it to do those things. And it’s not the A.I. — someday in the future, there could be a control problem where the A.I., on its own, through an unintentional interpretation of what it’s optimizing, could go off and do bad things. But we crossed the cyber threshold and we crossed the bio threshold early this year.

And my decision to take my voice and not just say: Hey, let’s eradicate polio, let’s be generous with foreign aid — the things that all of my money is going to, I am going to use my voice.

It’s something that’s more important, which is that we are not awake to where we are with A.I. and the choices that humanity — not a country, but all of humanity — has to make. Do we make the effort to shape this in a net-positive direction? That actually overrides my total commitment to the foundation’s health work.

What specifically was the threshold? What did you see that made you think we’re in a new reality here?

This notion that it can find bugs in code, including security bugs: The next releases leading up to Mythos are increasingly good.

And they’re finding bugs in code that humans have looked over for over 20 years and said: Boy, we see there’s no problem here.

And in a few minutes, the A.I. says: No, no, I can inject this over here and this over here — at a level of complexity where, when you see it, you go: Wait. Oh, yeah, you’re right.

The bioattack — the Gates Foundation, where we fund lots of medical research — the sophistication of coming up with new molecules, that’s really a good thing. But it’s ultimately dual use. Now that power has been passed into the hands of a small group just using the latest A.I. tools.

Well, I almost can’t believe you’re asking that. This is the most dangerous thing that humans have ever gone near.

I mean, we’ve created a society that tries to keep people safe not by saying: Oh, we can bankrupt the person who does that.

No, it’s fair to say that outside of the industry, the awareness of the dangers of A.I. is extremely low. And you can say that of academia, you can say that of think tanks, you can say that of policymakers, politicians.

The only question in my mind is: Do we wait until a cyberattack causes massive damage and a bioattack causes massive damage, and then the monitoring safeguards are required in these models to minimize the chance of that happening many, many more times? Or can we be wise enough to put these things in and require these things to be put in before millions of deaths?

OpenAI said this about GPT-6 Astra, and people inside OpenAI have been raising the alarm that the systems seem to know when they’re being tested. There’s more situational awareness, and so the testing environment is no longer as indicative necessarily of what they will do. So that’s one.

And the second is that all the labs are moving as quickly as they can toward recursive self-improvement, where you have the A.I. coder moving not just from speeding up the engineer but really taking over the coding. Well, so you’re not focusing on the whole problem there.

I’m surely not. [Laughs.]

The fact that, at some point, the A.I. system itself may do something that’s against our interests — that is absolutely a risk, and the symptoms we’ve seen through aspects of Hugging Face and other problems point out that the way we do the reinforcement learning today, the fact that we don’t have a supervisory layer that has some absolutes, like: You’re not supposed to take over other computers. You’re not supposed to break out into the internet.

The control problem is a serious problem, but the imminent risk is not recursive self-improvement. The imminent risk is: These are the most powerful tools ever, and unlike every other dangerous technology, they were not funded by government research and development, and the government is not a significant purchaser of these products. It’s not like rockets or nuclear weapons.

So what does that imply? If you’re more worried in the near term about what human beings do with A.I. than loss of A.I. control, then what does that imply for what your first steps need to be?

There is no supervisory layer today. That supervisory layer is needed urgently to prevent bad people from using today’s A.I.s to shut down economies or kill millions of people.

These models, the ability to separate out making molecules for good and making them for evil — that is so hard to distinguish. Anthropic released Mythos and Fable, where they had turned the filters up so high that you can literally ask questions about cancer and, next thing you know, you’re down at Opus and then Sonnet, and then Haiku is the only A.I. willing to help you.

And there are humans who, for bad reasons, will be able to use these models. And so unless we put in safeguards and monitoring and require that in all models, then we’re just going to have some gigantic events of that type, and then finally we’ll respond.

So there’s no doubt that to date, A.I. has created more jobs than it’s destroyed. The demand for the skill sets, even just to build the data centers, is very, very high. We have a reasonably low unemployment rate.

So the two counterarguments I’ve heard people make on this: One is that you have a Jevons paradox effect, where the cheaper, more widespread availability of this kind of intelligence leads to a massive increase in the demand for this kind of thing.

So, yes, you have many more A.I. chatbot nurses, and that leads to more people being sent to the hospital, being sent to the doctor, where real nurses take care of them.

Yes, it is making a human-provided resource much cheaper, but because it’s going to expand the demand so much, it will sort of work itself out — create jobs in other areas, create new demand. How do you see that?

Well, Jevons is just a referral to the fact that parts of the economy are subject to demand elasticity. And yes, in the case of software, if you’re, say, three times as fast and there is still some role that only humans can perform, then as you lower the cost, you induce demand. So it’s fair to say that the equilibrium today so far for software is not a loss of employment.

When we invented radial tires that lasted four times as long, for some weird reason, people didn’t drive four times as much. And factories that make tires employ a quarter of as many people. When you replace people in Amazon warehouses with robots, people don’t buy more because of that.

So anybody who’s numeric can say to themselves: What portion of the economy is subject to demand elasticity, and what are those tasks that will still be human-necessary?

As soon as you’ve completed the entire task, it doesn’t matter that there’s demand elasticity. That goes into the token budget. It doesn’t go into the human salary budget.

The cost for some of these things is so much less than the cost of the human labor, and so as you cross reliability thresholds, both with white-collar and humanoid robots, you destroy jobs and you leave no high ground.

But A.I., because of the efficiency and invention that comes with it — over the 20-year period, you do get mind-blowing advances in things that people can relate to: the cost of their food, shelter and education. Because those are highly regulated areas. And so the good stuff, if we’re not careful, arrives more slowly than the bio and cyber risks, the psychosocial risk and the jobs risk. Those things in the next five years are very significant.

And so people will decide — although it’s hard for a single country to check out — people will decide whether to slow down, stop or get rid of A.I. And yes, it will have political difficulties.

Stopping data centers isn’t going to slow this thing one iota. So anybody who’s against data centers because they think that’ll slow down A.I., that’s a waste of effort. Now, the data centers are going to get built somewhere.

So the broad view of the technology — that has to be expressed in some other form.

I want to get at something you’re saying here because it’s something that I’ve thought about, too, which is that there are a lot of rate limiters, a lot of weak links in the chain when you try to take, even in an optimistic view, A.I. advances that then have to be built in the material world.

You have an acceleration of good candidates for pharmaceutical development, but you still need to find rats to test on, monkeys to test on, human trials. You have slow regulatory agencies, etc.

And then you have this tremendous acceleration of intelligence that is, for lack of a better term, native to the digital world and is acting there in a constant way.

I mean, right now you see this. You can accelerate A.I. with very little regulatory overhang, but you cannot get the OpenAI parking lot covered in solar panels without permits.

So I think you have a very high chance of getting into a very weird economic and social world, where the digital world is spinning into this other thing, but most of the things human beings need ultimately come out physically. We need shelter and we need food and we need all this, and they run through institutions.

And so a lot of the ways it could actually make our lives better are limited by normal human factors, but a lot of the ways it could make them worse or weirder are not.

Well, we definitely need to look at the things that slow down the good stuff. So for example, because the Gates Foundation is a nonprofit, we can work with regulators on how they use A.I. to do their jobs. Whether it’s organoids or biological models, we can speed up that regulatory piece. And there are some countries that are very much engaged in that type of acceleration.

The one application that’s going full speed ahead, and it kind of amazed me, is the agricultural one, because they’re getting better weather data to these farmers in Africa. We have over one million farmers in India already using the system. So it tells them what crop disease they have, what fertilizer to use, what varieties to plant. We’ve even put a bunch of services they can take advantage of on there. That one is going full speed ahead.

The health and education — you could say, will it be the rich countries, the middle-income countries or the low-income countries that get there first? Because some of the barriers are different.

For the low-income countries, it’s not regulatory. It’s: Is anybody providing the tokens? Do they have the smartphone and the connectivity, which are the basics, and the language thing that we’ve talked about?

So they’ll proceed at different paces. Ideally, we’ll learn from each other. I mean, China actually banned young people from having social relationships with A.I. Do they know something we don’t know? Can we look at outcomes of different experiments? So there’s going to have to be a lot of that learning.

But you’re right — if the benefits aren’t coming quickly, then the permission to operate, particularly if we don’t put on the safeguards for the cyberattacks or the bioattacks, this is going to be a very tough issue to stick up for.

When I was preparing for this episode and telling people I was interviewing you, one of the big spaces of skepticism people now have is around what they’ve heard about you and Jeffrey Epstein.

I’ve looked at your House testimony, but what do you say to people who have lost some faith in you and just see you differently now, linking your name and his?

They should read what I said to Congress. I got to answer all the questions. In trying to raise money for global health, I thought that Epstein could connect me because of his relationships with them, and I had meetings with him ——

Relationships with whom?

With billionaires.

But, you’re a billionaire — I mean, you’re the billionaire, on some level.

I’m giving all my money away, and I spend a lot of time trying to raise money for global health.

And so you felt that he had connections that would be of value to you in that?

To raise money for global health, yes. I mean — did you read it?

I did read it.

That’s what we met about. I mean, other than — OK, there was a dinner with Larry Summers where we talked about the economy. The whole discussion was: Is there a chance here to help out?

Spending time with him was clearly a mistake. I’ve changed my bar for even somebody in a nonpaid intermediate role. I’ll never take any risk on that again because our work is very reputation sensitive.

The hole at the center of that story, for me, is how this guy was so compelling to so many very smart, very wealthy people.

There are a lot of people who want your attention and don’t get it. People want Larry Summers’s attention and don’t get it. But there’s something about Epstein’s charisma or the way he presented himself that drew people into at least thinking he could be very useful to them.

What was that? I’ve read his emails; he does not seem like a pleasant person to email with. What was the factor about him that allowed him to weave this web that you and so many other people were in?

Well, I wasn’t in a web. I was in discussions about raising money for global health. I didn’t go to any island or meet any women. Anyway, don’t call it a web.

How he performed the bootstrap of owning the fanciest house I’ve ever seen in New York City and having Larry Summers and the No. 2 guy at J.P. Morgan there — that was an interesting dinner, even if Jeffrey never said a word.

I don’t know how that bootstrap took place. But there were lots of billionaires that he was involved with in the moment where you decide: OK, what am I doing with my wealth? How do I minimize taxes? What do I do with my family? That type of thing.

And so I don’t think anybody else was drawn in for that reason. My case is kind of a unique case in that he said: Oh, you’ll have more money than you’ll know what to do with, and eventually I insisted that he take me around to see billionaires.

He had me meet with five. It turned out that none of them had a near-term intent, and I ended the relationship with him within a month of that.

And so the thing he was able to do, because that’s interesting to me, is even for you to walk into the house — it was that fancy. The people around him gave him credibility, and so he was able to put on a show such that what he was able to offer was of value. There was all this social capital and wealth floating around him.

Well, some people socialized with him. I did not, other than, to my surprise, after dinner, a magician coming in — David Blaine.

Oh, really?

I didn’t spend one minute socializing with him. He offered — come to the island or come to some show in Paris, and I said I would not choose to do that. That would not be a good idea.

I want to widen back out to the Gates Foundation. You said you’re going to spend down its money, an estimated $200 billion, by 2045.

Given everything we’ve talked about here with A.I., how has your vision for how that spending plays out changed?

I mean, there’s two dramatic things that have happened: One is the incredible A.I. capabilities, which continue to be exponential. And the second is the reduction in overall generosity toward the poorest in the world.

So I have one piece of enablement, which is: We’ll discover drugs faster, we’ll discover new seeds faster, and we can talk to those farmers and get them to buy the right seed, or talk to the person living with H.I.V. and help them seek the care they need.

So A.I. can be a big enabler for our goals, including malaria eradication, polio eradication, cutting childhood death in half again. But now the amount of resources available is way less than a golden-rule view of the world would suggest it should be.

There is, from the people connected to Anthropic and OpenAI, this sense of an amount of nonprofit money coming online in the next couple of years that will dwarf any moment in philanthropy before it.

I know people in that world — the sense of this being something very unusual is very present. Does that change what’s possible here?

Well, be numeric. Take the cuts in overseas aid ——

I’m not saying it answers the cuts in overseas aid.

But that’s — we save lives for $1,000 per year. And so getting less money from philanthropists net doesn’t save those lives. The amount of money to save lives at $1,000 per life saved will be dramatically less.

So when I’ve looked at the way your foundation is spending on A.I. — and tell me if I have this wrong — it’s about 40 percent on education, 40 percent on health, 10-ish percent on agriculture and 10-ish percent on institutions. Do I have that ——

I mean, it’s a little more in agriculture. Almost nothing we do — because we’re like a pharmaceutical company inventing new drugs. And do you call that A.I. or not call that A.I.? We didn’t put any of that in our $1 billion commitment we announced. We just put in A.I.-specific things, like understanding African languages.

Tell me a bit about your views on A.I. and education. This is a place where I’ve seen a lot of studies now, and they have very, very mixed results depending on how they’re used.

So where do you think it is valuable, and where is it a risk?

Well, the contrast between the ambitious goals that the Gates Foundation set near 2000 — our goals for global health and our goals for education.

In global health, we thought: Wow, African governments, traditional beliefs — are we going to have any impact at all?

Much to my surprise, our work on global health — together we create, with others, Gavi, the vaccine alliance; the Global Fund; George W. Bush does the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief.

A ton of things happen, including primarily vaccines — rotavirus, pneumococcus — and childhood deaths more than halved, from nearly 10 million a year to under five million a year. So we more than exceed any goal we would have set for the field in global health.

In education, we thought we could just go see what really great teachers do, videotape that, understand it, create a feedback system for teachers to hear that, improve their practice — constant learning on that — and that we could make education a lot better.

As you’ve just seen from the latest numbers, kids are learning less today in most rich countries, including in the United States, than they learned 10 years ago or 20 years ago. So people start, appropriately, with a very high degree of skepticism ——

Before we go to A.I., tell me why you think that. Those numbers have been very, very striking. — Why do you think that is? Why are we seeing learning loss in rich countries to the extent that now I think you’ve got to have — not you, but one has to have a broader answer than the pandemic?

Oh, it’s definitely — we are postpandemic. And people debate: Is it the use of cellphones? Is it something to do with affluence?

Overall, there are some outliers. England is countertrend, and they went back to basics in terms of how they teach reading as well.

And so high expectations are winning out over just free-form creativity. But there’s something clearly large in those statistics. It’s very concerning.

And so you can almost say: Why do we continue to do education? Well, education is key. I’m stubborn. We’ve got A.I. now, and we have people for whom the A.I. is playing a very specific role.

Each student, at the end of the day — this is here in New York City classrooms where they’re using a curriculum called Kiddom — spends less than 10 minutes answering a few questions. And then the teacher’s given, right away, a sense of: OK, which concepts are the kids struggling with? Which ones are struggling with them? How might you organize the classroom?

The data on that, which are small-scale, are one of these stunning results that make you want to really scale it up. When you scale up in education, you go from the teachers — who willingly engage in experiments and are probably self-selected for flexibility — to the broad population.

So the number of things in education that look good in the small, that either don’t affect it when you scale up or the quality of implementation degrades so much that the effect is basically washed out — that’s the history of education innovation.

I do think A.I. helps you with motivation. Many of these software tools have helped motivate students, but actually created more of a differential. It’s a kid like myself who goes home and used Khan Academy for two hours at night, and it’s the median kid who comes in and sees: Wow, he’s just so much better. That’s discouraging. That probably hurts.

So unless you believe in trickle-down or something, this is not equity at work. Can the A.I., not only through personalized learning but personalized motivation, overcome that? And I really believe that we can get that right.

Well, there’s a question here of A.I. tools that are specifically designed for this, and then a question in what we were just talking about with cellphones and smartphones and social media, and of how A.I. will diffuse through society.

And I think the big concern here, and one I have as well, is this — but now it gets called cognitive offloading. That what A.I. is being used for in mass numbers by students, and being really quickly adopted for, is: I didn’t do the reading; summarize it for me. Or: I have to write this essay; draft it for me. Or: Help me with these math problems.

And even, I think — we saw a big study out of China that was striking to me, where you saw kids using A.I. had increases on their homework scores, and then when they had to test outside of that context, their test scores began falling pretty sharply.

And so certainly one can imagine A.I. programs that’ll be good here. But in terms of a technology and a way of interacting with the world diffusing through society, well, of course it could help people learn linear algebra or whatever it might be.

Then, in practice, what it’s going to do is people will be using it to help them, and both from a student level and up through the professional level, it will begin to degrade the learning — the creativity that happens through the hard work of drafting and struggling and challenging yourself.

Yeah. Well, you clearly would get bimodality, where a student can use A.I. to be lazy and corrupt the measurement system, or a student can use A.I. to help them learn more.

I have to say, in terms of my learning about subjects, this is the best time of my life. I mean, I take YouTube videos and put them into the chat, I have A.I.s talk with each other — what a nirvana.

I always had the ability to send mail to somebody like the Intellectual Ventures C.E.O. Nathan Myhrvold, who knows physics. Well, now I discuss the physics thing with the A.I., and then if it’s a super important decision — for example, I’m going to invest $1 billion — I’ll send it to Nathan and say: Could you look this over? But 24 hours a day, keeping up-to-date on the latest malaria thing or vaccine thing.

So that bimodal modality is going to be there, and it really does go back to this motivational part of it.

Is that a place where there should be more limits on the systems?

You mentioned a few minutes ago China — which, for all we’ve talk about, it’d be impossible for us to strike a deal with them. But China currently has stronger national-level regulations on A.I. than we do, including things like social companionship for kids.

One of the places that you talk about in the essay, where maybe we want to be more aggressive, is around children. And that’s a place where I think it is reasonable for the government to be paternalistic. We should be paternalistic.

And social media always feels to me like an experiment we ran on kids. A lot of the internet does. And I don’t so much mind us running the experiment on adults, but I wonder if we want to be more aggressive in what we don’t let kids do with A.I. until we have a better sense of how it affects them — everything from learning relationships to trying to make it harder to have A.I. help you cheat on your homework.

Yeah, I don’t think a black-and-white ban is necessary, because I do think with monitoring — which I’m a broken record on that — making sure it’s staying within the bounds of what’s appropriate, what the parents want, our capabilities there are very strong.

There are many systems that try to help by, instead of telling you the answer, they engage with you on how you reason through the problem. And so then the question is: Can you make sure the student isn’t going to those outside systems and just getting the answer? Instead, they’re engaged in the system that brings them along step by step in that reasoning process, so that they’ll be more capable the next time.

And so, yes, seeing what that student is doing and deciding: OK, do you call in a psychiatrist? Do you call in the parents? In a lot of these systems, the idea of monitoring will be very important. And at different ages, the visibility of the parent about what’s going on and how time is being spent.

At, say, some very young age, a parent probably should have complete visibility into the exact dialogue that the student’s engaged in. As the child gets older, there are things about sexual identity or things that, really, it’s beneficial for that to at some level be private or not. I think there’s a lot of tuning to go on with this.

One of the partners the foundation is working with is Common Sense Media, who do a very good job of saying to parents: This TV show or this movie, this is what it exposes you to.

But this is a much tougher area. Most of these systems that have been set up with parental control, the parent’s lack of technical sophistication is such that it doesn’t really matter that you tried to engage the parent. Nothing happens.

In my case, I didn’t know that my daughter had a second cellphone, so that was a fairly straightforward way that she, in late hours, was able to stay on social networking when I hoped that she would be sleeping. And so we have to be realistic about how these things are designed.

People will worry about the privacy issues there. That’s fine. It’s not an argument for being unmonitored in terms of what your kid is doing.

So the next two years, then, politically: You have the midterms coming up, then you’ll have a presidential election in 2028.

So if this were to go, not just in terms of passing laws the way you want it to, but because you center your call on this coming together of society to discuss, debate, respond — what are you actually envisioning here?

So I’d have two metrics. One is the obvious safeguards to minimize the cyber and bio risks, and then the second would be the nature of the dialogue.

If the dialogue ends up being one party is for A.I. and the other party’s against, then we’ll have the climate change scenario again, which is not a great place to be. You don’t have room for debate when you only have the two extremes.

And the default case, at least right at the moment, seems to be very little middle ground about how we should manage A.I.

Let’s say that a very different administration and a very different composition of political power exists in 2029, and there’s interest in rebuilding American foreign aid. What would your advice be on how to build it back so it’s effective — so the American people understand what they’re getting for that spending, and so it’s actually doing good?

So if you ask the American people what portion of the budget’s going to help people in poor countries, it’s generally more than 5 percent. People say 10 or 15 percent. So the fact that it was about a half a percent and now it’s going down toward a quarter of a percent, that would be pretty shocking to people.

Understanding that the money is well spent, that it really does save millions of lives, that it made every bit of difference in terms of H.I.V. and malaria and tuberculosis and maternal survival — Americans should hear what they should be proud of, even at that half-a-percent level.

So a moral argument will be made. It will be made in the face of an overall debt level that will be very tough. And whatever safety network needs to be created because of A.I. impacts, that will be competing for those dollars.

Always our final question: What are three books you’d recommend to the audience?

Well, one I literally binged this weekend was “The Correspondent” by Virginia Evans. That’s fiction — very touching, very upbeat.

Apropos of what we’ve just discussed, there’s one called “Into the Wood Chipper” by Nicholas Enrich, which talks about how somebody didn’t go to a party one weekend and they decided instead to put U.S.A.I.D. into the wood chipper.

About a month ago I read “The Infinity Machine” by Sebastian Mallaby.

An A.I. book.

Yeah. A history of Demis Hassabis and DeepMind, but you get a sense of the whole founding of the A.I. industry. It does an incredible job.

Bill Gates, thank you very much.

Thank you.

SUMMARY

President Trump is such an awful human being that just writing about him feels degrading. Alas, though, when someone as morally warped as Trump — whose first secretary of state called him a “moron” — assumes this much unchecked power at the dawn of the Age of Artificial Intelligence, he can’t be ignored. Because right now Trump is leaving America exposed to dangerous viruses: digital, biological and diplomatic.

ARTICLE

Trump Is Going Viral in the Worst Ways
On the technological, diplomatic and biological fronts, Trump is creating a disaster.
By Thomas L. Friedman
Published 2026-09-29 21:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/trump-mideast-diplomacy-iran-ai.html

President Trump is such an awful human being that just writing about him feels degrading. What president would denigrate his predecessor in front of China’s leader the way Trump mocked Joe Biden, now suffering from cancer, by pointing out that a framed picture of an autopen was hanging in the White House instead of Biden’s portrait?

Alas, though, when someone as morally warped as Trump — whose first secretary of state called him a “moron” — assumes this much unchecked power at the dawn of the Age of Artificial Intelligence, he can’t be ignored. Because right now Trump is leaving America exposed to dangerous viruses: digital, biological and diplomatic. Something bad is going to happen to us as a result. We and our children are going to pay for this, and not only at the gas pump.

Let me start with the digital virus now on the loose. Recently, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google all disclosed incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their controls and gallivanted about hacking other computer systems — including an Australian government website, the Hugging Face platform and websites of the U.S. Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission. Remember, these are infant A.I. systems; they’re still in diapers and yet to be supercharged by fully training themselves and leaving their human designers behind.

And remember, too, the stories above are about what the good guys are doing. Talk to any major cyberprotection expert at any major U.S. company, and you’ll be terrified by stories about what the bad guys are doing with smaller A.I. models that they have gotten their hands on, with the controls stripped out.

The CrowdStrike Global Threat Report said attacks by “A.I.-enabled adversaries” increased by 89 percent in 2025 compared with the previous year, Infosecurity Magazine reported in February — and the rate has soared since.

But fear not, because our president, who doesn’t even use email, told the United Nations last week that he knows that our fears about A.I. safety are fraudulent. He referred to “the very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming.” He added: “And nobody was dead. These are the same people that are now saying that A.I. is going to kill us all.” (Untold thousands have died in catastrophes worsened by climate change in the last decade, and only in Trump’s fetid imagination did anyone say, “Sir, we’ll all be dead in 12 years.”)

Trump and his party — and the A.I. tech bros who have effectively paid them to keep their hands off their industry — had better pray that the “October surprise” in this coming midterm election is not a major, destructive A.I. event. If it is, they’d better have their spaceships ready to whisk them off to another planet where they can live forever, because this one may make their existences a living hell.

This A.I. threat is not a hoax (nor is the climate threat a hoax, as Trump would know if he ever looked at his own administration’s NASA website). The only hoax is that Trump, who once suggested injecting bleach might be a good way to rid yourself of Covid-19, thinks he knows anything about A.I. or climate change — or bleach.

“It’s not a hoax at all,” Bill Gates said in an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday. Gates said that the United States should restrain A.I. development until tougher safeguards are in place, and he argued that China would most likely do the same if Washington took the initiative to draft new rules to regulate the use of A.I.

A.I. without proper regulation is “completely irresponsible,” Gates said. “You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like.” He concluded: “A.I. is certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths.”

Precisely because there has never been such a tool, despite its destructive potential, with so much promise to solve so many energy, climate and medical problems for humanity, I want to see A.I. thrive, as does Gates. Which is why we should all want to prevent now an A.I.-driven Sept. 11 that would completely delegitimize artificial intelligence in the public eye. That would be a double tragedy.

I wish that the only threat to us from Trump’s unrestrained ignorance were an A.I. virus. Sadly, last week, my Times colleague Apoorva Mandavilli reported that America’s Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, long the “undisputed global leader in public health,” has been so systematically dismantled by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. that it is now “a skeleton of the powerhouse it was.”

Not only has the C.D.C.’s staff been reduced by some 30 percent, but, Mandavilli reported, citing current and former employees, “the changes have hindered the C.D.C.’s ability to respond to outbreaks as measles spreads at home and Ebola abroad, and to issue timely guidance on vaccinations as cooling temperatures kick off the respiratory season. … Entire divisions have been shuttered, including teams that worked on smoking, sexual violence, child abuse and falls among older adults.”

The Guardian newspaper carried a story about the spreading outbreak of measles in Pennsylvania, which has now topped 900 cases. Dr. John Goldman, an infectious disease specialist at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, said that between 1992 and 2026, he hadn’t seen a single case, The Guardian reported. Now, “We’re seeing at least one every day,” and he added, “Never in my life did I think I was ever going to see measles again.” This is an example of how Trump’s negligence is helping to spread actual, biological viruses.

But don’t forget the anti-diplomatic virus also sapping our strength. What is that? Check out this story in the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, by its Middle East affairs expert Zvi Bar’el. It was about how the diplomatic incompetence of the Trump administration and the malevolence of the cabinet of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have combined to grind the 20-point Trump peace plan for Gaza to a halt. So Gazan civilians, many living in war-broken buildings, one of which collapsed on Sept. 16, killing at least 21 people, including 11 children, remain in total squalor.

When Trump launched his vaunted Gaza Board of Peace and made himself chairman, participating countries pledged $17 billion for Gaza. But “as far as is known, less than $300 million has been transferred,” Bar’el reported.

Moreover, the peace plan’s international stabilization force has yet to be established. The Palestinian police force to replace Hamas, which is supposed to operate under a Palestinian technocratic government, was supposed to receive training in Egypt, “but Israel is preventing them from leaving Gaza,” according to Bar’el.

Then Bar’el peeled back the real story: “The stalemate in Gaza serves Israel. Hamas no longer poses a security threat, but as long as it holds territory, Israel retains a pretext for resuming the war. And as long as the Strip remains devastated and unlivable, the pressure on the people to leave only grows.” He added that Netanyahu’s defense minister, Israel Katz, after being criticized by a rival politician for not achieving a more decisive victory over Hamas, declared that the Israeli military was ready, if ordered, to eliminate Hamas “so that the emigration plan can be implemented.”

So that the emigration plan can be implemented.

Really? What is that? That is Orwellian speak for the ethnic cleansing of Gaza of Palestinians by the Netanyahu government. And what have Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said in response? Zilch.

I’ve learned over the years that diplomacy operates like a virus as well, beneficially or detrimentally: The more success you have, the more respect you get; the more respect you get, the more success you have. Conversely, the more failure you have, the less allies trust joining you, so the more failure you have.

Example: Between March and October 1991, Secretary of State James A. Baker III made eight diplomatic trips to the Middle East to put together the Madrid peace conference — the first among Israel, the Palestine Liberation Organization and several Arab states. I made all eight trips with him as The Times’s diplomatic correspondent. He failed on the first seven, but Baker would not quit and he got it done on the eighth.

Show me a single diplomatic initiative the Trump administration has built since the cease-fire in Gaza, which Trump has left to languish. It’s as if all he cared about was the headline from the signing, after which he amazingly declared last Oct. 13: “Together, we’ve achieved what everybody said was impossible. At long last we have peace in the Middle East.”

Now that’s what I call a real hoax.

There is no energetic, focused follow-up because there are no clear lines of authority. You have Thomas Barrack, who is the special envoy for Syria and Iraq and the ambassador to Turkey, making his own policy statements. You have Massad Fares Boulos, the father-in-law of Trump’s daughter Tiffany, serving as a senior adviser to the president of the United States on Arab and Middle Eastern affairs. You have part-timers, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. You have various assistant secretaries of state and defense. And you have Trump on his social media feed. (Somebody is going to make this into a musical!)

What you don’t have is a secretary of state like Baker, relentlessly focusing and leveraging American power and making trip after trip after trip until he gets the job done.

The only thing Trump relentlessly follows up on is harassing the press. Last Saturday, after being forced by a judge to allow CNN reporters back in the White House after Trump illegally banned them because their coverage was not fawning enough, the president nevertheless blocked CNN from accompanying him on Air Force One to attend a football game in Tennessee.

When it comes to denouncing the press, Trump is laser-focused. But when dealing with the digital, biological and diplomatic viruses weakening our national immune system, not so much — to our great peril.
