A Tough Ad Reminds Nebraska Voters About a Brutal Crime and a Pardon
A group supporting Dan Osborn, the independent Senate candidate in Nebraska, is airing an ad attacking Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican, for pardoning a man convicted of sexual assault.
By Lisa Lerer
Published 2026-09-29 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/ad-watch-nebraska-senate-race.html

A super PAC supporting Dan Osborn, the independent candidate for Senate in Nebraska, is airing a graphic new 60-second ad attacking his opponent, Senator Pete Ricketts, the Republican incumbent, for pardoning a man convicted of sexual assault nearly three decades after the assault.

Here’s a look at the ad, its accuracy and its major takeaway.

On the Screen

The ad opens with a “content warning” about sexual assault and the phone number for the National Domestic Violence Hotline.

It cuts to a narrator, called “Jody S.,” who says she has a “story to tell” about Mr. Ricketts.

The woman describes being violently assaulted by an intruder in her home.

The style is spare, with limited music and images of an empty home. Some of the woman’s words are rendered in white type over a black background.

The ad pans to a series of newspaper headlines from the 1990s showing that the woman’s attacker pleaded guilty to sexual assault and was sentenced to prison.

Later, a black-and-white image of a smiling Mr. Ricketts flashes on the screen. The woman says that the senator, then serving as governor and as a member of the state’s pardon board, had voted to pardon her assailant.

Viewers next see a mug shot of the woman’s attacker on Nebraska’s official sex offender registry, part of the state government website. The man’s image then disappears. His pardon, the woman explains, meant that his name was removed from the registry.

The Script

“I have a story to tell about our senator, Pete Ricketts. On April 30, 1993, John Arias broke into my home, tied me up with parachute cord and violently raped me. My children heard everything that happened. He was caught, pled guilty and went to prison. He said I should watch my back for the rest of my life. Pete Ricketts cast the deciding vote to pardon this man.”

“Governor Ricketts.”

“Yes. But with that, you’ve got your pardon.”

“That pardon brought back all the nightmares. I found out just totally by accident. I thought impossible that anyone would make that decision without contacting the victim. Because of Pete Ricketts, my attacker is now allowed to own a gun and had his name removed from the sex offender registry. I have no idea why Senator Ricketts chose my rapist over me.”

“Nebraska Values PAC is responsible for the content of this advertising.”

Accuracy

The assailant, John Arias, pleaded guilty to first-degree sexual assault and was sentenced to 15 to 30 years in prison. He was released in April 2008, after serving nearly 14 years, according to state records.

In September 2022, he requested a pardon from the state board of pardons, which included Mr. Ricketts, who was then governor; Doug Peterson, then the state attorney general, and Bob Evnen, the secretary of state. A pardon would not erase the crime from state records but would remove his name from the state’s sex offender registry.

According to an audio recording of his 28-minute pardon hearing, Mr. Arias did not deny the assault, though he appeared to question some of the details of the victim’s account.

Mr. Ricketts and Mr. Peterson ultimately voted for the pardon. Mr. Evnen opposed it, saying that he didn’t think Mr. Arias had “fully come to grips with what happened that night.”

Mr. Peterson described the request as “on the bubble,” but cited Mr. Arias’s military service and volunteer work with the American Legion.

“We historically have taken these types of criminal acts, like sexual assault and child abuse, very seriously,” he said.

Mr. Ricketts agreed that Mr. Arias’s request was “on the bubble” but announced “you’ve got your pardon” — the line clipped in the ad.

Weeks after granting the pardon, Mr. Ricketts issued a statement defending his decision, saying that Mr. Arias “has shown to be remorseful.”

A few months later, the victim, who said she was not notified about the pardon or invited to participate in the hearing, testified before the State Senate in support of a bill to ensure that crime victims are notified of Nebraska Board of Pardons meetings.

“His rights were restored,” she told the legislators. “I ask you, where do my rights fit in?”

The Takeaway

Mr. Osborn, a union leader and Navy veteran, is in a tough race against Mr. Ricketts, who served two terms as governor and won his Senate seat in a 2024 special election. While Mr. Osborn is an independent, Democratic candidates cleared the field to ease his path, and he has been endorsed by the Nebraska Democratic Party.

The spot is an effort by Democrats and their allies to gain traction in a red state, where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats nearly two to one. Mr. Osborn has repeatedly cast Mr. Ricketts, one of the richest members of the Senate, as uninterested in the concerns of everyday Nebraskans. The ad is an effort to undermine his character and reinforce that image.

ARTICLE

Democrats in Congress Embrace a More Punitive Posture Toward Israel
Nearly every Democratic senator voted to advance a measure calling for a human rights report on Israel’s conduct in the West Bank, as some in the party propose punishing settlement activity with sanctions.
By Robert Jimison and Annie Karni
Published 2026-09-30 00:12 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/democrats-congress-israel.html

Democrats in Congress are increasingly adopting a more punitive approach to dealing with Israel, taking a series of steps in recent days that suggest they would pursue sanctions for building new settlements and other actions against the Jewish state should they win majorities in November’s elections.

On Tuesday, all but one Senate Democrat voted to advance a measure that would force the Trump administration to produce a human rights report examining violence by Israel in the West Bank, including the deaths of Palestinian American citizens, in a rebuke that would once have seemed unthinkable.

The bid failed, but the near-unanimous level of Democratic backing for it reflected the party’s new willingness to embrace steps that had long been considered anathema given the relationship between the United States and its closest Middle East ally.

At the same time, top Democrats in the House and Senate have proposed legislation that would impose sanctions on Israel for building settlements, making it clear to Israeli companies and banks that if they were involved with settlement building they would be penalized. The steps, months after almost half of House Democrats voted to cut off aid to Israel, are the latest sign of an expanding appetite in the party to move beyond expressions of disapproval and toward measures that could reorder the U.S.-Israeli relationship.

“While I was pleased so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland and the author of the human rights measure. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of U.S. taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values.”

He added that “this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”

The measure was blocked on a vote of 51 to 47. But it attracted support from almost the entire Democratic caucus, including from Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader and a staunch supporter of Israel. The sole Democratic “no” vote was from Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, who is an unequivocal backer of Israel.

One Republican, Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, voted with Democrats in favor of the resolution.

The issue of Israel and Gaza has repeatedly exposed divisions in the Democratic Party throughout this year’s midterm campaign. But in this case, the vote demonstrated near unity on an issue that drew far less support just two years ago.

In 2024, when Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent, forced a vote on a similar resolution seeking a State Department report on whether human rights violations had occurred in Gaza, just 11 Democrats voted to move the resolution forward.

Mr. Van Hollen’s measure invoked a never-tested section of the Foreign Assistance Act that allows Congress to demand information about the human rights practices of countries receiving U.S. security aid, and to cut off the money if an administration refuses to disclose it.

It would have required the State Department to produce an unclassified report examining Israel’s human rights record in the West Bank, including any effort to investigate the cases of nine U.S. citizens “killed by violent Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces.”

Coming just weeks before the midterm elections that have been shaped by Democratic voters’ mounting hostility toward Israel, it was seen by some senators in the party as a way to register opposition to the conduct of Netanyahu government without going as far as cutting off military aid. Still, it marked a clear break with the past, when most Democrats would reflexively vote against any measure that challenged Israel.

“That we’ve gotten to the point of a unanimous rebuke is astounding,” said Jeremy Ben-Ami, the president of J Street, the center-left lobbying group. “It used to be there was unanimous Democratic support for every pro-Israel resolution. Now it’s unanimous to take on their human rights violations.”

The debate has taken on new urgency during another burst of violence in the West Bank, where attacks by Israelis and Palestinians have fueled an increasingly volatile cycle.

Earlier on Tuesday, more than 100 Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians and soldiers in the West Bank when the military tried to return a Palestinian family to its home months after being forced out following a long campaign of violence.

As the violence continues, some Democrats are moving beyond investigations and are instead seeking to impose direct consequences on Israelis involved in expanding settlements.

Last week, Senator Chris Coons, the Delaware Democrat who would be in line to become the chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee if his party were to win control of the Senate, introduced legislation that would impose sanctions on Israel for the construction of settlements in the E1 area of the West Bank, a strategically significant patch of land that would split the West Bank in two and complicate the potential creation of a Palestinian state.

The move was notable for Mr. Coons, who has joined with Republicans to oppose his party’s bids to block U.S. weapons sales to Israel, saying that he would not “abandon our steadfast ally.”

Representative Joaquin Castro of Texas, a senior Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, on Thursday is set to introduce a broader bill that would punish Israel for the construction of any new settlements throughout the West Bank and Gaza, as well as the expansion of existing ones. It also would prohibit the import of goods made in the settlements.

The bill is expected to be cosponsored by Democratic Representatives Don Beyer of Virginia, Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania, Greg Casar of Texas and Sara Jacobs of California.

In a statement to The New York Times, Mr. Castro said that the record expansion of West Bank settlements was one of the top impediments to peace.

“Democrats must face this with urgency — act now or watch the prospect of Palestinian self-determination slip away forever,” he said. “Congress should and can be using every tool we have available, including sanctions.”

The recent moves come just weeks after Britain, France and Canada announced coordinated sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

From the first primaries in March through the final ones in September, Democrats’ turnout outpaced Republican voters in many key states that will decide congressional majorities next year. In red states like Texas, battlegrounds like Georgia and bluer ones like New Hampshire, Democrats have raced to the polls to choose their nominees, while Republicans have not kept up.

“There’s been historic enthusiasm gaps this cycle, that are real reasons to be optimistic,” said Meredith Kelly, who was a top official for the House Democratic campaign committee in 2018, the last midterm election with President Trump in office.

Furious Democratic voters emerged during that campaign’s primary season and maintained their energy into November. The party flipped 42 House seats, taking the majority. Republicans gained Senate seats that year in deep-red states like Indiana, Missouri and North Dakota where they ousted Democrats who had been elected during Barack Obama’s second presidential campaign.

This primary season, perhaps the starkest example of Democratic enthusiasm came in Texas, a state Mr. Trump carried by 14 percentage points two years ago. Both parties had hard-fought and expensive Senate primary campaigns there this year.

About 150,000 more people voted in the Democratic primary between James Talarico, the victor, and Representative Jasmine Crockett than in the Republican contest between Senator John Cornyn and the state’s attorney general, Ken Paxton, who would go on to win in a runoff.

That’s a major change from four years ago, when there were 900,000 more votes in the state’s Republican primaries for state offices than in its Democratic contests. Even in 2018, during the last Democratic wave election, 500,000 more people voted in the Republican Senate primary than in the Democratic one. That year, the last midterm election with Mr. Trump in office, Democrats flipped seats across Texas as Beto O’Rourke came the closest any Democrat had gotten in decades to winning a Senate race in the state.

The lopsided Democrat turnout didn’t extend to every state, and was most notable in battleground states.

Going back farther, Michigan and Wisconsin held competitive Democratic primaries in both 2018 — which drew record turnouts at the time — and 2026, and both saw huge turnout increases this year.

In Wisconsin, David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, narrowly defeated Francesca Hong, a state legislator from Madison, in a race that saw turnout jump by more than 250,000 votes — a 47 percent increase. Michigan’s numbers were nearly as striking. The state’s 2018 competitive Democratic primary for governor drew 1.1 million voters. The Senate contest last month had 1.5 million.

Eight years ago, on the eve of the 2018 primaries, Nate Cohn wrote in The Times that the vote in primary races generally provides “a rough if imperfect indicator of the national political environment.”

But Republicans are better prepared for a wave of Democratic enthusiasm than they were during the “blue wave” in 2018. Republicans redrew House districts across the country to create more potentially safe seats for their candidates, and the party has a large cash advantage. As in 2018, this year’s Senate battleground is being fought in red states Mr. Trump carried two years before, giving his party a distinct advantage.

Tom Perez, who was the Democratic National Committee chairman in 2018, acknowledged that voter enthusiasm among Democrats wouldn’t go as far in the new political environment.

“I really do believe that people are going to come out in abundance,” he said, but he added that it would require more financial investment in potentially competitive races.

“You don’t want to wake up the day after and see that you lost by three points somewhere because you didn’t do anything,” he said.

“I don’t think you know we have this stuff, so I’ll give you a second to process it so you don’t perjure yourself,” Mr. Schmitt said, even as the poster board was swiftly taken down, too quickly for most in the room to read it.

When the former special counsel insisted he had not gone to see the Atlanta Hawks play in that time period, Mr. Schmitt declared, “I think you’ve already perjured yourself,” and called Mr. Smith a “dirtbag.”

The accusation appeared to unravel almost immediately.

Invited to respond by Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat, Mr. Smith said he had, in fact, attended a basketball game on that day, but it was to see the Iowa Hawkeyes at the University of Maryland. That night, Caitlin Clark, the star point guard who now plays in the W.N.B.A., scored 38 points and had 12 assists.

Ms. Klobuchar suggested that Mr. Schmitt’s accusation was rooted in the senator’s confusion between the “Hawks” of Atlanta and the “Hawkeyes” of Iowa.

Mr. Schmitt declared that he still stood by calling Mr. Smith a “dirtbag,” then left the hearing.

The exchange took up just four minutes of the hearing. But it showed how eager the Republicans were to paint Mr. Smith as an out-of-control partisan — and to find a basis to accuse him of a crime at a time when the Justice Department has proved receptive to pursuing the people who investigated Mr. Trump.

A central issue was Mr. Smith’s subpoenas for lawmakers’ phone records as he and his team sought to trace Mr. Trump’s pressure campaign on Congress to block Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s Electoral College certification.

As part of that effort, investigators also examined whether Mr. Trump had defrauded his supporters when he raised vast sums after the election promising to expose fraud that did not happen. They also subpoenaed financial records of Republican-aligned groups as they traced what actually happened to the money.

That effort did not result in charges.

Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, and others argued that when Mr. Smith subpoenaed phone records of Republican lawmakers, and sought court orders keeping those subpoenas secret, he showed that his prosecutorial ambitions extended far beyond Mr. Trump.

“Is it a crime to be a Republican?” Mr. Cruz asked angrily. “Absolutely not,” replied Mr. Smith.

Senator Darline Graham, the sister of Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July, also confronted Mr. Smith over a subpoena of her brother’s phone records. Like Mr. Cruz, she focused on how an application for nondisclosure order to the phone companies raised the risk that if the subpoena became public, a target could destroy evidence or intimidate witnesses.

“Do you really believe that Lindsey was going to destroy evidence that was not even in his possession?” she asked.

“No, I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant. He was not a target of our investigation, and in fact he likely would have been a witness in our case” against Mr. Trump, Mr. Smith replied.

He told both Mr. Cruz and Ms. Graham that his team sought the records to investigate the conduct of Mr. Trump, not the lawmakers. The concern was not whether the lawmakers would destroy evidence or intimidate witnesses, but whether Mr. Trump or his associates would seek to do so.

Democrats countered Republican accusations by pointing to the evidence Mr. Smith gathered against Mr. Trump, leading to indictments for his efforts to undo the results of the 2020 election, and for his handling of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago home in Florida.

Senator Adam Schiff, Democrat of California, said the G.O.P. anger directed at Mr. Smith and the F.B.I. was a smoke screen for facts they would rather not face — that the former president had engaged in wrongdoing, and that the witnesses against him in both cases were largely Republicans.

Senator Cory Booker, a New Jersey Democrat, called the hearing “a farce.” The Republicans attacking Mr. Smith, he added, “choose Trump over truth, corruption and crimes over the Constitution, and I’ve had enough of it.”

For his part, Mr. Smith maintained a measured, even meek, tone as lawmakers on the panel alternated between describing him as a pinnacle of his profession and a poster boy for improper conduct.

“If asked whether to prosecute a former president today, based on the same facts, I would do so regardless of whether that president was a Republican or a Democrat,” he said, adding: “I will not be silenced by continued threats of prosecution from the president or others.”

In early 2022, the Justice Department opened two investigations involving Mr. Trump. One was into his campaign’s plan to create false slates of electors as a pretext to block Mr. Biden’s certification, and the other was into Mr. Trump’s hoarding of classified documents while out of office, and his obstruction of efforts to retrieve them.

In November 2022, after Mr. Trump announced he would run for president again, Mr. Smith, a former prosecutor of federal corruption and international war crimes, was tapped to take over the inquiries as a special counsel. The next year, Mr. Smith brought two indictments against Mr. Trump.

Mr. Smith insisted that he brought charges because Mr. Trump “engaged in criminal activity,” and not because of any political agenda to stop Mr. Trump’s resurgence, as the president’s Republican allies have asserted. Mr. Trump triumphed over the two federal cases by winning re-election in 2024, leading to Mr. Smith’s resignation.

Since leaving government, Mr. Smith has said that the Justice Department has been “corrupted” by Trump loyalists who have wrecked its credibility and sought to undermine the rule of law.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in testimony to Congress in July, suggested the department would investigate Mr. Smith to determine if he had lied to Congress.

Much of Tuesday’s hearing covered familiar ground — including whether investigators’ effort to collect lawmakers’ call records violated the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause, as Republican lawmakers insisted.

That issue is contested. Everyone agrees members of Congress cannot be prosecuted or forced to testify about their legislative acts. But appeals courts have disagreed about whether it also creates a confidentiality shield, and no court has interpreted it as barring subpoenas to phone companies for call logs.

The Justice Department’s public integrity section signed off on the subpoenas, Mr. Smith said. But while he defended the investigation’s work as carefully following the law, Justice Department rules, and best practices for prosecutors, he did offer one regret for how he had done the job.

Mr. Smith noted that he had come from a generation of prosecutors who spoke almost exclusively in courtrooms, and not in public, even to defend the integrity of the work or the prosecution team.

Following that tradition proved costly in the cases against Mr. Trump, he said.

“I do agree that prosecutors in the future need to learn to be able to communicate to the outside world,” Mr. Smith said.

Glenn Thrush contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

Top Democrats, Long Hesitant to Spend Money in Texas, Start to Back Talarico
The main super PAC for Senate Democrats will begin to run digital ads in the state’s Senate race, in a sign of the party’s growing confidence.
By Theodore Schleifer and Lauren McGaughy
Published 2026-09-29 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/james-talarico-ken-paxton-texas-senate-race-money.html

Top national Democrats are preparing to make an initial investment in the Texas Senate race, a strategic shift that speaks to the party’s growing confidence in a state that has dashed its hopes for decades.

The main super PAC for Senate Democrats, Senate Majority PAC, said on Tuesday that it would begin an advertising effort meant to help James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, by targeting his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton.

The super PAC, which is aligned with Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, had so far resisted spending money in Texas, viewing the party’s path to a majority as running through smaller states where advertising is cheaper.

The group declined to provide a figure or a range for its planned spending in Texas. For now, it will run statewide ads only on YouTube and other digital and streaming platforms and forgo more expensive television ads that could drain the super PAC's resources. That suggests that national Democrats are not yet prepared to go all-in for Mr. Talarico.

Mr. Talarico has narrowly led in polls and his campaign has raised much more money than Mr. Paxton’s, but national Republican groups have begun spending enormous amounts to prop up their nominee, giving him an overall financial advantage. G.O.P. groups have reserved about $167 million in ads for the final two months of the race.

Because the cost of political advertising in Texas is so high, with its large size and many media markets, both parties have been reluctant to invest in the state, worrying that doing so could divert resources from other top Senate races. When Senate Majority PAC announced its initial advertising plans this year, it focused on eight states and left out Texas.

Unless Democrats sharply ramp up their spending, Republicans are likely to hold an advantage on television in the final weeks of the race. As of Monday, Mr. Talarico was set to be outspent by nearly five to one on all advertising in the final two months before Election Day, with only about $35 million booked on his behalf, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm.

Lauren French, a spokeswoman for Senate Majority PAC, said that its ads would run through Election Day and “focus on Paxton as a corrupt, dangerous individual.”

The first ad, which will come from an allied super PAC that was created last week and is called Texas Forever, targets Mr. Paxton, the state attorney general, over his office’s handling of a prominent child abuse case.

Adam Hoffman, a lawyer in Waco, Texas, was accused of sexually abusing a local boy for years. After the victim declined to testify again when the trial resulted in a hung jury, lawyers in Mr. Paxton’s office cut a deal in which Mr. Hoffman served less than a month behind bars and did not need to register as a sex offender in Texas.

The arrangement set off a local outcry and allegations that Mr. Paxton had given Mr. Hoffman a sweetheart deal. Mr. Paxton has denied any wrongdoing and defended his office’s work on the case, saying it was the best deal possible while honoring the victim’s wishes. Gerry Morris, a lawyer who represented Mr. Hoffman, told The New York Times in June that while he disliked Mr. Paxton, it was “an absolute 100 percent lie” that the attorney general had done anything to sway the case’s outcome.

Some Democrats have privately pined for Senate Majority PAC to get involved in Texas. Mr. Talarico’s fund-raising emails have pointed to the challenge he faces, using words like “beyond ridiculous” to describe the tens of millions of dollars flooding into the state for his opponent.

Garry Jones, who leads a different pro-Talarico super PAC, Lone Star Rising, argued that money alone would not swing the race for Mr. Paxton.

“We’re a few weeks into the deluge, and what we’re seeing is that there isn’t enough money in the world to make Texans forget they hate Ken Paxton,” Mr. Jones said.

Lone Star Rising said it planned to spend at least another $10 million for Mr. Talarico.

Mr. Paxton, who won a hard-fought Republican primary on the back of his support from President Trump and the party’s right-wing base, has long been trailed by scandal. He was indicted in 2015 on felony fraud charges, but cut a deal in 2024 to avoid trial without admitting guilt. He was impeached in 2023 over allegations of corruption but was acquitted in a State Senate trial. His wife, a state senator, has filed for divorce, citing adultery.

Anthony Holm, a longtime Republican consultant who once worked for Mr. Paxton, said that for the better part of a year, Mr. Talarico had been the one with an advantage in fund-raising, and therefore in messaging.

But now that Mr. Paxton has the financial edge, Mr. Holm said, he can use the influx of cash to target the meaningful chunk of voters who are still undecided.

“As long as Paxton has the money,” Mr. Holm said, “he’ll be fine.”

ARTICLE

Supreme Court Allows Rapid Third-Country Deportations, for Now
The court also announced it would hear arguments in December on the legality of the Trump administration policy to swiftly deport immigrants to countries not their own.
By Abbie VanSickle
Published 2026-09-29 19:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/supreme-court-deportations-third-country.html

The Supreme Court on Tuesday gave President Trump a temporary victory on a central piece of his mass deportation agenda, agreeing the administration can, for now, resume rapidly deporting immigrants to countries other than their own.

Although the justices cleared the way for the policy to continue, they also announced that the court would fast-track the case and hear oral arguments about it in December, setting up a final ruling on the issue next year and a new test for presidential power at the court.

The one-page emergency ruling was unsigned and gave no vote count, as is typical in such cases.

On the line in December will be Mr. Trump’s policy of sending people to countries where they have no ties, including nations that have faced allegations of human rights abuses. Among the countries migrants have been sent to are Liberia, Equatorial Guinea, Costa Rica, Honduras and the Central African Republic.

The court’s three liberal justices noted that they would have denied the government’s request to resume the deportations.

The justices asked the lawyers for the administration and the immigrants who challenged the policy to focus their briefing for the December argument on whether the lower court judge who had paused the swift deportations had the authority to do so, and whether the policy violated the Constitution and international protections against torture.

James Percival, the top lawyer at the Department of Homeland Security, celebrated the court’s ruling. In a statement, he called it a “victory.”

“A bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike,” he said. “It’s not too late to get $3,000 and a flight home.” He ended his statement with a link to department instructions for immigrants on how to self-deport.

Trina A. Realmuto, a lawyer for the National Immigration Litigation Alliance and part of the team representing the immigrants, called the emergency decision “a devastating result.” The court, she said in a statement, “has allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture.”

But she pointed out that the court had agreed to hear full argument in December, saying that Tuesday’s decision “does not decide that the policy is lawful.”

The deportations had been blocked recently after a federal court ruled the administration could not deport migrants to third countries unless they were given an opportunity to contest their removals, including to voice concerns that they might be persecuted or tortured abroad.

The justices’ ruling means that the administration can, for now, continue its program and conduct rapid deportations including to countries like Equatorial Guinea, where U.S. deportees were hooded, bound and beaten by the police, according to reporting by The New York Times.

The justices had weighed in previously on the administration’s efforts to send immigrants to third countries.

In May 2025, the Trump administration asked the justices to step in and clear the way for third-country deportations after a federal judge in Massachusetts temporarily blocked the administration from sending people to countries not their own — in that case South Sudan — without the chance to object.

In a one-paragraph ruling, the court’s conservatives allowed the administration to continue the deportations over the noted dissents of the three liberals.

Since then, the Trump administration has continued to deport immigrants under the program, including to authoritarian countries with histories of human rights abuses. So far, the administration has sent more than 25,000 people to third countries as part of its mass deportation efforts, according to a social media post by Mr. Percival.

Some immigration and human rights experts have asserted that the third-country deportations may be part of a broader strategy by the Trump administration to encourage undocumented immigrants to leave on their own, rather than face the fear of being sent to a country where they have no ties.

In his brief, Solicitor General D. John Sauer characterized the third-country deportation program as “an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens.”

Mr. Sauer wrote that the appeals court ruling had “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations,” including canceled deportation flights and disrupted delicate diplomatic negotiations with other countries.

Lawyers for a group of immigrants challenging their removals said in a brief that the Trump administration had ignored “the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime U.S. residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there.”

They argued that the Trump administration could avoid any delays in its deportation program simply by “providing the notice and opportunity to be heard that the law requires.”

ARTICLE

How a Planned Steel Mill in Iowa Reveals Trump’s Midterm Strategy
As President Trump travels the country, he is expected to focus on his economic accomplishments at a time when Americans have expressed deep frustration with his policies.
By Katie Rogers and Farah Stockman
Published 2026-09-29 00:19 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/us/politics/trump-steel-plant-iowa-midterms.html

President Trump, staring down a rough midterm season for Republicans, unveiled plans for an Iowa steel mill project on Monday that he said would plug billions into the economy and create construction jobs in a state hit hard by his policies.

Voters in Midwestern states were crucial to delivering a second election win to Mr. Trump, but now, those voters are among the hardest hit by tariff-driven manufacturing costs and a rise in fuel prices driven by the war in Iran. When a reporter in the Oval Office asked him on Monday why several Republican candidates in Iowa were working so hard to protect their seats, Mr. Trump seemed mystified.

“I don’t know,” said Mr. Trump, who is traveling to several states this week ahead of the midterm elections. “I love Iowa. I’ve always been very strong with Iowa.”

The project in Iowa is one of several job-creation announcements Mr. Trump is expected to make as he traverses the country. He will travel to several reliably conservative states this week, including Oklahoma and Alabama. He is also scheduled to visit Ohio this weekend in support of Senator Jon Husted, an embattled incumbent facing several challenges, including a lack of name recognition among some of the state’s most devoted conservatives.

Mr. Trump said on Monday that he would also visit Iowa, where he hopes the planned steel mill will boost prospects for Republicans in tight races — and perhaps his own fortunes as a kingmaker who has asked supporters to pretend he is on the ballot in November. Americans have signaled that they are doing just that, but in a way that could backfire on him. The war in Iran and the cost of living have both eroded his support.

So Mr. Trump has leaned into the promise of the mill, which is part of an $18 billion investment from Mesabi Metallics. Supporters of the project say it will be one of the largest steel mills in the world when it is completed.

In the Oval Office on Monday, Mr. Trump, several cabinet members and Iowa Republicans said the project would remind voters that Mr. Trump’s policies have created jobs. Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, who is facing a tough re-election race and who last week voted to curb Mr. Trump’s war powers, appeared to be behind Mr. Trump, telling reporters that the steel mill could create some 6,000 construction jobs and 1,750 permanent jobs, with salaries that could exceed $100,000 a year.

“We’re going to mine it in America. We’re going to mill it in America, and we’re going to make it in America,” Ms. Miller-Meeks said.

Mesabi Metallic is owned by Essar Group, a Mumbai-based conglomerate controlled by one of India’s wealthiest families. The Iowa mill project follows another initiative led by Mesabi: a $2.5 billion iron-ore mine and pellet plant in Nashwauk, Minn.

That project, described as the first new operation of its kind in the state in about 50 years, has been supported by EXIM Bank, a U.S. federal import-export bank that announced it would extend loans to the company worth up to $10 billion. Some analysts consider the EXIM loan to be risky, because Mesabi has faced financial problems and significant delays over the years.

Alec Varsamis, a spokesman for EXIM, said that Mesabi had so far been granted a $770 million loan for the iron-ore mine in Minnesota.

“We are operating at no cost to the taxpayer, and we are on track to repay our congressional appropriations to the U.S. Treasury,” Mr. Varsamis said.

In the Oval Office on Monday, Mr. Trump said that the project would go forward even if control of Congress changed hands, or if a “less friendly” president took over. Rewant Ruia, chairman of Mesabi’s executive board, and Ravi Ruia, co-founder and vice-chairman of the Essar Group, were also in the Oval Office for the announcement.

The company filed for bankruptcy protection in 2016, and has been entangled in a lawsuit with Cleveland-Cliffs, another steel manufacturer.

Mesabi executives have leaned on a Trump-world insider as the company has sought to expand its footprint in the United States. The company hired Jason Miller, a longtime Trump adviser, as its lobbyist, paying him at least $240,000 through his company SHW Partners, according to lobbying disclosure records. The government of India also hired Mr. Miller’s company, paying $150,000 per month for “strategic counsel, tactical planning and government relations assistance on policy matters before the U.S. government,” according to federal filings under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

Mr. Miller said in text messages that he had stopped his work as a lobbyist for Mesabi, adding that he deregistered with the company at the end of July, and deregistered as a lobbyist for India in June. He has since joined the administration as an unpaid special government employee. He was not present in the Oval Office and said he had “recused” himself from Monday’s announcement.

Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy organization that tracked Mr. Miller’s lobbying on behalf of Mesabi and the Indian government, said that the extension of potentially billions in taxpayer-backed loans from EXIM Bank deserved more scrutiny because of Mr. Miller’s role.

“In any other administration, this would be treated as a monumental scandal,” Mr. Weissman said. “But in this one, it’s just another day.” Rewant Ruia, chairman of Mesabi Metallics, spoke in the Oval Office on Monday, and said the new steel plant in Iowa “will use the latest technology and will compete head-to-head with any steel plant in the world on size, quality and on cost.”

Gov. Kim Reynolds of Iowa, a Republican who attended the Oval Office event, said in a statement that the deal would be transformative for her state.

“Our commitment in Iowa to fiscal responsibility, tax competitiveness, and long-term economic stability has created one of the nation’s strongest environments for business investment,” she said. “Now, this opportunity will fundamentally change the economic trajectory of our state and the entire region for decades to come.”

The steel mill project is part of a broader election-season attempt by Mr. Trump to push back against widespread voter frustration with his policies, including tariffs that have been punishing for American manufacturers, particularly in the Midwest.

Mr. Trump and his advisers believe that any polling predicting a blowout for Democrats is overrated, and to some degree, they have history on their side. On Monday, Mr. Trump again called recent polling “fake,” and complained that the news media had not appropriately trumpeted employment numbers, 401(k) account gains and a host of other accomplishments.

“Nobody talks about all of the incredible things,” Mr. Trump said.

But this is not 2016, or 2024. In 2026, Americans are deeply unhappy with the cost of living and frustrated with the war in Iran, which has driven up prices further. In response, Mr. Trump has taken to calling the concept of affordability a Democratic hoax, while promising that prices will come down as soon as the war ends.

“We’re going to win that war very soon. That’ll be over, and the gases, gas prices, will come tumbling down,” Mr. Trump said. “So nobody else could have done that. Nobody else.”

Mr. Trump’s self-congratulatory messaging on the war has done little to help G.O.P. candidates in tough races across the country. In the past week, Republicans running for Senate seats in Iowa and Michigan have called on Mr. Trump to end the conflict. A slate of other candidates, including two running for governor in Wisconsin and Michigan, and Mr. Husted in Ohio, also have said that the war needs to end, and soon.

ARTICLE

Ad About Welfare Fraud Draws MAGA Backlash
Far-right influencers piled on Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, President Trump’s former press secretary, over a campaign ad about Medicaid work requirements in Arkansas.
By Bayliss Wagner
Published 2026-09-29 22:32 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/sarah-huckabee-sanders-campaign-ad.html

The MAGA world is turning on one of its own.

Pro-Trump, far-right influencers attacked Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders of Arkansas, who served as President Trump’s press secretary from 2017 to 2019, after she posted a campaign ad promoting her state’s work requirements for many Medicaid recipients.

In the ad, which Ms. Sanders posted on social media on Monday morning, an unkempt, young white man named Brad mashes the buttons of his video game controller. He throws cheese balls and potato chips into his mouth, often missing.

“Brad has turned relaxing into a full-time profession,” Ms. Sanders tells the camera. “But you, you actually work hard. You pay taxes to cover welfare for guys like Brad, who just choose not to work. That’s why I launched a welfare-to-work requirement.

“Now, more Arkansans are working than ever before,” Ms. Sanders says. “Even Brad.”

In the next frame, Brad is shown with freshly combed hair. He adjusts his tie and flashes a thumbs up.

The ad instantly drew blowback from the kinds of once-fringe figures that the Republican Party brought into the fold under Mr. Trump. Critics almost exclusively expressed anger that the protagonist was a white man. Several of them demanded that Ms. Sanders take down the ad, issue an apology and fire the staff members who helped produce the TV spot, accusing her of engaging in “anti-white racism.”

Jack Posobiec, a right-wing commentator best known for fueling the “Pizzagate” conspiracy theory about a child abuse ring at a Washington restaurant, called the ad “Antiwhite” and criticized Ms. Sanders for airing it in the run-up to the midterm election, suggesting it would alienate white voters.

“It’s a lesson in what not to do when it comes to optics,” Mr. Posobiec said in a video accompanying his post, while saying he supported Ms. Sanders’s policy.

Many of her critics claimed the ad gave a false impression about the demographics of welfare recipients. Yet enrollees of Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion — the focus of the “welfare to work” program — are overwhelmingly white, according to an analysis of data from August that the State Department of Human Services provided to The New York Times. They are slightly more likely to be female than male.

More than 60 percent of the roughly 218,000 Medicaid expansion enrollees in the state reported that they are white, 18 percent reported that they are Black and 16 percent did not report their ethnicity. More than three-quarters of them are between 18 and 49 years of age. Women make up 54 percent of the program’s beneficiaries, according to the data.

In a social media post, Sean Davis, the co-founder of The Federalist, a conservative online magazine, said, “Our government has systematically discriminated against white men for decades now, and yet now has the audacity to dishonestly mock young white men as welfare queens.”

Will Chamberlain, a conservative lawyer and influencer who worked on Ron DeSantis’s presidential campaign, accused Ms. Sanders of “anti-white racism.” In a video posted on social media on Monday, he said the ad was “how you end a national political career before it even begins.”

Also joining in the criticism were Matt Walsh, a right-wing podcaster and prominent Trump supporter; Mike Cernovich, a Trump defender and far-right commentator; and Caleb Pascoe, a lobbyist for the American Principles Project, a social conservative advocacy group.

Ms. Sanders’s ad seemed to provoke some of the anger that Mr. Trump capitalized on during each of his runs for office: A feeling among men, and white men in particular, that the country has turned against them.

The onslaught of criticism prompted Ms. Sanders to defend the ad, but she did not address accusations of racism.

“Some critics online don’t like my welfare work requirement ad,” Ms. Sanders said in a post on X on Monday afternoon. “Next thing you know they’ll say I should have used cookies instead of cheese balls. If you are able-bodied you should not collect welfare simply because you choose not to work. Period.”

Arkansas is rolling out the new work requirements for many Medicaid recipients — or the “welfare to work” program, as Ms. Sanders calls it — as part of mandates in Mr. Trump’s sweeping tax and budget bill.

The Medicaid expansion program allows adults who make up to 138 percent of the federal poverty level in Arkansas to qualify for government-funded health care. Officials in Arkansas expect enrollment in the program to decrease by 20 percent once the new federal work requirements take effect on Jan. 1, according to The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette.

A March report from the Urban Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, found that 23 percent to 45 percent of enrollees in the state could lose coverage by 2028. In total, more than 800,000 Arkansans benefit from Medicaid coverage; more than half of them are children.

Arkansas’ population is 75 percent white and 15 percent Black, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Roughly 10 percent of Arkansans identify as Hispanic or Latino.

Mr. Trump won Arkansas by more than 30 points in 2024, and Ms. Sanders is favored to win re-election in the red state. Her campaign has continued to air the ad on cable television across Arkansas, according to data from the media-tracking firm AdImpact.

SUMMARY

Q: I’ve heard that I should eat at least 30 unique plant foods a week for my health. When Kathryn Smith, 26, a surgical athletic trainer in Atlanta, first heard on a podcast that eating 30 different plants every week could improve her health, she liked the idea of having a tangible goal. Eating 30 plants a week, some influencers, podcasters and physicians say, will diversify your gut microbiome and in turn, improve your health.

ARTICLE

Do I Really Need to Eat 30 Different Plants Each Week?
The 30-plant goal has crept into the lexicon of the online wellness world. We asked experts where it came from, and whether it’s legitimate.
By Alice Callahan
Published 2026-09-29 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/well/eat/nutrition-30-plants-a-week.html

Q: I’ve heard that I should eat at least 30 unique plant foods a week for my health. Is that true?

When Kathryn Smith, 26, a surgical athletic trainer in Atlanta, first heard on a podcast that eating 30 different plants every week could improve her health, she liked the idea of having a tangible goal.

She began making homemade granola with oats, nuts and seeds; salsas with chili peppers, cucumber, avocado and herbs; and bean salads with corn, tomatoes and mango.

The idea of eating 30 (or more) plants each week — including fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, seeds, herbs and spices — has taken the wellness world by storm. It has spawned apps that track how many plants you eat and supplements advertising 30 or more plants per capsule or scoop. Thousands of social media posts have mentioned the practice, with many touting benefits like lower inflammation, better heart health, more energy, a stronger immune system and a longer life.

Eating 30 plants a week, some influencers, podcasters and physicians say, will diversify your gut microbiome and in turn, improve your health. Does the evidence match the buzz? We asked experts to help us break it down.

What the Research Suggests

Eating 30 different plants per week is a catchy notion, said Justin Sonnenburg, a professor of microbiology and immunology at Stanford Medicine. But while consuming plenty of vegetables, whole grains and other plants is good for your health, there isn’t strong evidence that the 30-plant target is a “magical threshold,” he said.

Its origin traces back to an analysis from 2018, in which researchers compared stool samples from 85 adults living in the United States and Britain. About half of the adults said they typically ate 10 or fewer unique plants per week; the rest said they ate 30 or more. Those in the latter group had significantly more diverse gut microbiomes, said Rob Knight, a microbiome scientist at the University of California, San Diego, who led the study.

It makes sense that eating a variety of plants could encourage microbiome diversity, Dr. Knight said. Gut microbes are primarily nourished by fiber, so in theory, eating different types of fiber promotes the growth of different kinds of microbes. Researchers have found that less diverse gut microbiomes are generally associated with poorer health.

The study had limitations, however, said Anissa Armet, a nutrition researcher at the University of Alberta in Canada. It was small and relied on participants’ estimations of how many plants they typically ate each week, which could have been inaccurate, she said. And it showed only an association between eating more plants and microbiome diversity; it didn’t prove causation.

When Dr. Knight and his colleagues did a larger analysis using data from more than 3,000 adults, they found that eating 11 to 20 plants per week was associated with similar microbiome diversity as eating 30 or more. Meaning, it wasn’t necessary to eat 30 plants to see the benefits, Dr. Knight said. That analysis, however, has not been peer-reviewed or published.

A few limited studies have since tested variations on the 30-plant target, Dr. Armet said. In a 2025 trial involving 25 adults with chronic kidney disease in Australia, researchers found that consuming 30 or more plants per week (compared with 15 or fewer) led to less constipation and more favorable markers of gut health. And in a trial involving about 400 adults published in July, researchers found that those who took a “30-plant” supplement for six weeks reported less constipation, but had no increase in microbiome diversity, relative to study participants who took a probiotic supplement or a placebo made from bread croutons. (The study was funded by ZOE, the company that sells the supplement.)

Because the participants in both studies increased their fiber consumption in pursuit of the 30-plant goal, the researchers couldn’t say whether the increase in the variety of plants, the extra fiber or a combination of the two was responsible for the benefits, Dr. Armet said.

And contrary to some online claims, she added, there’s no evidence that 30 plants per week is an optimal amount to reduce inflammation, improve heart or immune health, increase energy or prolong life-span.

That said, research generally supports the benefits of eating a variety of plant foods; it just doesn’t back the 30-plant target, Dr. Sonnenburg said. People’s microbiomes are complex and unique; there’s no one-size-fits-all advice, he added.

The Bottom Line

If you enjoy the challenge of eating 30 plants a week, go for it, said Lourdes Castro, a dietitian and adjunct professor of nutrition at New York University. It may help you eat more fiber and more diverse foods, which can benefit your health, she said.

But some people might feel overwhelmed by tracking their meals or anxious about meeting the target, Ms. Castro said.

A more evidence-based goal, Dr. Armet said, would be to consume the recommended amount of fiber — 21 to 38 grams per day, depending on your age and sex — from a variety of plant foods.

And skip the supplements, Dr. Sonnenburg said. “Whole foods are better.”

endometriosis-diagnosis-tests.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 30  Words: 1302/1304

SUMMARY

Getting an endometriosis diagnosis is notoriously hard. The Food and Drug Administration has not approved any noninvasive endometriosis test. In both cases, a majority had endometriosis.

ARTICLE

Do Endometriosis Tests Really Work?
Patients and doctors are eager for a noninvasive way to diagnose the disease, and several start-ups are offering new options. Here’s what to know about them.
By Maggie Astor
Published 2026-09-29 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/well/live/endometriosis-diagnosis-tests.html

Getting an endometriosis diagnosis is notoriously hard.

It takes seven to nine years on average, and patients are often told their agonizing pain is normal menstrual cramping or in their head. If they do find a helpful doctor, many need surgery to confirm the diagnosis, because imaging doesn’t reliably show it. The disease, in which tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, is estimated to affect at least one in 10 reproductive-age women.

For many, a reliable noninvasive test feels like the holy grail. Now, several start-ups claim to have found it, offering to diagnose endometriosis by examining RNA molecules in saliva, proteins in blood or electrical signals in the gastrointestinal tract.

“The premise is a good one, because currently the standard of care is invasive,” said Dr. Ja Hyun Shin, a gynecologic surgery specialist at Weill Cornell Medicine.

But so far, she and other experts said, the evidence for the new tests is limited to small studies of patients who may not be broadly representative.

Katherine Burns, an associate professor at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine who studies endometriosis and has it herself, said she understood why patients were eager: She suffered for about 10 years without a diagnosis and would have tried anything to get answers and relief. “But one of the things that I’ve learned along the way is, you have to ask questions,” she said.

Here is what we know about the new tests.

What’s being marketed?

The Food and Drug Administration has not approved any noninvasive endometriosis test. But several companies are offering products “for research purposes only,” or through a regulatory loophole that the F.D.A. has sought unsuccessfully to close.

Endometriosis sometimes appears on M.R.I.s or ultrasounds, but often not — so for many women, the only way to get a definitive diagnosis is for a surgeon to search for lesions and take biopsies. The premise of the new tests is that they can detect biomarkers, or changes in body fluids or functions, associated with the disease.

One, called Endotest, checks saliva for a pattern of microRNAs, molecules that are involved in regulating genes. Another, EndoSure, measures gastrointestinal electrical activity. A third, EndomTest, checks blood for two proteins. Each test is backed by at least one peer-reviewed study run or funded by its manufacturer.

A fourth test, from Xella Health, uses a proprietary artificial intelligence algorithm to analyze blood biomarkers, symptoms and medical history for endometriosis risk, but its accuracy has not been publicly assessed. Xella is also developing a menstrual fluid test, based so far on an unpublished analysis of 28 samples — not enough to draw conclusions from, given how different endometriosis can be in different patients, said Stacey Missmer, a professor of women’s health at the University of Michigan Medical School.

What’s the evidence?

The initial studies of Endotest and EndoSure found that they accurately identified more than 90 percent of people both with and without endometriosis. But the studies had limitations, many experts said, including size, types of patients and the fact that they were funded or conducted by the products’ manufacturers.

Endotest’s main study involved 971 patients; EndoSure’s had 154. In both cases, a majority had endometriosis. Tests can perform misleadingly well in such “high prevalence” populations, because they have little opportunity to misdiagnose people who have other conditions, said Dr. Tamer Seckin, an endometriosis surgeon and founder of the Endometriosis Foundation of America.

A recent study of Endotest by independent researchers found less impressive results, but it was small and conducted in an unrepresentative population. Two small studies in Belgium and Brazil have also examined EndoSure, but they haven’t been peer-reviewed, and included so few people without endometriosis that researchers couldn’t reliably estimate how well the test identified them.

Ziwig, Endotest’s manufacturer, said “prospective real-world studies involving up to 25,000 women” were underway. Dr. Mark Noar, EndoSure’s executive chairman, said it was also working on studies in broader populations.

Many experts said they considered the microRNA technology behind Endotest promising, if not yet perfected. While there haven’t been many studies of Endotest, microRNA’s overall potential as a biomarker has been studied more.

The evidence for EndoSure’s technology, examining gut electrical signals, is more preliminary, said Dr. Seckin, Dr. Shin and Dr. Ted Lee, the director of minimally invasive gynecologic surgery at NYU Langone Health.

Christine Metz, a professor at the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research at Northwell Health, said EndoSure’s initial study was promising. But Dr. Metz noted that numerous diseases, medications and other factors can affect gut motility, so more research is needed to confirm whether the signals EndoSure measures are specific to endometriosis.

As for EndomTest, the protein-based option, a small study by its developer showed nearly no false positives but many false negatives: It only identified 46.2 percent of people with endometriosis. (Andrew Levin, the chief executive of the company that has licensed it, said further studies were underway.) And despite the lack of false positives in the study, the test relies in part on a protein that rises with many diseases. The company says examining two proteins together makes the test more accurate, but Dr. Seckin and Dr. Missmer were skeptical.

A British health agency is considering allowing Endotest, the microRNA alternative, to be used temporarily in the National Health Service to generate more evidence. But the agency said the other new tests weren’t ready for that yet.

Experts emphasized that, while reliable noninvasive tests could speed up diagnosis, they may not provide the information that surgery can about the severity and location of endometriosis lesions — and tests with unproven accuracy are risky. False positives can lead to unnecessary surgical treatment, and false negatives can prevent diagnosis.

A false negative from a test advertised as reliable is “the worst thing that can happen,” said Semir Beyaz, an endometriosis researcher at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, because being told nothing is wrong is “what they have been going through forever.”

What comes next?

A test that is now on the market, or a modified version, could conceivably be validated within a few years.

“I find these things very promising first steps,” Dr. Beyaz said.

In the meantime, experts emphasized that doctors can be confident many patients have endometriosis based on symptoms and a physical examination, and treat them accordingly. “We could really be doing much, much better immediately if we just listened to our patients,” said Dr. Hugh Taylor, a professor and chair of obstetrics, gynecology and reproductive sciences at Yale School of Medicine who studies microRNA as an endometriosis marker.

New tests might be most useful in patients whose symptoms are ambiguous, like those with unexplained infertility but no pain, or adolescents with mild symptoms that could be early signs of endometriosis.

In addition to Endotest, a large clinical trial is looking at a microRNA blood test called DotEndo, based on Dr. Taylor’s research. (Dr. Taylor is on its scientific advisory board.) The trial was designed in consultation with the F.D.A., said Heather Bowerman, the founder and chief executive of DotLab, which makes the test. If the results are good, she said, DotLab may seek F.D.A. approval as soon as 2027, though it hasn’t decided which regulatory route to take.

At the same time, new discoveries are underscoring how much researchers still may not know.

A recent paper from Dr. Taylor’s team was one of the first to report that adolescents with early-stage endometriosis may show different microRNA markers from adults. That could mean different tests are needed, said the lead author, Dr. Alla Vash-Margita, an associate professor of obstetrics, gynecology and reproductive sciences at Yale.

Dr. Taylor said he believed “we will have noninvasive diagnostics for endometriosis in the near future.” But, he added, “Whether any of the ones we’re seeing now are going to be the best test is hard to know.”

SUMMARY

On the morning of Aug. 4, two Russian guided bombs, each weighing more than 1,000 pounds, struck the residential block where I grew up in Kramatorsk, eastern Ukraine. Russian forces have been advancing on Kramatorsk slowly but steadily, and I long knew that my childhood home would eventually find itself in the fight. Two months after the war broke out, I returned to Kramatorsk to report on Russian advances in the eastern Donetsk region.

ARTICLE

Bomb by Bomb, the Slow Death of My Hometown in Ukraine
It was possible, for a time, to think that Kramatorsk, where I was born and raised, would survive the war mostly unscathed. Not any more.
By Olha Konovalova
Published 2026-09-29 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/world/europe/ukraine-kramatorsk.html

On the morning of Aug. 4, two Russian guided bombs, each weighing more than 1,000 pounds, struck the residential block where I grew up in Kramatorsk, eastern Ukraine.

I learned of the attack from social media, scrolling through videos until I recognized a neighboring building in flames. Then came the frantic search for any piece of information on whether my home had also been destroyed.

Finally, a man who still lives in my building sent me a video, filmed from inside my flat. The fire had spared it, but not the blast. Shards of glass covered the floor. In the kitchen, the window frame had been torn from the wall. In the living room, the windowsill was gone entirely. Even the bathroom tiles had cracked.

Russian forces have been advancing on Kramatorsk slowly but steadily, and I long knew that my childhood home would eventually find itself in the fight. Still, nothing prepares you for seeing the place you were born torn apart by bombs.

This is an experience shared by millions of people across Ukraine over four and a half years of war — those now watching their homes being damaged by the approaching fight, and those who’ve already lost them.

As a journalist, I have covered such stories repeatedly, watching city after city being destroyed: Sievierodonetsk, Bakhmut, Avdiivka, Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka. Now, it’s my hometown’s turn.

Kramatorsk is a small city filled with parks and childhood memories. I remember splashing in a fountain in the city center on hot summer days and sledding down the hill near my school in winter. On weekends, my mother and I would walk to the local farmers’ market to buy fresh milk and homemade cheese that we would devour with breakfast. A Georgian restaurant near our home became a favorite spot for family evenings over a khachapuri and wine, a birthday celebration or just a cup of coffee.

Everything changed on Feb. 24, 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion. Explosions woke my parents in Kramatorsk and they called me in a panic to ask what they should do, where they should go and what they should take with them.

I was in Mariupol that day, more than 100 miles to the south, working as a producer with a CNN team. Trying to organize my parents’ evacuation over the phone, I told them to pack the essentials — documents, a change of clothes and our cat — and get out of town.

They left the apartment tidy, expecting to come back soon. They’re still in Norway today, under refugee status.

Two months after the war broke out, I returned to Kramatorsk to report on Russian advances in the eastern Donetsk region. Russian troops were closing in, capturing village after village. Shelling had become an almost daily occurrence. It seemed like my last chance to see home.

When I opened the door, the first thing I noticed was the smell. Our apartment used to smell of my mother’s cooking. Now it smelled empty. Everything was covered in dust. Knowing I might not be able to return, I wanted to take as much as I could: family photo albums, my father’s chessboard, my grandmother’s hand-embroidered bedsheet. But it turned out a life doesn’t fit into a suitcase, and I had to leave much behind.

Outside my flat, though, Kramatorsk carried on a life that was both strange and strangely ordinary. There were constant reminders of the war, of course, like gasoline shortages and the absence of Coca-Cola from supermarket shelves; we managed to get both on the black market. But food delivery services still ran, and hotels were full of journalists.

Ukrainian forces pushed the Russian troops back and the city grew safer. Residents began to return. Kramatorsk became a rear base for journalists and humanitarian group staffers working at the front. Businesses reopened, including our favorite Georgian restaurant. As I began visiting Kramatorsk more often, I had lunch there.

Sitting in the same place my family used to gather, it was easy to believe that Kramatorsk had escaped the fighting. The same town, the same restaurant, the same me.

That, it turned out, was an illusion.

I had seen it play out before, in the town of Pokrovsk, about 40 miles southwest of Kramatorsk. Pokrovsk, too, had returned to something resembling normal life after the initial Russian invasion. For the news media teams I worked with, Pokrovsk was a safe place, somewhere to sleep and eat a good meal at the end of a day at the front.

But as the fighting closed in, guided bombs started to hit Pokrovsk more often. Starting in the fall of 2024, the streets grew emptier as people evacuated and shuttered their homes and businesses. Within months, Pokrovsk had emptied out, inhabited only by the soldiers preparing for the coming street fighting.

On my trips back to Kramatorsk, I began to recognize the same pattern in the past few months. As Russian forces pushed closer, their drones began reaching the city, flying through my neighborhood on the eastern edge of the city.

Bombs hit areas I have known my whole life. This spring, an airstrike hit the street I used to walk down to go to art school as a child, where I would stop at a little shop to buy a chocolate bar and cherry juice before class. The bomb landed a few meters away from the shop.

Finally, on Aug. 4, bombs landed near home. One struck the building next to mine; the other reduced the Georgian restaurant where I had spent so many happy family moments to rubble. All around, trees were uprooted and burned-out cars lay overturned in the street. In my own building, alongside blown-out windows, damaged balcony frames hung from the upper floors. Then, in late September, another attack sparked a large blaze that ravaged several dozen flats next to mine.

My home has survived, but will I have anywhere to return to, when the war is over? Deep down, I know how this story will end.

Constant Méheut contributed reporting.
