SUMMARY

“The beliefs of James Talarico are certainly wrong. Talarico is running for Senate in Texas, and he has a chance to be the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the state since Lloyd Bentsen defeated a Republican congressman named Beau Boulter in 1988. The race between Paxton and Talarico could be the most consequential in the country.

ARTICLE

The ‘God Gap’ Is Narrowing in Texas
It may not be enough for James Talarico to win. But might it also be a sign of a change to come?
By David French
Published 2026-10-04 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/opinion/talarico-paxton-texas-senate-evangelicals.html

Robert Jeffress, the senior pastor of First Baptist Dallas, a 16,000-member congregation, stepped to the microphone at the Republican Party’s midterm convention last month and issued what sounded like a declaration of a religious cold war:

“The beliefs of James Talarico are certainly wrong. But they’re more than wrong. The beliefs of James Talarico are blasphemous. They are evil, and they are not beliefs that any true Christian could support. Ever.”

Talarico is running for Senate in Texas, and he has a chance to be the first Democrat to win a Senate election in the state since Lloyd Bentsen defeated a Republican congressman named Beau Boulter in 1988. Republicans are worried, and as a consequence their rhetoric is getting wilder and wilder.

According to Talarico’s critics, he’s a heretic. He’s a wolf in sheep’s clothing who will lead God’s people astray. President Trump calls him “Talafreako,” and he’s apparently so dangerous to Republicans that, as The Wall Street Journal reported last month, right-wing podcasts are mentioning Trump less and less while attacking Talarico more and more.

He’s young, he’s polished and he is, heaven forbid, a seminarian (on leave from his studies at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary). Talarico is running one of the most faith-forward campaigns in the country, along with other Democratic candidates like Adam Hamilton in Kansas (a pastor running for senator) and Rob Sand in Iowa (running for governor).

Democrats have run a version of this playbook before. The Rev. Raphael Warnock has prevailed in two Senate elections in Georgia, winning a partial term in a 2021 runoff against Kelly Loeffler and then a full term in 2022, against a MAGA favorite, Herschel Walker. Democrats nationwide are trying to close the “God gap” that has been the Republican Party’s not-so-secret weapon since the 1970s and the advent of Ronald Reagan.

Talarico’s Christian faith, though, is more liberal than the Christian faith of many Republicans. It’s more liberal than mine (which isn’t hard). But for many fundamentalists, Talarico’s theology makes him the wrong kind of Christian. And to some, no Christian at all.

His opponent is Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general of Texas, whose wife is divorcing him for infidelity and who was impeached by the Republican-led Texas House of Representatives for misconduct that included bribery, obstruction of justice and disregard of official duties. (The Texas Senate acquitted him.)

Trump calls him “the greatest attorney general in the United States of America.”

This frontal assault on Talarico’s faith comes after much of the right has spent more than a decade telling voters that they’re electing a president and not a pastor, that they should pay no attention to the religious beliefs (much less the personal conduct) of the Republican president they love. But now the message has changed. In Texas, one of the candidates — Talarico — is treated more like a pastor than a potential senator, and his theology is treated as the true threat to our Republic, and to our souls.

Paxton? He gets a pass. Just like Trump.

The race between Paxton and Talarico could be the most consequential in the country. If Democrats win in Georgia and North Carolina, that’s to be expected, this time around anyway. If they win in Ohio and Maine, it’s troubling for Republicans, but hardly catastrophic — Maine leans blue, after all, and Ohio was a swing state until recently.

But Texas? A Democratic win there would be monumental. It’s not just that Texas is red — Trump won by more than 13 points in 2024, and he won convincingly in 2016 and 2020 as well. It’s not just that no Democrat has won statewide office in more than three decades. It’s that Texas is arguably the cornerstone of both Republican and evangelical political power in the United States.

Its 40 Electoral College votes are indispensable to the party. Were Texas to go or even trend blue, G.O.P. presidential victories would become far more difficult.

It’s the Republican state with the largest economy, and it’s arguably the most important culturally (though Tennessee would like a word). It has long been a magnet for internal migration. The South tends to dominate the G.O.P., but it’s a Texas-flavored version of the South. To quote the country singer Ella Langley, when it comes to finding a home in Red America, an extraordinary number of Americans are “Choosin’ Texas.”

But Texas isn’t just a symbol of Republican power; it’s also a symbol of Democratic defeat. Democrats used to run the state, and the story of Democratic decline in Texas is also a story about religion. When the religious right emerged as one of the most potent voting blocs in the nation, it ultimately routed Democrats in the South.

And yet, as of Friday, a key polling average has Talarico leading Paxton by three points. And he’s leading in poll after poll. Beto O’Rourke — the last great blue hope — never achieved such lofty polling heights in his Senate race against Ted Cruz. Is the era of Democratic decline at an end?

But there’s a question that’s even more important: Will Talarico’s religious faith help put him — and his party — over the top?

To try to answer that question, I went on a reporting trip that became a journey — from Zoom calls in my home office to meetings in coffee shops in Austin to walking the streets of Beaumont, which is where I met Brady, a shirtless Marxist-Leninist in a kilt.

But I’m getting ahead of myself. To understand the religious dynamics of the Texas race, it’s important to absorb the true depths of the “God gap” in American politics. That gap isn’t just about white evangelicals (although it certainly is partly about them), and it’s one of the Democrats’ chief obstacles to obtaining a durable political majority.

Any discussion of the God gap does have to begin with white evangelicals. Their numbers are vast (far more than twice as large as Black Protestants, the most loyal religious Democratic voters), and they vote in lock step.

In 2024, white evangelicals voted for Trump by a 65-point margin, 82 percent to 17 percent. Trump lost all other voters by 18 points, 58 percent to 40 percent.

Lost, however, in that top-line number is an additional fact that should disturb Democrats: In 2024, virtually every Christian denomination — evangelical, mainline and Catholic — shifted to the right.

Last year, Ryan Burge, a political scientist who is one of the nation’s foremost statisticians of religion, published an analysis of 22 Protestant denominations, and he found that all but four shifted to the right from 2020 to 2024, and some of them shifted rather significantly.

The predominantly Black National Baptist Convention had an immense rightward shift. In 2020, 10 percent of its members voted for Trump. By 2024, that percentage almost tripled, to 29 percent.

And what about the Catholic vote? In Texas, 22 percent of the adult population is Catholic, the only religious group that comes close to evangelicals, who represent 27 percent of Texas adults. Nationally there was a 13-point Catholic swing toward Trump.

There are two ways of looking at this data. One is deeply depressing for Democrats: The religious vote is sliding away, and in a country as religious as the United States still is, despite recent declines in religious faith and practice, losing the religious vote means losing elections time and time again.

The other is a bit more hopeful. The religious vote is sliding, but that’s recent — and reversible. Joe Biden, though well past his prime in 2020, did substantially better than Kamala Harris. People of faith may not be lost to Democrats forever so much as they’re punishing Democrats — warning with their votes against the secularization and social radicalization of the far left.

As I talked to Paxton supporters, angry anti-Paxton Republicans and wary but hopeful Democrats, a picture began to emerge. Talarico can win his race, but it will take MAGA pushing Christians out and Talarico pulling Christians in. Anger at Paxton alone won’t be enough for Talarico to prevail.

My first conversation was with Robert Jeffress. I reached out by email, and he graciously agreed to chat, even though we’ve been on opposite sides of the conservative civil war for a very long time. He’s been one of Trump’s most prominent evangelical supporters since 2016; I — to put it mildly — have not.

When we connected via Zoom, he was a bit less fiery than he was on that stage in Dallas, but he still made his beliefs crystal clear. First, he emphasized that “I don’t endorse and haven’t endorsed anybody in this race. I don’t endorse, except for president.”

So, if he’s not endorsing, why did Jeffress speak to the Republican convention in Dallas? “Because of some of the erroneous things Talarico said that I don’t reconcile with the New Testament,” Jeffress said. “And I was criticizing him not for his political beliefs, but his religious beliefs.”

“His religious beliefs certainly don’t disqualify him from being a senator,” Jeffress continued. “They do disqualify him from being a follower of Christ.”

I asked Jeffress to specify his religious objections to Talarico, and he named three key issues — that Talarico had “said that he believes there’s a spectrum of genders,” that Talarico’s spiritual mentor had said that he’s uncomfortable using words like God and Father, and that Talarico had “very recently indicated that all religions were basically different paths that led to the same truth.”

If that seems like thin gruel to you to condemn someone to hell, you’re not alone, but that’s not the central flaw in Jeffress’s analysis.

If conservative Christians are supposed to reject Talarico’s religious views, what are they supposed to make of Paxton’s conduct, and isn’t his conduct both in and out of office more relevant to voters than Talarico’s theology?

Paxton has reportedly cheated on his wife more than once, and his wife, a Texas state senator named Angela Paxton, has filed for divorce, citing “biblical grounds.” (Even the divorce filings in Texas invoke the Bible.) He was recently spotted overseas, during the thick of the campaign, with a woman who appears to be his current girlfriend.

And his misconduct isn’t just private. Paxton was impeached after seven of his top deputies at the attorney general’s office blew the whistle on him, claiming that he’d engaged in bribery and abuse of office to provide favors for an investor named Nate Paul.

Paxton was accused of providing favors to Paul, including providing him with “highly sensitive information” about an F.B.I. raid on Paul’s home. In exchange, Paul reportedly helped Paxton remodel his home, and Paul employed a woman who was Paxton’s mistress at the time.

But Paxton isn’t just corrupt. As The Associated Press detailed in a report last week, he lives a “jet-setting lifestyle” that takes him across the country (and the world) and leaves immense blank spaces in his official calendar.

Earlier in his tenure as attorney general, The A.P. reported, Paxton’s “official calendars were packed with job-related duties. In 2021, more than 90 workdays were blank — a number that reached 112 in 2024, the last full year The A.P. had records for.”

“Over a two-year period ending in 2024,” The A.P. noted, “Paxton flew to the Caribbean, Israel, India, Taiwan, South Africa; made three trips to Europe; and hit five different ski towns in the Rockies, including numerous visits to Park City, Utah, among other destinations, records show.”

Here’s one way to think of Paxton — he possesses all of Donald Trump’s corruption and none of Trump’s charisma.

These details are supposed to matter to Southern Baptists. In 1998, at the height of the scandal surrounding Bill Clinton’s relationship with Monica Lewinsky, the Southern Baptist Convention passed a resolution on the moral character of public officials, and a key clause said, “Tolerance of serious wrong by leaders sears the conscience of the culture, spawns unrestrained immorality and lawlessness in the society, and surely results in God’s judgment.”

I asked Jeffress about that resolution and its impact on Southern Baptists today, and his response confirmed the views of skeptics who believed that Baptists cared more that Clinton was a Democrat than they cared that he had cheated on his wife.

“What was going on in 1998?” he asked, and then answered his own question: “Monica Lewinsky and Bill Clinton, and that was an emphasis on that, and I think it could have been partisan, very much a partisan reaction to that.”

And what is his own view? The Book of Romans, he notes, “teaches that God has given government the role of protecting society.”

“And I’ve said before,” he continued, “when I look for somebody who does that, I don’t want somebody with a demeanor of Jesus necessarily — be nice if they did — but I want the meanest, toughest S.O.B. I can find.”

Raise the subject of Ken Paxton to a conservative supporter of Senator John Cornyn, the incumbent Paxton defeated in the Republican primary, however, and you’re very likely to get a much different reaction.

Trump endorsed Paxton late in the primary race, and Paxton won by a stunning 28-point margin.

Many Cornyn supporters are still furious. Why mount a primary challenge to a man who almost always voted with Trump? Why risk a Senate seat to put a corrupt man in Washington?

The answer, it seems, is a version of a MAGA purity test. Cornyn has been with Trump almost all the time, but it’s the “almost” that counts. Cornyn, for example, supported a modest gun control compromise after the massacre at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas. Perhaps most important — to Trump at least — is that Cornyn voted to certify Biden’s election.

Paxton, on the other hand, abused the power of the attorney general’s office to file one of the most specious and frivolous lawsuits I’ve ever read.

In December 2020, he sued Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin to try to block them from voting in the Electoral College. The suit was so frivolous that Texas’ respected solicitor general, Kyle Hawkins — who was appointed to the post by Paxton — refused to add his name to the complaint. The Supreme Court dismissed the case without even granting it a hearing.

The Texas Republicans I talked to were divided on whether Trump’s endorsement was fatal to Cornyn, or if Cornyn was going to lose no matter what Trump said. Karl Rove seems to think Trump made a difference. During a conversation at the Texas Tribune festival in Austin, Rove not only attacked Paxton for his record of corruption but also said that tracking polls showed Texas Republicans breaking toward Cornyn before Trump’s endorsement, a trend that decisively reversed itself when Trump weighed in.

As Matt Mackowiak, a former senior Cornyn campaign official, told me, Paxton’s supporters were “trying to exterminate RINOs” — referring to the ultimate Republican insult, “Republican in name only” — “but they’ll turn the state blue.” Though Cornyn, he hastened to add, was no RINO: “Cornyn cannot be a RINO if he voted 99 percent with Trump.”

I asked Mackowiak about the idea I mentioned before, that anger at Paxton alone won’t do the trick for Talarico. It’s not enough for Paxton to merely push voters out; Talarico has to pull them in.

His answer focused on “permission structures.” By emphasizing his own faith and — perhaps more important — by trying to explicitly welcome disgruntled Christians into his coalition, Talarico was creating a permission structure for Republicans to support his candidacy.

The more I talked to Cornyn Republicans and dissenting evangelicals, the more I realized that Jeffress’s theological attack was missing the mark. The permission structure that Talarico was creating had little to do with theology and everything to do with decency. Voters were less interested in what Talarico believed (they weren’t seeking to join his church) than how he behaved.

It’s almost as if they’d listened to the words of Jesus Christ in Matthew 7: “By their fruit you will recognize them.”

As the head of an Austin-area evangelical nonprofit who insisted on anonymity for fear of retaliation told me, “I’ll bank on basic character, and the ability to actually listen and respond.” Talarico, he said, “seems like a genuinely good guy.” In a Christian version of the beer test, he said, “I’d like to have a coffee with him.” Or as a former Republican and former Texas public official told me, “I would want him as my neighbor.”

It was difficult to find any conservative evangelical leaders who were willing to go on the record with their support for Talarico. As that same former Republican told me, “there is a massive social barrier” to saying that you’d vote for a Democrat.

Evangelical cancel culture is real, and there are few better ways to land in its cross hairs than saying nice things about James Talarico.

I wasn’t content, however, with talking only to pastors, consultants and public officials in the Texas political elite. I wanted to see the race at the grass roots. So I got in my rental car and drove down to a neighborhood in Beaumont, in southeastern Texas, to walk along and listen as Talarico volunteers and local Democratic Party candidates and officials went door to door trying to turn out the vote for Democrats.

(I contacted the Paxton campaign also, but my messages went unanswered. Neither candidate would speak to me about the issue of faith — or any other issue.)

I met the Talarico crew in the parking lot of a local seafood joint. The day was hot, but not too hot, and the volunteers who’d gathered there were excited about Talarico. They were also nervous, maybe very nervous.

They’d been through 2018, when they thought Beto O’Rourke might win. And they’d been through many more drubbings when the Democrat never had a ghost of a chance. As Samantha Bartley, a member of the Hardin County Democratic Party, told me: “I’m praying we aren’t like the Dallas Cowboys, OK? We can beat some booty until the fourth quarter, we got two minutes left, and we can drop the ball and lose every time.”

But they still had hope. Shannon Heath, a precinct chair in Hardin County, said that membership in the local party had doubled, and that while she wasn’t seeing any movement in what she called “Mega MAGA,” the core of Trump’s base, Democrats were focusing on “Republicans who are still Republicans, and a lot of them have changed their minds.”

I walked with Bartley and Heath through a working-class neighborhood in Beaumont. They both said they were still at least a tiny bit nervous. It’s socially awkward to knock on a person’s door.

But there was no cause for concern. Real-life contact with these ordinary Texans was as different from online political conversations as Venus is from Mars.

Everyone was unfailingly polite and gracious, but in one key way my (admittedly anecdotal) grass-roots experience was identical to my conversations at the grass tips. Republicans were everywhere, but actual Ken Paxton supporters — people willing to say nice things about him — were hard to find.

The neighborhood was surprisingly ideologically diverse. We encountered roughly equal numbers of Republicans and Democrats, and most of the time that was the extent of the conversation — a person pleasantly identified as being Republican or Democratic and that was that.

But two voters stood out — Sharon and Brady (I agreed not to use the voters’ last names). Sharon was an older woman who said she leaned Republican. She listened patiently to the Talarico volunteers but interrupted them to say that she’d supported Trump. He’s “rude and crude,” she said, “but things had to change.”

She paused for a moment, however, and blurted out, unprovoked, “I hate Ken Paxton.” She didn’t commit to Talarico by any means, but she had no affection for Paxton at all, and in the intensity of her feelings you could see the difference in at least some Republican perceptions of the two men.

Trump was “rude and crude” but had his uses. Paxton? There was nothing good to say about him.

Brady was the shirtless man in the kilt I mentioned earlier. He was the last house of the day, and he was delighted to talk to the Talarico volunteers — and to me. Before our brief interview he dashed inside to put on a shirt. He identified himself as a “Marxist-Leninist” who “chronically doomscrolls” on social media and votes Democratic.

He was unconvinced, however, that people were changing their stance. “Everyone’s kind of dug in,” he said. “Everyone’s doing what they’ve been doing.”

In 15 minutes I felt like I’d met the two farthest poles in the Talarico tent. To win, his campaign had to capture all the Sharons, all the Bradys, and everyone in between.

That sounds like a daunting task, and it is. I can see the polls showing Talarico in the lead, but I keep hearing a voice whispering in my head, “This is still Texas.”

At the same time, something is stirring. It’s hard to take evangelical attacks on Talarico’s theology seriously when evangelicals have flooded the polls to support Trump, a man without a visible theology other than the worship of the self, and whatever else we say about him, Donald Trump is no god.

It’s also hard to take seriously the attacks on Talarico’s pastor for his supposed heresy when Trump’s most prominent faith adviser, Paula White-Cain, is also a person whom many Southern Baptist and other evangelical supporters of Trump would consider a heretic. She preaches a form of the prosperity gospel — the belief that if you have the right kind of faith (and donate to her ministry) that health and wealth await you.

But there is something else in play — something that was a common theme in every conversation I had with a disgruntled Republican. They’re not just tired of Paxton, and they’re not just growing tired of Trump. They’re especially tired of Trump’s most zealous supporters, the people who are happy to blow up the Republican Party to make sure that MAGA stays in charge.

Some of these disgruntled Republicans could swallow Trump, but not the mini-Trumps. Amid all the arguments about policy and ideology, some religious voters are willing to try decency for a change. As one evangelical told me about supporting Talarico, a man he admired but disagreed with on some important things: “It’s an experiment. Let’s see what happens.”

There was one more thing that caught my attention — a surprising hint of grace from all sides. And I wonder if that hint of grace might doom Paxton more than any policy or scandal. His movement feeds off the fear and fury of its members. That’s what causes them to overlook — or perhaps even cheer — his cruelty and corruption. There are no lines he won’t cross to take on the people he hates. He is indeed a mean S.O.B.

But what if hatred starts to fade?

One of the Talarico supporters who showed up at the seafood place in Beaumont was Julie Stephenson, a pastor at First Christian Church in Beaumont. Her church is part of the Disciples of Christ, a mainline denomination, and like most mainline congregations, hers has red and blue members. But “there’s no animosity,” she said. “It’s not red against blue in our congregation.”

Nor did I hear an insulting word from any Talarico volunteer I spoke to. I asked Heath, the Democratic precinct chair, if she was angry at MAGA supporters, or if she had any serious conflicts with people on the other side, and she looked at me with a hint of incredulity.

“They are our neighbors,” she said.

There was even a glimmer of hope and reconciliation from Pastor Jeffress. Throughout my conversation with him, he was certainly unsparing in his criticism of Talarico’s religious beliefs, but he also repeatedly said that Christians should vote their conscience.

“What if a parishioner comes to you and says, ‘My conscience is telling me Talarico’?” I asked.

“Follow what you feel like God’s leading you to do,” he responded. “Period. I wouldn’t hesitate to tell them why I’m not voting that way and made sure they were aware of some of the statements he had made about Jesus and the Bible, but if they say, you know, ‘I just can’t overlook the other. This is the way I’m going’?

“I’d say, ‘Fine, I’ll see you in church next Sunday.’”

SUMMARY

Even in 2026, the fastest way to get from Singapore to Malaysia is a five-minute ride on the diesel-powered Shuttle Tebrau, which takes passengers from the Woodlands train checkpoint in Singapore to the Johor Bahru Sentral transport hub in Malaysia. ARTICLE

1,200 Miles by Train, From Singapore to Bangkok
A writer takes a weeklong journey, from the island city-state to the Thai capital, in the final days of a historic rail connection.
By Nicholas Yong
Published 2026-10-04 04:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/travel/singapore-bangkok-train-historic-shuttle-closes.html

Even in 2026, the fastest way to get from Singapore to Malaysia is a five-minute ride on the diesel-powered Shuttle Tebrau, which takes passengers from the Woodlands train checkpoint in Singapore to the Johor Bahru Sentral transport hub in Malaysia.

But the shuttle’s time is soon coming to an end. By mid-2027 it is scheduled to end operations and be replaced by a new rail link connected to Singapore’s subway system that will depart nearby.

The coming change had me thinking about the rail connections between the two countries. Journeys into Malaysia by train were one of the most common holidays for Singaporeans before the rise of the low-cost regional airlines in the early 2000s. Rail connections were also disrupted by political developments. That’s too bad, because a long rail journey is a great opportunity to see the Malaysian countryside, and there are plenty of places to stop along the way.

And so, on a sweltering afternoon in March, I paid 16 Malaysian ringgit ($5) for a seat on the shuttle, kicking off my weeklong journey to Bangkok, with stops in the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur and the state of Penang, to eat and explore.

Each leg took between an hour and four-and-a-half hours, except for an overnight ride to Bangkok. The whole trip took seven days and six trains. Train tickets cost $135 in total, and I stayed two nights in each city, spending approximately $1,400 on hotels, meals, transport and other expenses.

Delights of the Malaysian Capital

After my shuttle journey, I took the Electric Train Service, an intercity rail service, from JB Sentral to Kuala Lumpur. The direct connection, which had begun service three months earlier to great fanfare, has cut travel time between the two cities to four-and-a-half hours, from seven. Tickets can be purchased via the rail operator KTMB’s app.

The six-car train is not the equal of the high-speed rail services of China or Japan, but business class — at a cost of 171 ringgit — had reclining seats and plenty of legroom.

One of the best places to eat in Kuala Lumpur, renowned for its food scene, is the open-air Jalan Alor Food Street. A century old, it has everything from barbecued seafood to Chinese Muslim cuisine to the ubiquitous Satay. I grabbed a magnificent rougamo, often called a Chinese burger, consisting of small strips of slow-cooked pork stuffed into a flaky bun.

But arguably my best meal was lunch the next day at the renowned Village Park Restaurant in nearby Petaling Jaya. I sampled nasi lemak, the national dish: coconut rice accompanied by crispy fried chicken, peanuts, strips of cucumber and sweet sambal chili with a real kick.

Before lunch, I ventured to the otherworldly Batu Caves, a limestone cave complex on the outskirts of the city housing a series of Hindu temples and shrines. Inside the caves, a major pilgrimage site, the air was redolent of incense and long-tailed macaques gamboled everywhere.

Every tourist wanted a selfie. “Oh, she’s got a baby!” exclaimed a British woman about a monkey cradling her infant. Fittingly, there was a giant statue of the monkey-like deity Hanuman.

A 140-foot-high golden statue of the war god Murugan perched near a colorful 272-step staircase that leads to the Sri Subramaniar Swamy temple. It was a dizzying climb in the midday heat, accompanied by nonchalant monkeys leaping everywhere. At the top, I was rewarded by the sight of the towering rock formations that had formed over millions of years.

Street Food and Murals in Penang

My trip resumed the next day with a three-and-a-half-hour business class ride (175 ringgit) on a sleek and modern train to the town of Butterworth, alongside many British and Australian families. When we disembarked for a catamaran to George Town — the capital of Penang and a UNESCO World Heritage Site — I also overheard many Chinese and Korean accents. Tickets were two ringgit for the 10-minute ride.

Penang is often called Malaysia’s culinary capital. You can find an amazing variety of street food, such as char koay teow, or flat rice noodles stir-fried with ingredients like prawns, chives, bean sprouts and lard. A plate at the Michelin-rated Siam Road Charcoal Char Koay Teow cost me just 10 ringgit, and it was savory and spicy, infused with a wok hei, or smoky flavor.

Penang has also become associated with the murals of the Lithuanian artist Ernest Zacharevic, who rose to global acclaim in 2012 after creating a series of six street art murals depicting daily life in Malaysia. A combination of painting and objects like a bike or a motorcycle, the murals invite interaction, and tourists gather to get photos with them. Other murals have also sprung up around them.

At Penang Hill, a nature reserve just outside the city, another train awaited: a 1.2 mile funicular railway to the summit. Built by the British in 1924, it is reminiscent of the funicular at The Peak in Hong Kong. To enjoy the panoramic view of George Town, I sat at the bottom of the train for the five-minute journey.

I then ambled to The Habitat, a mile-long nature trail built by the British East India Company in the early 1800s. It sits on the edge of a rainforest reserve. With the sounds of cicadas ringing and the sight of langurs casually grooming each other, I wiped the sweat off my brow and took time to savor the trail.

Three Trains to Bangkok

The longest leg of the trip began with a two-hour train ride from Butterworth to the town of Padang Besar, which straddles the border between Malaysia and the Thai province of Songkhla. I jostled with backpackers and day-trippers en route to the Thai town of Hat Yai, a popular weekend destination for Malaysians, where I would catch a sleeper train to Bangkok.

While the popular option is to hire a communal van for a 90-minute ride, there are three trains a day from Padang Besar to Hat Yai; tickets can only be bought on site for eight ringgit. The six-carriage train operated by State Railway of Thailand was decidedly spartan, with overhead fans and a thick sheen of dust on the windows. It also left around 20 passengers wilting in 90-degree weather for 30 minutes.

When I finally got off at Hat Yai Junction station, I was greeted by the evening crowd, as vendors carrying their wares in baskets reached up to sell food through the train windows. There, I boarded the sleeper train bound for Krung Thep Aphiwat Central Terminal Station in Bangkok, the largest railway station in Southeast Asia. The train, an air-conditioned oasis in the heat seating more than 400, departed on time for the 15-hour ride.

For about 1,800 baht (about $54), a first-class seat gets you a private cabin with two seats that convert into beds, lockable doors and a sink, albeit shared with another passenger. My seat in a second-class carriage had cost just over 1,000 baht. Tickets can be purchased from platforms like Thai Railways or Baolau.

A couple of hours later, train workers converted the seats into upper and lower berths with curtains for privacy. It was reminiscent of my time in Singapore’s military a lifetime ago, when a dozen men shared double-decker bunks in a single room. It was cozy, if somewhat claustrophobic, and the ride tested the limits of my 45-year-old spine.

In spite of numerous travel influencers’ warnings that train engine noise makes it hard to fall asleep, I slept through the night. My only regret: not choosing the lower berth, which had a window. On the top berth, all I could do was stare at the ceiling.

In the morning, I was awakened by a staff member impatient to convert the berths back into seats as the train rolled into Bangkok. It was time to explore, starting with a meal at Funky Lam Kitchen, where the descendants of two Laotian princes serve up modern Lao cuisine. The spicy, earthy and sour flavors left me wanting more.

On my last day, I headed to Song Wat, a trendy district brimming with cafes, street art and amazing food. The streets and narrow alleyways held surprises around every corner — here a building adorned by a mural of two tumbling elephants, there a delightful cafe sitting in a two-story shophouse.

At the Michelin-rated Urai Braised Goose, chaos reigned amid a questionable queue system governed not so much by the sequence of numbers as it was the mood of the servers. It took me almost an hour before I got a seat, but I was rewarded by thin, flavorful strips of goose meat with a spicy dip and rice.

Despite the humidity, I explored Song Wat for hours, before taking refuge at the Sleep Like Cats cafe. As I sipped on an iced milk tea, the owner’s orange tabby — or perhaps the real owner — ambled past and stared at me curiously. I stared back and reflected on how far I had traveled to get here.

Nicholas Yong is a Singaporean freelance journalist based in Seoul, and the author of “Seven Sacks of Rice and Other Baggage.”

SUMMARY

Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak has sickened 977 people as of Oct. 2, with Lancaster County and its large Amish population accounting for about 40 percent of cases.

ARTICLE

Measles Outbreak in Amish Country Forces Some to Rethink Vaccines
The spread of measles in Pennsylvania and Ohio is largely affecting Amish communities where vaccinations levels are low.
By Anemona Hartocollis and Madeleine Hordinski
Published 2026-10-04 21:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/us/amish-vaccines-measles.html

The Amish family thought the chills and fever that had hammered their second oldest son was strep throat. Then a ringing came from the phone shack in the yard: A friend was calling to say the measles had been lurking at a horse auction in Lancaster, Pa.

The 15-year-old boy and his father, an Amish horse breaker, had been there just a few days before.

“We knew it was the measles,” Emma Miller, the boy’s mother, said.

Measles cases have been reported in 45 states in 2026. In Pennsylvania — where state officials say five have died in connection with the outbreak — and Ohio, the Amish people are bearing the brunt of the sickness. They are also taking a share of the blame from outsiders, owing to a lifestyle that tends toward shutting out modern medicine, along with other aspects of contemporary life.

But two days of traveling with a health practitioner through the pastoral Amish country of northeastern Ohio found that despite the stereotype, the Amish are not anti-vaccine. Their reasons for rejecting vaccination are more nuanced.

Like most other Americans, many had never seen a case of measles before, and were not aware of how dangerous the virus could be, leading to deafness, brain swelling and even death. They thought measles would not find them, and it did.

The contagion, officially declared vanquished by vaccination, ripped through the Miller family over the summer, sickening six of the seven children and their mother. It skipped only their father, Marvin Miller, and one daughter, Mary Ann. Both had been vaccinated.

Through the fog of her own illness Mrs. Miller struggled to nurse the sick children, including the baby, as she dispensed Tylenol to battle the fever that accompanies measles. It was left to 12-year-old Mary Ann to sweep the floors and do the baking. Neighbors left food at the door.

The family stayed home from church to protect the congregation. But for all their precautions, the sickness jumped to their cousins, who had visited before there was any thought of measles.

“I didn’t imagine it would be so bad,” Mrs. Miller said.

The Amish are sometimes depicted as objecting to vaccination on religious grounds, but getting vaccinated was a matter of personal preference, families said, again and again. Often it came down to a matter of family practice, or tradition. If their parents or grandparents had been vaccinated, they probably would be, too.

Vaccinations rates are also low because the Amish generally do not have commercial health insurance or credit cards. They pay for medical appointments in cash. In an emergency, they turn to their mutual aid fund.

The measles vaccine came into use in 1963, when the virus was killing 400 to 500 people a year in the United States.

In 2000, measles was declared eliminated, but not eradicated, a subtlety of terminology that allows for a recurrence of the disease. That status is now in jeopardy. There have been more outbreaks in recent years, as hesitancy over vaccines has been fueled by Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the secretary of health and human services, who has long been a skeptic of their efficacy.

“The memory of the vaccination coming in and immediately dropping the death count across the country is for some people two to three generations away,” Cleveland’s director of public health, Dr. David Margolius, said. “That, coupled with more vocal people in positions of power saying, ‘Hey, you don’t need these vaccinations anymore.’”

Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak has sickened 977 people as of Oct. 2, with Lancaster County and its large Amish population accounting for about 40 percent of cases.

It has hospitalized 195 people and been associated with five deaths, according to the state’s public health department. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists just two deaths, disputing the state’s tally.

Ohio has logged 206 cases this year, with the highest numbers in three Amish-heavy counties: Geauga, with 49; Wayne, 44; and Ashtabula, 32. Last year there were 46 measles cases statewide. The state has shipped about 7,100 doses of outbreak-related vaccine to providers this year, up from just over 1,000 last year.

The Pennsylvania and Ohio contagions are most likely linked. Health investigators say some of the Ohio contagion began just as the Miller family’s did, with exposure at horse sales in Lancaster, Pa., and in Bloomfield and Sugarcreek, Ohio. From there, it spread to weddings, funerals, parties and church services.

* * *

During the lockdowns of the Covid years, Stephanie Truckey, a registered nurse based in northeast Ohio, noticed that the Amish had become even more distanced from medical care because they shied away from technology like telehealth.

Ms. Truckey formed a service called Angels to Amish to make house calls and provide basic medical care to patients in parts of Ohio, Pennsylvania and Indiana. She does not administer measles shots. But patients often ask about them, and she connects them with providers.

On a recent Thursday morning, she was driving along streets dotted with scooters and horse-and-buggies, answering calls from Amish people with ailments ranging from a persistent cough to anxiety or depression. After visiting their homes and doing the initial intake, she would set up a video conference on her laptop with a nurse practitioner, who was able to make a diagnosis and write a prescription.

She could spot the Amish houses, she said, because they are painted white, as befitting the “Plain People,” as they call themselves. The family laundry usually flapped on a line in the yard.

Her first patient, Lorene, complained of congestion that kept her up at night. She was 30 years old and living at home with four of her seven siblings. Amish children live with their parents until they marry, she said.

Lorene’s mother, who had called Ms. Truckey, stood by. All her children have been vaccinated, she said. Within the community, “there’s a lot that do, and there’s a lot that don’t,” she said. “It’s each individual choice.”

The nurse practitioner detected a brewing sinus infection, and Lorene’s mother handed over a check for $140. (Most patients asked to be identified by first names or to be anonymous to protect their privacy.)

The next patient, Rosanna, was covered in an itchy red rash — not measles. She had vaccinated all six of her children.

“I didn’t want my children to get measles and suffer,” she said. “I heard how sick they can get.”

But they did not get the Covid vaccine. “Some people have their doubts,” she said.

The evidence that Rosanna might be too busy for doctor’s appointments was everywhere: a pile of freshly dug potatoes on a table, tomatoes ripening on the porch, an ancient Maytag washing machine with a hand-wringer. She does laundry every day but Sunday.

At the Hickory Grove School, an Amish school, a teacher in her early 20s came out barefoot to chat. She was vaccinated as a child, she said, and so was her mother. There was no requirement for the students to be vaccinated in order to enroll in the school, unlike in a public school, she said.

Apart from the usual head colds, none of the 26 students in the school have been sick, she said. The children could be heard inside the school singing old-timey songs — “I’ll Fly Away” and “This Land Is Your Land.”

The Amish housewives, for the most part, seemed distant from the wars over whether vaccines caused more harm than good. They didn’t seem to know of Mr. Kennedy. They said they were largely sheltered from such debates because they did not read newspapers or watch television.

“Who?” said Nancy Miller, a 24-year-old mother of two young boys, when asked about Mr. Kennedy. She said she got her news primarily by word of mouth. (Miller is a common name among the Geauga County Amish.)

She and her husband decided to vaccinate their boys when measles “started getting around,” she said. Her husband had been vaccinated as a child. She could not be vaccinated because she was pregnant.

For Emma Miller, whose family were among the first to get measles in their community, it was a difficult summer.

Her husband, being immunized, had encouraged her to get early childhood shots for her children, who are 9 months to 17 years old. But until last summer, she had never heard of anyone having measles, so it did not seem like a priority, she said.

But being sick with measles had been grueling, and the experience had motivated her to get the children their shots.

“We’re getting them all,” she said.

ARTICLE

Court Tosses Sentence After A.I. Video of Victim ‘Forgiving’ His Killer Is Played
An appellate court in Arizona threw out the prison sentence of a man convicted of manslaughter after an A.I.-generated video of his victim was played at a trial.
By Adeel Hassan
Published 2026-10-04 20:31 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/us/manslaughter-conviction-overturned-ai-video-statement.html

Oct. 5: This article was updated after publication to include a statement from Stacey Wales.

An appeals court in Arizona on Wednesday threw out the prison sentence of a man convicted of manslaughter after a video created by artificial intelligence depicting the victim forgiving his killer was played in court.

The three-judge panel reaffirmed the conviction of Gabriel Horcasitas, 55, who had been sentenced to 10.5 years in prison, but said that he must be resentenced in the 2021 road-rage shooting death of Christopher Pelkey, 37.

The judges concluded that the sentencing judge committed a “fundamental error” by allowing and relying on an A.I. video that generated a likeness of Mr. Pelkey’s voice and appearance.

The appeals court found the video did not “reflect actual events” while presenting statements in the footage as if they were coming directly from the victim.

The appeals court noted the use of the A.I.-generated video posed a novel legal issue and that no prior Arizona case had addressed the admissibility of such a depiction of a victim during sentencing.

The video was used with victim-impact statements made by members of Mr. Pelkey’s family and friends in the courtroom during the sentencing of Mr. Horcasitas last year.

At the sentencing, Mr. Pelkey’s older sister, Stacey Wales, presented the A.I. video depicting Mr. Pelkey addressing Mr. Horcasitas.

“I believe in forgiveness and in God who forgives,” the video said.

The video also portrayed Mr. Pelkey as addressing the court, saying, “This here is a true representation of who I was.”

The sentencing judge, Todd F. Lang of Maricopa County Superior Court, praised the video, saying, “I loved that A.I.” He called it “genuine” and noted that the victim was allowed to “speak from his heart.”

However, he then imposed the maximum sentence, which was more than the nine years that prosecutors had sought.

Critics have argued that the introduction of A.I. in legal proceedings can open the door to manipulation and deception, compounding the already emotional process of giving victim-impact statements.

The appeals court held that a victim’s right to speak cannot trample a defendant’s right to be sentenced based on accurate and reliable information.

The video “erases the interpretive distance between the family’s belief about what the victim would have said and the victim’s own voice and opinions,” the judges wrote.

They decided that the reliance on the video made the sentencing procedure fundamentally unfair.

A lawyer for Mr. Pelkey did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Sunday. Kristen Reller, a lawyer for Mr. Horcasitas, said on Monday that she could not comment on the decision because the case was still active.

Ms. Wales was preparing her own victim-impact statement for two years, she told The New York Times last year, but believed that it was missing a critical element.

“I kept hearing what Chris would say,” she told The Times.

Ms. Wales said that her husband and the couple’s longtime business partner had used A.I. to help corporate clients with presentations, including one featuring the likeness of a company’s chief executive who had died years ago.

With the help of her husband and business partner, she took Mr. Pelkey’s voice from a YouTube video of him speaking after completing treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder at a facility for veterans, she said.

For his face and torso, they used a poster of Mr. Pelkey from a funeral service, digitally trimming his thick beard, removing his glasses and editing out a logo from his cap, she said.

Ms. Wales said that she had written the script that was read by her brother’s A.I. likeness.

“Nobody lied or attempted to deceive the court into believing Chris was alive or had recorded the video before he died,” she wrote in an email late on Sunday. “Everyone that reached out to me that saw it that knew Chris emphatically agreed and affirmed the message in the A.I. video is what Chris believed and could hear him saying in real life.

Ms. Wales added that she disagreed with the ruling.

“The appellate court drew an arbitrary line between media formats,” she wrote. “Families routinely play slide shows, display collages, recite hypothetical conversations, or read poetry to convey their grief.”

She compared the inclusion of A.I. video with the first use of photographs in courts.

“It took 15 years of landmark cases around the 1860s before photography was widely accepted in courts.”

On Nov. 13, 2021, Mr. Pelkey was stopped at a red light in Chandler, a Phoenix suburb, when Mr. Horcasitas pulled up behind him and honked.

That caused Mr. Pelkey to leave his vehicle and approach Mr. Horcasitas’s car and gesture with his arms as if to say, “What the heck?” according to a probable cause statement.

Mr. Horcasitas then fatally shot Mr. Pelkey in the chest.

The case will be returned to Maricopa County Superior Court for a new sentencing hearing, without the A.I.-generated video of Mr. Pelkey giving his statement.

Neil Vigdor contributed reporting, and Georgia Gee contributed research.

ARTICLE

What to Know About the Medical Plane That Went Missing Near Nantucket
A Gulfstream G100 carrying six people was flying from Bermuda to Boston when it lost contact near the Massachusetts island. A search for survivors has ended.
By Bernard Mokam and Georgia Gee
Published 2026-10-04 17:47 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/us/missing-medical-plane-nantucket-what-to-know.html

A medical transport plane lost contact near Nantucket, off the coast Massachusetts, in the early hours of Oct. 3, a Saturday. It prompted a federal and state search to find the aircraft and the six people who were on board that lasted nearly two days.

A debris field was located hours after the plane went missing.

The plane, a Gulfstream G100, lost communication with the Federal Aviation Administration just after 1 a.m. Eastern time. It was traveling from Bermuda, the British territory off the coast of North Carolina, to Boston.

There were four Canadian citizens and two Bermudian nationals on board.

Here’s what we know:

What Happened

The plane took off from Bermuda’s lone airport, on St. David’s Island, at 11:41 p.m. Eastern time on Friday, according to data from the website FlightAware.

Flight data shows that the air ambulance was flying consistently at an altitude of 24,000 feet before it plummeted several thousand feet around 1:05 a.m.

The F.A.A. lost contact with the plane and issued an alert around 1:20 a.m., activating search operations from the Coast Guard, the Massachusetts authorities and the New York Air National Guard.

The missing plane was operated by an Ontario-based medical evacuation company, Latitude Air Ambulance, which flies people to hospitals and offers repatriation services, according to its website.

On board the plane were two Canadian pilots, two Canadian medical staff members and two Bermuda nationals. All are still unaccounted for.

The pilots were reportedly trying to declare an emergency before it lost contact, said Preston Harimon, a spokesman for Nantucket Memorial Airport.

The Search

A continuous search for the six people traveling on the plane ended at sunset on Sunday, the Coast Guard said in a post on X. The six have not been publicly identified.

An interagency effort canvassed more than 2,800 square miles.

“This is a large and demanding search area,” Rear Adm. Matt Lake of the Coast Guard said on Sunday morning.

Rescue teams used fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters in the search. The Coast Guard also worked with Massachusetts authorities to use an aircraft equipped with sonar to help with the search.

Crews located a debris field about 20 miles south of Nantucket.The authorities did not specify what they recovered in the crash area.

The depth of the water in the area was approximately 80 to 90 feet, Admiral Lake said.

Cause for Concern

Experts agreed that the plane’s reported rate of descent was unusual and concerning.

According to data from FlightAware, the plane was flying consistently at an altitude of 24,000 feet before it rapidly descended 13,000 feet at around 1:05 a.m.

Brad Wheeler, a retired commercial pilot who flew for nearly 40 years and has flown between New York and Bermuda, said the maneuver indicated a “significant problem.”

Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general for the Transportation Department, said that the speed adjustment just before the plane’s descent showed the situation had gone awry.

“They were responding to something,” she said.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

Some Democrats, Scarred by 2024, Take a Harder Line on Trans Athletes
Democrats competing in historically conservative territory in the midterms are more aggressively responding to Republican attacks casting them as extreme.
By Tim Balk
Published 2026-10-04 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/us/politics/democrats-trans-athletes-midterms.html

In Ohio, a longtime Democratic congresswoman in a tough race, Marcy Kaptur, is running an ad in which she says she thinks “boys should not play in girls’ sports” and that she is focused on “making your life more affordable.”

In North Carolina, a vulnerable Democratic congressman, Don Davis, has released a commercial that shows him stalking a football field and saying that there are “real concerns about fairness and safety” in youth sports and that there “should always be a safe and fair space for women and girls in sports.”

And in several of the country’s most competitive congressional battlegrounds, a leading progressive super PAC is running ads describing Republicans as “obsessed” with transgender people and distracted from rising prices.

As the midterm election approaches, some Democrats in battleground races are moving to respond to Republican attacks casting them as extreme on transgender issues. In some cases, Democrats have reacted by accusing Republicans of being out of touch with voters’ economic concerns, or desperate to change the subject. In others, Democrats have voiced their opposition to transgender female athletes participating in girls’ and women’s sports. At times, their opposition has drawn criticism from other Democrats.

The strategies show how the party has shifted on the issue since the last nationwide election — a pivot that has played out in various ways since early 2025, when Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat from deep-blue California considering a run for president, suggested that the participation of transgender athletes in women’s sports was “deeply unfair.”

Democrats remain divided on the issue. Many of the party’s candidates are wary of either angering the base by taking a position that would limit transgender rights, or taking a position at odds with most voters, who polls show overwhelmingly agree with Republicans on the issue of transgender athletes’ participation in women’s sports.

But a number of Democrats are trying to actively parry Republican attacks, which haunted them in 2024, when Kamala Harris largely elected not to address a torrent of ads from Donald J. Trump that declared: “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.” Democratic strategists judged the ads to have been highly effective.

In the midterms, Republicans have again put the issue at the center of their message, part of a broader effort to cast Democrats as outside the mainstream. One ad, targeting Mr. Davis, said that the congressman was “fighting for they/them, not us.”

This time, Democrats are not letting the attacks go unanswered.

“For the first time ever, Democrats are strongly on offense on this,” said Christina Freundlich, a Democratic strategist. She added that, while approaches varied across the country, Democrats were broadly focusing on “clarifying the record — but then moving onto groceries.”

Republicans are still directing far more attention and resources to the issue. AdImpact, a media tracking firm, said on Friday that it had observed more than eight times as much Republican spending as Democratic spending on midterm ads focused on L.G.B.T.Q. and transgender issues. Mr. Trump, in a video about the midterms released on Saturday, said that “We’re not going back to transgender for everybody.”

But Republicans have been unable to move the topic to the center of voters’ attention. A CNN poll last month found that “policies regarding gender identity and trans people” did not make the top 10 issues that were most important to voters. (The issue ranked last out of 11 that CNN tested.) A Supreme Court decision in July upholding restrictions on transgender female athletes prompted a flurry of celebratory statements from Republicans, but scant expressions of disappointment from leading Democrats, depriving the G.O.P. of a chance to highlight a contrast.

“Democrats have figured out how to navigate this,” said C. Stewart Verdery Jr., a Republican consultant, though he added that the issue had not fully lost its salience, pointing to polling showing that roughly 80 percent of Americans opposed allowing transgender athletes to participate in women’s sports.

At a moment when Democrats have advantages on many of the other core issues animating the midterms, Republicans have seized on the topic as a way to put Democrats on the defensive. They have framed the issue as one of basic fairness, and say that Democrats want to ignore it.

In some of the country’s most high-profile races, Democrats have sought to take center-ground positions. When Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate nominee in Iowa, said on the day of the primary that her Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, was “extreme on gender ideology,” his campaign rushed to release a statement saying that he did not believe that “males should be playing female sports.”

In Texas, the Democratic Senate nominee, James Talarico, who has faced a drumbeat of Republican attacks over his past support for allowing transgender athletes in girls’ sports, told Fox News in September: “I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness.”

The pivot has been sharpest among Democrats trying to compete in historically Republican territory — like Iowa, Texas or Mr. Davis’s district, a freshly gerrymandered swath of North Carolina that Mr. Trump won by nearly 12 percentage points in 2024.

In Ohio, Ms. Kaptur, a 22nd-term Toledo Democrat, faced local Democratic backlash over the ad in which she says that “boys should not play in girls’ sports.”

“We wanted her to take it down,” said Schuyler Beckwith, the chair of the Democratic Party in Lucas County, which includes Toledo.

Ms. Beckwith said that Ms. Kaptur was “stooping to the level” of Republicans’ “disturbing” rhetoric on the issue. Still, she added that Ms. Kaptur was in a “really tough race” and that she remained focused on helping the congresswoman’s re-election effort.

(On Saturday night, the Republican challenging Ms. Kaptur, Derek Merrin, assailed Ms. Kaptur over the issue at a rally with Mr. Trump, saying she was running from her record. A spokeswoman for Ms. Kaptur, Kylie Blitzer, said in a statement that Mr. Merrin was “desperate to change the subject” and that politicians should not set the rules for girls’ sports.)

In bluer areas, Democratic voters have seemed less forgiving. Representative Seth Moulton, a Democrat who said after the 2024 election that he did not want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete,” lost last month by 30 points in a primary against Senator Edward J. Markey. The senator focused heavily on the issue, accusing his challenger of throwing transgender children “under the bus.”

The Transgender Freedom Alliance, a research group advising Democratic candidates, has both urged candidates to respond to the attacks and frowned on the idea of Democrats fully embracing Republicans’ positions on the issue. The group says its research has found that the most effective Democratic answer is to argue that Republicans are fixating on transgender issues at the expense of economic ones.

Adrienne Kimmell, who is leading the group’s research, said Democrats did not need to say that “boys should not play in girls’ sports.”

“It’s just not necessary,” Ms. Kimmell said.

She said she favored the approach of former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, a Democrat running to return to the chamber, who has run an ad featuring a voter who asks, “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?” Another speaker in the ad points to existing restrictions in Ohio on minors seeking gender transitions, and a third blames Mr. Brown’s opponent for rising grocery prices.

Kelley Robinson, the president of the Human Rights Campaign, a prominent L.G.B.T.Q. advocacy group, praised Mr. Brown’s ad. But in a Substack post last month, she expressed concern about the way many Democrats were handling the issue.

“Turning on a vulnerable community is not a winning political strategy,” Ms. Robinson wrote. Addressing Democrats, she added: “It legitimizes their side and weakens ours. And it harms transgender people.”

Representative Vicente Gonzalez, a Texas Democrat who has joined Republicans in voting to criminalize providing gender transition treatments to minors, said it would be “really foolish” for Democrats running in tough races to stake out progressive positions on the issue.

He ran an ad in 2024 in his swing district highlighting his position on gender transition procedures.

“I was the only one who addressed it head-on last cycle,” Mr. Gonzalez said. “I know some folks were critical of it. But the fact is it played well in my district.”

Evan Gorelick contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

In the last hours of Kristi Noem’s tenure as the homeland security secretary, her agency delivered a windfall to one of her political donors by buying five airplanes from the man’s firm at a substantial markup, documents show. The agency also paid the company $45 million apiece for a pair of 17-year-old Boeing 737 passenger planes, the documents show. The Times requested a copy of the contract that the Department of Homeland Security signed to purchase the planes, but the agency has not released it.

ARTICLE

Kristi Noem’s Agency Gave Her Donor a Lucrative Contract Just Before She Left
The Homeland Security Department signed a multi-million dollar agreement to buy five aircraft from a company owned by a political contributor of the secretary on her last day, documents show.
By Hamed Aleaziz, David A. Fahrenthold, Nicholas Nehamas, Tyler Pager and Niraj Chokshi
Published 2026-10-04 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/04/us/politics/kristi-noem-planes-donor.html

In the last hours of Kristi Noem’s tenure as the homeland security secretary, her agency delivered a windfall to one of her political donors by buying five airplanes from the man’s firm at a substantial markup, documents show.

The Department of Homeland Security agreed to pay the donor’s firm $108 million for a Boeing 737 airliner that had been converted into a massive private jet, complete with a stand-up bar, two bedrooms, marble showers and a table covered in manta ray skin.

The firm, Daedalus Aviation Corporation, had bought the same plane a few months earlier from a seller who had asked for less than $90 million, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times.

At the same time, the agency agreed to buy two smaller Gulfstream luxury jets at prices that also seemed to yield a hefty profit for the seller. Daedalus spent about $83 million to buy the pair, but resold them to the agency for $106 million, the documents show.

The agency also paid the company $45 million apiece for a pair of 17-year-old Boeing 737 passenger planes, the documents show. The Times spoke to six aviation experts, who said that those prices were millions of dollars higher than the typical market value for jets of that age.

President Trump announced on March 5 that he was firing Ms. Noem after a series of controversies, including questions about her agency’s awarding of contracts. But she remained in the position until her successor, Markwayne Mullin, was approved by the Senate and could take over on March 24.

After taking over, Mr. Mullin explored backing out of the deal, according to two White House officials, but feared a significant financial penalty. The officials said that Mr. Mullin consulted the White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, who shared his concerns about the possible financial ramifications and told him that he should not seek to block the purchase. He did not.

Mr. Mullin’s staff did not address specific questions about that account, but provided a statement saying that “these planes were purchased prior to Secretary Mullin’s arrival at D.H.S.”

The Times reported in August that the Department of Homeland Security bought 10 airplanes from Daedalus during Ms. Noem’s tenure, paying the firm $464 million. Those planes have already become a symbol of government waste. The agency said that they were needed urgently for deportation flights, but it lacked the crews to fly them. The department leased one of the planes to the F.B.I. and left the rest largely idle.

Through the newly acquired documents, The Times is now revealing fresh details about five of those planes: the three luxury jets and the two $45 million passenger planes. They were the most expensive planes the agency bought from Daedalus, and were purchased in a bunch on Ms. Noem’s last morning in office.

What the documents do not explain is why the agency went through with such a costly transaction just before the arrival of a new leader.

Ms. Noem, who is now a special envoy at the State Department, declined to answer specific questions about the sale or the prices that her agency had paid. Instead, she provided a statement identical to the one she shared with The Times in August.

“The purchase of these planes was not completed during Secretary Noem’s tenure at D.H.S.,” Ms. Noem’s statement said. “Funding for the 10-aircraft acquisition was made available during the leadership transition, and the acquisition process continued, and the purchase was finalized under Secretary Mullin’s leadership.”

Though the sale was approved under Ms. Noem, government documents show the planes did not formally change hands until April, when Mr. Mullin was in charge.

Daedalus’s chairman is William Walters, who gave $10,000 to Ms. Noem’s American Resolve political action committee in 2024. The company said Mr. Walters did not know the group was associated with Ms. Noem at the time, though the group existed to support her. Its website prominently displayed a photo of her face.

After Ms. Noem took office, her agency awarded more than $900 million in contracts to companies led by Mr. Walters. It hired his company Salus Worldwide Solutions to encourage immigrants to leave the country voluntarily, and to fly her and her aides on chartered jets. Then it gave Daedalus a no-bid contract to procure planes for deportation flights, under an arrangement in which the company could buy planes from others and resell them to the government, in essence as a middleman.

In a statement, the firm defended its prices, saying they reflected a market with a limited supply of suitable planes.

“Daedalus Aviation is proud to have delivered aircraft of the highest available value under very tight time constraints in an incredibly competitive market for aircraft acquisition,” the firm said.

Asked about the account of Mr. Mullin seeking advice about whether to follow through with the sale, the firm said that it believed the contract was already final when Mr. Mullin took office.

The Times requested a copy of the contract that the Department of Homeland Security signed to purchase the planes, but the agency has not released it.

The Times also requested documents laying out the agency’s rationale for awarding Daedalus its no-bid contract. The law generally requires such documents to be made public, but the agency declined to do so in this case, saying that releasing the documents would “compromise national security or create other security risks.”

To assess whether the Department of Homeland Security got good value for its purchase, The Times talked to government officials and aviation industry experts familiar with the aircraft. Reporters also reviewed records detailing how the jets were sold and resold.

The records made clear that the purchase of the expensive luxury planes was one of the last acts of Ms. Noem’s turbulent 14-month tenure.

Mr. Trump said in early March that he would replace Ms. Noem, after she struggled to answer questions about a different set of contracts in which her agency had hired some of her political allies to work on a $200 million-plus ad campaign.

But Ms. Noem remained in office for 18 more days.

On March 24, Mr. Mullin was scheduled to take over the role in the early afternoon. Ms. Noem was in Guyana that day, starting her work as a special envoy.

Late that morning, with Ms. Noem still in charge, the department approved the significant change to its contract with Daedalus.

Previously, the agency had purchased only aging Boeing airliners from the company, in line with its mission of finding aircraft for flying deportees en masse. It had paid the firm between $17.6 million and $35 million each to buy five planes that were between 17 and 23 years old, the documents reviewed by The Times show.

But under the new agreement, the agency contracted to buy three luxury jets that Mr. Walters’ companies had been using to fly government officials.

One was the Boeing 737 with the manta ray skin table. The sale of that plane for $108 million was first reported by The Daily Beast.

The plane’s previous owners were Frank and Lorenzo Fertitta, brothers who live in Las Vegas and lead the Station Casinos chain. The brothers had put the jet on the market in early 2023 for $89 million, according to documents that Mr. Walters’ companies provided in response to questions from Democrats on the House Oversight Committee. The sales brochure promoted electronic bidets, a wine chiller and four televisions.

But the plane sat unsold for more than two years. In early 2025, its broker was still hawking it online for less than $90 million.

Daedalus bought the plane in September 2025. The Fertittas are prolific Republican donors, and their cousin Tilman Fertitta is Mr. Trump’s ambassador to Italy. They declined to say how much they had sold the plane for, citing a confidentiality clause in the deal.

While the Department of Homeland Security was paying to charter the plane for Ms. Noem’s travel — but did not own it — Daedalus repainted it the same red-white-and-blue color scheme as Mr. Trump’s redesigned Air Force One.

Ms. Noem had made clear that she supported buying the luxury plane and others. In testimony before a Senate committee on March 3, two days before Mr. Trump announced she would be replaced, she said that buying the planes would save taxpayers money by reducing the department’s reliance on chartered aircraft. She implied the planes could have dual purposes.

“There are aircraft being purchased that will be utilized for executive air travel and for deportations,” Ms. Noem said.

At the time, the department was already paying another vendor to deport immigrants on a network of chartered planes. The agency did sometimes use smaller planes like the Gulfstream jets.

In the hearing, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, Democrat of Rhode Island, pressed Ms. Noem about the luxury 737. Would a plane like that really be used for deportations?

“In the past, we have used jets of this size, in this configuration, for deportations,” Ms. Noem said. She added that she thought the plane was being refurbished to remove a bedroom.

Daedalus said that after the department purchased the plane, the government paid to replace one of the two bedrooms with a conference room. The agency left the rest of the plane’s interior, including the bar and manta ray skin table, in place, the company said.

On March 24, the Department of Homeland Security also agreed to buy the two 10-year-old Gulfstream jets, which both seat about 14 people.

Daedalus had bought one last December for $41 million, and another — with a longer range — in January for $41.8 million, both roughly in line with the market prices for planes of that age, according to records kept by Aircraft Post, a market intelligence firm that gets reports from aircraft brokers. A representative for the cheaper of the two planes also confirmed the sale price.

The records obtained by The Times indicate that the Department of Homeland Security then paid $53 million for each — a markup of more than $11 million per aircraft.

Among the five planes in the March 24 purchase were the two Boeing 737 airliners. Like the airliners it had previously bought from the firm, they were more than 17 years old, and had been used by Southwest Airlines and the low-cost carrier Avelo Airlines.

But this time, the department paid much more than it had for similar planes: $45 million for each.

Daedalus declined to answer specific questions about the prices it charged for those planes, or what it had paid to purchase them. The planes’ previous owners declined to comment. The Times was unable to ascertain what Daedalus paid for them.

The Times talked to a half-dozen experts on the valuation of aircraft, who said the prices appeared to be far higher than market rate. They estimated that jets of this make, model and age typically sell for anywhere from $15 million for a modestly maintained plane to $30 million for one in unusually good condition.

Prices can rise with included extras, like maintenance or spare parts. But even then, experts said it would be difficult to imagine an airline paying $45 million for a plane of this type.

“I hope they came with buckets of caviar each, otherwise it doesn’t make a whole lot of sense,” said Richard Aboulafia, a managing director at AeroDynamic Advisory, an aerospace consulting firm. “This does not resemble any aspect of an airline marketplace.”

After buying the planes, the government needed a place to store them. It turned again to Mr. Walters.

Under Ms. Noem, the agency had hired his other company, Salus Worldwide, to maintain the first five planes it had purchased from Daedalus. Now, under Mr. Mullin, the agency continued that arrangement, and put the new planes in that company’s care as well. Contracting records show that the department paid the company more than $2 million in both May and June.

In August, the agency hired a contractor unconnected to Mr. Walters, Eastern Air Express, to take over caring for most of the planes. The contract does not cover the 737 luxury jet. The Department of Homeland Security has sought to transfer it to the Pentagon, but a spokesperson there said no agreement had been signed.

Department of Homeland Security officials now say that four of the 737 airliners will not be used for deportation flights, but rather will be used to fly government leaders and members of Congress on overseas trips.

The agency declined to say when, if ever, one of the 10 would be used for a deportation flight.

Julie Tate and Andrea Fuller contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

When President Trump decided in his first term to host the annual Group of 7 summit of world leaders at his own private golf club in Miami, the act of self-dealing was so astonishing that it incited an uproar among fellow Republicans, forcing him to scrap the idea. Now in his second term seven years later, Mr. Trump has decided to host the Group of 20 annual summit of world leaders at his private golf club in Miami in December — and this time the plan has generated practically no protest.
