ARTICLE

Mayors Are Filming Videos, Mamdani Style, With Varying Degrees of Cringe
The growing use of walk-and-talk social videos can be traced to Zohran Mamdani’s successful campaign for mayor of New York City. But not all candidates are naturals on camera.
By Julie Bosman
Published 2026-10-05 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/us/mayors-tiktok-video-instagram-mamdani.html

Susana Mendoza, the Illinois state comptroller and a candidate for mayor of Chicago, was not going to let the crummy weather get in her way. She had videos to shoot.

Sheltered on a drizzly recent afternoon under the overhang of a building along the Chicago River, Ms. Mendoza, in a black suit, high heels and her signature updo, faced a cellphone held aloft by a staffer — then flubbed her line.

“I’m the only candidate for mayor with the financial management experience and backbone to manage this crisis,” she said confidently, pointing at the camera as she walked.

Tackle the crisis, an aide corrected. Ms. Mendoza clapped her hands, then jogged in reverse to try the shot once more.

“This is how it works,” she said cheerfully.

And this is how mayors and mayoral hopefuls are talking to constituents these days: with snappy, walk-and-talk, make-policy-personal videos that reach potential voters on TikTok or Instagram.

The videos’ growing popularity can be traced to New York City and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a digital native who is widely seen as a master of the art. His campaign relied on viral social media posts to get his message out and help propel him to victory last year.

But not all candidates are as skilled on camera. Some videos are charming, real-life glimpses into the day of a mayor trying to solve problems. Others come across as stilted, overproduced or even awkward. Most candidates are learning as they go.

“They can be effective, but the person has to be genuinely likable or it doesn’t work,” said Aviva Bowen, a political strategist in Chicago. “They’re supposed to be raw and gritty and a peek behind the curtain.”

Last month, Mayor Brandon Johnson of Chicago publicized his re-election bid with a video of himself dancing, albeit stiffly, on a rooftop. Mayor Daniel Lurie of San Francisco took to video to warn residents that a mountain lion was spotted at the corner of 44th Avenue and Ulloa Street. Jacob Frey, the mayor of Minneapolis, recently showed off his between-the-legs dribble — and a few bricked jump shots — while telling residents about a basketball tournament returning to the city.

Good or bad, the videos are increasingly a staple in the day of an American mayor — or an aspiring one.

Campaign strategists say that the videos — which are also being adopted by governors, members of Congress and other elected officials — can be deceptively tricky to pull off. They are most compelling, the consensus goes, when they are candid, honest and shorter than 30 seconds. Success is measured in shares, views, likes and comments.

The videos can also help push an obscure candidate into the spotlight. In Seattle, Katie Wilson was running for mayor last year as a nearly unknown community organizer and socialist when she released a video of herself standing on a sidewalk holding an $8 slice of pizza and explaining how the cost was connected to the city’s housing crisis. Her campaign took off, and months later she was elected, unseating the incumbent, who had led Seattle since 2022.

Ms. Wilson’s videos worked because they leaned into her image as an awkward policy nerd who isn’t natural on camera, said Sandeep Kaushik, a Democratic political strategist in Seattle who was not involved with her campaign.

“They come across as really honest and authentic,” Mr. Kaushik said. “And they showed you who she is as a person. They weren’t formal or antiseptic or cerebral in the way most campaign communications are.”

Annie Gabillet, the deputy communications director who oversees digital work for Mayor Lurie in San Francisco, said that his videos are an outgrowth of the early days of his campaign. Mr. Lurie had never run for office before and was fighting for name recognition. So he began making candid, in-the-moment videos, sometimes dropping in on small businesses or art galleries, places around the city that he loved.

“He didn’t set out to become an influencer, so as he’s filmed more videos himself, it’s become more natural, as if he’s just talking to San Franciscans,” she said.

Mr. Lurie’s Instagram audience is largely San Francisco-based, and he relies on Instagram reels to get his messages out. Some of his highest-performing videos this year have been snapshots of life in the city: a new Jollibee opening on Market Street, a how-to on cleaning storm drains, a scene of Mr. Lurie stopping by a salsa dancing event in Union Square.

But mayors have to be careful to exude not just authenticity, but competence, as Mayor Karen Bass of Los Angeles learned the hard way.

After Mr. Mamdani touted his administration’s pothole-filling prowess, a Los Angeles resident posted a video asking Ms. Bass to fill a hole on her street. Ms. Bass responded with her own video — explaining why the pothole could not be addressed right away.

Social media mockery ensued. Ms. Bass followed up the next day with a video showing the fixed pothole.

“Sometimes content lands differently than you intended,” said Leslie Gamboni, senior director of digital communications for Ms. Bass, adding that the reaction didn’t necessarily make the video a failure. “We did see that the video reached a lot of people, and hopefully people came away understanding more about 311 and how to report an issue.”

As next year’s mayoral election in Chicago begins to heat up, mayoral hopefuls are elbowing each other for attention in real life — and on Instagram reels.

Alexi Giannoulias, the Illinois secretary of state and a mayoral candidate, has been making the rounds of block parties, concerts and food festivals and posting videos of his interactions with voters online.

Last month, Mr. Giannoulias shared videos of himself jumping into the Chicago River, speaking at an event celebrating Chinese heritage and downing tequila at the city’s Mexican Independence Day parade.

“Alexi believes it’s important to communicate directly to voters where they are, whether that’s knocking doors or short-form video on social media,” said Jordan Abudayyeh, a campaign spokeswoman.

Mayor Johnson, who is running for re-election, has hired social media influencers to make posts promoting his campaign, circumventing traditional media. “We hope to showcase the mayor in his element,” said Christian Perry, a campaign spokesman.

Ms. Mendoza is not on the air with television ads yet, but she drops new social videos regularly, sometimes filming several at once.

In September, as rain continued to threaten her shoot, Ms. Mendoza said that she sees the videos — which she said she had been posting long before Mr. Mamdani’s rise — as crucial to her nascent mayoral campaign, less than five months from the February election.

“When I bump into people in real life, more and more and more, they’re like, ‘Oh my gosh, I love your videos,’” she said. “They feel like they already know me. Then I get to seal the deal with them.”

Cynthia Silva contributed video research and editing.

Family of Epstein Victim Appears in Ad Targeting Republican

A Democrat running for Congress in a competitive Colorado district released an ad on Monday that features the family of Virginia Giuffre, one of the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s most prominent victims.

ARTICLE

Supreme Court to Hear Major Environmental Lawsuit
The justices will begin their new term with a landmark case about whether local governments can sue oil companies over damages caused by climate change.
By Abbie VanSickle
Published 2026-10-05 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/us/politics/supreme-court-climate-change-oil.html

Who should cover the costs of climate change?

That is the question underpinning the first case of the Supreme Court’s new term, a landmark dispute over whether state and local governments can seek to hold oil companies responsible for billions of dollars in costs from floods, droughts, wildfires and other climate-related disasters.

The case before the justices pits officials from Boulder, Colo., against two major oil companies — Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil. The Colorado officials contend that they should be able to proceed with a lawsuit arguing that the oil companies violated state law and seeking to hold them responsible for the costs of environmental damages. The companies, joined by the Trump administration, argue that such lawsuits are barred by federal law and the Constitution.

A decision is expected by the end of June or early July. Depending on its scope, the ruling could have significant implications for similar efforts to sue fossil fuel companies for billions of dollars in damages caused by climate change.

If the court sides with the companies and finds that such lawsuits are not allowed, it could doom dozens of other such cases by local and tribal governments percolating in lower courts throughout the country.

A decision for Boulder could clear the way for similar cases to move forward, potentially opening up oil companies to enormous financial liability.

Only eight of the nine justices are scheduled to take the bench for the argument. Last week, Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. announced he would recuse himself from the case.

He gave no reason in the recusal announcement, but he had faced pressure from environmental and court watchdog groups to step aside because he has publicly reported owning stock in two oil companies that are not parties to the case but could be affected by the outcome, ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. He had also gone on a luxury fishing trip with an investor in a company involved in the dispute.

In an interview after his announcement, Justice Alito told Bloomberg that he had taken “into account the particular arguments that were made on both sides here” and decided that recusal was “the prudent step.”

Under the court’s ethics code, justices can recuse at their own discretion. They typically step aside if their impartiality could be questioned, including because of a financial tie to a party or a close friend or family member who is involved.

If the justices were to split 4 to 4 in Justice Alito’s absence, a lower court decision to allow the Boulder suit to move ahead would stand. Such deadlocked decisions set no binding national precedent.

The legal fight began in April 2018, when the city and county of Boulder sued Exxon and Suncor, asserting that the companies should be required to share in the costs of climate change, including damages from more heat waves, wildfires, droughts and floods.

Boulder argued that local governments and taxpayers “cannot pay the full costs of all that is needed, nor should they.” The suit contended that the companies “knowingly and substantially” fueled the climate crisis by “producing, promoting and selling a substantial portion of the fossil fuels that are causing and exacerbating climate change.” It also claimed that the companies concealed and misrepresented the dangers of their products.

After a decision by the Colorado Supreme Court to allow the case to continue in state court, the oil companies asked the justices to intervene. The Trump administration joined them, a reversal of the Biden administration’s stance on the climate lawsuits.

The oil companies argued that the case should be heard in federal court, not state. Federal courts are often thought to be a more business-friendly venue.

The companies claim that federal laws regulating the environment pre-empt Boulder’s lawsuit and that because climate change is a global problem, it cannot be handled in state courts.

They are joined by the lawyers for the Trump administration, who argue that a ruling for Boulder could spur a raft of litigation, allowing “every locality in the country” to “sue essentially anyone in the world for contributing to global climate change.”

Boulder has pushed back on those arguments, saying in its briefs that its lawsuit is part of a tradition “since the Founding” to use state law to handle cases where the harm comes from outside the state, including in environmental cases.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

How the Midterms Could Complicate the Supreme Court’s New Term
Even before the justices start their new term on Monday, the court has spent the summer resolving fast-moving requests on election-related disputes.
By Ann E. Marimow and Abbie VanSickle
Published 2026-10-05 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/us/politics/supreme-court-midterms-elections-trump.html

At a public appearance this spring, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. insisted, as he regularly does, that members of the Supreme Court are not “political actors.”

Yet with the court’s new term beginning Monday, scarcely a month before the closely watched midterms, the court may be unable to avoid getting uncomfortably pulled into electoral politics.

With partisans on both sides primed for potential election challenges, lawsuits to settle hotly contested elections could end up before the court, potentially with the control of Congress at stake. They would land on top of an already packed docket of cases on culture war issues and President Trump’s agenda that were selected by the justices to be heard from the thousands of petitions they receive each year.

The result could be another consequential and controversial span on the bench for the justices, even as their public poll numbers have dipped and elected leaders and candidates, particularly in the insurgent wing of the Democratic Party, have called for an overhaul of the court.

The court “knows what an extraordinary politicized moment we are in,” said Jeffrey Rosen, a law professor at George Washington University Law School. For that reason, the justices would prefer not to be involved in lawsuits that would affect results or allow state officials to affect results.

But, he said, if the justices see a true post-election emergency, “it’s hard to imagine they wouldn’t intervene” if called on.

The court will hear oral arguments in about 60 cases, starting on Monday with a major environmental lawsuit, and continuing through late April. During that period, they will deliberate at private conferences, draft and exchange opinions and release the court’s rulings. The most closely divided decisions are typically announced on the final days of the term in late June or early July. But the justices also field emergency requests and issue quick-turn orders without a lengthy briefing period or hearing arguments.

The new term was foreshadowed by a busy summer for the court, which grappled with a series of emergency requests critical to the nation’s political system.

The justices blocked both President Trump’s plan to dramatically overhaul how Americans vote by mail in the upcoming election and three separate times stepped in to block Missouri from using a congressional map drawn to advantage Republicans. At the same time, they allowed the administration to deploy an online system combining citizenship information, Social Security numbers and other sensitive data about millions of Americans to help states hunt for supposedly ineligible voters.

In each case, the majority issued unsigned orders that academics and advocates said suggested that the justices were trying to avoid changing voting rules or creating confusion for state election officials ahead of November.

“There is a robust majority of the court that does not want to be the decision maker that’s going to be the one allowing the chaos to happen,” said Roman Martinez, a lawyer who argues frequently before the court and is a former law clerk to Chief Justice Roberts.

In the mail-ballot matter, election officials from both parties had cautioned that Mr. Trump’s mail-in ballot plan would be disruptive and confusing, potentially putting millions of votes at risk. In the Missouri case, the court warned of “electoral chaos” if the state were to change course so close to the election and use the GOP map, as pressed by Republican officials.

Even in the online database case, where the court sided with the Trump administration, the justices seemed to try to dampen the impact on the upcoming election. They noted that their own ruling could be limited by what’s known as a 90-day “quiet period” before elections that prevents elections officials from making broad changes to state rolls ahead of the vote.

Erin Murphy, another former law clerk to Chief Justice Roberts, said the court seemed to be sending the message: “Stop doing this to us because we really don’t want to be in this position.”

That posture could change after the election if there are disputes over vote counts or the certification of elections. There is already a flood of election-related litigation filed around the country by both parties and concerns about the possibility of voter intimidation and the seizure of ballots.

If the court were to get drawn into closely contested elections that could determine control of Congress, it would raise echoes of the post-presidential election period in December 2000. That was when the Supreme Court put a stop to a Florida recount in the election that sealed George W. Bush’s victory over the Democratic nominee, Al Gore.

The Supreme Court was likewise the final arbiter of Mr. Trump’s challenges in December 2020, rejecting post-election challenges involving the use of mail ballots in Pennsylvania and a Texas lawsuit seeking to throw out election results in four battleground states that President Trump lost.

“Everyone’s eyes are on the election,” said Cecillia Wang, national legal director at the American Civil Liberties Union, which is preparing for a possibly intense burst of post-election challenges.

Such challenges would pose a conundrum for the court, putting it at the heart of the deeply divided political landscape, even as polls show Americans increasingly disapprove of its work and worry the court is putting its thumb on the scale in partisan battles. Democrats particularly have grown to believe the court, with a 6-3 majority of Republican nominees, is too conservative, according to a new Gallup poll.

A poll conducted by Marquette Law School in September found that 57 percent of Americans, a sizable majority, now believe the justices are motivated mainly by politics rather than law. The percentage of those approving of the court dipped to 43 percent.

Those numbers were divided along party lines. Sixty percent of those surveyed said the court has ruled in Mr. Trump’s favor often or fairly often. Seventy-eight percent of Democrats said the court was going out of its way to avoid ruling against Mr. Trump.

In an interview with CBS News posted on Friday, Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr., who is one of the court’s most reliable votes in favor of the president’s agenda, insisted that the court “is not part of any political movement. And we are not attempting to further any political agenda.” He added: “We are trying to interpret the Constitution as best we can and apply it in the cases that come before us.”

The court’s poor showing in the polls coincides with a drumbeat of calls, particularly from Democrats, to change the structure of the Supreme Court should they win control of Congress next year. There is broad, bipartisan support for eliminating life tenure for justices and for enacting an enforcement mechanism for an essentially voluntary ethics code that the justices adopted in 2023, according to the Marquette poll. The public is more closely divided, however, on proposals to expand the number of seats on the high court.

Exacerbating the court’s unfavorable numbers, pollsters have indicated, could be its rulings against Mr. Trump and the anger those decisions have sparked from the president and his conservative allies. Mr. Trump has sharply criticized the court, particularly the three justices he nominated, who last term ruled against some of his signature policies, including tariffs and birthright citizenship.

The president said in an interview with Time magazine published last week that he regretted picking Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett M. Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett.

“I gave them the position of a lifetime,” he said, “and they voted against me often.”Major aspects of the administration’s agenda will once again be tested before the court. Notably, the justices will review the administration’s policy of deporting immigrants to countries where they have no ties and its practice of indefinitely detaining immigrants who crossed the border illegally years ago.

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, has also asked justices to clear the way for the administration to fully enforce its ban on transgender troops serving in the military and to make it easier for the president to install his allies as United States attorneys throughout the country.

And the justices have been asked to weigh in on Mr. Trump’s appeal of a $83 million jury award against him for defaming the writer E. Jean Carroll after she accused him of sexually assaulting her in the mid-1990s in a Manhattan department store. The court has already left in place a $5 million civil judgment against Mr. Trump after a jury found in 2023 that he had sexually abused and defamed Ms. Carroll.

Apart from Mr. Trump’s agenda, the court plans to hear a series of other consequential matters, including a blockbuster case dealing with gun control in December.

After years of ducking the question, the justices will consider whether state and local laws banning semiautomatic rifles violate the Constitution. The case deals with laws in Illinois and Connecticut but will likely determine the fate of similar laws throughout the country aimed at restricting military-style rifles.

The widespread availability of semiautomatic rifles, such as AR-15s, continues to be a deeply polarizing issue. Owned by millions of Americans, the rifles have also been used in high-profile mass shootings, including in the Sandy Hook and Uvalde elementary school massacres.

The legal battle over assault weapons bans is the latest Second Amendment fight to come to the court. Since 2008, when the justices declared an individual right to own a gun apart from military service, they have contended with how to evaluate the validity of gun restrictions.

Religious rights, particularly for Christians, have also been on a winning streak at the court and will be back on the docket this year.

In November, the court will hear a case brought by the Archdiocese of Denver challenging Colorado rules that require preschools that receive public funding to accept the children of gay and transgender parents.

Accepting those students would be at odds with the church’s teachings and mission, said the archdiocese and two Catholic schools. But lower courts upheld Colorado’s law, saying the state could require participating schools to abide by anti-discrimination rules, as long as the requirements were applied to schools across-the-board and without regard to religion.

The justices have also been asked to hear a case from Texas challenging a state law that requires every public school classroom to display a Protestant version of the Ten Commandments. Three other states — Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana — have recently enacted similar laws.

Facing Backlash, Trump Says His Super PAC Will Pay for Taxpayer-Funded Ads
The president said that his PAC, MAGA, Inc., would pay for TV ads promoting him that had been paid for with taxpayer money.
By Shane Goldmacher, Theodore Schleifer and Maggie Haberman
Published 2026-10-05 22:54 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/us/politics/trump-taxpayer-funded-ads-pac.html

President Trump reversed course on Monday and announced that his super PAC would now pay for the television ads promoting him that have been airing nationwide at taxpayer expense.

In a post on his social media platform, Mr. Trump wrote, “I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.”

More than $10 million in taxpayer-funded ads have run since September, according to AdImpact, the ad-tracking service. The ads, which are running on cable and network television, were paid for through a $20 million contract that used funds from the Department of Homeland Security.

Democrats — and some Republicans — have criticized the ads as a possible violation of federal laws for using taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes.” The ads were broadcast in the heat of the campaign for the midterms, as Republicans are trying to hold control of Congress. At least one of the ads featured footage that originally had appeared in a 2024 Trump campaign video.

The White House had defended the ads as simply public service announcements. But the use of material that had originated in a campaign provided further fuel to critics of the ads.

There were four different ads and each featured an unusual disclaimer: “Paid for by the U.S. government.”

One of them featured images of Mr. Trump as the song “Love Me” by Christian Berishaj played. The artist, who performs as JMSN, has complained about the use of his song.

The New York Times wrote over the weekend that Mr. Trump had personally instructed his budget director to use taxpayer money for TV ads. Federal records show that U.S. Customs and Border Protection, which falls under the Department of Homeland Security, awarded a contract to LMD, a Maryland marketing firm, on Sept. 20.

Mr. Trump referred to the backlash in his post.

“The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money,” he wrote, defending them as “a rather standard thing to do.”

The White House did not immediately respond to an email for comment or how the president’s super PAC would pay for the ads. A spokesman for MAGA Inc. did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Trump has rarely acknowledged bowing to popular pressure in his second term.

Mr. Trump’s claim in his social media post that he would pay for the ads “myself” through his super PAC is likely to add fodder to another formal complaint against the president.

A campaign watchdog group, the Campaign Legal Center, accused Mr. Trump of violating federal election laws by directing his super PAC in a complaint to the Federal Election Commission because of his previous claims to control the super PAC.

Mr. Trump has referred to the super PAC’s funds as “my money that I control” in the past.

Federal law bars federal office holders from directing spending decisions for a political organization with no contribution limits, such as a super PAC.

Alex Pfeiffer, a spokesman for the super PAC, MAGA Inc., said at the time, “MAGA Inc. fully complies with the law.”

Mr. Trump’s political committee can certainly afford to pay for the ads: MAGA Inc. entered September with about $415 million on hand. MAGA Inc. and two super PACs affiliated with it have since set aside about $194 million for advertising ahead of November, according to AdImpact data.

Mr. Trump had defended the use of taxpayer money for the spots just five days earlier. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, the president said: “If somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money.”

“But these are ads for the country,” he said. “You have to understand. I’m not promoting a candidate. I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office. I’m promoting the country.”

Who’s Winning the Race for Congress?
It’s Oct. 5 — 29 days away from the midterms. Here’s the state of play.
By Lisa Lerer and Shane Goldmacher
Published 2026-10-05 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/us/politics/whos-winning-the-race-for-congress.html

“It’s a five-alarm fire.” A “slow moving car crash.” Republicans are “hemorrhaging” and “should brace for losing everything.”

Republicans have been full of doom in recent days, as they confront the reality that their political prospects do not seem to be improving. And their candidates are rapidly running out of time for a turnaround.

With less than 30 days before the election, Democrats are reaching deeper into traditionally conservative areas while Republicans find themselves fighting to save their incumbents.

Decisions last week by Republicans to pull money out of the North Carolina Senate race and divert resources to Kansas demonstrated the depth of their party’s challenge, as new New York Times/Siena University polls found strength for Democrats in five reliably Republican states that could determine control of the chamber.

The first events in what President Trump has promised will be a series of midterm appearances — all in deep red states — underscored the anxiety among Republicans that even some of their most loyal voters could stay home from the polls in November.

And a series of economic indicators released last week, showing job growth slowing, mortgage rates rising and unemployment climbing, only reinforced the difficulties of the national environment for Republicans.

To be sure, a wave of red cash could save Republican seats. But it’s also clear that Democrats are playing hard on their turf.

The Battle for the Senate

Republicans have made some significant moves on the Senate map.

The Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate super PAC, pulled money from North Carolina, a sign that some top party strategists doubt that Michael Whatley can defeat former Governor Roy Cooper in the perennial battleground state. Even Trump, who tapped Whatley, the former Republican National Committee chairman, to run for the seat, said he was “worried about him” on Friday before leaving for his campaign swing.

The group made its first investment in Kansas, where Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican seeking a second term, appears increasingly embattled. The more than $10 million in ad reservations comes as both sides increasingly view Kansas as a late-breaking battleground. Democrats are considering spending there to support Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor and Democratic challenger.

In Texas, Republican spending smashed records as the party frantically tried to boost Ken Paxton, the scandal-tarred attorney general running for Senate. This week, Trump will host a rally in San Antonio — his second trip to Texas in two weeks, and an indication of the party’s worry about a seat it has held since 1961.

The Race for the House

The House map keeps growing and growing for Democrats.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added eight districts to its list of seats to flip on Friday, pushing the total number of competitive districts for the party to 66. That’s nearly double the number the party ended the 2024 cycle with, the committee said.

The committee expanded its electoral frontier deeper into Republican areas, adding races that included seats in rural Virginia, Oklahoma and a Houston-area district that was redrawn to favor Republicans. All eight seats were considered safely Republican when the midterm campaign began in earnest at the start of the year.

The expansion comes a week after The Cook Political Report shifted 15 races toward Democrats, creating three new “tossup” districts, in conservative swaths of North Carolina, Texas and Florida.

Inside the Air Wars

The campaign arm of House Democrats is planning to spend $13 million in the coming week in 35 House districts, according to an ad-buy plan shared with The New York Times.

The spending includes some new districts, most notably Pennsylvania’s First Congressional District, a seat held by Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, one of the only Republicans seeking re-election in a seat that President Trump lost in 2024. The other new districts are California’s 48th, Michigan’s Fourth and Seventh, and New York’s 19th.

Of the races the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is spending in, most are on offense. The party is spending on 21 seats currently held by Republicans and 14 held by Democrats.

One Key Metric

The average 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage, the most popular home loan in the United States, rose to 7.28 percent, according to the mortgage financing giant Freddie Mac. That’s the highest since November 2023.

Top Talker

Strategists on both sides of the aisle were buzzing after a report on Thursday that Paxton told a group of conservative donors and lobbyists that Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas had hurt him politically.

“Do you feel like he’s a little bit of a drag?” Paxton is heard being asked in an audio recording obtained by The New York Times.

Paxton responded: “So to be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”

What captivated Republicans about the report was simple: Paxton, a longtime Trump loyalist, said aloud what they were all whispering but didn’t dare say for fear of provoking the president.

Paxton just had the misfortune of being caught on tape.

One Poll Number

84 percent.

That’s the percentage of independent voters who disapprove of Trump’s handling of gas prices, according to the NYT/Siena poll released on Saturday — a figure that has alarmed Republicans.

On the Ground

Hispanic voters along the border are voicing frustration with the president’s approach to immigration and the economy, raising questions about whether Republicans could lose districts in South Texas that the party redrew to tilt in their favor.

Ariel Salinas, the owner of a construction company in McAllen, Texas, blamed the president’s immigration crackdown for his inability to reliably find laborers for his work crews.

“Years ago, you put a fence up because people were stealing stuff. Now you put the fence up because ICE is stealing the workers. There was even a fence shortage in the summer. It caught all of us off guard,” he said.

Quotes of the Week

“It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president. At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing.” — Vice President JD Vance

“In my experience, people engage in political bomb-throwing when they’re feeling insecure. So he’s welcome to make whatever comments he likes. I’m going to keep focusing on the midterms and helping us win on Election Day in the next 30 days.” — Senator Ted Cruz

Vance and Cruz, two potential presidential candidates, engaged in a bit of early 2028 sniping last week, trading barbs about their midterm campaign schedules. Vance suggested that Cruz was more focused on laying the groundwork for a 2028 primary bid than helping Republicans win the coming midterm elections. Two days later, Cruz shot back, brushing off Vance’s jab.

SUMMARY

Before any criminal charges were filed, before any weapons were drawn, before anybody mentioned the president, a dog named Bob wanted to go to the park. So Mr. Mattai drove to his favorite dog park in Bainbridge Township, Ohio. Mr. Mattai entered the park again and told Mr. Mathews that he should be the one to leave.

ARTICLE

They Argued About Trump at a Dog Park. Then They Pulled Their Guns.
What happened between two dog owners one April afternoon in Ohio will soon be scrutinized by a judge and jury as both men grapple with the consequences.
By Jessica Contrera
Published 2026-10-05 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/us/trump-ohio-dog-park-shooting.html

Before any criminal charges were filed, before any weapons were drawn, before anybody mentioned the president, a dog named Bob wanted to go to the park.

Bob’s owner, David Mattai, had the week off from his job as a forklift mechanic. Mr. Mattai, 55, first tried taking Bob on a hiking trail, but the spaniel refused to walk. So Mr. Mattai drove to his favorite dog park in Bainbridge Township, Ohio.

At a picnic table inside the park that April afternoon was Emmanuel Mathews, 80, and his corgi, Frankie.

Mr. Mathews was retired from a career as a meat distributor, and on the days when his back wasn’t causing him problems he was a regular at the park. He had brought a copy of The Wall Street Journal with headlines that included “Trump Grapples With Fears on War.”

The events that unfolded over the next 20 minutes — pieced together from interviews, records and body camera footage — would be unusual, but hardly unthinkable in a country where political tensions so often combust. Two men, one Black and liberal, one white and conservative, would disagree about President Trump. Their disagreement would become an argument, then a screaming match and then, because both men had guns in their cars, a crime.

What happened at the dog park — and who is to blame — will soon be scrutinized by a judge and a jury, as both men face the possibility of time behind bars and grapple with the lifelong consequences of division turning violent.

Likely to take the stand in both cases is Jamie Jedlinsky, 70, the singular witness to what went down.

Mr. Jedlinsky’s mother had taught him that you didn’t have to tell people who you voted for, so he never did. If someone brought up politics, he would usually change the subject to birding. But on this day, Mr. Jedlinsky and his pit mix, Willow, had walked into the park and greeted Mr. Mathews, with whom he had become somewhat friendly over the years. When he noticed the newspaper in Mr. Mathews’s hands, he decided to gesture to the headline about the Iran war and say, “That sucks, don’t it.”

Mr. Mathews, who goes by Mike, disagreed. In his cardigan, he began to discuss his support for the president’s choices.

Mr. Mattai, who had arrived moments earlier in sweatpants, was listening. He considered himself a democratic socialist before it was trendy. He owned a collection of bumper stickers with messages such as “Trump Is a Felon” and “Hicks Don’t Mix With Politics.” In his solidly Republican patch of Northeast Ohio, he considered it his moral duty to “comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable.”

Mr. Mattai, who had struggled with alcoholism for most of his life, would later say he had been drinking that day.

He decided to butt in. “Trump is the worst president in history,” he said, to which Mr. Mathews replied, “Trump is the best president in history.”

The spat quickly grew in intensity and volume. At one point, Mr. Jedlinsky recalled, they were saying, “You shut up!” and “No, you shut up!”

“Just two guys, mad at themselves, mad at the world,” Mr. Jedlinsky said. “They both wanted to just yell at someone, and they ran into the perfect storm, where there’s somebody yelling back.”

Mr. Jedlinsky was relieved when the younger man finally heeded his advice to both of them to let it go. Mr. Mattai leashed Bob, returned to his Hyundai and began to drive toward the park’s exit. But then Bob started to whine.

“Man, you did want to stay at the park,” Mr. Mattai recalled telling his dog. He turned his car around.

Some of the specifics of what happened next remain in dispute. But Mr. Jedlinsky, Mr. Mattai and a lawyer for Mr. Mathews agree upon a certain set of facts. (Mr. Mathews declined to be interviewed.)

Mr. Mattai entered the park again and told Mr. Mathews that he should be the one to leave. Mr. Mathews began to move toward his Cadillac, which was adorned with a corgi sticker. When he made it to the other side of the fence, he turned around.

“Did your mother drop you on your head?” he asked.

“You talking about my mother?” Mr. Mattai responded. He reached across the fence and grabbed Mr. Mathews by his grayish white hair. Mr. Jedlinsky pushed them apart and told them both to go home. While the three men were putting their dogs in their cars, Mr. Jedlinsky heard Mr. Mattai say: “Oh you’ve got one? I’ve got one, too.”

Then Mr. Jedlinsky heard gunshots.

Mr. Mathews had a .45-caliber handgun in his car. He fired first; when he pulled the trigger a second time, no bullet came out. Mr. Mattai had a 9-millimeter pistol in his car. He fired back at least four rounds. The bullets sprayed across Mr. Mathews’s car and into his open window as Mr. Mathews drove away. They pierced his door frame and the driver’s seat, missing him by inches.

Mr. Jedlinsky crouched behind his wheel and called 911.

“It escalated,” he told the dispatcher.

When a police officer arrived, he found Mr. Mattai splayed on the pavement. There was a hole in his lower back where Mr. Mathews’s bullet had entered, and another in his abdomen where it had exited.

The passenger-side door of his Hyundai was open. Bob was in the front seat, unharmed, tongue out.

‘I Shot Him’

Mr. Mathews peeled out of the parking lot and drove toward the Bainbridge Township police station. In this area of Northeast Ohio, where the Cleveland suburbs begin to meet rural farmland, Mr. Mathews was familiar with law enforcement. Before he retired, his meat company had provided burgers and cutlets for police events.

He had made it about four minutes up the road when he saw a Bainbridge Township police cruiser, siren on, coming toward him. Mr. Mathews stopped his car and flashed his lights. The officer pulled over.

“You going to the shooting?” Mr. Mathews asked. “I was part of it.”

The officer, whose body camera was rolling throughout their interaction, confiscated Mr. Mathews’s handgun, patted him down and removed a piece of paper from the pocket of his cardigan.

“That was my list for the day,” Mr. Mathews told the officer. “This wasn’t on it.”

He quickly informed the officer of his local connections: the cops he knew, the poker game he used to play with the former police chief, and the fact that he happened to be living with the mother of the county’s top prosecutor. Before long, Mr. Mathews was telling his side of the story from the back of the police cruiser.

He lifted his handcuffed wrists to wipe tears from his eyes. There was a small cut on his cheek. He said the other man had not just grabbed his hair, but also head-butted him before they went to their cars.

He did not say who pulled a gun out first.

“I said, ‘I feel my life is in danger.’ I said that ’cause I know that’s what they say,” Mr. Mathews told the officer. “And he went around the side of his car and started coming at me, and I shot him.”

At the police station, he kept talking as the officer confiscated the cross around his neck, the Greek coin ring on his finger and the $890 in his wallet.

“That’s a bad thing I did, but it really wasn’t,” Mr. Mathews told the officer. “This guy had a gun in his hand.”

In the back of the police car and while being booked, he asked four times about the well-being of his dog, Frankie. He did not ask about the condition of the man he had shot.

‘We’ve Seen This Movie’

At the hospital, Mr. Mattai’s wife, Sally, couldn’t stop crying. The doctors had explained that her husband was in emergency surgery, and they couldn’t say for sure if he would make it through.

When he did, Mr. Mattai learned that the bullet had torn through his intestines and fractured his spine. He had a second surgery the next day.

It didn’t surprise his wife to learn how the confrontation at the dog park had started. It was politics, in part, that had brought her and Mr. Mattai together about a decade earlier, in a Facebook group where they shared memes.

Mr. Mattai had told her how he had immigrated from Guyana at 10, become an American citizen and joined the Marines. He worked as a paramedic in California until his alcohol addiction cost him his job. When the two met, Mr. Mattai had moved in with his father in New York and was trying to start over. He went to welding school.

When he moved to Ohio to be with Sally, they lived on nearly four acres in a rural area. They flew a Kamala Harris flag in 2024, but took it down the morning after the election. One of their neighbors, they said, kept up a cardboard cutout of Mr. Trump showing two middle fingers.

Now, Mr. Mattai's wife felt certain that what happened to him was a result of Mr. Trump’s disparaging of minorities.

“We’ve seen this movie before, the whole, ‘I feared for my life because it was a Black guy’ crap,” she said.

Her husband agreed. He initially told the police, from his hospital bed, that he had not touched Mr. Mathews and did not speak to him after seeing his gun. Mr. Mattai later told The New York Times that he had grabbed Mr. Mathews by the hair, but said that had been the extent of the physical contact.

“I was in the infantry for 10 years,” Mr. Mattai said. “If I had head-butted him, he would not have driven off anywhere.”

Though Mr. Mattai told The Times that he had served in the Marines for a decade, the Marines said his length of service was less than a year. Asked about the discrepancy, Mr. Mattai apologized, saying he had become accustomed to embellishing his military record because he was embarrassed about his past.

“It’s like the facade I made up for the world,” he said. “I didn’t want to tell them that I just, kind of, had this life of a bum.”

Two weeks after the shooting, Mr. Mattai was released from the hospital. He struggled to walk with a walker and had severe pain down the right side of his body. He needed months of rehab. But first, he had plans.

As soon as he got home, he said, he poured all his vodka down the drain. Then he went to his garage, where he kept his collection of political bumper stickers. He threw them in the trash. From then on, he said, he wasn’t going to drink and he wasn’t going to confront anyone about their political views.

Mr. Mattai concluded that it must have been God who sent Mr. Mathews and his gun to the dog park to teach him a lesson.

“I needed violence done to me to correct the path that I had put myself on,” he said.

But he still wanted to see Mr. Mathews sent to prison.

‘My Own Life Sentence’

Mr. Mathews was charged with felonious assault, a second-degree felony. If convicted, he could face up to eight years in prison and would be required to serve at least three. After posting a $50,000 bond, he was released with a GPS ankle monitor.

His trial is scheduled for February. His lawyer, Ian Friedman, plans to argue that the shooting was justified. Under the “stand your ground law” passed by Ohio Republicans in 2020, someone facing an imminent threat of serious harm does not have to try to escape before using deadly force.

“This case was never about politics or any other motivation, other than Mike being faced with a life or death situation and acting to save his life,” Mr. Friedman said.

In recent years, Mr. Mathews had endured a heart attack, a stroke and two back surgeries. Now at 80, he was reckoning with the possibility of spending what could be his final years in prison.

On the day he was arrested, Mr. Mathews told the police, “I should have been more of a coward, and this wouldn’t have gone this far.”

The local prosecutor — the one whose mother lives with Mr. Mathews — recused himself from the case and brought in the Ohio Attorney General’s Office.

That office was not asked to consider potential charges against Mr. Mattai, according to a spokesman.

But in August, four months after the shooting, Mr. Mattai received a call from his lawyer telling him that there was a warrant out for his arrest. He turned himself in.

The next morning, he learned that a prosecutor from another county had been brought in on the case. The prosecutor was charging Mr. Mattai with misdemeanor assault and disorderly conduct based on Mr. Mathews’s claim that Mr. Mattai had head-butted him. Mr. Mattai faces up to six months in jail.

He said he was willing to plead guilty or no contest when he returned to court in late October, if it meant avoiding jail time. He now walks with a limp and says he can’t return to his forklift mechanic job because he is unable to lift heavy objects.

“I got my own life sentence from this,” Mr. Mattai said. He has not taken Bob back to the dog park.

Mr. Jedlinsky, the man who tried to break up the fight, spent months away from the park, too. He said he was so shaken up in the aftermath that he didn’t sleep.

He didn’t remember seeing a head butt. He couldn’t say what Mr. Mattai was doing when the bullet entered his back. He wasn’t taking sides, in this fight or any other.

“This country is in a big divide right now,” Mr. Jedlinsky lamented. “It’s, ‘You’re either with us or against us.’ You’ve got to pick a side and hate the other side.”

Mr. Jedlinsky had spent months thinking about that day when his life had been put in danger. After everything it had cost the men involved, he was certain of one thing: Nobody’s mind had been changed.

ARTICLE

How One Boeing 777 Exemplifies Iran’s Riskiness and Resilience
The Trump administration says all Iranian airlines are being “shut down.” So why is this jumbo jet still flying from Tehran to Southeast Asia?
By Damien Cave
Published 2026-10-05 04:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/world/asia/boeing-777-plane-iran-us-sanctions-flights.html

The travelers speaking Persian at Ho Chi Minh City’s international airport last Monday dragged their bags toward an old Boeing 777 flying a new route — to and from Tehran. Many said they recognized it was a risky venture.

The plane, owned by Mahan Air, Iran’s largest private carrier, is one of just a few still defying a widened American effort to isolate Iran with threats to punish any entity that engages with its airlines. And because previous sanctions have barred suppliers from selling parts or services to Mahan for years, the dangers are also mechanical.

Iran’s aging aircraft — like the 23-year-old jetliner on the tarmac in southern Vietnam — are what sanctions experts often describe as “disasters waiting to happen.” Oman, Turkey and Iraq have stopped accepting Mahan’s flights. But not Vietnam, nor a few others. Recent stops for the 777 with tail sign EP-MTE also included Bangkok, Beijing and Moscow.

“Even if you don’t want to think about it, the danger is in your mind,” said Amir, 66, an Iranian in a golf shirt who was leaving Ho Chi Minh City, sharing only his first name to avoid trouble in Tehran. “Hopefully we’ll land safely. Hopefully nothing will happen.”

The story of Mahan Air’s old Boeing wide-body illustrates the risks that come with the Trump administration’s amplified campaign to make civil aviation a tool for coercion. In the aircraft’s travel record and reputation — pieced together with documents, tracking data and interviews with aviation and sanctions experts — there are warning lights aplenty.

Alongside the potential danger for civilians are hints of Iranian resilience and third-party resistance that suggest American threats can only go so far when so many still rely on energy from the Middle East.

Direct flights from Tehran to Vietnam only started in August, with plans to run weekly. Thailand added flights in July. The new routes appeared not long after Iran, in May, allowed several tankers heading for the region to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

For the countries still receiving Iranian flights as of early October (along with China and Russia, the list includes Afghanistan, Armenia, Malaysia, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Thailand, Uzbekistan and Vietnam), the promise of future energy supplies appears to be a draw. And not just now. What if Iran keeps control of the Strait of Hormuz with tolls for adversaries, and expedited service for friends?

“That may be the trade off,” said Emanuele Ottolenghi, a senior fellow at the Center for the Research of Terror Financing who has studied Iran’s networks for decades. “Keep our flights open and we’re going to let your tankers travel.”

Some countries may also be trying to do a bit of superpower hedging.

The latest round of U.S. sanctions targeting companies that service, ticket or provide fuel to Iranian airlines threaten to exclude violators from the dollar-based financial system. China, a strong critic of that very system — and what it calls America’s “illegal unilateral sanctions” — has increased flights between Tehran and several cities, including Guangzhou, Shanghai and Beijing.

For countries determined to avoid the perception of alignment with either superpower, offering limited service to Iran lets them “more or less sit in the middle,” said Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow with the Washington Institute for Near East Studies. “The new Mahan flights look like modest commercial and tourism links.”

Indeed, a dozen people in the airport check-in line said they had arrived with a packaged tour that delivered a week’s worth of beaches and sites across Vietnam. A few carried teal cone-shaped hats as souvenirs. Many described the trip as a way to convene with relatives coming from outside Iran and find respite from the grinding strain of life in a low-grade war.

But analysts doubted that tourism was, or will be, the plane’s only mission.

Mahan has been under sanctions from the U.S. Treasury Department since 2011 for alleged “dual use” violations that have included transporting weapons, military personnel, bulk cash and gold for the Iranian regime. Among Western intelligence agencies, it is known primarily as the airline run by and for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps.

In April, EP-MTE was specifically identified and sanctioned by U.S. officials in a statement accusing Mahan Air of transporting unmanned drones around the world.

A few months later, President Trump updated executive orders aimed at terrorism with broader sanctions targeting Iranian aviation. The Treasury Department justified the measures by pointing to Mahan Air.

“Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a September statement. “You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system.”

The state-run company that operates Vietnam’s airports did not respond to requests for comment, nor did Vietnam’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Despite the American threats, EP-MTE is still flying.

Aviation records show it was one of five Boeing 777-200ERs delivered to Singapore Airlines between 2001 and 2003 that later moved to a Thai discount airline that went bankrupt during the pandemic. That led to nearly three years of storage in the Australian desert. Then, in 2023, a shell company registered in Florida, Ion Aviation, bought the planes and moved them to China, before another company, Udaan Aviation, registered the lot in Madagascar. Tracking data showed that the planes traveled from Cambodia to Iran in July 2025.

“This is a classic scheme that the Iranians have used for decades to acquire used aircraft, using an intermediary in some funny country,” Mr. Ottolenghi said. “They’ve used Armenia, Iraq, Malta and Madagascar.”

Such a large acquisition carried legal risks; 22 people in Madagascar were detained last year and accused of forging documents related to the transfers.

But safety is the lingering concern. Aviation enthusiasts have noted that for all five planes, the extended stay in an Australian boneyard most likely degraded fuel lines, rubber seals and metal engine covers. With the plane subject to an export ban, factory-certified reactivation — the industry standard after years of deep storage — did not occur.

Russian airlines, under sanctions since the country’s attack on Ukraine in 2022, have faced similar challenges. One company, S7, grounded its fleet of Airbus A320/1neo planes in 2024 for lack of maintenance.

“This highlights how sanctions on civil aviation can bite, but only slowly,” said Agathe Demarais, a senior policy fellow with the European Council on Foreign Relations. “Such sanctions are essentially a ticking time bomb for a country’s airlines.”

During the brief period when the nuclear deal that President Barack Obama had negotiated with Iran was in place, exemptions for aviation sales were granted, perhaps giving Iran a chance to stockpile vital components. Analysts said Iran could also be cannibalizing other planes for parts. Josefine Petrick, a policy fellow who focuses on the negative impacts of sanctions at the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, a London think tank, called it “puzzle piecing a plane together.”

It can work, for a time. Flight trackers show that Monday’s flight landed safely in Tehran. But there is no denying the additional danger.

EP-MTE is one of at least two old 777s being used by Mahan to fly across Asia. The other is EP-MTB. Each one can hold more than 200 passengers. And with time, the mechanical risk compounds like interest, prompting complex questions about responsibility.

Who or what country or company would be blamed if one of Mahan’s 777s crashes?

“Sanctioning countries need to be aware and factor in the indirect effects of the policies that they push for,” Ms. Petrick said.

“Airplanes in Iran often operate twice as long as they would in other countries,” she added. “To some extent, these really are disasters waiting to happen.”

Tung Ngo contributed reporting from Hanoi.

ARTICLE

Russia Moves to Tamp Down Speculation About Plague in Siberia
The country’s consumer watchdog has said only that “an employee of an anti-plague institute in the Irkutsk Region” contracted pneumonia.
By Ivan Nechepurenko
Published 2026-10-05 14:40 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/world/europe/russia-plague-siberia.html

The rumors have been swirling for days. That a young lab worker died of suspected plague in Siberia. That the authorities feared an epidemic might spread and had quarantined hundreds of people.

While concrete information is scant, conflicting reports abound.

Russia’s consumer watchdog, which oversees disease control, has said only that “an employee of an anti-plague institute in the Irkutsk Region” was “diagnosed with pneumonia” of unknown origin.

With the Kremlin on Monday urging people to ignore speculation, here is what to know.

The official line

The Russian consumer watchdog did not name the employee. In a statement carried by state news outlets and published in pieces, the agency said that “no microorganisms linked to her professional activity were identified in the patient’s samples” and that “no health changes related to infectious pathology” had been identified among her contacts.

A commission also checked the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk for compliance with “biological safety requirements,” the agency said, and “no emergency situations involving pathogenic microorganisms were identified.”

The Irkutsk institute conducts research on a number of infectious diseases, including plague, which is caused by a bacterium. While there are a few hundred cases globally every year, mainly in Africa, plague can be easily treated with antibiotics if caught early.

In its statement, the consumer watchdog added that the “sanitary and epidemiological situation” in the Irkutsk region was “stable.”

The statement was issued on Sunday, two days after initial reports emerged about something more concerning happening in the Irkutsk region, which is about 2,600 miles east of Moscow.

Contradictory statements

The first signs of a potential issue came on Friday, when the Irkutsk regional governor said that he had held “an extraordinary meeting” with Russia’s chief sanitary physician about “a suspected case of a particularly dangerous infection in a resident.”

“All identified contacts” of the resident “have been placed under medical observation,” the governor, Igor I. Kobzev, wrote in a statement on social media.

That day, the mayor of Shelekhov, a town close to the city of Irkutsk, the regional capital, said that he had received “many inquiries” from residents and could confirm that the local hospital’s inpatient department was closed for quarantine. The mayor, Maksim N. Modin, said the hospital’s laboratory had suspended operations. He urged residents “not to spread rumors.”

The governor of the neighboring Buryatia region, Aleksei Tsydenov, was the first to officially raise the prospect of plague. He said on Friday that “the woman who died of plague in the Irkutsk region” had not visited Buryatia. His post on a state-linked messaging app was later updated to read “possibly died of plague.”

The following day, the authorities in Baikalsk, a town about 50 miles from the city of Irkutsk, cited “unofficial information” about “a case of plague” in a statement advising against travel to Shelekhov. That statement, on Telegram, was later deleted.

So were at least three posts by Ren-TV, a federal news network, including one that named the deceased lab worker and reported that she had researched plague.

Mr. Modin, the Shelekhov mayor, said on Monday that the consumer watchdog had the situation “under strict control,” adding, “a set of anti-epidemic measures is being carried out.”

Theories and speculation

Local news media have painted a bleaker picture. Lyudi Baikala, a regional outlet, reported that in addition to the Shelekhov hospital, other clinics and a maternity ward had been closed in Irkutsk.

Pavel Stepanov, a local journalist, wrote on his Telegram channel that a young laboratory assistant had broken a test vial and died. In a subsequent post on Monday, Mr. Stepanov defended his reporting and questioned why some government agencies and Kremlin-friendly news outlets had deleted statements and stories about Irkutsk.

The authorities, he said, “should investigate whether all this is not a sabotage by our enemies, who are acting with increasingly sophisticated methods.”

Any reason to be scared?

Officials in the United States and the European Union have said they are aware of and monitoring the reports about Irkutsk.

A potential lab leak and a feared disease prompted some comparisons with Covid-19, but experts said that even if plague were confirmed, the risk would be limited. Human cases of plague occur each year and are relatively simple to treat.

Professor Ian Jones, a virologist at the University of Reading, England, said in an emailed statement that the Irkutsk case “seems like a rare lab accident and is unlikely to go much further.”

Oleg Matsnev, Michael Mason and Koba Ryckewaert contributed reporting.

glacier-archaeology-melting-alps.html

SUMMARY

The Alps are losing ice faster than almost anywhere on the planet. Secrets like an enigmatic, 2,500-year-old ski that melted not long ago out of a strip of dying Swiss ice. It would be the latest in a growing trove of tools, garments and human remains that archaeologists have recovered from the Alps’ shriveling ice.

ARTICLE

A 2,500-Year-Old Ski? The Melting Alps Release Ancient Secrets.
Archaeologists are scouring mountain passes as artifacts from a bygone world all but tumble out of Switzerland’s shrinking ice.
By Raymond Zhong, Giacomo d’Orlando and Mira Rojanasakul
Published 2026-10-06 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/06/climate/glacier-archaeology-melting-alps.html

The Alps are losing ice faster than almost anywhere on the planet. And, as the glaciers and ice patches disappear, they are releasing secrets that had been locked away for millenniums.

Secrets like an enigmatic, 2,500-year-old ski that melted not long ago out of a strip of dying Swiss ice.

On a bright recent morning, Romain Andenmatten, a 42-year-old archaeologist, peered down at his discovery. Exploring the paltry remains of the ice at a mountain pass called Col de Barberine, he spotted a three-foot-long slat of grayish wood, nestled between rocks at the ice’s edge.

Three years ago at this same pass, elevation 7,500 feet, Dr. Andenmatten found a similar plank, also with a tapered end suggesting a ski or snowshoe. Carbon dating revealed it to be from roughly the fifth century B.C., when, on a certain day in the Iron Age, its owner might have been crossing the Alps and lost his footing.

Now Dr. Andenmatten wondered whether he’d found the second in the pair. It would be the latest in a growing trove of tools, garments and human remains that archaeologists have recovered from the Alps’ shriveling ice.

Between a winter of little snow and a summer of broiling heat waves, this year has been another devastating one for Switzerland’s glaciers. They have shed nearly 20 percent of their volume over the past five years, scientists said this month. At the current pace of global warming, 97 percent of today’s glaciers across the Alps could be gone by century’s end, posing big challenges for the tens of millions of Europeans for whom the ice is a vital reserve of water in dry years.

In much of the world, it’s mostly stone, metal and pottery that survive from ancient times. Not in the Alps, where the ice has preserved organic materials — leather, wood, textiles, body parts — that can tell a richer, more human story about the past.

“The Stone Age was not really a stone age,” said Regula Gubler, an archaeologist for the Swiss canton of Bern. “Most of what people used and wore was made out of organic materials,” she said. To find the leather shoes that protected their feet, the baskets of woven lime bark they carried into the mountains, “that’s just really special,” Ms. Gubler said.

The objects that have welled up out of Switzerland’s ice span the ordinary to the beguiling.

A fragment of an elm wood bowl from the fifth millennium B.C., long before the pyramids of Egypt and Stonehenge. A birch bark quiver with two flint arrowheads tucked inside, from around 2800 B.C. A two-foot-long statuette sculpted from larch, with a human figure at one end and a sharpened point at the other, from the last two centuries B.C., its purpose unknown.

Such discoveries are challenging old ideas about how early societies interacted with the alpine environment. Far from being forbidding, off-limits zones, the icy mountain passes apparently bustled with traffic: hunters, herdsmen, traders bearing barrels of wine on mules.

“The Alps were always used; it wasn’t an empty space,” Ms. Gubler said.

Nor, evidently, did early populations limit themselves to the gentlest routes. Their preferred paths between valleys seem to have been the shortest ones, never mind the steepness or the elevation.

There’s an urgency to the archaeologists’ work. Once organic materials are defrosted and exposed, they decompose quickly, or are snatched up by private treasure hunters. In 2024, the police and the archaeological authorities in the canton of Valais seized a collection of 11,000 artifacts, including coins, tools and decorative objects from as far back as the Bronze Age, and questioned a man for using a metal detector to scavenge them without permission.

With so many small glaciers and ice patches disappearing each year, some relics are probably doomed never to be found, to be consigned to oblivion simply because no one was in the right place, at the right moment, to spot it.

“An archive of human existence in the Alps is being lost,” said Marcel Cornelissen, an independent archaeologist based near Bern.

Archaeologists in Valais are maximizing their eyes on the ground with an app they developed, IceWatcher. Anyone — hikers, shepherds, crystal collectors — can use it to report potential finds in the mountains.

It was through IceWatcher that Dr. Andenmatten, an archaeologist for Valais’s cantonal government, heard in 2024 about some fragments of wood in an ice patch. He hiked up to a crossing called Restipass and collected some pieces that he later dated to the Bronze Age, making them perhaps 3,000 years old. Some might have been stakes in the ice that marked paths for travelers and warned of crevasses. Others might have been pieces of a sled or scraps of firewood.

Now, he and a colleague, David Gucker, were going back to see what this year’s sweltering temperatures had uncovered.

They drove up switch-backed roads and hiked for two hours through steepening alpine meadows. Finally, they clambered up to the pass and got a shock: The ice was all but gone. When Dr. Andenmatten was here two years ago, it had carpeted the slope where they stood. Now it was barely an icy area rug, leaking streams of water.

Sometimes, the ice in these passes can shrink noticeably over the course of a single day of fieldwork, Dr. Andenmatten said. “In the past, climate change might have unfolded over several generations, or over a lifetime,” he said. “Today, we experience it almost day to day.”

He and Mr. Gucker scoured the gravel and stones. They were well above the tree line, so any wood here had to have been brought by humans. The question was when: five years ago, or 5,000?

Dr. Andenmatten was in his element. He leaped from rock to rock like a mountain goat, flashing an impish, gaptoothed grin.

Something caught his eye: two slender pieces of wood, with smooth, squared-off edges. Delicate tree rings ran through them like flaky layers of mille-feuille pastry.

Dr. Andenmatten rotated the pieces this way and that. It wasn’t obvious they’d fit together. But miraculously, they did, and with that they transformed from lifeless fragments into an implement, something crafted by human hands.

“Really nice, this piece,” Dr. Andenmatten declared, before tucking it into a plastic bag.

Using satellite images and topographic maps, Swiss archaeologists are working with environmental scientists to predict where the next discoveries might emerge.

It would be “amazing” to find something atop a mountain peak, not just in the passes below, said Albert Hafner, an emeritus professor of archaeology at the University of Bern. Prehistoric people crossed the Alps, but we don’t know whether they scaled them, or, if they did, why. “We know that mountains were sacred in many cultures,” Dr. Hafner said. A religious object on a peak might reveal something about early people’s curiosities, their beliefs, their inner lives.

The next morning, Dr. Andenmatten hiked into the mountains again, to Col de Barberine. There, he found the possible second ski.

A ski might not tell us much about inner lives. But “the thing that is for me more spectacular is that it’s conserved,” Dr. Andenmatten said — that an accident of nature has allowed this modest object to speak across the ages.
