I mean, it’s fine as far as it goes, but how far does it go?

Sure, we should provide useful tools to lots of people. But we’re talking now about a level of risk that, if correct, nobody wants to be taking.

Internally, there would be these conversations where we would talk about the idea of falling off the frontier, and sometimes there was this straw man that would come up where someone would say, “Well, would the world be better if OpenAI weren’t here at all?” in skeptical response to someone who had suggested that we ought to either slow down or stop in a particular way that somebody thought we shouldn’t. That’s a straw man.

If we need to train these models because of the international balance of power and because Americans won’t be safe unless we do, that’s one reason to do something dangerous.

But “do this or else brand X will ship first” is not the same kind of reason.

Well, let me try to steel man this case, because I hear this from people all the time, including people I really respect. One response I got to my piece on “let’s not do recursive self-improvement until we’re sure it’s safe, let’s just ban it and begin to carve out exceptions as we know the exceptions are safe” ——

Just to be explicit, I agree with that.

I’m happy to hear that, but as of now, it seems like we’re not doing it.

But somebody said to me, “In your imagined world here, can Americans not use a Chinese open-weight model that has been improved using recursive techniques? Can they not use a Chinese closed-weight model? Does this apply to everybody?”

There is this issue of both the fear that the other companies will launch ahead of you, and, if they are doing the same thing anyway, then what does it matter that you didn’t do it? And maybe they’re going to do it in an even less safe and even less transparent way.

And then, of course, if we slow down, China speeds up, and then is it really better that China’s in control of this technology and Americans are going to use a Chinese one anyway?

How do you think about that set of claims?

No one wants to lose control to the robots. I definitely don’t want to see A.I. become a reason that China dominates the United States.

I’ll also say that I think the spirit of our times, Ezra, is that you choose what to do based on some complete unified theory of the political outcome that you are ultimately going to achieve, and for me, this is not like that.

Part of what I hear in your question is the idea of the Overton window on: Would the Chinese ever agree to XYZ?

When I first joined OpenAI, I remember telling friends that it felt like the Overton window had become an Overton door that I had stepped through into some strange world where what was reasonable and what might happen was totally outside what I had thought of as normal.

And I am, as you said earlier, kind of a normal person.

At least you were. [Both laugh.]

Yeah, I was. But I think that the changes in what’s happening can drive big changes fast in what seems politically plausible, and I definitely believe that that could happen with respect to U.S.-China cooperation on A.I.

So let me ask you what you actually want to see happen at these companies. Maybe it’s worth getting this into conversation first: Are you saying that OpenAI has an unsafe culture or the A.I. industry has an unsafe culture?

The A.I. industry has an unsafe culture.

So you’re not saying there’s a particular OpenAI problem, or at least that’s not how you see it?

No, that is not how I see it.

OK, so what do you want to see happen?

We should have a level of operational rigor and safety control that at least matches the most dangerous other things that people know how to do, like nuclear.

For example, in a nuclear power facility, there’s this idea of triple redundancy. Someone can have a bad day; someone can push the wrong button; there’s still not going to be a meltdown.

When you talk about aviation and nuclear, those are interesting examples in two ways that I’d like to hear you respond to.

One is — putting my “Abundance” hat on — the way we regulated nuclear power basically took nuclear power to a standstill. We so aggressively regulated nuclear power — in my view overregulated nuclear power — that nuclear power broadly stopped being built in this country. And instead, we used more natural gas and, in many other countries, more fossil fuel of different kinds.

There’s a real question of whether or not, in our effort to make nuclear power safe, we made it fundamentally unbuildable.

Now, aviation is different. We launch a lot of planes and they do fly very safely. So that’s one layer of my not exactly objection, but it is the case that a lot of regulation can dramatically slow something down.

Can I reply on nuclear?

Yeah.

I agree we over-regulated nuclear and that we didn’t end up in the optimal place.

And it’s not just that we made nuclear hard to build; we made nuclear hard to make safer because building new, safer reactor designs was hard and getting them approved was hard. I’m sure there are lessons there for how to be safe. There were other things, too, things you’ve written about in the “Abundance” context, like the NIMBY idea of not wanting nuclear in your backyard was part of how it became hard to do.

But I would much rather have those problems than the ones we do now.

So you’re saying you would prefer the problem of a little bit of overregulation and going too slow to the potential problems of under-regulation and going too fast.

At least to the extent we have now.

If you think of it as there being some sort of Goldilocks middle and we’re trying to get near it, I think we’re pretty far from it in the direction of being too dangerous.

So maybe the grass is always greener on the other side, but I’m looking at it and thinking we really ought to be willing to risk some overregulation in order to make sure that this is safe.

So that’s one level, and I would describe that as almost like the level of organizational design and engineering.

When I talk to someone like Jensen Huang, he says, in a way that makes some sense, “Look, these companies need to mature. They need to become bigger. They need to be putting much more of their both resources and personnel and compute into validation and verification and safety and scaling and liability and all these things that mature companies do.”

And then there’s this other side where maybe this is not like aviation or nuclear or chip design. You are building increasingly intelligent systems, and every time you build a new one, it has new capabilities, and maybe it’s trying to outsmart you, and maybe it wants things in the world and has goals in the world that you don’t actually understand. You think you taught it one thing and actually you taught it another, and we don’t really know how to operate with that. So our best guess is maybe we’ll have A.I. systems sitting on A.I. systems sitting on A.I. systems watching each other. But actually, we’re entering into totally new territory, honestly, without very thoughtful discussion of whether or not we should. We just went from “We are” to “It’s happening” very, very quickly.

I’m just curious how that sits in your thinking — whether or not we really do, in your view, have analogies that work here for things that are fundamentally intelligent and goal-oriented and becoming more so?

I’m suspicious of the idea whenever someone says, “This is without parallel.” We have a blank page.

I mean, not to put words in your mouth, but people are good at figuring [expletive] out, and I think we have valuable tools for this.

Yes, it’s not precisely like anything that we have had before, but nuclear is an analogy, aviation is an analogy, dealing with people and organizations is an analogy.

I think one of the most fascinating things about these recent incidents with the swarms, including but not only Hugging Face, is that groups of agents have cultures. And we should care about those cultures, and we should think about how to make them good.

And we’re just beginning to even realize that that’s a real thing. We’re just beginning to inhabit a world in which that’s a real operating reality, that there are cultures among groups of agents.

So I think we need to use everything that we have to figure things out. And certainly, regardless of whether we’re speeding ahead on capabilities, or “paced” or stopped, we need to figure out how to align these systems. There’s no version of the path of futures that we’re on where that isn’t a vital thing to figure out.

Well, I’ll admit, I do sort of buy the argument that the train has left the station, but I think it’s worth entertaining this for one minute.

And the way I describe it is this: Obviously, if A.I. is unsafe and kills us all or takes over the financial system or something, that’s bad. Everybody agrees we don’t want that to happen.

But let’s take the more positive view — the world where alignment roughly works out, but this world where we actually have created something smarter and more capable than we are. Donald Trump, in this very weird way, has been talking about how he wants to rename this “superintelligence” from artificial intelligence. And then Sam Altman got asked about this, and I thought his answer on that was interesting:

Archival clip of Brendan Bordelon on “Decoded”: So that’s why I’m curious whether you think this rebrand will actually have any impact on the public perception of this technology. Sam Altman: Yeah, it’s not clear to me that superintelligence is a less scary term. I do think it’s a more accurate term.

I thought that was very telling, in a way, because superintelligence is a much scarier term. And if it is in fact a more accurate term, I do think, just at a first principles level, if you said to me, “Should human beings create something more intelligent and capable than they are? In the long run, will that be good for them?” Probably not. Or at least it’s not obvious to me why it would be.

Yeah.

And sometimes when I hear even the good versions of this, they seem to have this world where it’s like we’re being taken care of by these A.I.s ——

That’s right. Like pets.

Like pets, a little bit. And that vision sucks, too. [Laughs.]

Yep, it does. I don’t want that for my kids.

So I guess I’m trying to ask you: The company you worked for, the guy who runs it says he thinks superintelligence is a better term for it. The chief scientist is like, we’re making an “alien mind.”

Even if it works, do we want this?

Maybe not. It depends on what the “this” is, and I don’t think we know what the “this” is.

Again, the future has a lot of uncertainty in it. And it has always been very striking to me from the beginning, from when I joined, that I would ask people, “Well, what does the good future look like? Where are we trying to get to?” And I would elicit humility from people that are otherwise very proud and very confident, and I would get a lot of, “Well, that’s above my pay grade.” Or “People will figure it out.” Or “Whatever people want.”

And it just struck me that the sense of the good that was under this was impoverished.

What was it for you? You were there. You’re a thoughtful person. You’re a Rhodes scholar who studied philosophy and then founded a civil rights NGO. What were you trying to create?

I thought that we were building powerful tools that could do a lot of good in the world on a day-to-day level, and I didn’t think that we were going to be able to create something fundamentally smarter than we were.

And this is something I can say with full confidence only in hindsight. Because it was only when this stopped being true — when I thought, “No, we really are going to have something that thinks circles around us” — that I thought, “Oh, we’re in a totally inappropriate part of the possibility space here in terms of how safe the industry is actually being relative to that reality.”

It’s one of these things, people have said to me, “It must have been a hard decision.” Or “How brave of you” or whatever. But when it became clear to me that we were going to build something — we, the industry, were on track to build something that could think circles around us — and we were this far from being ready for that at a safety and alignment level, it just became apparent to me that my time helping build it was over.

So I feel like there’s a tension between some of your recent answers here. On the one hand, I asked you a few minutes ago about what we need to do, and you’re like: Look, humans are good at figuring things out. We’re good at solving problems. You know, we can build a better organization.

And then when I say: Is this thing we’re building a world we should want, even if it succeeds? You sound very ambivalent about that, and almost ambivalent at best.

Yeah.

So where are you personally? I’m curious — I’m not saying I think we’re going to stop. I’m not saying you think we’re going to stop. But is the thing you wish we would do to add an aviationlike layer of safety to this?

Or is the thing you wish we would do to pause and think through whether superintelligent or very intelligent A.I. is really consistent with the human good?

Are you where the Anthropic C.E.O. Dario Amodei is, or are you where Pope Leo is?

I mean, it’s odd to say this as a Jew, but closer to the Pope.

It is urgent that we think carefully about the kind of future that we want to build. My personal belief is that once we have found that this is possible, once we have made the discoveries, I don’t think there’s a back button where we get to live in a world where this doesn’t, in some form or other, eventually happen, whatever it is that can happen.

In my ideal world, there’s space to be thoughtful and take a breath and really, really think about what kind of future we want to build.

Silicon Valley — part of what happens is we’re always removing friction. There’s always this sense of trying to just get the answer. And I think there are all these activities in life that are so important for us, that are meaningful, that have also been necessary in the past. Like, I go to work to provide for my wife and children. And the fact that I am able to shelter and protect them is part of what gets me up in the morning. And so I’m doing work.

Or another example is learning. We have to go to school in order to learn how to do skills that we then use, because they are valuable in the economy. But if we’re in a world where all of that stuff is automated, then if we learn, it’s only from first principles or only because we want to.

I mean, people will talk about this idea of a leisure society — they may not use that word, but the basic idea is: You can do whatever you want. There’s nothing you have to do. Maybe you’ll take up painting. I think that would suck for a lot of people.

I think right now we see that when people do not have enough to do, it does not tend to go well for them.

Right. What’s really important? What’s really valuable? I don’t have the answers here, but those are the questions, at a personal level, that I would like to turn to.

I feel like because of the safety situation that we’re in, and because of the work that I did, I need to do what I’m doing now and have these serious conversations about exactly what’s happening in safety.

But my vocational pull is toward these wisdom questions, for sure.

I think that is a good place to end. Always our final question: What are three books you’d recommend to the audience?

OK. No. 1: “The Challenger Launch Decision.” This is a book about why the Challenger exploded, and it’s by Diane Vaughan, who’s a social scientist.

I thought I knew the story of why the Challenger blew up. I thought what happened was that middle managers cut corners, and there was this rubbery O-ring that got brittle in the morning cold, and it snapped. And the idea was that these people were foolish.

Turns out, the risk of that O-ring breaking because of the cold had been known and documented and accepted in the safety documentation — they had great safety documentation — over and over and over.

Even the night before the launch, there was a late-night conference among the engineers who were worried about whether this particular launch would be safe because it was so cold.

Huh. Why is this book feeling relevant to you? [Laughs.]

Yeah, well, I think we’re in this place.

So if they had said, “It’s not this launch” — the Challenger launch was not that different from earlier launches that had gone safely. It was only a little bit colder and a little bit windier. And if the people involved said, “This launch is not safe enough,” then it would reopen a can of worms about whether the earlier launches had been safe or not, even though, in the event, they had gone well.

And I worry we could have that with what we’re doing in the industry, where we accept a risk, nothing horrible happens, and then the next thing is not so different. There are, as we were talking about earlier, the changes — instead of being a whole new world every few months, it’s more like a little bit different every week. So you can imagine going by shades into a level of risk that does not make sense.

And it has crossed my mind that I should be sending copies of this to my former colleagues.

The second book I will name — I have a 2-year-old and a 4-year-old — “Little Witch Hazel.” It’s a picture book by Phoebe Wahl. It’s just absolutely beautiful, and my daughter’s eyes light up every time we pull it off the shelf. So if there are parents out there looking for a good one, I would recommend it.

And then third — and most importantly, I guess, if you were going to pick one — would be “The Sabbath” by Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel.

One of my favorite books ever.

It’s a wonderful book. It happens to be from my tradition. I’m Jewish. And ——

Well, it’s worth it for anybody, really.

It is worth it for anybody. It’s true. The famous line is “The Sabbaths are our great cathedrals.”

That tradition of stopping and taking a breath, he says, is more important than any temple. And ——

Yeah, cathedrals in time. I always think about that.

Yes, cathedrals in time. And I pointed to this — maybe I’ll just quote the last line of something I said to colleagues as I was leaving: “We have to make good choices. We have no time to rush.” So I hope we take that wisdom.

David Robinson, thank you very much.

Thank you.

SUMMARY

At the recent White House tech summit, Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, sat in the chair next to President Trump — his literal right-hand man. Later that day, Mr. Huang used the term “super intelligence,” just as the president prefers. Before Mr. Trump, Mr. Huang didn’t show much interest in politics.

ARTICLE

He’s the Most Powerful Engineer on Earth. Here’s Why He Thinks A.I. Is Going Great.
Our fate may be very well be in the hands of Jensen Huang.
By Stephen Witt
Published 2026-10-07 15:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/opinion/jensen-huang-ai-tech-nvidia.html

At the recent White House tech summit, Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, sat in the chair next to President Trump — his literal right-hand man. Later that day, Mr. Huang used the term “super intelligence,” just as the president prefers. In the aftermath of this summer’s rogue A.I. attacks, Mr. Huang has emerged as a leading skeptic of the danger this technology poses. As his biographer, I understand why he dismisses the risk. I also worry that he’s not seeing the whole picture.

When I first interviewed him, Mr. Huang told me that every problem — business, personal, whatever — is actually an engineering problem: You study the inputs, you study the constraints and then you get the outputs that you want. While writing his biography, I watched Mr. Huang put this approach into action. He engineers his business to ensure that Nvidia will be the default platform in industries like robotics and health care. He engineers his products to be better than the competition’s. And in 2025, he began to engineer the president of the United States.

Before Mr. Trump, Mr. Huang didn’t show much interest in politics. Now Mr. Trump and Mr. Huang talk on the phone often and seem to have a genuine personal rapport — Mr. Trump even picked him up in Alaska to go to China on Air Force One. Mr. Trump wants to be close to Mr. Huang because the president likes winners — and Jensen Huang is the biggest winner of all. Since its inception in a Denny’s restaurant in 1993, Nvidia has grown to become the most valuable company in American history, even taking inflation into account.

Driving the growth is the unprecedented data center boom behind A.I., which Mr. Huang has termed a “new industrial revolution.” Data centers can hold thousands of tall metal cabinets called “racks” that wire together dozens of Nvidia microchips into a modular computing unit. A new rack, about the size of a refrigerator, can cost around $8 million and, by some estimates, can draw more power than 70 single-family homes. In 2026, Nvidia will net around a quarter of a trillion dollars selling this and similar equipment.

The data center boom has made Mr. Huang the emperor of A.I. — the other big tech companies are borrowing money to access his products. It is a testament to Mr. Huang’s engineering prowess that no competitors have yet managed to gain significant market share in Nvidia’s core business of A.I. chips. Engineers simply prefer Nvidia. These are the self-described “systems guys” responsible for implementing A.I. at the circuit-board level.

Mr. Huang is himself a systems guy and that informs his view of A.I. I’ve interviewed at least a hundred GPU engineers by this point, and I have yet to meet one who was seriously concerned about runaway A.I. On the other hand, most of the software engineers I talk to are extremely concerned. Bill Gates recently warned that A.I. could kill one billion humans.

The situation is baffling: here are two groups of rational, high-IQ technical experts looking at the same data and reaching totally opposite conclusions. It reminds of the viral image “The Dress,” where some people saw blue and black, and some people saw white and gold.

Here is what I think is going on: the basis of modern A.I. is the neural net, which draws direct inspiration from biology. In fact, a modern A.I. consists of many billions of artificial neurons, simulated in computer code. Thus, to the software experts, a modern A.I. looks something like a mass of undifferentiated brain tissue, mysterious and fundamentally difficult to control.

But that’s not how the hardware guys see it. They draw a clear distinction between actual neurons — which are biological cells that can be unpredictable — and synthetic neurons, which are simple mathematical models whose behavior can be forecast with perfect accuracy. When you work from the microchip up, maintaining control of A.I. is an engineering problem, and governed by the same input/output constraints as any other. To the A.I. doomer skeptics, safe A.I. is a math equation — or, in Mr. Huang’s words, just “software.”

When Mr. Huang began studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s, microchips had tens of thousands of components on them, and were typically designed by hand on paper. Today they can have more than a hundred billion components, and are designed using specialized software with assistance from A.I. Mr. Huang, at 63, has personally managed this exponential growth in capability. His generation of engineers built the tools to ensure that the hyper-complex microchip remains something that humans can interpret and control.

As a hardware guy, Mr. Huang spends more time in Asia than most Western tech C.E.O.s. He was born in Taiwan; his native language is Taiwanese, and Nvidia is building a satellite headquarters in Taipei. Mr. Huang is also supportive of mainland Chinese A.I. developers. I believe this also influences his thinking, as East Asia is much more optimistic about A.I. than is the United States. When I do speaking events in Asia, I never get questions about A.I. risk. In the United States, it’s the most common thing people bring up.

So perhaps it is unsurprising that Mr. Huang believes he can make the artificial neuron safe. From his point of view, if you can see every calculation the machine does, right in front of you, then the machine should remain entirely within your control. If the machine is misbehaving — well, that’s your fault. All you need is better engineering. He knows it can be done.

Thus Mr. Huang has dismissed all calls for any slowdown in A.I., or any regulations that would impede development of the technology. “There is 0 percent chance that’s going to be the end of the world,” he said in an interview with CBS News. At a Goldman Sachs conference last month, he suggested that cyber-security concerns were a marketing tactic. “What better way to create demand than to create a problem?” he asked. He also has suggested that the profit motive alone will be sufficient to incentivize companies to make A.I. safe.

Mr. Huang has succeeded in getting Mr. Trump to parrot his talking points. In September, Mr. Trump called Mr. Huang while he was onstage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles. He put the president on speaker, then held a microphone up to his phone, broadcasting to the audience Mr. Trump’s claims that any talk of risks to human life from A.I. was a “hoax.” “The robots are not going to be taking over the world,” the president said, following a round of applause.

The phone call, which had the feel of an orchestrated publicity stunt, was a public declaration of Mr. Trump’s resistance to A.I. regulation. But where others saw the president taking a forceful stand, I saw Mr. Huang engineering the president. The input was shameless public flattery: in the phone call, Mr. Huang called Mr. Trump “sir,” praised Mr. Trump’s intellect (“You know so much about A.I.,”) and stoked Mr. Trump’s bottomless need for validation. (“Did you hear that? Thousands of people are clapping for you.”) And the output? Little regulation on A.I. and freedom to export some of Nvidia’s hardware to China, and whatever else Mr. Huang wants.

This situation worries me. Mr. Huang is the most capable individual I have ever met — but, I fear, A.I. is more capable still. I suspect that the capabilities exist, today, for A.I. to enhance dangerous pathogens and to shut down electrical grids. At the same time, the science of interpreting and controlling A.I. is years behind the science of making it smarter. At a granular level, we can control the behavior of synthetic neurons, but technologists can’t currently explain how these neurons coordinate to produce intelligence. That gap in understanding is widening, and I don’t know if Mr. Huang can see it.

The future, even in the best-case scenario, will be extremely disorienting. But maybe it will be awesome. Maybe I will live to be 205. Whatever happens, it will happen because of the decisions and guidance of a singular, extraordinary man who directs the future of A.I. and much else besides. Engineering is powerful — and today, Mr. Huang is the most powerful engineer alive.

Stephen Witt is the author of “The Thinking Machine,” a history of the A.I. giant Nvidia.

Nelson: Well, I’ll talk about that specifically, the role that the media plays in understanding what the American military does, but then, also the steps that led us to the secrecy, as you point out, about the war in Iran with this Department of Defense.

ARTICLE

Pete Hegseth’s ‘Vast Overcorrection’
A Special Forces veteran joins the columnist David French to assess Pete Hegseth’s leadership.
By David French, Mike Nelson and Jillian Weinberger
Published 2026-10-07 09:07 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/opinion/pete-hegseth-pentagon-iran-war.html

What impact has the Iran war had on the U.S. military? As the conflict drags on, the Times Opinion columnist and Iraq war veteran David French speaks with the former Special Forces officer Mike Nelson about the way Pete Hegseth, the secretary of defense, has tried to remake the military in the midst of the war, and what the Democrats should do if they win control of Congress in January.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.

The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

David French: As some listeners might know, before I went into journalism, I served in the U.S. Army. I was a judge advocate general officer, an Army lawyer. I deployed to Iraq in 2007 and served for almost a year. So I can say from some degree of experience that I’m worried about the way Pete Hegseth, the secretary of defense, is managing the war in Iran.

News clip: There are new, concerning reports of deteriorating morale among troops. News clip: Months of strikes on Iran have severely depleted the U.S. military’s supply of missiles, especially advanced interceptors. News clip: Some family members expressed concerns — prolonged deployment is affecting sailors’ mental health.

My friend Mike Nelson spent more than two decades in the Army, retiring as a Special Forces officer. He is a fellow at the National Security Institute, and he joins me today. Welcome, Mike.

Mike Nelson: Morning, David. Thanks for having me.

French: Mike, before we dive into details, how would you rate how Hegseth is faring so far, sort of top line? How much is he changing the military under his leadership? And just putting aside the rhetoric, substantively, how much is he changing the military? How long-lasting could these changes be?

Nelson: Well, I’m going to surprise a lot of the people who have read anything I’ve written, primarily at The Dispatch, about Secretary Hegseth, and I’m going to say the truth is that not every one of Secretary Hegseth’s ideas are bad or wrong, but many of them are. And more important, many of his correct ideas are not necessarily where a secretary of defense should be focusing. He was correct to say that there had been myriad distractions that had been placed on the Department of Defense that took away from some of the war-fighting focus, or deterrence focus, being ready for future operations. We saw it in his speech last week. He’s primarily a showman, so he has his canned catchphrases that he likes to say.

Archival clips of Pete Hegseth: No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos. No wimps. No radicals. Just warriors. […] We do bad things to bad people. […] Maximum lethality, not tepid legality. Violent effect, not politically correct.

And for months, we have been hearing “No dudes in dresses,” specifically saying that he has changed the policy so that there cannot be transgender service members anymore. OK. That decision was made months ago, and he just continues to hit the greatest hits. All right, what next? The next part, the “no beardos” thing, right? He was correct that shave waivers were probably overused and oversought in a disciplined military, and too many people were getting them, and it took away from the overall military bearing. OK. That’s what we expect battalion sergeants major to focus on.

French: Yeah, I was going to say that this is not a secretary of defense-level issue, but ——

Nelson: So he is focusing largely on these tactical-level, really — he commands, or leads, the single largest organization in the United States, and he is focused on these very small-ball issues that we actually empower and pay really professional noncommissioned officers — these sergeants and sergeants major — to do on his behalf. All he has to say is: “This is the new policy. Go forth and do great things.” Instead, he’s bringing people to D.C. to make sure they hear it straight from him. I think a lot of his ideas, which might be correct, are distractions, or at least for what he should be focusing on, where he’s supposed to be at the strategic level, merging those tactical effects with the strategic goals of the United States — and that’s not happening, and we see that playing out with the war in Iran.

Additionally, before I move on, like I said, he has some good ideas. Recently, in his speech, he had Fortress America, I believe is what he called it, which was basically hardening U.S. installations to make sure they were on independent power grids and not susceptible to cyberattacks. That’s a good move.

Besides that, he is also making some really bad moves. So we’ve seen his focus on warrior culture and physical training, and things like that coming at the cost of some of the innovations that we should be focusing on as an American military. I think he is damaging not only our progress in getting ready for the next conflict, but he’s also potentially causing negative effects in military leadership by purging those innovators who currently exist and replacing them with sycophants who are primarily motivated by personal loyalty.

French: I’d love for you to tell listeners a little bit more about your service. I think it’s safe to say it was a bit different from mine. I served as a JAG officer in Iraq. You were a Special Forces officer, tip of the spear. And it seems to me that it’s as if Hegseth is kind of trying to reshape the military into that entire archetype: the Special Forces warrior. Do you think he’s trying to remake the military in that image of almost, like, the Spartan Special Forces warrior? What’s happening here?

Nelson: I think you’re right that there is this archetype that filtered out. And it’s kind of a disservice to what the military was doing as a whole.

The war, if you think about the way the war started and culminated, there are two examples that I think a lot of people have in their minds. There’s the beginning of the war with Task Force Dagger, my old unit, 5th Special Forces Group, riding horses with the Northern Alliance, which is one side of S.O.F., working by, with and through local resistance.

French: And just to interrupt you for a second — S.O.F., Special Operations Forces?

Nelson: Right. And then the other side of that, you have kind of — in Kathryn Bigelow’s movie “Zero Dark Thirty,” the raid on Osama bin Laden SEAL Team 6 conducting a direct-action raid — our most elite direct-action Tier 1 forces conducting these kinds of incredibly hard to pull off raids and doing them with great skill. That does not portray at all what the everyday experience of a lot of soldiers were, which was largely conducting patrols, conducting local governance, all sorts of things that went into the war that aren’t as easily translatable onto film or in really cool-looking Instagram pictures.

I do think that the secretary, his whole concept is predicated on the idea that the Joe Biden years particularly focused far too much on creating social experiments within the military, and that distracted from the core function of fighting wars. And there are certain examples where there were distractions. There were things that took away from just the time available to conduct training. But it’s a vast overcorrection that he’s engaged in.

And as we look at the transformation of war, we are going to need people who have that warrior ethos, but that’s only one part of the combined arms fight. We are also going to need a lot of innovators, a lot of analysts, a lot of people who can integrate the new technologies. So the secretary’s focus tends to be a little bit myopic just on one part, and one part that was applicable several years ago, but not necessarily looking at all the new layers that are required.

French: We’re going to get into this a little bit more, but I’m struck by the different image that he has of a soldier compared to what the Ukrainian Army looks like, which I think might be very indicative of your point, because the Ukrainian Army is not an army of extraordinarily heavily muscled, high-T special operators. The average age is shockingly high. I’ve seen some measures say the median age of a Ukrainian soldier might be in the late 30s or early 40s, which is more like the age I was when I dragged myself through officer basic at Fort Lee. And also, it’s got a — frankly, Mike — a bunch of nerds doing drone warfare. And so it strikes me that he’s articulating a kind of physical image of a warrior that, as you were saying, doesn’t match the diversity of the needs that we have.

Nelson: Right. We do need infantrymen to be able to move long distances, carrying large amounts of weight on their back, with very little sleep and very little food. But yes, Ukraine is right now what I refer to as the lethal laboratory. They are leading the way in demonstrating what is the future of warfare, and it is a mixture of both new technologies and old truths of war that will endure forever. We are missing the opportunity to learn from our Ukrainian allies, but the generals who were trying to do that are no longer part of the D.O.D. They’ve been purged out.

French: I’m so glad you raised the generals, because I had a conversation with one of the fired generals not long ago, and this person pointed out that, in essence, they were fired for following orders. In other words, the Biden administration handed down some edicts and some orders regarding D.E.I. — diversity, equity, inclusion and other things — and as loyal soldiers, whether they agreed or not, they saluted and they carried out those orders. And Hegseth comes in and essentially says: Well, if you were carrying out the orders that were the priority of the previous administration, you’re woke, you’re weak, whatever, and you’re gone.

And one of the fears that was expressed to me by this former general was that, well, does that then set a precedent that if you are a general officer and you follow the orders of an administration, that the next administration will come in and purge you, replace you with general officers who have to then follow their orders, who will then only be purged by the next administration?

It strikes me that the Trump administration is setting a precedent here that if actually carried out by other presidents would be catastrophic for the integrity of the military. And it’s setting a precedent that, given enough time under the current administration, could be catastrophic for the idea that merit matters as much as political fidelity. But it was very chilling to me to hear the general essentially say, “I was fired for following a lawful order.”

Nelson: Right. So a lot of the criticism that Hegseth has steered toward these generals — who implemented, as you said, the lawful orders of the previous duly elected president and the civilian leadership through the secretary of defense — focus on two things, largely. Well, three things, I guess: D.E.I. in general — kind of a big umbrella — the Covid-19 vaccine mandate and the withdrawal from Afghanistan. Everything that was just listed, we can disagree with or think were bad ideas or conducted poorly, and all of them were lawful orders from the duly elected president through the civilian leadership. Right now, there’s a great deal of discussion about generals rejecting Secretary Hegseth’s guidance. There are two places that I have concern about legality: One being the overall legality of the war with Iran, and the second being the Sept. 2, 2025, boat strike, at the beginning of Operation Southern Spear.

But outside of that, I think it’s fair to say that I disagree and think that most of Secretary Hegseth’s stuff or ideas are bad ideas — counterproductive and potentially damaging in the long term — but they are legal. And would he want these same generals that he’s propping up to be fired immediately in 2029, in January, because they implemented his orders? The secretary needs to remember that his predecessors gave legal orders, whether he agreed with them or not, and he is in a position now to implement new policy, and that’s fine. We may disagree with it, but they are legal orders.

French: Before we move on to the Iran war, there’s another element, and this is kind of the entree into it. So moving from what is the culture of the military, what’s happening with generals — the secrecy that we have seen around the Iran war. And I want to be really careful about this question, because there are ways in which secrecy is absolutely imperative. So, for example, there was a famous moment during earlier iterations of the Iraq war where Geraldo Rivera is embedded with American troops. And Mike, I don’t know if you remember this ——

Nelson: I do.

French: He essentially maps out an upcoming attack. In other words, he talks about what’s about to happen, what we’re about to do, and if Iraqi forces were watching these feeds, they would have had foreknowledge of an American attack. It’s an example where secrecy’s really important. You don’t broadcast what you’re about to do. And when we had embedded media, they would get briefings on upcoming attacks, but they were under an agreement that they were not going to discuss that until the appropriate time, when everything unfolded.

But I think a lot of listeners would be really surprised at how closely connected the media was, at least to my work, when I was in Iraq. We had embedded media throughout the entire period: L.A. Times, Reuters, Times of London, Stars and Stripes — and they were able to report from the front, what we were doing. And in my experience with the guys, the cav troopers I served with, 99 percent of them wanted to talk to the media. They wanted people to know what we were doing. But you were in a very different part of the world. You were in the Special Operations world, the ultimate level of secrecy applied to you.

Talk me through your own experience with the media, and how you see the connection between the media, the military and the American public.

Nelson: Well, I’ll talk about that specifically, the role that the media plays in understanding what the American military does, but then, also the steps that led us to the secrecy, as you point out, about the war in Iran with this Department of Defense.

I had a general officer that I worked for who I have near cultlike devotion to — one of the finest officers I’ve ever known, one of the finest human beings I’ve ever known. And I saw this person. I’ve worked for him twice: once in a Special Operations task force in Afghanistan and once at a much higher strategic level. And he used to always bring media with him on his in-theater engagements. And I heard a pretty prominent member of the media ask him once why he did so, because so many other members of the military were at least shy around the media, or maybe cautious around the media. And he said, “The American people deserve to know what their military does on their behalf, and you’re how they find out.”

And I thought that was just a distilled-down, virtuous statement about the role of military operations in a healthy republic. Right now, we are engaged in a conflict that started out unpopular and is growing more unpopular as it goes. There’s never been a less popular war since World War II, since modern polling.

And part of the problem is, because the American people do not trust what the government is telling them about the war, about the causes for it, about the conduct of it, about how it’s going, about how it’s going to be resolved at the end. And part of this, we know that the president has his own unique relationship with the media and unique relationship with how he presents the truth of what he’s doing or what his administration is doing. But the secretary and the Department of Defense as a whole owe a part of this, too, or are complicit in this, too. From the beginning, we saw that Secretary Hegseth had what seemed to be a primary motivation of controlling the narrative of what he was doing — not so much what the Department of Defense was doing, but what he personally was doing. Controlling his own image and those who had the ability to shape it.

He implemented attempts to control what the media would report from the Pentagon, famously purging out or at least having most of the legacy media leave physical spaces in the Pentagon when they wouldn’t agree to preapproval of their stories. They’ve been replaced largely with alternate media that are, in some cases, sycophants; in some cases blend the boundaries between what is media and what is public relations, because we’ve had people who are both wearing the hat of new media, credentialed by the Pentagon, and special government employees working for the Department of Defense without disclosure. We’ve had other people who haven’t been officially brought on as special government employees, but have publicly said that they’re advising the secretary on what to do. So he wants to tell his story through supportive media only. Additionally ——

French: Can I interrupt you on that real fast? I want to drill down on that, because that has not gotten the attention it deserves. Now, listeners, the conflict of interest should be very obvious.

And that’s something that, in my view, is utterly symbolic of the corruption around this administration. But that is a perversion of the role of the military. It’s a perversion of the role of the media, and I just wanted to put an exclamation point behind that. So, anyway, please continue.

Nelson: And we should be clear: In previous administrations, Republican and Democrat, we’ve seen the crossing over between media and government officials back and forth. People who were in the administration then became hosts on cable news. But there’s a clear delineation of which role they’re filling at which time. They’re never wearing both hats at the same time, and if they are, they’re never hiding the ball from the public that they’re attempting to influence. We’ve seen the secretary and Sean Parnell, his primary spokesman, respond to any critical stories by flatly claiming that everything is fake news.

Now we see, whether it’s stories about the damage done to Naval Support Activity Bahrain, the Port of Shuaiba, critical shortages on some of our interceptors — all of this is immediately reported as fake news: It’s not true; the war is going gloriously.

And there’s never a revisiting of the actual facts. Now, this is a problem because I don’t think, and I may be overstating things, whenever we go to war, there are going to be costs. The fact that the administration is trying to paint it as though there are no negative effects makes them seem even more disingenuous.

French: Well, you’re getting to something, and we’re sort of rolling into the war itself right now. And it strikes me — and this is something that I’ve been banging the drum on from the beginning — that, let’s suppose you’re a supporter of the war in Iran and, like I’ve said, I’ve long been an Iran hawk. There are circumstances where you could convince me, if you went to the public and you presented evidence, that striking Iran would be in the national interest, in compliance with the laws of war, that it would be the right thing to do. But it was never tried. They never went to us.

And one of the points that I’ve tried to make to people is that this isn’t just a matter of dotting the I’s and crossing the T’s on some sort of archaic constitutional requirement when everybody knows it’s just the president anyway. No. Democracies are supposed to go to war with the support of the people, because a democracy with the support of the people can be one of the most potent war-fighting enterprises in world history. But a democracy that goes to war without the support of the people can underperform, can fail at accomplishable tasks, because it lacks that support.

How have you seen this decision? We can set aside the legality, the constitutionality, just for a moment. Practically, how have you seen that decision to not go to the American people work itself out in the actual conduct of the conflict?

Nelson: Well, as you point out, they teach this in the woke war colleges that Secretary Hegseth has a problem with. There is this thing called Clausewitz’s trinity, right? And one of them is the will of the people, and you need popular support, particularly when we talk about a republic.

One of the, arguably, advantages that Iran has in this conflict is that they don’t have to have popular support. They are already repressing their people. You know, I don’t think they have too much concern for the suffering of the people as they endure the effects of the conflict. But in hindsight, a lot of people look at the war in Iraq and judge it as this horrible decision, and George W. Bush is ultimately responsible, and he needs to answer for what decisions he made, as any president does.

But people forget the Bush administration spent about a year making the case for a war with Iraq. The American people overwhelmingly agreed with it, and the Senate overwhelmingly agreed with it. We’ve either, as you said, sought congressional approval, as is required by the Constitution, or it’s been for limited national security means. But usually those have also come along with the “My fellow Americans” from the Oval Office statement, not a middle-of-the-night video released via Truth Social, where there are myriad reasons revealed.

In that statement on Feb. 28, the president said, “To the great, proud people of Iran, I say tonight that the hour of your freedom is at hand,” which sounds a lot like regime change, and that’s ——

French: That is the natural meaning of those words.

Nelson: Correct. Yeah. Why now was not entirely clear, and what we are trying to accomplish is not entirely clear. And that all leads into the fact that, as I said, starting on Feb. 28, this war was already underwater. The administration never felt like they needed to make the case for it, I think in part because they modeled this after Venezuela. It would be over before we ever had to make a justification, and it would be seen as gloriously victorious. That has not been the case. And I think part of that — I don’t know this for a fact — is if Secretary Hegseth is presenting all rosy information to the American people, he may also be doing that to the president himself, underplaying the risks and saying that the military can accomplish everything that he wants.

French: So let’s talk through the course of the war itself. And so there were a number of goals articulated. At first it seemed to be regime change — “The hour of your liberation is at hand.” And then, mainly through Secretary Marco Rubio, you began to see a bullet-point checklist that this is what we want to accomplish. They changed their tune on regime change pretty quickly. After a few days, it was: Regime change? What regime change? What we really want to do is sink the Navy, cripple the Air Force, degrade — to the point, at least, of potential destruction — their missile and drone arsenal, end any capacity for future nuclear development, and doing so while keeping the Strait of Hormuz open to minimize damage to the American and global economy.

And it seems like they’ve accomplished essentially one of those bullet points, which was destroying a big chunk of Iran’s conventional military. But, as you and I both know, the Iranian Navy and the Iranian Air Force were not keeping us up at night. That was not the source of the danger from the Iranian regime. And so it looks like none of the other objectives have been truly accomplished. And it seems like the definition of victory now, Mike, is changing to: But if we can pry the Strait of Hormuz back open, then we’ve won the conflict.

How are you seeing the actual course of the conflict, and if any of these other goals are going to be accomplished?

Nelson: So going back through, I’m going to go through the negatives and then maybe the causes for hope. So, as you said, regime change, we shouldn’t forget that really what started this whole interest in striking Iran again were the popular protests in January. We talked about the — a lot of talk right now — if there is a justification. As a matter of fact, the administration will counter those who express concerns about the war by basically accusing them of wanting to help Iran get a nuclear weapon, and we will never let Iran have a nuke. I agree with that premise. We did a ——

French: I don’t want that, either.

Nelson: Right. And we did a great deal to set back the Iranian nuclear program in the summer of 2025 with Operation Midnight Hammer. We haven’t done anything, really, since then to affect the nuclear program. We have probably incentivized the Iranians to have even more of a desire for a nuclear weapon as a deterrent, as a trump card to prevent any kind of future attacks. The way they see the president talk about North Korea — you pointed out that we have basically put the Iranian, or specifically the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps Navy, at the bottom of the sea — and that’s a good thing.

But that’s an operational effect. The fact that they are still able to threaten traffic in the Strait of Hormuz means they have found alternate means to affect the maritime domain. We have destroyed a fair amount of their missile capability, and they’ve used a lot of it. But as we’ve seen in reporting, Iran may have retained more of their missile capability than we originally thought, and also, as has been reported, we have used a fair amount of our interceptors defending the region against these.

Opening the strait, as you point out, it’s not a goal of the war because it was the condition that existed before. It’s just a condition that we need to correct because of the war. We have now, I believe, settled into the best of all bad options.

French: I was going to ask that. Have we learned here? Just from a military perspective, are we doing better? And if so, how?

Nelson: So there was a lot of focus last week, when Time released the transcript of their interview with President Trump, and they asked him why he had rejected an Iranian cease-fire negotiation, and he said: Because I wouldn’t agree to something now that I wouldn’t have agreed to a year ago, and it has to be more than the strait.

That was an excellent answer from the president. The resolution of the war has to be more about relieving those conditions I just listed, where we are, in almost every aspect, worse off than we were a year ago.

And the smart play is now the long-term blockade and economic pressure against Iran. The downside of that is that it’s going to exacerbate, or at least keep in the fore, some of the economic pressures that have affected American consumers. But again, the war’s unpopular. Gas prices are not going to go down before the midterms, which is, I’m sure, front of mind for the president, and it’s going to require — kind of like George W. Bush did after the 2006 midterm “thumping,” as he referred to it — he still, despite the unpopularity of the Iraq war, made the correct decision to pursue what was known in the United States as “the surge,” but which enabled the Sahwa, the Sunni Awakening in Iraq, and helped stabilize the region.

The president is going to need to resist the urge for dramatic means, and to keep the course of economic pressure, I think. That’s the best option he has.

French: I’m glad you brought up the surge because one of the things — as I wrote this some time ago — the only thing worse than starting an unconstitutional war is losing an unconstitutional war. And that seemed to be what we were on the verge of. Are you seeing this administration essentially reaching a point where, if it achieves reopening the strait, they’ll then just declare victory and then say, “It’s essentially over. We won”? How do you think this thing actually ends here in the real world?

Nelson: I think, and I don’t mean to overuse an expression, but the devil’s in the details. I do think that, No. 1, there’s going to be some agreement about reopening the strait, but there will probably, for the president to accept it, be some kind of language about an agreement on the nuclear program. I think the most likely place that we will fail to achieve our objectives is we are going to sell out the Iranian people. The Iranian people are going to continue to be oppressed, and probably even more so. In the memorandum of understanding, there was language about us not interfering with the domestic affairs of the Iranian regime, which meant, I think, de facto turning a blind eye to future repression, executions, human rights abuses, etc. So I do think there’s going to be a range of options.

We have the strait and nuclear program at the top, with the strait being the most easily discernible — whether it’s legitimate or not — and then support to the Iranian people at the bottom. Somewhere in there, we’re going to find a range of what we’re going to agree to.

French: I could talk to you forever, but let’s kind of wind down here. Let’s put on a different hat for you. We’re recording this less than a month before the midterms. All indications seem to be that the Democrats will improve their position — at the very least, maybe take one, maybe two chambers. If they do take control of Congress, what should they do to constrain Trump and Hegseth? What should they not do? Put on your “I’m advising Democrats for the good of the service and for the good of national security” hat.

Nelson: Well, I think one of the immediate questions is that the Massie-Hegseth impeachment motion will have to be voted on. So that’s going to, at a minimum, cause embarrassment for the administration and for Secretary Hegseth himself, because I don’t think it’s likely he’s going to be removed from office, but I do think it’s likely he’s going to get more votes against him than he probably realizes. And that will probably cause embarrassment for all involved.

I do think there’s a chance, if the president is unaware of how unpopular the Iran war is, that after the midterms he may seek to find someone, just as Secretary Donald Rumsfeld resigned after the 2006 midterms, that Secretary Hegseth may be not long for this world in the administration if the president looks for someone to point the finger to.

The other thing we’ve seen right now with the lame-duck Republicans who the president did not support in their primaries and now have basically nothing to lose — many of them went along with some of the War Powers votes to restrain the war in Iran. And I do think there’s a danger in those kinds of votes becoming more popular as, No. 1, after the elections, when there are more Republicans potentially who have nothing to lose during the lame-duck session; or in the new Congress, when there’s even less of a red representation in the legislature. I think that highlights the importance of the president making the case that he has not made yet, neither to the American people nor to Congress, why it is important. He defaults to these very short bumper-sticker answers: We should pay more for high gas prices than Iran getting a nuclear weapon.

There needs to be more of an explanation for what the long-term strategy is. Again, I think he has settled on the best option available, which is long-term imposition of economic pain and blockade of Iran. That is the one most likely to achieve any kind of success, but that’s going to require more support that he currently does not have.

French: All right. That’s a great way to end it, Mike. Thank you so much for joining me. I really appreciate it.

Nelson: Thanks for having me.

Thoughts? Email us at theopinions@nytimes.com.

SUMMARY

(It’s worth noting that many of the elite, popular and highly ranked private schools in Texas refused to accept vouchers this year.) In Iowa, which has a universal voucher program for private schools that’s similar to Texas’, the Democratic candidate for governor and the current auditor, Rob Sand, has made a similar connection between vouchers, special interests and corruption. Though the Texas vouchers prioritize students with disabilities, The Observer also noted that most of the private Texas schools they analyzed lack special education services.

ARTICLE

Billionaires Love This School Policy. Many Regular Parents Hate It.
In Texas and Iowa, Democrats are successfully tying universal school vouchers to corruption.
By Jessica Grose
Published 2026-10-07 09:07 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/opinion/school-vouchers-midterms.html

“I’ve been voting Republican my whole life. I’m super conservative,” Pine Tree superintendent Steve Clugston tells the camera in an Instagram reel. “I’m gonna tell you what, when Greg Abbott sold us out to the billionaires and sold out our schools, I’m done with his leadership.” In the Texas governor’s race, Clugston is voting for Abbott’s Democratic opponent, State Representative Gina Hinojosa.

The Pine Tree public school district is in the bright red, small city of Longview in East Texas, between the big cities of Dallas and Shreveport, La. The majority of its 4,400 students are economically disadvantaged. When I caught up with Clugston on Friday, hours before the Pine Tree football team trounced its opponents under the lights, he was at his farm. “My wife’s a teacher, my daughter’s a teacher, my son-in-law’s a teacher, both my sisters are teachers, my brother-in law’s a retired superintendent. So I’d say education’s kind of in our blood,” he told me over the phone.

Clugston told me he’s sick of his fellow Texas conservatives straying from their principles of fiscal common sense and straight talk; he even attempted a run for the Texas State Senate as an independent conservative. He is particularly appalled by Texas’ voucher program, known as Texas Education Freedom Accounts, which went into effect earlier this year. This program puts state money in accounts for Texas families to use outside the public school system: up to nearly $10,500 for children enrolling in private school, up to $30,000 for children with disabilities and up to $2,000 for those who are home-schooled.

The State of Texas has no say over the curriculum taught at the institutions that accept vouchers, and participating schools can discriminate against applicants for any number of reasons, including religion and disability status. Texas’ vouchers are universal, which means anyone can apply for them, regardless of financial means, though poorer students have been prioritized.

Around 70 percent of this year’s voucher recipients were already enrolled in private or home- school. Vouchers are costing the state about a billion dollars this year alone, and could ultimately end up costing $4.4 billion annually. While funding for vouchers comes from a budget that is separate from the public school pot, the state’s funding for public schools has not kept up with inflation.

Texas public schools will lose a projected $227 million just this year, as they shed head count, according to The Houston Chronicle. More public schools may close as a result of vouchers siphoning that money away from them. In Clugston’s opinion, vouchers are “a billion-dollar giveaway program for the rich and we’re gonna have no accountability in it. Zero.”

Hinojosa has made saving public education central to her campaign for governor, and it is what got her started in politics. Her child’s school was on the brink of closure, and she describes her political trajectory as concerned parent, to local school board member, to Texas House member. If elected, Hinojosa has vowed to “end the voucher scam.”

I have long been frustrated at the way both parties barely talk about K-12 public education, despite plunging test scores and post-Covid woes. But the reason politicians don’t talk more about education is because voters don’t care about it. What makes Hinojosa’s message on schools effective beyond irate public school parents and educators is that she ties the passage of vouchers to larger themes plaguing Republicans in the age of Trump: corruption and the outsize power of billionaires.

Vouchers failed in the Texas Legislature multiple times, with rural Republicans tending to side with Democrats to block the measures. In rural areas, “school choice,” even with vouchers, tends to be a mirage. There are few private schools, and public schools are often the biggest local employers and the heart of small-town life; nearly every Texan I spoke to for this newsletter said the reverence for “Friday Night Lights” is real.

When Gov. Greg Abbott couldn’t get vouchers passed the honorable way, he decided to primary Republican state legislators who opposed the policy. Abbott took $12 million from Jeff Yass, a pro-voucher Pennsylvania billionaire, got most of his preferred candidates into office, and got vouchers passed in 2025, as The Washington Post noted.

The outcomes for students participating in voucher programs in other states have been decidedly mixed, but Yass doesn’t give a rip. “If the mother or the parent wants the kid to go from one school to another, who the hell is anyone to tell them not to?” Yass told The Post. “I don’t care what the studies say.”

Yass isn’t the only billionaire who meddled in vouchers in the Lone Star State. The religious Texas billionaires Tim Dunn and Farris and Dan Wilks, have also poured money into pro-voucher candidates over the years. As The Texas Tribune explains, “Dunn is also the founder of Midland Classical Academy, a private school that offers its approximately 600 K-12 students a ‘Classical Education from a Biblical Worldview,’ according to its website.” (It’s worth noting that many of the elite, popular and highly ranked private schools in Texas refused to accept vouchers this year.)

Some voucher proponents claim that Texas offers more choice to underprivileged children in underperforming schools. But the data we have on other states with universal voucher programs, like Arizona’s, suggest that they are redistributing money to the highest income and most educated ZIP codes in cities and suburbs. An Arizona ABC station found that parents were spending their voucher money on everything from trampoline parks to ski tickets.

In Iowa, which has a universal voucher program for private schools that’s similar to Texas’, the Democratic candidate for governor and the current auditor, Rob Sand, has made a similar connection between vouchers, special interests and corruption. “The current school voucher program is an open invitation to waste, fraud and abuse of taxpayer dollars,” Sand explains on his campaign website.

Sand lists his voucher stance under the headline Accountability for All, where he also talks about protections for whistle-blowers and banning stock trading. By doing so, Sand is saying that you don’t have to care about what’s going on in the classroom to be outraged that a New York-based company called Odyssey, which manages his state’s voucher program, allegedly got a “sweetheart” deal for the work. As auditor, Sand found that the company “more than doubled its rate less than a month after signing their no-bid contract, costing taxpayers an additional $2.7 million.” (Odyssey, which has ties to Yass, also administers the voucher system in Texas.)

Whatever you think about public schools, it is difficult not to seethe at the fundamental unfairness of voucher programs that give money to schools that don’t have to educate all students. The Texas Observer found that of 291 private schools approved for voucher funds from the state, over 90 percent were religious or faith-based schools, “more than 100 of those schools require or prioritize for admission students of the same faith, and more than 60 have a written policy that discriminates against L.G.B.T.Q.+ students, the schools’ own data shows.”

Though the Texas vouchers prioritize students with disabilities, The Observer also noted that most of the private Texas schools they analyzed lack special education services. A Dallas Morning News analysis found that thousands of students with disabilities returned state money, in part because private schools either rejected them or didn’t even respond to their applications.

Some educators I spoke to in both Texas and Iowa told me that they’d already seen students ricocheting back to public schools because their private or home-school experience wasn’t all it was chalked up to be. Another outrageous part of this legislation is that Texas public schools are still required to do the disability testing for families that choose vouchers, and it’s straining their limited resources.

When put to a public vote, school vouchers have been unpopular; they’re perennial losers on the ballot. It’s maddening that ideologically motivated billionaires, who likely never sent their own children to public schools, have been able to push this policy through.

According to the latest New York Times/Siena University polling, Hinojosa is up by four points, and Sand is up by 11. Texas is obviously the tougher battle, but after spending the week talking to parents there, I’m cautiously optimistic. Rebekah Baus, who described herself as a conservative Christian and lives in the Dallas-Fort Worth area with her husband and two kids, told me she is so upset about the state of public school policy that she doesn’t know which way she is voting.

The State of Texas, Baus said, is trying to pretend “our public school system is failing, but in the reality, we’re failing our public school system by not funding them properly.”

End Notes

- Rural schools tend to be particularly ill served by vouchers. If your rural school is closing, or at risk of closure for any reason (including a declining population of children), I want to hear from you: drop me a line.
- ProPublica has been doing excellent work on vouchers and the lack of oversight into vouchers and private schools. They tried to start a fake private school as an experiment and found that the requirements were so scant, “we could enroll students in two states right now, if we wanted to. Arkansas even suggested ways our school could accept public money through the state’s voucher-style program.” They even created a quiz to show how “many states invite anyone with a dream and a heartbeat to start a school.” Take it here, you’ll be shocked.
- Given that I adored the Sharon Horgan show “Catastrophe,” I was not surprised to find that I also love her new HBO show “Youth.” Horgan plays Alex, a divorced literary agent who is struggling with sandwich generation headaches while she tries to get back into dating. Her 18-year-old won’t launch, her ex-husband pretty much stopped parenting and her parents are in poor health. Horgan always manages to make the mess of life into something funny and real, and I want half her outfits. (If someone can source her booties or the perfect cropped sweatshirt she wears in Episode 1, please tell me.)

The Trump Outrages Keep Piling Up
Readers react to President Trump’s “take out Los Angeles” remarks and his ethics flaws. Also: Climate risk; colleges and A.I.

Jonathan P. Levin Northampton, Mass.

twilight-zone-tv-america.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 16  Words: 1201/1290

SUMMARY

Before he created “The Twilight Zone,” Rod Serling was stuck. Serling didn’t want to make that kind of show. With “The Twilight Zone,” Serling realized he could use allegory to make his political points.

ARTICLE

America Feels Trapped in the Twilight Zone. This Man Can Help.
With “The Twilight Zone,” Rod Serling created a durable blueprint for understanding our surreal reality.
By Alan Sepinwall
Published 2026-10-07 19:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/opinion/twilight-zone-tv-america.html

Before he created “The Twilight Zone,” Rod Serling was stuck. He’d established a reputation in the TV industry as, basically, Aaron Sorkin before Aaron Sorkin: a celebrated writer of weighty adult dramas that grappled with big contemporary issues like political corruption or the dehumanizing nature of corporate life.

He also frequently battled sponsors over what he was allowed to write and how far his scripts could go. When he worked to create a fictionalized version of the 1955 lynching of the Black teenager Emmett Till, for example, the final product was so watered down by sponsor and network pressure that it resulted in what he’d later describe in an interview with Mike Wallace as “a lukewarm, vitiated, emasculated kind of show.”

Serling didn’t want to make that kind of show. So after he was instructed to remove virtually all references to contemporary politics from a teleplay about a United States senator titled “The Arena,” he had a realization: “I probably would have had a much more adult play had I made it science fiction, put it in the year 2057, and peopled the Senate with robots,” he wrote of that experience.

Serling apparently applied the lesson of “The Arena” to a broader canvas, as he started writing speculative stories that were at sharp right angles to our own reality, in an anthology series that premiered in 1959 with the title “The Twilight Zone.” Because the series, which often featured fantastical scenarios, always with a surprising final twist, was so stylized, Serling found he could finally tell the unvarnished truth.

Almost 70 years later, at a moment when our own situation can seem increasingly ominous and surreal — when it’s hard to look anywhere, from political corruption to corporate malfeasance to the barrage of everyday headlines, without feeling as if you’ve traveled into a fifth dimension, beyond that which is known to man — Serling’s shrewd tactic for addressing political subjects offers an instructive response.

Contemporary television has often struggled to respond to the current political darkness; while shows like “The Good Fight” directly confronted the first Trump administration, few shows have done that during the second term. Some satires like “South Park” have taken direct aim, while others like “Saturday Night Live” have often seemed at sea when it comes to dealing with political turmoil.

With “The Twilight Zone,” Serling realized he could use allegory to make his political points. After all, how could a network censor or a viewer angrily insist that a story was saying something controversial about the world when it centered on a three-armed Martian?

This might help explain why “The Twilight Zone” still seems so incredibly — and at times, depressingly — relevant. Serling and his collaborators repeatedly and stealthily tackled such subjects as prejudice, creeping authoritarianism, the dangers of humans being replaced by technology and the peril of conformity as a societal ideal in ways that still resonate. Many episodes, when rewatched now, feel like they could have been written five minutes ago.

The show hit on social questions we have yet to adequately answer. Serling, a Jewish American who enlisted in the Army to fight Nazis during World War II, wrote often with his collaborators about the dangers of fascism and how easily people can succumb to its allure, including in such episodes as “The Obsolete Man” (a librarian is sentenced to death in a dystopia where books are outlawed) and “He’s Alive” (a hatemonger rises to power through coaching from Hitler’s ghost). In “The Brain Center at Whipple’s,” an aloof owner of a manufacturing plant gleefully replaces his flesh-and-blood workers with machines, unmoved by pleas from his former factory manager about the value of human thought and emotion; eventually, he himself is replaced by a robot.

“Number 12 Looks Just Like You” is set in a future where everyone upon turning 19 is forcibly transplanted into one of a handful of conventionally attractive bodies. It’s like today scrolling an Instagram feed where everyone is using the same filters or going down a rabbit hole about looksmaxxing. And the impulsive, destructive behavior of President Trump has often been likened to aspects of the plot of “It’s a Good Life,” an episode about an omnipotent child named Anthony Fremont who holds an entire town under his thumb.

Serling’s influence is evident all over modern culture. A legion of current storytellers, in television, film and literature, owe him a debt, from Steven Spielberg to Guillermo del Toro, from Curry Barker (as seen in his 2026 horror hit “Obsession”) to Ryan Coogler (“Sinners”). Charlie Brooker, creator of the anthology series “Black Mirror,” has talked about what he learned from Serling’s use of genre devices and the freedom they gave Serling to say what he wanted to say. “If he hadn’t had that rock for the river to flow around,” Mr. Brooker told me, “would the stories feel so resonant now? Or would we only read about them in academic books about the history of television?” Mr. Brooker went on to note: “Because he was forced to enter the world of metaphor, it’s the thing that gives him a superpower.”

Serling’s storytelling superpower grew from a desire to regain a lost affection for humanity — another effort that might prove instructive to us today. During his service as a paratrooper in the Pacific theater of World War II, a teenage Serling witnessed people dying under gruesome, often pointless circumstances. At 20, he watched as a close friend was decapitated in front of him by, of all things, a supply crate dropped from an airplane, and soon came perilously close to death himself.

These experiences left him traumatized and despairing about the depths to which his fellow man was capable of sinking. They also forced Serling to examine why people so often make terrible choices and whether there’s hope for them to do better in the future, a theme that would animate his TV writing. In “The Twilight Zone,” characters are often offered a magical second chance — and the ones who can’t change frequently earn karmic justice of a supernatural variety.

Despite his celebrity and acclaim — and his unnerving prescience — Serling struggled with self-doubt for much of his career. In the years leading up to his 1975 death of a heart attack at the age of 50, he gave an interview suggesting his accomplishments would soon be forgotten.

“I’ve written articulate stuff, reasonably bright stuff over the years, but nothing that will stand the test of time,” he said in 1972. “The good writing, really good writing — like wine — has to age well with the years, and my stuff is momentarily adequate.”

Not only did Serling underestimate his influence, but he also failed to see how the tactic he adapted would prove to be the most successful way to process perilous times. If the Serling who gave that interview could, like some of his characters, travel forward through time, he might be dismayed that so many of the problems he wrote about still aren’t resolved decades later. But he would also see that the best way to describe the legacy of his work isn’t “momentarily adequate,” but a different phrase he repeatedly recited as the host of “The Twilight Zone”: “as timeless as infinity.”

Alan Sepinwall is a TV critic, most recently for Rolling Stone, and the author of the forthcoming “Serling: A Journey Into the Twilight Zone With TV’s First Visionary.”
