To students and teachers at Paul Éluard, that investment doesn’t do enough to reverse decades of neglect, both at the school and in the wider district.

ARTICLE

The School Near Paris That Shows Why French Students Are Protesting
Angered by poor classroom conditions, students at Paul Éluard High School in a suburb of the capital were among the first to blockade their campus during an ongoing round of unrest.
By Ségolène Le Stradic
Published 2026-10-07 09:55 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/world/europe/france-school-protest-paul-eluard.html

When students at Paul Éluard, a high school in a working-class suburb north of Paris, arrived for the first day of school, they found classrooms lacking chairs, tables and reliable electricity, students and teachers said. With the school under renovation, students were being taught instead in prefabricated buildings with bad insulation, filthy toilets and regular power outages, they said.

Then came the staffing shortage. Two mathematics professors were moved to another school, leaving no one to cover their classes for over a week. There were no replacements for the school’s absent psychologist or careers adviser, they said, and there was only a single part-time nurse to provide on-site medical care to roughly 2,000 students.

“It was a completely chaotic way to welcome students,” said Irène Cailleteau, a mathematics teacher at Paul Éluard since 2020. “It was an extremely difficult way to start the year.”

Those are among the frustrations that have fueled a surge of student protests since late September, both at Paul Éluard — one of the wellsprings of the unrest — and at hundreds of high schools across France.

Thousands of students, sometimes backed by teachers like Ms. Cailleteau, have blockaded their schools to protest widespread teacher shortages, creaking school infrastructure and grueling schedules — and to demand an overhaul of the national system that allocates places in higher education programs.

The movement, which was bolstered on Tuesday by union-led rallies in more than 40 French cities, has divided the country and inflamed political tensions, particularly after many demonstrations descended into violence. Some protesters have shot off mortar-style fireworks, burned public buildings and looted shops, while rights groups and jurists have accused the police of disproportionate force. In just over two weeks, more than 6,500 people have been arrested, and more than 750 police officers, as well as roughly 300 students and staff members, have been injured, according to French officials.

At the demonstrations at Paul Éluard, footage showed largely peaceful protesters, disrupted by some participants who pulled down part of the school fence and set fires in the street outside. That led the authorities in late September to order the school’s closure, ban protests in front of it and arrest several students.

The school’s principal and the local branch of the Education Ministry declined to comment on the accounts in this article. The office of the regional president, Valérie Pécresse, said that her administration had recently invested about $50 million to improve the school, which is among more than 50 in the area, a suburb called Seine-St.-Denis, that has been newly renovated.

To students and teachers at Paul Éluard, that investment doesn’t do enough to reverse decades of neglect, both at the school and in the wider district.

In Seine-St.-Denis, a sprawling area with a large immigrant community, the unemployment and poverty rates far exceed the national average. That inequity is mirrored in the district’s education system: 61 percent of middle and high schools in Seine-St.-Denis and its neighboring areas had a missing teacher at the start of the year, according to a survey by a major labor union of more than 1,000 French schools. That was eight points higher than the national average.

“The problem is national, but it’s three times as bad in the suburbs,” said Bilel Narjissi, a senior at Paul Éluard and a member of the school’s student council.

Recent students and teachers at Paul Éluard said classes had spent an entire school year without a professor in some subjects, including philosophy, which heavily affected students’ preparation for their senior exams.

France’s education minister, Édouard Geffray, said on Tuesday that the number of teaching vacancies had fallen by more than half over the past year.

But students said they had yet to feel meaningful change.

Zakarya Boukhadda, a 16-year-old at Paul Éluard, said at a rally this week that there weren’t enough special educators at the school, especially “for students with neurodivergent conditions or autism like myself.”

Frustrations That Boiled for Years

Paul Éluard, founded in 1965, was named for a French writer whose poem “Liberté” became a widely read ode to freedom during World War II.

Over time, the school bearing his name became synonymous with decline.

In May 2023, staff members created a social media account comparing the high school to the Titanic. Pictures and videos showed cracked and crumbling walls, leaking or collapsed ceilings, and flooded floors. Those conditions were also described in interviews with former and current students, who recalled rats scouring the hallways.

In late 2024, regional officials reported finding parts of the school in a state of disrepair, warning of fire doors that had been wedged shut, a blocked emergency exit and signs of vandalism.

Ms. Pécresse’s office said that the regional government had tried to resolve the structural problems at the school, including by waterproofing its buildings, adding fire doors and providing more security, as well as investing the $50 million, about 45 million euros, which would go toward “a comprehensive transformation of the entire site.”

But to the students and their supporters, those additions are too little too late and have left students cooped up in substandard temporary buildings while the renovation goes on.

Bally Bagayoko, a far-left local mayor, told journalists at a rally on Sunday that the regional council’s response was “contemptuous.”

“They say, ‘We’re giving you 45 million,’” said Mr. Bagayoko, who has often joined demonstrations in solidarity with the students. “That means, ‘Be satisfied with what we’re giving you, be happy that we’re giving you anything at all,’” he added.

Mr. Bagayoko, 53, grew up in the area and recalled studying in badly insulated buildings when he was a student himself.

“How many times did I sit in a classroom where there was so much construction going on?” he asked. “We were sitting there in our coats because we were freezing our butts off,” he added. “That’s why it’s unbearable to see those who have the power to act pretending that they’re just now discovering this.”

Ms. Pécresse has dismissed Mr. Bagayoko as a rabble-rouser, pledging on social media to send him “the bill for the 100,000-euro replacement of the gate at Paul Éluard High School.”

“Let the mayor take responsibility for his actions,” she added. “I’ve taken responsibility for mine: a complete renovation of the high school.”

For some at Paul Éluard, the conditions at the schools compound the perception that the national leaders care little for the area or its alienated and underprivileged residents, many of whose families come from France’s former colonies in Africa.

“They simply don’t care about us,” said Zorah Adrachi, 19, who graduated from Paul Éluard in the summer hoping to study psychology or train as a teacher. Despite passing her senior exams, an achievement that generally guarantees entry to university, Ms. Adrachi is among thousands of young high school graduates who have not been offered a place on a higher education program, leaving her in limbo.

Mr. Narjissi, the student council member, who wore the French tricolor on the collar of his woolen coat, said he would not give up the fight for better learning conditions.

“Maybe our parents didn’t dare pursue executive careers or positions of responsibility,” he said. “But tomorrow we’ll be the members of Parliament, we’ll be the mayors, and we’ll keep going and we won’t give up.”

SUMMARY

María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home two weeks ago prompted widespread protests in Spain and spurred the prime minister to call national elections, died on Wednesday. The eviction touched a nerve among Spaniards fed up with a housing crisis. Ms. Abascal’s eviction marked a “turning point” in Spain, putting housing at the center of the national debate, her representatives said.

ARTICLE

‘Maricarmen,’ Whose Eviction Enraged Spaniards, Dies at 87
María del Carmen Abascal, aged and ailing, became a symbol of the country’s housing crisis when she was evicted two weeks ago, prompting mass protests and triggering national elections.
By Carlos Barragán
Published 2026-10-07 19:34 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/world/europe/maricarmen-dies-spain-housing-sanchez.html

María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home two weeks ago prompted widespread protests in Spain and spurred the prime minister to call national elections, died on Wednesday.

“We regret to announce that Maricarmen passed away today,” her representatives said in a statement, using the shortened form of her given names, by which Ms. Abascal had become widely known across Spain. They did not give a cause of death.

Ms. Abascal was evicted on Sept. 23 from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than 70 years, after police broke down her door. She was carried out on a stretcher and admitted to a hospital suffering from exhaustion.

Days later, as her condition failed to improve, her lawyer reached an agreement with the company that owned the apartment that would have allowed her to return once she was discharged.

“This solution came too late,” said the statement, signed by the tenants’ union, her lawyer and her family. “An absolutely avoidable situation following an agonizing process.”

The eviction touched a nerve among Spaniards fed up with a housing crisis. Tens of thousands of people, many of them young, took to the streets for days across the country, protesting skyrocketing rents and evictions, and singing “we are all Maricarmen.” Hundreds have also camped in Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s most famous square, and have no plans to clear out.

“This is not an eviction, this is murder,” hundreds of demonstrators chanted in the square on Wednesday evening, according to footage from Spain’s public broadcaster.

The eviction also brought about the end of the minority government of the left-wing prime minister, Pedro Sánchez. He called snap elections for Nov. 29, after a housing bill he presented last week, aimed at restricting evictions and freezing rents, was rejected in Parliament by a majority of conservative legislators.

“My deepest sympathies to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” Mr. Sánchez said on social media. “A warm embrace as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today.”

Born in 1938, Ms. Abascal worked as secretary for a pharmaceutical company, according to the newspaper El País. She retired in 1998 and spent her retirement walking around her leafy, affluent Madrid neighborhood close to the Retiro Park and taking care of paintings and porcelain pieces at home.

She had moved with her family to the apartment in the 1950s. Her father held the lease and later passed it on to his wife, who in turn transferred the rent-controlled lease to Ms. Abascal in 2005.

In 2020, the property was bought by the company Urbagestión, which sought to more than triple her monthly rent, which had been 500 euros, or about $570, according to her lawyer, Beatriz Duro. That was far more than Ms. Abascal, living on a €1,450 monthly pension, could afford.

The owners of Urbagestión, who did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday, have previously disputed the account of the rent increase and said Ms. Abascal was simply not legally entitled to remain under the rent-controlled lease.

The yearslong legal battle between them ended with Spain’s Supreme Court siding with the landlord and approving the eviction.

On Sept. 23, after three failed attempts in previous months, the police removed Ms. Abascal from her apartment, after clearing out hundreds of activists who had barricaded the building to shield her. Her case quickly drew international attention and prompted the national government to respond.

“I wasn’t able to defend my home, but I did fight so that others can learn to fight for theirs,” Ms. Abascal said from her hospital bed after the eviction.

Days later, amid growing pressure, Ms. Abascal’s lawyer announced that she had reached a deal with the building owner that would allow her to return home. Under the agreement, she would have received an eight-year lease with a monthly rent equal to 30 percent of her pension, or about $460.

Ms. Abascal’s eviction marked a “turning point” in Spain, putting housing at the center of the national debate, her representatives said. Spaniards, especially young people with low salaries, are finding it increasingly difficult to rent homes in many cities, as an influx of tourists, immigrants and wealthy foreign buyers adds to demand, while sluggish construction and a shortage of public housing constrain supply.

Spain has a housing shortfall of about 755,000 homes, according to the Bank of Spain.

Despite a sharp decline in evictions — to about 25,000 last year, from around 68,000 in 2014 — the issue remains politically delicate for the government, particularly after Mr. Sánchez promised before taking office to end them. The role of a real estate company in Ms. Abascal’s eviction also angered many on the left, who accuse private investment firms of driving up housing costs in Spain.

Mr. Sánchez blamed his conservative opponents for Ms. Abascal’s eviction, pointing to their role in defeating legislation in February that would have restricted evictions like hers.

The prime minister’s previous housing polices expanded tenants’ rights, but right-wing parties have argued that they hurt small property owners and encourage squatting. In 2025, the conservative regional president of Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, called Mr. Sánchez an “accomplice” of squatters.

On Tuesday, after calling snap elections following the defeat of his recent bill, Mr. Sánchez said his government would pass a similar measure through a smaller parliamentary body that remains active after Parliament is dissolved. He also called on voters to deliver a “progressive majority in Parliament,” framing the election in part as a choice between moneyed elites and everyday people.

“When Congress turns its back on what people are experiencing in the streets, the government cannot look the other way,” Mr. Sánchez said.

The full ramifications of Ms. Abascal’s eviction remain to be seen. The tenants’ union, along with labor unions, has called a general strike for November in response, and her case is likely to loom over the election campaign.

Ms. Abascal’s representatives, who asked that the family’s privacy be respected, said her death would strengthen their determination to “defend the right to housing and fight against speculators.”

“And above all, we will honor what she always asked of us,” the statement said: “Fight, keep fighting for what is yours.”

Rubio Urges Europe to Awaken From ‘Slumber’ and Uphold Western Dominance
In Greece, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Western nations must embrace an earlier ethos of exploration and conquest as part of their civilization, to remain ‘at the head of the world.’

Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Wednesday for Western nations to rejuvenate their civilization so they can maintain their dominance in a world of wars, economic uncertainty and technological change.

“Today, we find ourselves at a crossroads,” Mr. Rubio said in a speech in Athens, with the Acropolis and Parthenon bathed in the golden light of a Mediterranean sunset behind him.

“The next decade will write the story of the next century,” he said. “The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, servitude and decline. We’ll either choose to act now, or lose the choice to act at all.”

Mr. Rubio’s speech sought to highlight the ideological tenets of an American conservative movement whose adherents see President Trump as their leader.

Some of its intellectual architects argue that citizens of the United States and Europe should not apologize for the choices made by their ancestors, including exploration and conquest of other peoples and lands. Instead, they say, citizens should embrace that earlier ethos, as their countries seek an edge in the military and economic competition with China and other non-Western powers.

Men of ancient Greece, Mr. Rubio said, “knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor in fighting to defend its interests above all else.”

“They believed — fiercely — in the ideal of the ‘great man’: the exceptional individual who obtains immortality through his own deeds,” he added.

Mr. Rubio’s visit to Greece was the centerpiece of a three-nation European tour, and it was the second time he has used the continent as a backdrop for an ideological speech.

His remarks in Athens echoed lines he delivered to European leaders in a February speech at the Munich Security Conference, where he spoke of the possible “civilizational erasure” of Europe. However, in the new speech, Mr. Rubio did not use that contentious phrase — one embraced by far-right American and European nationalists pushing for strict limits on immigration.

As he did in Munich, Mr. Rubio praised the builders of empires — Alexander the Great, who conquered the “entire known world” (an exaggeration of the size of the territory he controlled), as well as Julius Caesar, Charlemagne and Hernán Cortés — the Spanish conquistador whose troops violently toppled the Aztec rulers of Mexico.

Mr. Rubio also talked about crimes committed against ancient Greece by a Persian army that ransacked Athens 2,500 years ago. He invoked “the legendary last stand of 300 Spartans” at Thermopylae against the Persians.

With those references, Mr. Rubio was adopting the rhetoric of some conservative commentators, who, during the American wars in the predominantly Muslim countries of Iraq and Afghanistan, emphasized the heroism of the 300 Spartans faced with what they called rapacious warriors from another civilization.

Later in the speech, Mr. Rubio denounced the “radical mullahs of Iran” — the country located on the land of ancient Persia.

He went on to link the philosophical and political pursuits of ancient Greece to “the architects of European Christendom,” who designed soaring cathedrals, and to colonial settlers, who embodied “the American frontier spirit.”

“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was here millennia ago,” he said.

Nations, he said, must have “the ability to wield force when prudence and diplomacy fail.”

Mr. Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, criticized Western governments that had “opened our borders” in recent decades, a theme he also addressed at a news conference on Wednesday morning.

There, he called for greater cooperation between the United States and Greece to restrict migration and immigration.

“Greece is also a very close strategic partner on border security and the fight against mass migration,” Mr. Rubio said while standing beside Giorgios Gerapetritis, the Greek foreign minister.

“What we do not wish to see under any circumstances is that the birthplace of the West is threatened by bad decisions, by actions, by failure to address challenges,” Mr. Rubio added.

Mr. Gerapetritis told reporters that Greece was trying to address “challenges” from “mass migration.”

Mr. Rubio also praised Greece for being on track to spend at least 5 percent of its annual gross domestic product on defense, a benchmark that Mr. Trump insists NATO allies must meet.

Mr. Rubio is scheduled to fly to Portugal on Thursday, his third stop on a tour that started in Iceland.

After the news conference, he visited the U.S. Embassy, where he was introduced to a crowd by Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former romantic partner of Donald Trump Jr., the eldest son of the American president.

When asked at the news conference about the allegations, Mr. Rubio said he would not discuss them in public.

“Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here,” he said, as Ms. Guilfoyle sat in front of him.

SUMMARY

Is there an outbreak of plague in Russia? The slightly longer answer: A woman who works in a remote Siberian lab that studies plague has died of pneumonia. Based on what we know so far, no. For all the unknowns, experts say that even if plague were confirmed in Shipilova’s death, the risk of widespread contagion would be limited.

ARTICLE

What to Know About the Fears of a Plague Outbreak in Russia
Russian authorities aren’t saying much about the death of a woman who worked in a lab studying plague. But experts say any risk of contagion would be limited.
By The New York Times
Published 2026-10-07 19:30 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/world/europe/russia-plague-fears-what-to-know.html

Is there an outbreak of plague in Russia?

The short answer: We don’t know. The slightly longer answer: A woman who works in a remote Siberian lab that studies plague has died of pneumonia. The lab has been locked down and the Russian authorities aren’t saying much, which has fueled speculation and rumors.

There’s a lot we still don’t know. The Times has gathered all the available information and talked to experts to try to make as much sense of it as possible. (Spoiler alert: Don’t panic.)

Who died, and how?

Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of Irkutsk’s Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, seems to have died of a mysterious pneumonia earlier this month. Her death prompted Russian health authorities to quarantine the hospital where she died, along with the institute’s staff and other people who were in contact with her. So far, so unsettling.

The plague still exists?

Yes. The plague has been with us a very long time. There are still a few hundred cases every year, mostly in Madagascar and Democratic Republic of the Congo, but also in the United States, Russia and other countries.

Many people know the plague as the “Black Death,” a pandemic that is thought to have killed at least a third of Europe’s population in the 14th century.

Yersinia pestis, the bacteria that causes plague, has infected humans for thousands of years, also circulating among rodents and other small mammals, which serve as long-term reservoirs, and fleas, which spread it.

Are we talking about the bubonic plague?

There are three main ways that plague can infect humans: Bubonic plague occurs when the plague-causing bacteria multiplies in the lymph nodes, usually after a bite from an infected flea. Septicemic plague occurs when the infection spreads to the bloodstream. The most virulent type is pneumonic plague, which causes a severe rapid-onset lung infection and can be spread through a cough or sneeze.

Left untreated, pneumonic plague can kill a victim within days. But all three types of plague respond well to antibiotics if they are taken quickly. Based on the information we have so far, most experts aren’t too worried.

Then why the sense of alarm?

The fact that Shipilova worked in a lab studying plague, which is supposed to have robust protections against the microbe escaping, is concerning.

The lack of details from the Russian authorities has unnerved many around the world who remain scarred by the Covid-19 pandemic. At that time, it was an authoritarian government in China, where the virus originated, that covered up information.

In the immediate aftermath of Shipilova’s death, Russian authorities were very terse. They failed to clarify her whereabouts before her death or to address questions about whether an accident had taken place at the institute.

When health officials and the United States government began asking questions, the Russian authorities gave additional information. (On Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it was “incumbent” upon Russia to share more with the world. “We’re watching it very closely, hour by hour,” he said.)

Russia said yesterday that Shipilova had been vaccinated against the disease and no “emergency situations” had been identified at the lab. (One caveat: It’s not clear how effective the available vaccines are.)

Russia’s health regulator also said there are “no epidemiological risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region.”

Has plague ever been used as a bioweapon?

Maybe — but it’s been a while. In the 14th century, according to one account, a Mongol army catapulted plague-infested bodies into the Crimean city of Caffa.

In the modern era, a defector from the Soviet Union’s bioweapons program once claimed his government stockpiled “dozens of tons of smallpox and plague” that could be loaded onto bombs and missiles.

The existence of an active biological weapons program in Russia, which has historically sourced strains from anti-plague institutes, has added to global concerns.

In an annual threat assessment this year, U.S. intelligence agencies said Russian scientists were continuing to develop new chemical and biological weapons capabilities. The State Department, in its arms control compliance report last year, said Russia maintained an offensive biological warfare program in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention.

So should I panic?

Based on what we know so far, no. For all the unknowns, experts say that even if plague were confirmed in Shipilova’s death, the risk of widespread contagion would be limited.

Reporting by Paul Sonne, Edward Wong, Chris Buckley, Oleg Matsnev Milana Mazaeva and Alina Lobzina

ARTICLE

Russia Says It Found No ‘Emergency’ in Plague Lab
New information around the death of a lab worker, including a statement that she had been vaccinated against the plague, came as U.S. officials demanded more data.
By Paul Sonne
Published 2026-10-07 10:39 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/world/europe/russia-plague-us-trump-state-department.html

The Russian authorities said on Wednesday that a researcher at a Siberian anti-plague institute who died from a mysterious pneumonia had been vaccinated against the pathogens she worked with and that no “emergency situations” had occurred at the lab.

Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian health regulator, issued the statement after the United States urged Moscow to be more forthcoming about the possible public health incident and the World Health Organization asked for more information to make an accurate assessment of any threat.

The paucity of details in Russian official statements and the absence of international health officials on the scene have led to questions about the Russian government’s insistence that it has the situation under control. The world has remained on high alert about public health threats in the aftermath of the Covid-19 pandemic.

On Oct. 2, Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old researcher at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Irkutsk, died from pneumonia of an unknown origin at a hospital in Shelekhov, the town where she lived, prompting fears of a pneumonic plague outbreak.

Ms. Shipilova had been vaccinated and therefore “had immunity to the dangerous infections she worked with,” the Russian health regulator said on Wednesday. The statement implied that Ms. Shipilova had a lower risk of contracting the plague, though vaccination would not definitively rule out becoming ill with the disease.

Rospotrebnadzor also said that two commissions monitoring biological safety had inspected the institute. “No emergency situations were identified during work with pathogenic microorganisms,” the health regulator said.

Tests on Ms. Shipilova’s remains, the regulator previously said, had not found evidence of any of the microorganisms she worked with at the institute.

Medical observation has been completed for more than 90 percent of the people Ms. Shipilova had been in contact with, and “no health impairments related to infectious pathology were detected,” the Russian regulator added. Nearly 5,000 laboratory tests revealed no hazardous pathogenic microorganisms, its statement said.

“Preventive and anti-epidemic measures have been organized to an exhaustive extent,” it said in the statement. “There are no epidemiological risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region.”

The Russian authorities released the additional information after the State Department sent a formal diplomatic note, known as a démarche, asking for more detail about what happened.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio also voiced the request publicly on Tuesday during a trip to Iceland, noting that the United States was monitoring the situation.

“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” he said. “We’re watching it very closely, hour by hour.”

Ms. Shipilova’s unexplained death prompted the Russian authorities to quarantine part of the hospital where she was taken, as well as the institute’s staff and other people whom she had come into contact with in her final days. Other facilities in and around Irkutsk also implemented restrictive measures, in some cases as a precaution.

In the immediate aftermath of Ms. Shipilova’s death, the Russian authorities gave only sparing public statements, failing to clarify the researcher’s whereabouts before her death or to address questions about whether an accident had taken place at the institute.

Aleksei Tsydenov, the governor of the Buryatia region, which borders Irkutsk, initially said that Ms. Shipilova had died of the plague, without naming her, and then edited his statement to say that she had “possibly” died from the illness.

The Russian health regulator also waited five days after Ms. Shipilova’s death to reveal her vaccination status. An independent Russian publication, People of Baikal, cited a former intern at the institute who said all employees were vaccinated against the plague as a precaution.

The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, has regularly referred questions to Rospotrebnadzor, which has not held any news conference on the matter. President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia has not publicly commented.

The existence of an active biological weapons program in Russia, which has historically sourced strains from anti-plague institutes, has added to global concerns.

In an annual threat assessment this year, U.S. intelligence agencies said Russian scientists were continuing to develop new chemical and biological weapons capabilities. The State Department, in its arms control compliance report last year, said Russia maintained an offensive biological warfare program in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention.

The relatively thin details from the Russian authorities have unnerved U.S. officials and others around the world who remain scarred by the coronavirus pandemic and efforts by the authoritarian government in China, where the virus originated, to cover up information.

The Chinese government has so far offered a muted response to the reports from Russia.

“China and Russia maintain close exchanges and cooperation in the field of infectious disease prevention and control, including the plague,” Guo Jiakun, a spokesman for the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said on Tuesday in a brief response to a question about whether Moscow had notified Beijing about the possible plague case.

Pneumonic plague causes a severe, rapid-onset lung infection and is considered the most virulent form of the plague. It results from the same bacteria that cause the bubonic and septicemic plagues.

Unlike Covid-19, the disease can be treated effectively with antibiotics, but it must be caught very quickly.

Plague is endemic to Siberia and Russia’s Far East, where the bacteria that causes the disease circulates in wild rodents and their fleas. One of the tasks of institutes like the one in Irkutsk is epidemiological surveillance of such threats.

Experts have said that even if plague were confirmed in the Russian case, the risk of widespread contagion could be limited.

In a statement on Monday, the W.H.O. said that based on available information, “the public health risk to the general population appears to be low.” But on Wednesday, the organization said it had not received sufficient information from Russia to complete a full risk assessment.

The organization’s leader, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said in a statement that the Russian health authorities had informed the W.H.O. that the Irkutsk region had not registered any confirmed cases of the plague. Russia told the agency that an epidemiological investigation had been conducted, with contacts of the deceased observed and tested, and “no high-threat pathogens had been detected.”

Mr. Ghebreyesus said the W.H.O. had requested further information to clarify the cause of the severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures, and media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause.

The New York Times was not immediately able to identify any credible media reports of a second employee from the Siberian institute coming down with pneumonia. In a news conference on Wednesday, Mr. Ghebreyesus said the W.H.O. did not assess whether such reports were credible and could ask for information even based on unverified social media posts.

“We have asked Russia to respond to this,” he said. “Any reporting that comes, we cannot ignore it. And credibility of the media is not our mandate.”

W.H.O. officials said they wanted to establish what caused the pneumonia in Ms. Shipilova and could offer Russia help with additional testing.

Her mother, Svetlana Shipilova, said in an interview with a local Russian news outlet, Glubina, that she was upset about friends believing “nasty stuff” about her child, including an unverified report that suggested her daughter had become ill after breaking a test tube.

“Not all doctors even realize that a test tube is impossible to break. Even if you throw it against a wall,” she said from quarantine. “Only an amateur could say that. Even hypothetically, it’s simply impossible to spill or break. They’re so protected.”

Three people who knew Darya Shipilova echoed that sentiment in comments to The Times, describing her as a diligent and responsible person who was being tarnished with unverified reporting that she had made some sort of mistake at work.

President Trump has offered help to Russia in dealing with the situation, but Russian officials have responded by saying that they have it under control.

“It is always very good when offers of mutual assistance are made,” said Mr. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump told reporters that he would hold a call “very soon” with Mr. Putin to discuss the matter.

Elena Sofina, the deputy mayor in Shelekhov responsible for social affairs, said in a statement on Tuesday that Russian officials could handle the situation themselves. She called the matter “completely under control.”

“A dangerous diagnosis has not been confirmed, but we are still following all protocol measures,” she said, adding, “We continue to work.”

ARTICLE

At Nearly $300,000, Some Recent Duke Graduates Out-Earned All Their Peers
Federal data show Duke math majors earning a bigger median income four years after graduation than any other majors from any school. It’s a small cohort.
By Ron Lieber
Published 2026-10-08 02:58 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/07/your-money/duke-math-major-salaries.html

If you earn $297,029 four years out of college, something probably went right during your four years as an undergraduate.

But neither the math majors at Duke — the school and program that are responsible for that median figure — nor the faculty are doing a chest-beating victory dance.

Duke math majors sit atop a relatively new set of federal earnings figures that became available thanks to legislative and regulatory changes in recent years. To provide both transparency and accountability, the federal College Scorecard website, among other places, now shows what people with different majors earn after graduating from particular institutions.

The current data set has just 17 people from Duke’s math program, since the data measures only graduates from a two-year period starting in 2017 who received federal financial aid. “That definitely made my eyebrows go up,” said Katie McKeown, a Duke math major from the class of 2019 who went on to get a Ph.D. in math and now works for a nonprofit.

A 2025 law designed to provide accountability for schools that produce low earners has also shined a light on schools that lead to affluence. My colleague Arfa Momin and I created a tool where you can search it all — and build a custom list of schools and majors that interest you.

Right behind Duke, in the second and third slots, is Carnegie Mellon University. Its computer science graduates earned $268,121, and its electrical, electronics and communications engineering specialists clocked in at $250,168. Both groups have over 100 people in the data set.

Carnegie Mellon appears three times in the top 30, more than any other school. The university is poised to expand the number of students who can aim that high, thanks to a $3 billion donation last month that will help pay for a new campus in Miami.

The HEA Group, a higher-education research organization and consultancy, sorted and published the new data this year.

In interviews, Duke math whizzes tried to express what the field meant to them and how interested students ought to evaluate the school.

Irina Cristali is a native of Romania who graduated in 2019 and now works as a machine learning research scientist at an artificial intelligence start-up. In trying to figure out who the high earners were, she tried to recall classmates who might be, say, vice presidents of engineering now and could have cashed in for $300,000 or more.

Her stronger memories of Duke were things that college shoppers should seize on beyond earnings. There were opportunities to get one’s name on published research as an undergraduate. Faculty members helped her get an internship offer and counseled her when she felt uneasy about her career direction.

“It was the American mind-set that you don’t have to have your life figured out at 18 or 22,” she said.

Indeed, Dr. McKeown barely had math figured out. She grew up in a single-wide trailer in rural Arkansas and spent two years at Duke in more remedial math classes. She got a 27 percent mark on her first quiz, but free tutoring and an instructor who believed in her helped her stick with the subject.

Duke math majors often study something else, too. “I don’t know a single math major who was only doing math,” said Faisal Alsaadi, who graduated in 2019 and has worked at start-ups in Saudi Arabia. He double-majored in math and economics.

“I like it when I’m able to train young people to think mathematically and then they take it into every part of the world,” said Ezra Miller, a Duke professor. He pointed to three current undergraduates — all double majors — who just won an international math competition by building models to maximize the performance of a soccer team.

Professor Miller does not shy away from the fact that if you want to get a job, it’s good to major in math. “But it does also attract people who are interested in beauty and truth,” he said.

According to math majors from the era in question, professors maintained a kind of studied neutrality about their students’ futures. And they remain wary of narrow methods of measurement.

“I am hesitant to celebrate earnings as the sole marker of educational success,” said Greg Herschlag, a Duke math professor, via email, while emphasizing his enthusiasm for the field and any teenager who pursues it. “I would rather universities and departments be judged not simply by how well their graduates do for themselves, but by how much value they create for others: how much they contribute to society, who benefits from that labor and whether that work is improving people’s lives.”

A Top Fed Official Casts Further Doubt on a Rate Rise This Month
The Federal Reserve is poised to raise interest rates further as it seeks to tame inflation, but that is unlikely to happen until the end of the year.
By Colby Smith
Published 2026-10-08 08:38 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/business/federal-reserve-christopher-waller-rates.html

The prospects that the Federal Reserve will deliver a second straight interest rate increase this month dimmed further on Thursday after a top official joined other central bank policymakers in suggesting that they have flexibility in determining the timing of subsequent moves.

Christopher J. Waller, a Fed governor, emphasized in a speech on Thursday that the Fed still had more work to do to bring inflation back to its 2 percent target after nearly six years of overshooting it. Mr. Waller endorsed “additional hikes” to support a speedier retreat to that level, but he did not convey an immediate urgency.

“If the economic data continue to come in as expected, I anticipate additional hikes to support a timelier return of inflation to our 2 percent goal,” Mr. Waller said in a speech at an event in Istanbul. “But there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur.”

He added that further moves to raise borrowing costs “do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time.”

Mr. Waller’s comments solidify a reset in expectations about when the Fed will next raise rates. Just two weeks ago, financial markets were putting 70 percent odds on a second consecutive rate increase at the Fed’s meeting at the end of October, just days before the midterm elections.

But those expectations plummeted to around 20 percent last week after two speeches by members of the central bank’s three-person policy-steering group led by Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed’s chairman. Two members of that “troika” — John C. Williams, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and Philip N. Jefferson, the Fed’s vice chair — suggested that the central bank could take its time before raising rates again after a unanimous vote to do so in September. That view was buttressed on Friday when September’s jobs report showed slowing monthly growth.

Mr. Waller explained on Thursday why, after supporting the Fed’s decision to hold rates steady over the spring and summer, he eventually backed an increase. By the time the policy-setting committee met in mid-September, he said, there was a “preponderance of evidence over several months that the risks for monetary policy had shifted.” That included signs that the labor market had stabilized as well as a proliferation of inflation risks.

Those risks include the extended war with Iran, which has raised prices for oil and other goods. Mr. Waller also cited emerging price pressures from the surge in spending to expand artificial intelligence capabilities as well as the prospect that President Trump may impose new tariffs.

“When the first inflation reading for August came in hot just before the F.O.M.C.’s September meeting, it was impossible to deny that inflation was still too high and not making sufficient progress toward our target,” Mr. Waller said.

He said inflation remained his top concern, especially the possibility that consumers begin to question the central bank’s resolve to get back to the 2 percent target.

“With evidence that economic activity is strengthening in the second half of this year, I am not greatly concerned that tighter monetary policy threatens a damaging slowdown in the economy,” he added.

Mr. Waller did not articulate how he would determine the timing of subsequent rate increases, but he emphasized the importance of the Fed’s communicating clearly about its thinking. That approach stands in stark contrast to Mr. Warsh’s preference for the central bank to be more circumspect in signaling about the future. The chairman has said that doing so ties the Fed’s hands and makes it harder for officials to pivot if the economic backdrop calls for a different response. He has also rejected quarterly forecasts that officials provide about their thinking on the path for policy and the outlook for inflation, growth and unemployment.

These projections are just one aspect of the Fed’s communication strategy that Mr. Warsh has directed a group of external advisers to look into as he seeks to make good on his promise to enact “regime change” at the central bank.

But according to Mr. Waller, opting against sending a clear signal about the policy path has downsides. It could “surprise markets and create volatility,” he said.

It also could make the Fed’s job of influencing the economy harder, Mr. Waller added.

“The point is that if too few or too many hikes are priced in, the change in financial conditions would mean too little or too much of an effect on economic activity,” he said.

SUMMARY

Emily Bazelon: Hi David, it’s great to be back here with you for the beginning of the Supreme Court’s new term. But there has been so much action from the court over the last few months on the emergency docket that I don’t feel like we had a break. Many district court judges feel like the Supreme Court does not have their backs when they rule against the Trump administration.

ARTICLE

Third-Country Deportations Are Only the Half of It
The real-world consequences of the Roberts court are coming into view.
By Emily Bazelon and David French
Published 2026-10-08 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/opinion/alito-supreme-court-deportation-colorado.html

Emily Bazelon: Hi David, it’s great to be back here with you for the beginning of the Supreme Court’s new term. Usually, this is like the first day of school for me — a fresh start. But there has been so much action from the court over the last few months on the emergency docket that I don’t feel like we had a break. I hope this is a fleeting feature of Trump’s second term rather than the new normal.

David French: It’s the new normal, I’m afraid. At least for the foreseeable future — for as long as presidents try to rule through executive actions rather than actually govern by executing laws passed by Congress.

Emily: I think it’s bad for two reasons: I am not a fan of the emergency docket except in actual emergencies and I liked having a break to think about other things. (I bet the justices did, too — remember the teaching gigs in Italy and Austria?) Oh well. Let’s pretend it’s time to get all dressed up and start with the first big case of the term. On Monday, the justices heard arguments in Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. Boulder, Colo., wants Exxon Mobil, the biggest energy company in the country, and Suncor, a company based in Canada that operates two oil refineries in the state, to pay the state back for some of the costs of dealing with climate change.

Boulder says this is like the public health damage unleashed by tobacco or opioids, which states have sued companies for causing in the past, settling for large sums. A lawyer for Exxon and Suncor says this is an “unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct,” clearly pre-empted by federal law. Their best argument, I think, is that federal laws have historically governed interstate pollution. The open question, however, is whether that rule applies to carbon-dioxide emissions.

A few weeks ago, I thought that this pro-corporate court, as I see it, would be a sure bet for ruling in favor of big oil. But last week Justice Samuel Alito recused himself (he did not say why), taking out one likely vote for the companies and creating the possibility of a 4-4 split. Then at oral argument, Chief Justice John Roberts asked some intriguing questions suggesting that he has doubts about whether Boulder’s suit is in fact pre-empted by broad principles of law. Justice Elena Kagan did a good job of pressing the point by asking for the source of this pre-emption — “Where is the text for that? Where’s the support for that?” Seems like the answer was weak.

What do you think about where the justices will land and also the underlying question — should a state or county or city be able to sue a company for this kind of harm, or is it a problem Congress is supposed to pass laws to address?

David: This is one of the rare cases where I must confess that I’m a bit stumped, even after reading the oral argument more than once. I don’t know how it will turn out and — quite frankly — I’m a little bit stumped on how it should turn out.

I’m clear on what I think the ideal legal regime should look like, and that’s a comprehensive, sensible federal system that provides rational legal uniformity across the country. After all, as Kannon Shanmugam, who argued the case for Exxon and Suncor, pointed out (and here I should note that Kannon is a friend of mine), a patchwork of state and local cases would almost certainly create a chaotic legal environment. Shouldn’t industries that create interstate effects be subject to interstate regulations? And that can only really come from the federal government.

But we don’t decide cases on the basis of what the law should be, but on the basis of what the law is. And it’s far from clear that the Constitution or any currently enacted federal statutes mean that state law can’t be used to impose liability on energy producers.

Chief Justice Roberts came out swinging, confronting Kannon with a number of scenarios in which states can impose liability for harms that occur inside a state, even if the initial action occurs outside the state. (He used the simple example of someone throwing a rock from State B and hitting someone inside State A).

Justice Kavanaugh argued that the court’s precedents “make crystal-clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law.” But after reading the argument, I’m not sure that a majority of the justices see the same clarity.

Add Chief Justice Roberts’s aggressive questioning to Justice Alito’s recusal, and you’ve got the possibility of a very unsatisfying 4-4 decision that would leave in place the Colorado decision allowing the lawsuit against Suncor and Exxon to go forward without really resolving the underlying issue.

Also, we should mention that there’s at least some chance that this case might also get tossed out of SCOTUS on jurisdictional grounds. So there is a good possibility that arguably the most important case of the term could go out with a fizzle and not a bang. I honestly don’t know how it’s going to go.

Emily: Last week, the court put two huge cases about deportation on the upcoming docket. One of them, Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., is a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting people to “third countries,” meaning countries with which they have no ties (often when their countries of origin refuse to take them back). This case is a big deal for several reasons. The administration has deported at least 25,000 people through this avenue, according to human rights groups. The evidence suggests that the government is in fact doing this with little or no regard for human rights. Some people wind up indefinitely detained or in awful and dangerous conditions. Trump officials appear to view this as a feature, to deter immigration, not a bug. They’ve spent or pledged more than $400 million to persuade 31 countries to take people.

David: This is yet another example of how the Trump administration sometimes treats undocumented immigrants worse than we treat many of the most hardened criminals in the United States. Under the relevant federal statute, third-country removals are to take place when conventional deportation is “impracticable, inadvisable or impossible.”

That’s a last-resort provision, not a loophole. It’s not a catchall provision that gives the Trump administration carte blanche to punish immigrants by sending them to nations where neither human rights nor the rule of law are paramount. American deportees should not be imprisoned in conditions that would violate both the United States Constitution and international treaties prohibiting torture.

Emily: Another big issue in D.V.D.: The Trump administration violated Judge Brian Murphy’s order in April 2025 to halt third-country deportations to places like Libya and South Sudan — not safe — if the deportees had no meaningful chance to object. Yet in an emergency docket ruling last week, a majority of the justices gave the Trump administration a pass for now, saying that the third-country deportations can continue until the court issues a permanent ruling. The case is fast-tracked for arguments in December. But it’s remarkable and dismaying that in the meantime and maybe forever, a majority of justices is willing to look the other way on disobeying a court order. Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote a powerful dissent to an earlier stay, but only her two fellow liberal colleagues joined it. She describes people narrowly escaping arrivals amid violence in Libya and writes, “Only the District Court’s careful attention to this case prevented worse outcomes. Yet today the Court obstructs those proceedings, exposing thousands to the risk of torture or death.”

Many district court judges feel like the Supreme Court does not have their backs when they rule against the Trump administration. This case illustrates why and the attending harms.

David: You raise an important point — litigants are required to follow court orders until those orders are reversed. In my law practice, for example, I didn’t ever tell my clients, “Sure, the judge ruled against us, but keep doing what you’re doing; I’m confident we’ll win on appeal.” Nope, that would be a great way to be hit with a contempt order.

Even if the Supreme Court ultimately reverses the lower courts, I do think it needs to make it very clear that defying orders on the expectation of reversal is completely unacceptable and that contempt orders are an appropriate response.

Emily: One more note about these third-country deportations: Many of these people are deportable because they committed crimes, often serious ones. The question of where they should live after they complete their prison sentences is also serious. But effectively disappearing people to places where they are mistreated and have no recourse is the equivalent of the United States abusing them.

David: You raise an important point — many, but certainly not all, of the people who’ve faced third-country deportation are violent criminals. There are no easy solutions in those cases where they’re deportable and their home countries don’t want them back. But one thing I do know is that deportation to countries that impose indefinite detention and engage in systematic human rights violations is morally grotesque.

To actually celebrate Trump’s policy is more grotesque still. At a minimum, there should be no deportation to countries that violate the Convention Against Torture, an international treaty that President Ronald Reagan signed and the Senate ratified.

When President Reagan transmitted the treaty to the Senate, he sent a message to the Senate declaring that ratification “will demonstrate unequivocally our desire to bring an end to the abhorrent practice of torture.” The Trump administration has no such desire.

Emily: The second big immigration case, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, is perhaps even more chilling.

David: I feel the same way.

Emily: It’s about whether ICE can detain anyone who crossed the border illegally, no matter how long ago and how law-abiding they have been since then, without a bond hearing before an immigration judge — in other words, no court review unless and until you can bring a habeas petition. When ICE adopted this position in July 2025, some government lawyers said they couldn’t believe it. “Mandatory detention is the dream of every hard-line anti-immigration activist,” one ICE lawyer told me. “This is as big a deal as ending birthright citizenship. If the Trump administration does that, then they have changed immigration law forever. If the Supreme Court signs off on this, it’s effectively saying we don’t do asylum here anymore.”

The appeals courts have split on whether the Trump administration’s expansion of mandatory detention is allowed by the 1996 immigration law that it is relying on. This statute is a notorious mess, but still, I think the answer is no. When this litigation started, I thought this was pretty much a slam-dunk. District Court judges largely rejected the Trumpian interpretation. But now I see two appellate courts twisting the text in the government’s anti-immigrant favor and while nine have ruled the other way, I’m not at all sure what the Supreme Court will do.

I have to point out that Congress could fix this problem. It’s supposed to write laws, not cede its power to the president and the justices. But I realize that is a futile point to make at the moment, though I keep trying.

David, do you think this case is chilling because mandatory detention with no bond hearing is bad, because it locks up so many people, including those with deep roots in our country, or bad and also illegal?

David: I think it’s terrible and illegal, but I’m not completely confident the court will agree, in large part because, as you say, the statutes are an absolute mess.

Emily: Is this 1996 law — an update of the Immigration and Nationality Act — one of the worst-written statutes ever? It’s a product of Newt Gingrich’s House leadership, but passed with Democratic support. (It was part of the budget bill that year, so voting no meant risking a shutdown.) The thing about this law is that it had draconian provisions that were not enforced because Congress did not authorize the spending for huge numbers of detention beds. Until, that is, last year, when Congress sharply increased the budget for ICE. We don’t have a new immigration law. We have new immigration policy because we made ICE the law enforcement agency with the highest funding in the country.

David: There’s serious competition for the title of worst-written statute, but it’s definitely a contender. I wrote about this issue at length in February, but here’s the short version. One statute, 8 U.S.C. Section 1225, says that “an alien who is an applicant for admission” shall be detained unless he or she is “clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted.”

Another statute, 8 U.S.C. Section 1226, says that an alien may be “arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States,” but in that circumstance they may be released on bond.

For roughly 30 years, presidents of both parties harmonized those statutes by applying the detention requirement to people stopped at the border and applying the bond provision to people arrested in the interior of the country (often after they’ve been living in the United States productively for years). No president read those statutes as requiring mandatory detention, much less permitting indefinite detention.

And there’s a good statutory reason presidents from both parties adopted the same reading. As Judge Dale Ho, a federal judge in the Southern District of New York, put it in a 2025 ruling, “Someone who enters a movie theater without purchasing a ticket and then proceeds to sit through the first few minutes of a film would not ordinarily then be described as ‘seeking admission’ to the theater.”

I believe the Supreme Court will agree with Judge Ho, but I’m far from certain. Let’s check in again after oral argument.

Emily: Gulp, yes, let’s.

Speaking of close textual readings, which you are carefully doing, what do you think of Justice Alito’s recent op-ed in The Wall Street Journal laying out his “Text? What text?” theory of originalism?

Here is the part that made me grind my teeth the morning I read it (not a metaphor). Alito goes after what he calls “insecure originalism” (subtext: any analysis he doesn’t like by a colleague, especially if her name is Amy Coney Barrett). Alito writes: “Insecure originalists remain in what Prof. Adrian Vermeule has called a ‘defensive crouch.’ Wary of being charged with ‘results-oriented’ decision-making, they are allergic to any evaluation of results. That is a mistake.”

Alito continues, “Insecure originalists may worry that they are subconsciously engaging in ‘judicial activism’ in the service of their own policy preferences. As a result, they may welcome occasions when their originalist analysis leads to results they dislike.”

Well, yes. Isn’t this the whole justification for originalism? The method’s claim to superiority is that it binds judges to the text of the Constitution as it was understood in 1788. They can’t take into account results because that would mean making a judgment call based on the outcome they would prefer, which could reflect their values. They are proud of reaching decisions they don’t personally like because this proves they are dutifully following the instructions of the framers.

Justice Antonin Scalia, originalism’s most brilliant salesman, often cited his vote in favor of ruling that the First Amendment protects flag burning. In 1989, Scalia published an essay in which he admitted to a bit of Alito-like wobble: “I hasten to confess that in a crunch I may prove a fainthearted originalist,” he said. “I cannot imagine myself, any more than any other federal judge, upholding a statute that imposes the punishment of flogging.”

But many years later, Scalia said, “I repudiate that,” in an interview in New York Magazine with the journalist Jennifer Senior. I think Scalia had no choice. If you can make an exception to the rule whenever you feel like it, then it’s not a rule. “I will take the bitter with the sweet!” Scalia said. “What I would say now is, yes, if a state enacted a law permitting flogging, it is immensely stupid, but it is not unconstitutional.”

I don’t think the court has ever consistently applied originalism (or the conservative justices’ latest expandable “history and tradition” test). Of course judges take into account real-life consequences and reach different results in difficult cases informed by who they are. But isn’t Alito giving away the game here? David, you are a committed originalist. If Alito gets to have no bitter with the sweet, can I have a world in which the Constitution reflects today’s reality? I look forward, for example, to the Supreme Court upholding the ban in Cook County, Ill., on many semiautomatic rifles, the big Second Amendment case on the docket this term. Now originalism will not bar the justices from letting the people of Chicago do their best to address the modern — that is to say, decidedly not pre-1800 — crisis of gun violence, right?

David: I had three thoughts about Justice Alito’s op-ed, two positive, one negative. First, I’m glad he wrote it. I want justices to be more transparent about their legal philosophies. I think he did a great public service in explaining how he approaches cases and explaining his own ideas about originalism.

Second, it’s important that people understand that originalists can and do disagree all the time. Originalism isn’t a plug-and-play form of legal philosophy that creates precisely predictable results in every context. It’s a way of thinking about the law. It’s not an outcome-generation machine. That’s why the conservative majority isn’t a monolith. They disagree all the time.

But on to my beef. I strongly disagree with his framing of “insecure originalism,” beginning with the word “insecure.” It echoes a particular New Right style of argument that claims that conservatives failed in the past because they lacked courage or craved the affirmation of elites. Think of it as the “if only Mike Pence had the courage” argument.

I don’t think Alito is going as far as all that, but I wasn’t the only person to read Alito’s piece and see echoes of the New Right.

As Jack Goldsmith, a Harvard Law School professor who served as assistant attorney general for the Office of Legal Counsel under President George W. Bush, wrote in The Atlantic on Tuesday: “In their attacks on the Court and its moderate conservatives, the Trump administration and its allies are articulating a New Right idea of conservative judging. That view despises originalism’s value-neutrality, prizes conservative results, admires judges with the ‘courage’ and ‘loyalty’ to uphold Trump’s program, and views adverse decisions as evidence of timidity, establishment capture, or betrayal.

“Alito claims no association with the New Right, but his essays and work on the Court make plain why its legal camp venerates him.”

I’m very worried about the future of originalism. One of originalism’s appeals is that it was supposed to diminish judicial discretion (by privileging the text above all else) and make legal outcomes more predictable and durable.

For example, to come full circle: My originalist approach to the Suncor case isn’t to ask which outcome I’d prefer (federal regulation), but rather which outcome the text of the Constitution and the relevant statutes requires, and that may well mean that Boulder, Colo., wins, at least until Congress says otherwise.

But in the wrong hands, originalism can become exactly what it was supposed to combat — a malleable doctrine that answers the “living constitutionalism” of some more left-wing judicial philosophies with what Sherif Girgis, a conservative professor at Notre Dame Law School, calls “living traditionalism” that can rest too much on the accidents of history, much less the judge’s own interpretations of that history, or personal preferences.

Emily: Indeed. At some point, let’s talk about Dobbs, Exhibit A of Alito opinions and Supreme Court jurisprudence based on misleading, cherry-picked history. I think you strongly disagree. But that’s for another day and the draft of the book I’m working on (more on that at some point, too. I hope).

For now, I will note that three red states (Alabama, Arkansas and Louisiana) are suing three blue states (California, Massachusetts and New York) over the blue states’ telemedicine shield laws, which protect abortion providers in their states who prescribe abortion pills to women in states with abortion bans. This one is worth the whole conversation next time! But let’s see whether the Supreme Court accepts the invitation to exercise original jurisdiction, meaning it acts as the trial court, an option that exists when states sue each other. I doubt it. (During this administration, I keep having to pretend I remember bits of the Constitution I’ve forgotten from law school or maybe never learned. Thank you, President Trump, for your attention to this matter.)

What movies or TV shows do you have for me? I offer you “Colin From Accounts,” a light but sometimes deep Australian comedy that features a dog on wheels. My dog likes it. I bet you will, too.

David: As you suspected, Emily, we’ll have to agree to disagree on Dobbs for now, though I’d love to have a real discussion with you about that case. I thought it was one of Alito’s best opinions (though I have small quibbles at the edges).

But let’s end with a point of agreement. I loved “Colin From Accounts.” My wife and I watched that some time ago, and if you like that show, I’ve got one I recommended on The Opinions last week. The Apple TV show “Last Seen” stars Patrick Brammall (the same actor who starred in “Colin”), and it’s about a missing child who … might have been found.

I won’t say more, except that Episodes 4 and 6 are among the most gripping episodes of television I’ve ever seen. Enjoy!

Nonconsensual sex is always wrong, but that doesn’t mean consensual sex is always right. Whether or not the student who would come to be known as Jane Doe — at the time under the influence of alcohol and ketamine, in an upstairs room full of fraternity brothers — had agreed at some point to sex has become a flashpoint in the discourse around Cornell University’s rape investigation. ARTICLE

The Cornell Case Exposes What We Can’t Say
We are unable to recognize and critique bad behavior outside of a narrow definition of criminal sex.
By Christine Emba
Published 2026-10-08 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/opinion/cornell-sex-consent-rape-criminal.html

Nonconsensual sex is always wrong, but that doesn’t mean consensual sex is always right.

Whether or not the student who would come to be known as Jane Doe — at the time under the influence of alcohol and ketamine, in an upstairs room full of fraternity brothers — had agreed at some point to sex has become a flashpoint in the discourse around Cornell University’s rape investigation. But regardless of where one falls on that debate, we should all be able to name the way a 20-year-old sophomore was treated by her peers as degrading and perverse, deserving of sanction regardless of the legal outcome of the case. And while the dozens of frat brothers who were sent a Snapchat message advertising an intoxicated woman as “free pussy” were not under legal obligation to intervene, their broad refusal to do so should also be regarded as a moral failure.

The lurid account has haunted the public imagination since The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper, published the details in mid-September. While the alleged assault happened in 2024, its re-emergence this year has resulted in a steady drip of shocking and at times conflicting evidence into the public conversation.

Campus sexual assault isn’t new. Something about this case — the coarseness, the extremity, the failure of trusted institutions to forcefully respond — has triggered widespread revulsion, a sickening shared sense that a boundary no one thought to name has been broken. It has attracted a different kind of attention, as well — with some observers defending the perpetrators, some interrogating the rush to judge them.

There are discussions to be had about agency, responsibility and justice. But we don’t have the shared language to talk about what, exactly, went wrong.

Not that we aren’t trying to talk about it. It’s just that our public conversation feels quibbling, inadequate to the outrage at hand and insensitive to the victim’s humanity. Where does this fall under New York State’s laws? Don’t some women like rough sex? Was it a rape, or was it just a bad experience regretted after the fact?

The last question is at the heart of our shrunken moral vocabulary. “Consent” has become the consensus standard of our time, a compromise between “her body, her choice” sex positivity and a societally necessary condemnation of sexual violence. The consent standard is meant to remove ambiguity without prescribing a larger framework: Sex without consent is rape, and rape is a crime. The certainty of those categories fits neatly into our existing accountability mechanisms as defined by the legal system. Anything outside of rape is a personal affair.

In a society that treats judging others as inappropriate — or at least unfashionable — consent has the appeal of being values-neutral: It defines harm without requiring anyone to make the case for a certain idea of the good. Our reliance on consent as the ultimate arbiter of acceptability has left us unable to recognize and critique bad behavior outside of its narrow definition of criminal sex.

After all, consent here is a legal criterion, not an ethical one — a floor, not a ceiling. It defines the bare minimum, but it doesn’t define the good. That gap between “legal” and “decent” is where moral criticism does its work, but a lack of a moral language strips us of the nuance needed to empathize with victims and to come up with a social, not just a juridical, response. Without that vocabulary, it’s difficult to express what we want our shared sexual culture to look like.

Consent doesn’t help us account for the power differentials of age, gender, experience or intoxication. It doesn’t ask whether the alleged victim entered into the encounter out of genuine desire or because of social pressure, or where one stops and the other begins. It doesn’t leave room to acknowledge that even “just” a regrettable experience can cause lasting harm and that the woman involved is deserving of compassion. What do we owe to each other? Is there no higher standard to which we can hold ourselves?

Any eventual court verdict won’t cure a culture in which misogyny is gaining traction at the highest levels of government and society, embodied by a president who has sheltered virulent misogynists and has himself been found liable for sexual abuse. It won’t reassure skeptical young women that they should trust their male peers. But restoring a moral framework from which to explain why certain beliefs and behaviors are either good or bad would make us better at holding our institutions — and one another — accountable.

“I was a sex doll for all intents and purposes, which is sad,” Jane Doe told a police interviewer in the weeks after her assault. It would be tragic to have the conversation end there.

Christine Emba is a board member of the American Institute for Boys and Men and a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.
