SUMMARY

And does the city believe in its mayor? If you’re going to advance anything big as a mayor, you have to have a coalition on the City Council. Look, we know this: There are three major areas that a city, a mayor have to deal with.

ARTICLE

Opinion | Who Should Be Los Angeles’s Next Mayor?
Times Opinion convened a panel of experts to help voters make sense of the race.
By New York Times Opinion
Published 2026-10-08 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/08/opinion/los-angeles-mayor-election.html

Karen Bass

Nithya Raman

Our Panel’s Ratings

We asked panelists to rate the leading candidates on how they would approach governing. Each chart reflects an average of their individual ratings.

This is the most frustrated L.A. residents and L.A. voters have been in the 40 years that I have been observing and studying Los Angeles. At Loyola Marymount, we conduct one of the largest annual surveys in urban America on Los Angeles, more than 2,000 residents every single year. When we ask about trust in government, efficiency in government, does government care about you, can government solve problems — all have declined dramatically. Voters have no belief in the ability of local government to improve their lives.

In any mayor’s race, we ask the question: Is the city working for us? Are residents able to get basic services? And does the city believe in its mayor? And I think all of those questions are up for debate right now because a lot of community members, people that we talk to every day, are feeling that services are not being delivered.

Everybody is either frustrated, unhappy or angry. And as a consequence of that, they’re uninspired by leadership. A mayor’s race often can be a moment of civic inspiration and of civic imagination, right? In 2013, Eric Garcetti had a vision for Los Angeles that he was selling to voters: a forward-leaning city. In 2005, Antonio Villaraigosa had a very clear vision of Los Angeles. “Come dream with me” was sort of the slogan of his inauguration speech. And in this campaign, I’m not seeing anybody articulating a vision for Los Angeles and trying to sort of lead people to a common civic mission.

Los Angeles has undergone two major catastrophes in the last two years — first, the ones with the Palisades and the Eaton fires. And even though the Eaton fire was in Pasadena, it’s still part of our larger community. The second major crisis we’ve had most recently is the Lineage fire in Boyle Heights, where a cold storage warehouse burned and the decomposing food took a long time to clean up. That’s of great concern to the community right now because it kind of traffics a longstanding history of people being promised so much by these candidates.

Right now, if she were to get elected today, her mandate is she’s not Bass. But that’s not the same thing as an agenda, and that’s something she should focus on building in the final weeks of the campaign. She can be very, very good at articulating a vision for Los Angeles when she wants to; she has a sense of the future, of what a multiethnic, complex city is supposed to be. And if she can articulate that, that will be a real strength. She is also very good at identifying and fixing the things that prevent government from working right.

I think if Raman wins, it’s notable that she’s not endorsed by her colleagues on the City Council. If you’re going to advance anything big as a mayor, you have to have a coalition on the City Council. And if you’re a council member that wants to advance anything big, you have to work with the mayor. So how does she reset relationships should she win, not just with the council, but also with labor and with the business community, in order to make some big moves and shift this mood?

I feel like she’s still learning how to be a politician. She has learned how to deliver her message better. I definitely do think that she will bring an outsider’s perspective. We haven’t really seen that in the city leadership. Most of the mayors that we’ve had have all had those traditional coalitions and things behind them, though she has very interesting people that are behind her, including the pro-transit community and environmentalists. We’re watching, I think, the plane being built in real time.

She understands policy and systems at a very minute level. And I think that was the strength of hers going into this race. I would say the biggest question, I think, from my perspective as a civil-rights leader in South L.A., is: Can we trust you on issues around race and equity in our community? I’ve seen her doing more work with the immigrant and primarily Latino community. But what about the other, more solidly Black communities that have been a part of this coalition bloc?

Bass has a truly cross-sector coalition. She has the business community behind her. She has older white liberals behind her. She has sizable support from the Latino community. So what is she going to do with that cross-sector coalition should she win? Every re-elected mayor has about a year, year and a half to do something really interesting and sort of ride that wave of optimism that may come from a victory. What will she do with that?

Mayor Bass spent a lot of time in Washington as a legislator. It’s like if you were used to driving a gas-powered car, and you came back to L.A. and the whole city is an electric vehicle. You have to learn how to work the machinery. Over the last couple of years, she’s been trying to figure out how the machinery actually works. If there is a second term, it’s got to be about implementation. We know what did not work around homelessness. What big tweaks are you making to actually move that forward? We know you did the executive directives around land use. But improving permitting is not the same as completing units. So if she wins a second term, the challenge would be how to get more completed units online. The strength is she knows the machinery better. The question I think most people are asking is: If we give you a second term, can you actually effectively drive this car, which is L.A. city? Can you actually effectively manage the department managers to get what we need?

Bass has tremendous relationships at all levels of government. She has been effective at leveraging that for support from Sacramento and Washington. That is a huge asset, and if Democrats retake the House and Senate, it be very helpful. The mayor’s biggest weakness is that she acts more like the legislative leader she was for two decades than as the executive and a manager a big city mayor is supposed to be.

One of the things that’s really disappointing about this race is that I had thought that with two smart, policy-savvy, progressive candidates, we would have some thoughtful conversations about housing policy, and we’re not. And to the extent that we have, it’s basically been: Should we build any apartments in what are exclusively single-family neighborhoods now? That’s a question, but there’s so many others that aren’t being asked.

Look, we know this: There are three major areas that a city, a mayor have to deal with. First and foremost is public safety. Second is land use. And then the third area is city services. Public safety, I think, is going OK for Bass. It’s that land use, the inability to build housing and affordable housing. One of the root causes with homelessness is the rent. That’s going to be Bass’s legacy if she gets re-elected, whether she wants it or not. She cannot give up on that issue of homelessness and housing.

The basics around housing are the three P’s, right? How are you doing protection, preservation and production? And what I’m hearing with Raman, it’s a lot about production. Her biggest challenge would be convincing these neighborhood associations that you could actually build density in your area and not disrupt the historical fabric of your neighborhood.

So I’m going to come at it a little bit differently, as someone who does work with the developer community quite a bit. I’ve worked for affordable housing developers and regular market-rate developers. And I will tell you that people aren’t interested in building in Los Angeles. A lot of times, the people who are opposed to a project, they are very savvy, with requirements and conditions on these projects, knowing that they won’t get built. We need a real sherpa in city hall to get us over the hump, to rebuild the trust of people who want to invest in our city at all levels of housing and bring all parties to the table, especially developers. And I think we have to figure out that we can’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good.

The other big question is: What generation do we have at the front of our minds when we’re talking about housing policy? Are our decisions on housing policy being dictated by the needs of people my age, who are homeowners? Or are they being dictated by thinking about kids who are in kindergarten and high school now, and what Los Angeles they get to live in or not?

The median age right now to buy a home in Los Angeles is much higher than in most of the country. I have two daughters in their 20s. To know that they would not be able to buy a home — a single-family dwelling or even a condo — for a long time is concerning. When younger voters are looking at this race, I think they’re thinking about that.

It is a generational issue. Most of the people in Los Angeles rent. But we’re kind of still beholden to the homeowners. It has huge implications: There is a concentration of intergenerational wealth into the hands of a minority of the city, which was on display with the first debate these candidates had, which was hosted by a homeowners’ association.

The most important thing the mayor needs to do — and it isn’t easy, cheap or fast — is to create enough long-term housing for people who are currently unhoused. Inside Safe isn’t housing. It is temporary shelter, in a motel or hotel room, to get people safely off the streets. The city should focus more on leasing apartment units, for a likely cheaper cost, and it is actually long-term housing.

While L.A. overall needs a much greater supply of housing, preventing homelessness could best be achieved by specifically constructing units that offer below-market rent.

The next mayor needs to focus on a sustained cost-of-living reform program that decreases the cost for all renters in L.A. Too many families find themselves in precarious housing situations where they need reliable, clean and affordable pathways to long-term housing, including public housing, new development and land trust options.

The next mayor needs to build a robust coalition of serious public and private leaders to streamline the intake pathway, and deploy prevention dollars — like basic income, or utility rates cuts and freezes to stabilize affordability — alongside coordinated services.

It’s the major event in Los Angeles since Covid. And it has structured the narrative about how a city can respond, how a city can prepare. And then the mayor being out of the country when the fires broke out symbolized the city being out of touch and not engaged. And so all of that, I think, is where we are right now for the mayor’s race, but also the way people view the city. Some of this is unfair when you look at the overall pace of response compared to other places. But the fires just showed the inability of communications with the fire department, how they deployed, all of that. It’s just a reflection of the inability of the city to respond and communicate.

We’re now at a point where we know we are going to have crises that we have not experienced before. We’re going to have coastal crises. We’re going to have more environmental crises. I don’t think we think enough about the potential for cyberattacks that could shut the city down or screw up the entire water system.

To go back to our discussion about coalitions, it doesn’t matter if you have a coalition if you don’t do anything with it. Then it’s just optics and representation. The city needs more than that. It needs action. We need strong leadership to solve some of the biggest crises we’re going to face. We’re about to face a big El Niño. Are we really prepared to take that on? Are we in communication in pushing the federal government to provide us greater resources so we can tackle some of these needs?

I think first and foremost, being the mayor of the second-largest city in the United States is a sort of right and responsibility all in itself. You absolutely have the bully pulpit. You absolutely have the ability to share your opinions. You can call upon the council to do all sorts of things. You hire general managers. You establish budgets. You appoint some seats to the Metro board, to the air quality management districts. It’s a myth that we don’t have the power. It’s just a matter of learning how to use it and being willing to use it.

The bully pulpit point is so important — we’ve seen Mayor Bass do that on a couple of occasions. With ICE, she was very strong. People heard it. They saw it. But I’m not sure in other areas we’ve seen it in the same way. Many of us are looking right now at New York City, and people are seeing what appears, at least, to be bold leadership and use of a bully pulpit in multiple ways. There is a little bit of envy and a desire to have that in our city.

There’s also an element to the job that involves diplomacy skills and a lot of soft skills to build a coalition on the City Council, to be able to build a coalition on the board of supervisors, to mobilize other mayors, to mobilize legislators so you could advance a policy at the state level. A mayor has a tremendous amount of power through appointment of general managers and commissioners, though, as well as being the most recognizable public figure in Southern California. It gives them the ability, if they are able to use it effectively, to make bold and ambitious moves.

The mayor has a lot of power on paper and controls some major entities, like power or the port. But in total, the mayor of New York has more power specifically for a few issues that cities are dealing with right now. The mayor of New York controls health, education and social welfare. The mayor of L.A. doesn’t. Those are three very important policy areas that many Angelenos believe that the mayor controls. And when you’re trying to deal with homelessness, let me tell you, it’s really tough when you don’t have health and welfare under your control.

I remain optimistic that it is possible. A lot of people believe that L.A. is ungovernable. It’s very difficult to achieve your goals when you’re not exerting that level of focus and discipline, and there’s not the engagement, there’s not the communication. I think there are ways to identify some simple, quick wins that, if I were advising her, I would sit down and say, three to five things, what can we do infrastructure-wise? It’s not sexy, but Zohran Mamdani is doing it. He’s fixing the play equipment in New York City. He’s getting after Amazon for their unpaid parking tickets.

I just want to say that as a person who is a millennial in this city and a renter, the biggest frustration is that the city does not work, meaning that there’s potholes, the sidewalks don’t work, that El Niño’s going to come, it’s going to be flooded. And the question is: Why are you paying so much money?

What I’ll add, as someone who had to vote on budgets and try to get services done, is I do not envy whoever is in office next year in trying to dramatically improve the quality of city services because it’s going to be very, very difficult. We still haven’t recovered, in terms of city services, from the Great Recession era. And the funding situation is not good.

Bass did a great job in terms of ICE. But part of it is because she hardly had to spend any money. It wasn’t budget constraints. She didn’t have to deal with the City Council on that. This was on her own, her instincts of having been a coalition builder and knowing to respond. She did a great job.

We know that undocumented immigrants generate tremendous income in our city — around $250 billion, I believe, every year. That’s 17 percent of the county’s G.D.P. The L.A. Economic Development Corporation in their survey found that 82 percent of businesses reported negative impacts. And of those experiencing declines in revenue, nearly half said that those declines were over 50 percent. So I think when we’re thinking especially about Latino communities, A.A.P.I. communities impacted by ICE, we get back to the question of: How is this city delivering services for them that enable them to thrive? That’s where the rubber meets the road on this, is that it can’t just be about symbolism. It’s got to be about the delivery of services by the city as well.

The mayor does have to thread a needle when it comes to the president of the United States, whoever that is. I think the mayor has a duty to stand up for their citizens and to speak out against what’s morally wrong. But at the same time, they can’t afford to be an ideologue all the time. The job requires that the mayor solve problems and deliver city services. So that might take a different approach, a different strategy, depending on what the need is, whether it’s working behind the scenes, in front of the scenes to get to solutions with the federal administration. Sometimes that’s being inspirational and taking a moral stand. And sometimes it’s being a pragmatist.

Just don’t poke the bear. Basically, ignore Trump unless it’s about ICE, unless it’s about the Olympics. Don’t give in to Trump just because of the Olympics. He’s going to want to make it a showcase for himself anyway; he will be investing money in that. And if not, that’s the risk we’re going to have to take. I wouldn’t give up the soul or the identity of L.A. just because the Olympics might have a cost overrun.

L.A. is a city that you have to find. There are hidden pockets of nature; there’s urban grit; there’s every ethnicity and all the food and all the things. But you have to go find it. It operates very much like a small town in a lot of ways. The politics are very hyperlocal.

L.A. is the epitome of everything that the Trump administration is against. Cultural diversity — we have a large population of foreign-born people. We have creative capital that’s not seen anywhere else in the world. And we have a vibrant democracy where, on a cultural level, on a citywide level, people come together all the time, every single day.

L.A. is one of the most diverse and segregated cities in America. But the beauty of Los Angeles is that it is filled with people who believe that the possible is possible. We show up because we believe the possible is possible for everyone, even though we are very diverse and segregated.

L.A. remakes itself constantly, and we are a city of entrepreneurs. And I don’t mean that just economically, but also socially, culturally, in every single way except for city government. And that’s the disconnect. We are a bunch of cultural, social, economic entrepreneurs, and city government is not.

Whoever takes office needs to have a tremendous amount of courage. I know we gave a lot of credit to Mayor Bass, but the real people that stood up to ICE were your everyday citizens. It was people getting arrested, getting deported in some cases. There’s so much a mayor can do. But how does a mayor take the cues from their citizens? It’s this big city that’s very diverse and very complex. We disagree on a lot. But there are certain things that we will all stand by. We’re an immigrant city. And we’re going to stand by our people.

SUMMARY

Surveillance technology has spread quickly through Uganda since 2019, when the government installed a $126 million closed-circuit television network from the Chinese telecommunications conglomerate Huawei to monitor public spaces. That’s not to say it was free: Uganda now owes China about $2.6 billion. Speaking to his Chinese counterparts “with an air of enthusiasm and shared objectives,” according to a party write-up, Mr. Todwong secured a funding pledge from China that would “apply these transformative lessons within Uganda.”

ARTICLE

The Authoritarian Future Is Already Here
A crackdown in Uganda shows how new technologies, Chinese influence and America’s moral retreat are making the world safer for autocrats.
By Megan K. Stack
Published 2026-10-08 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/opinion/surveillance-autocrats-uganda.html

This essay is part of “The New World Disorder,” a series exploring the disintegration of the postwar international system and how countries are adjusting as America steps aside.

Plainclothes thugs frog-marching a radio commentator from the microphone mid-broadcast. An opposition activist dying after reportedly being barricaded in his house, which was then set on fire. Security forces raiding a powerful independent media company, cutting electricity and imposing a monthlong closure.

A reign of terror grips Uganda. Specifically, the reign of Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the country’s belligerent and erratic military chief, who also happens to be the only son of Yoweri Museveni, the octogenarian autocrat who’s ruled Uganda for four decades. Critics of General Kainerugaba, who recently announced his intention to become Uganda’s next president, risk finding themselves in the “basement,” his nickname for the torture chambers he brags about on social media.

Ugandans have discovered that, increasingly, there is nowhere to hide. Civic life here is defined by thickening webs of state surveillance built with foreign help. Chinese cameras and facial-recognition software monitor the streets; Russian radio frequency chips implanted in license plates have been tracking cars in real time; Israeli software plunders the private contents of phones. Technology has created an intrusive eye that never blinks — a stealthy weapon for dictators keen to stifle speech and thought.

Welcome to our menacing new world, a place where authoritarians — established and aspiring alike — enjoy tolerance from the international community; wield cheaper, quieter and far more powerful surveillance tools at home; and reach across borders to help one another hang on to power.

Africa has become a testing ground for all of this. Authoritarianism is spreading on the continent, where Freedom House’s 2026 report found that only 10 percent of people now live in countries classified as “free,” a dismal statistic outdone only by the Middle East.

China has quietly fueled this political hardening. With unparalleled trade reach, a voracious appetite for natural resources and a compelling authoritarian model, Beijing has deepened its economic and political presence across Africa. Along the way, it has exported many of the technologies that the Communist Party uses for political and social control at home. African governments have spent at least $2 billion on the Chinese artificial-intelligence-powered surveillance systems that hound dissidents from Mozambique to Zimbabwe to the Republic of Congo.

China is not the only one. Israeli spyware such as the notorious Pegasus piracy software, which can use a phone to spy on its owner, has been snapped up by rulers around the world. And companies from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Germany and other European states have all exported surveillance technologies to Africa and other regions. Such tools have sometimes been used to target opposition figures, journalists and activists.

I visited Uganda recently to explore the aftermath of President Trump’s abrupt retreat from human rights, clean government and public diplomacy. I was told, over and over, that American silence during this clampdown has made it easier for other Western countries to remain similarly quiet and has radically emboldened an increasingly ruthless Ugandan regime.

This is not to overstate past U.S. altruism. America has always chased its interests overseas — sometimes violently, often cynically, selectively calling out the abuses of disfavored regimes while ignoring repression carried out by strategic allies. But it’s also true that America stood up for dissidents and human rights defenders when it was not inconvenient, and sometimes when it was. It pressured despotic governments, criticized rigged elections and sanctioned officials.

Now, suddenly, Beijing’s rules prevail: Make money, extract resources, turn economic ties into leverage. Whatever you do, respect local power — don’t criticize other governments for tyranny or abuse. Mr. Trump plays by those rules, too — “trade, not aid,” his administration pithily calls it.

“I really believe, if we look at the next 20 years, our politics will be influenced by the Chinese very, very much,” said Job Kiija.

I met Mr. Kiija in Kampala, the Ugandan capital, at a coffee shop wedged over a gas station on a ramshackle street fringed with palms and groaning with traffic. He runs Innovations for Democratic Engagement and Action, a civil society group that now works in the legal shadows since it was shuttered and defunded by government crackdowns.

He showed me threatening texts he’d been receiving on his phone (“U said some not nice things … U mayb in trouble soon”). He fretted about whether his group should publicly release an extensive report about the much-criticized elections this year that — yet again — kept Mr. Museveni in power.

To depend upon international law or support from friendly Western diplomats, Mr. Kiija said, is “no longer sustainable.”

“You live knowing you’re in danger,” he said. “But if you don’t do something about it, nobody will.”

It’s a mask-off moment in Uganda. For people caught in the cross hairs, these are days of dread.

Kakwenza Rukirabashaija has read the classified documents that list, in black and white, the arms of state power and surveillance tech that attacked him.

Mr. Rukirabashaija is a Ugandan lawyer and novelist. His first book, “The Greedy Barbarian,” is the sprawling, satirical story of a president who becomes a dictator, spiraling deep into greed and corruption until he is finally ousted by popular revolt.

The regime was not amused.

Over the next two years, Mr. Rukirabashaija was repeatedly detained and tortured. He was viciously flogged and beaten so badly that his ankle bones were fractured, his kidneys damaged and his back laced with scars from being whipped. Mr. Rukirabashaija said that General Kainerugaba, the president’s son, twice visited him in detention.

During the first visit, he said, the general ordered the author — the taller of the two men — to bend over to make himself shorter and to remove his pants to reveal the size of his penis. Then, as the general recorded the exchange on his phone, he told Mr. Rukirabashaija to kneel on the floor and apologize, the author said.

On the second visit, he said, General Kainerugaba offered him a bribe to keep quiet about the abuse he had suffered. Mr. Rukirabashaija was stunned.

“I just looked at the floor. I couldn’t believe what he was telling me,” Mr. Rukirabashaija said. “He could see that I could not even stand.”

Even upon release, awaiting what he considered to be a show trial, Mr. Rukirabashaija remained in the virtual prison of constant surveillance. Soldiers surrounded his house. He was certain his phone was compromised. In 2022, he managed to smuggle himself out of his house and sneak to the border, leaving his phone back at home to mislead the authorities tracking its location. He now lives in Germany.

It wasn’t until Mr. Rukirabashaija read his classified police file — sent to him in Germany by his lawyer — that he was confronted with the full machinery of his suffering. The secret court order authorizing the search of his phone. The tables laying out how a person identified only as Investigator No. 9 began to extract data from his phone at 3:44 p.m. The software tools the government had bought from the Israeli firm Cellebrite to analyze his social media posts and the Canadian company Magnet Forensics to pull his data from the cloud.

Mr. Rukirabashaija knew Uganda’s government was brutal, and he says he didn’t expect much from an Israeli company, either. But the cameo appearance of a Canadian company rankled him — the cold, corporate touch of a Western democracy. He wondered whether the people involved in these deals ever questioned their moral responsibility for the products they sold.

“When they see what happened to me, when they see my pictures — all the mutilations, all that software extraction, all that information,” Mr. Rukirabashaija said. “What do they think about?”

A Cellebrite spokeswoman told me the company has stopped selling technology in Uganda “based on our ethics and integrity standards and risk assessment framework.” Magnet Forensics did not reply to a request for comment.

Surveillance technology has spread quickly through Uganda since 2019, when the government installed a $126 million closed-circuit television network from the Chinese telecommunications conglomerate Huawei to monitor public spaces. Uganda is among dozens of countries worldwide to buy such security packages, which are typically marketed as “smart city” systems — cutting-edge weapons against crime.

Huawei engineers were embedded in the offices of Uganda’s security forces, according to reporting by The Wall Street Journal. At the same time, Uganda made a deal with a shadowy Russian firm called Joint Stock Company Global Security to buy a license plate monitoring system, which Human Rights Watch has called a threat to privacy. The Russian company was to help operate the system for the first 10 years.

Huawei declined to speak on the record, but it has previously denied that it or its staff helped Uganda’s government spy on political opponents. My efforts to speak to the Ugandan government resulted — after many unanswered calls and ignored messages — in nothing. As for the Russian company hired to install trackers on cars, the Ugandan attorney general this week declared the contract null and void. The future of the license plate monitoring project is unclear.

Ugandan dissidents have rarely been so vulnerable. State security apparatchiks who once relied on radio transmitters and word-of-mouth informants now wield technological superpowers, vastly expanding their ability to keep tabs on even ordinary citizens in far-flung corners of the country who criticize the regime online.

“They can pinpoint exactly where you are, and there’s no due process,” the Ugandan writer Mable Amuron told me. “I feel like, right now, we are in a military state.”

It is perhaps no accident that Uganda’s surveillance buildup came just as a credible, popular opposition was gaining ground against the 82-year-old Mr. Museveni. That challenge arrived, somewhat improbably, in the figure of Bobi Wine, a reggae and Afropop singer affectionately nicknamed the Ghetto President.

Mr. Wine, who grew up in the Kampala slums, gained fame churning out dance hits and songs that addressed social problems like corruption, poverty and police violence. In 2017, he pivoted to electoral politics, galvanized young Ugandans with his charisma and talk of clean, democratic government and easily won a seat in Parliament. The crowds thronging his campaign rallies suggested that Mr. Wine, whose real name is Robert Kyagulanyi, had awakened a dormant political energy.

Mr. Wine became a prime target for a paranoid and ossifying regime, which used Huawei technology to penetrate his encrypted messages, according to The Wall Street Journal. (Both Huawei and the government have denied that allegation.) In 2018, Mr. Wine was arrested, tortured and charged with treason. His outraged supporters filled the streets, where they clashed violently with security forces.

Undeterred, Mr. Wine went on to run for president twice against Mr. Museveni, first in 2021 and again in January of this year. Both times, Mr. Wine lost in elections that were marred by violence and allegations of vote-rigging and intimidation. At least 16 people were “likely killed” by security forces during and shortly after this year’s election, according to Amnesty International, including a woman who was shot in the back of the head while walking home after casting her ballot. People were detained (or abducted, in at least one case) and interrogated about their support for Mr. Wine.

While campaigning, Mr. Wine and his supporters say they were placed under tight surveillance and often arrived at events and rallies to find security forces waiting. The police have acknowledged using facial recognition and license plate readers to track Mr. Wine’s supporters.

In Kampala, I visited the headquarters of Mr. Wine’s party, National Unity Platform, to meet its secretary general, David Lewis Rubongoya. Within the walls of the sprawling compound, we crossed a courtyard ringed with murals commemorating slain party activists interspersed with Nelson Mandela, Malcolm X and Bob Marley. No matter where we stood, we couldn’t seem to escape the view of cameras mounted on a tall mast just outside the walls, angled to peer down.

“They’re aware that you’re here right now,” Mr. Rubongoya told me cheerfully. “They monitor everything that happens.”

After the 2026 election, when the president’s son took to social media to say he was praying for Mr. Wine’s death and threatened to “handle him accordingly,” Mr. Wine went into hiding, and eventually fled Uganda to live — temporarily, he insists — in the United States. I asked several people close to him how he managed to evade security and leave the country. Mr. Wine, I was told, was helped by supporters inside the security forces.

“Not everyone in the security establishment is pro-government,” Mr. Rubongoya said. “The country is silent, but there is a lot of anger.”

Uganda’s other major opposition figure hasn’t fared any better. Kizza Besigye was Mr. Museveni’s comrade and personal doctor back when they were rebels fighting their way into power from the bush in the 1980s. Mr. Besigye eventually turned on his old friend, accusing the president of selling out their shared principles, and challenged him in elections starting in 2001.

In recent years, Mr. Besigye had drawn closer to Mr. Wine, and formally endorsed his candidacy in the 2026 election. The regime appeared to be rattled by a burgeoning political alliance between the young, trendy singer from the slums and the 70-year-old, establishment-connected physician: Mr. Besigye, like Mr. Wine, was hunted down.

Mr. Besigye was abducted while visiting Kenya in 2024 for a book launch and was transferred illegally back to Uganda, where he was charged with treason and illegal gun possession. The Kenyan government at first denied any involvement, but its foreign minister eventually admitted cooperating with the Ugandan regime in an extrajudicial operation that bypassed Kenya’s Extradition Act.

Like-minded regimes, many of them in Africa, have increasingly colluded in this manner to silence or seize critics, according to the U.S.-based Action for Democracy, which has built a searchable online index tracking global collaboration among authoritarian governments. The group says “autocrats are treating repressive techniques as portable assets that can transcend borders.”

Mr. Besigye’s ongoing trial is, to put it mildly, flawed. A former mayor of Kampala signed on as Mr. Besigye’s lead defense lawyer, but he was grabbed from his home and forced into General Kainerugaba’s torture chamber for two days before being charged with failing to report a treasonous plot. Other lawyers for Mr. Besigye have been arrested, jailed or barred from entering the country. Last month, a key prosecution witness shocked the courtroom by testifying that the guns allegedly in Mr. Besigye’s possession when he was arrested in 2024 were planted by the police. The case is continuing regardless.

General Kainerugaba has repeatedly vowed to hang his father’s old friend, calling Mr. Besigye “a dead man walking.”

Abuse and repression are not exactly new phenomena in this young, volatile country, which has never experienced a peaceful transition of power since gaining independence from Britain in 1962. But the current crackdown is moving so fast, so publicly and with such impunity that several Ugandans I met likened it to the violent excesses of the infamous dictator Idi Amin, who oversaw the killing of untold thousands of Ugandans in the 1970s.

Some in Uganda see it as a project by General Kainerugaba to terrify critics into silence and weed out any officials perceived as insufficiently loyal to a man who would soon, if he has his way, be president. The general banters on his infamous X account about kidnapping and torturing people, posting pictures of battered captives, taunting enemies and threatening his next prey. Over the years, Ugandans have grown accustomed to disappearances and street clashes surging as elections approach, then receding once the results are announced. But this year, after the January election, the crackdown persisted.

Perhaps there is a method to the madness of the president’s son, who trained both at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst in England and the U.S. Army college at Fort Leavenworth, Kan. Maybe he, or the people around him, has cannily read the moment and wagered that the United States and other governments in a newly indifferent West will not complain over Uganda’s sharply repressive turn.

The United States used to push back. The Biden administration called Uganda’s 2021 election “neither free nor fair,” restricted the visas of Ugandans blamed for “undermining the democratic process” and, as political repression continued, kicked Uganda out of a program offering crucial tax and customs waivers to African countries.

Then Mr. Trump returned, and America stopped complaining. In July 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio effectively forbade his staff to utter so much as a euphemism that might hint at criticism of undemocratic values or flawed elections in other countries.

In describing their government’s relationship to the United States, almost every Ugandan I met pointed to Mr. Trump’s abduction of President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela and the U.S. seizure of that country’s oil. They saw Ugandan officials as anxious to do whatever the impetuous Mr. Trump asks because, if he gets angry, who knows what he may do?

That may explain why Uganda accepted some of Mr. Trump’s third-country deportees, and offered to send troops to Gaza. The government has uncomplainingly moved ahead with a health funding deal allowing the United States access to Ugandans’ private health data, ostensibly to monitor disease outbreaks. The political opposition is concerned that the United States may use the agreement to press for preferential rights to minerals or oil. Similar deals have been frozen or rejected in Zambia and Zimbabwe.

A Ugandan human rights lawyer, Agather Atuhaire, who says she was abducted in 2025 by security forces in Tanzania during a trip to the country and that she was tortured and dumped near the Ugandan border, can pinpoint when the change in the U.S. government’s attitude became clear. After security forces mercilessly beat voters and journalists during a 2025 by-election, Ms. Atuhaire, who now lives in Kenya, called a friend at the United States Embassy in Uganda to describe the violence she had documented. Just the previous year, she’d been flown to Washington and feted by Jill Biden and Antony Blinken as one of the State Department’s “International Women of Courage.”

This time, Ms. Atuhaire recalled, the message was different. Washington had told the embassy it didn’t give a damn, her friend said, using a harsher expletive.

The Trump administration’s moral retreat has effectively opened the field for China.

Beijing has cultivated political ties across Africa since the Cold War, when it backed anticolonial liberation movements with arms, money and training, and courted newly independent governments with aid. As China’s economy boomed and its global influence grew, it expanded its presence on the continent with loans, investment, infrastructure projects and resource deals. Unlike the aid doled out by Western governments, Chinese cash generally came without any fretting over human rights or the environment. That’s not to say it was free: Uganda now owes China about $2.6 billion.

“It’s like we’ve mortgaged our country,” said Joel Ssenyonyi, the leader of the opposition in Parliament. Speaking of China, he added, “The time will come when they will have all these countries on a very short leash.”

China played a major part in building and financing projects, including two of Uganda’s major hydroelectric power plants; oil fields to extract recently discovered crude oil that Mr. Museveni has proudly branded “Pearl Sweet”; a massive pipeline that will move the oil to port in Tanzania; and an expressway from the capital to the Entebbe airport. The terms often favor China: A $200 million loan from the Export-Import Bank of China to upgrade the airport, for example, requires the Ugandan government to fork over airport revenues for 20 years to ensure the debt. Arrangements like this already have caused debt distress in some countries, and a backlash against doing business with China.

Chinese construction sites, factories and industrial parks are scattered in and around Kampala. Thousands of teenagers are learning Chinese through the government curriculum, imports from Chinese factories dominate shops and markets, and Chinese investors have been buying up and leasing land. China is also deeply enmeshed with the Ugandan military, inviting officers to train in China, equipping soldiers with armored vehicles and air defense systems and teaming up with Uganda to manufacture explosives and drones.

Perhaps it was only a matter of time before China began exporting not just consumer goods and surveillance systems, but its political and governance ideas as well. Autocracies, after all, make for stable trading partners. They don’t badger Beijing about human rights and can push deals through without messy debate. Fostering such systems is good business for China.

That may explain why Chinese officials are working with local ruling parties to create leadership training schools that blend local nationalist and Pan-African traditions with Chinese Communist Party approaches to party discipline, political organization and governance. This suggests China is quietly working to undermine weak multiparty systems by nudging ruling parties in the direction of perpetual domination.

China has an undeniably enticing model: a durable ruling party with a rigid grip on power. Decades of extraordinary economic growth. Clean, safe streets with low crime. Foreign dignitaries, including officials from Uganda and other states that buy Chinese surveillance systems, get whisked off on junkets to the northwestern Chinese region of Xinjiang, where Beijing is accused of crimes against humanity over its mass detention and severe repression of ethnic Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim minorities. Visitors tour the sites and marvel at the harmonious streets gripped by an extraordinarily intrusive high-tech mass surveillance apparatus. Chinese officials deny committing crimes against humanity, saying the security crackdown combats Islamic extremism and terrorism.

When Richard Todwong, the secretary general of Uganda’s ruling party, visited China in 2023, he announced plans to open an Ideological Orientation School in his country. Speaking to his Chinese counterparts “with an air of enthusiasm and shared objectives,” according to a party write-up, Mr. Todwong secured a funding pledge from China that would “apply these transformative lessons within Uganda.” The school is yet to open. Similar schools already exist in Tanzania and Zimbabwe, with another planned for Kenya.

Still, I detected strains of buyers’ (or borrowers’) remorse.

At Kampala’s Makerere University, I met Nansozi Muwanga, one of Uganda’s leading political scientists. Ms. Muwanga was born into the churn of Ugandan politics. Her father, Paulo Muwanga, was vice president, prime minister (briefly) and de facto president (even more briefly) in the tumult of the 1980s. Her office is set in a cottage on the edge of a rolling, sun-dappled lawn where clusters of students picnicked under the trees.

When China first began to take a keener interest in Uganda, Ms. Muwanga said, it was regarded as a useful counterweight to the “sense of being constantly threatened” by the United States and Europe. “If you don’t have multiparty democracy, we’re going to take the money away,” she intoned. “Accept L.G.B.T.Q. rights or we’ll take it away.”

Lately, though, “the honeymoon is over,” Ms. Muwanga said, referring to China.

Unlike some Ugandans I met who are convinced their rulers would have found novel ways to spy on them with or without Beijing’s help, Ms. Muwanga believes China influenced the government to build up its surveillance state. When I asked her what Beijing’s motivation might be, she responded, to my surprise, by talking about land. China has a huge population, she pointed out, and Uganda has plenty of empty space.

“The Chinese have proved they don’t have to bend to your rules or way of life,” she said. “They can come and create a little China in Uganda without being disrupted.”

I was struck by this leap from explaining the tools used to control people to anticipating another round of colonization — the idea that the unspoken final prize was not the resources contained in the land, but the land itself.

People feel keenly the retreat of the Americans, Ms. Muwanga said. She feels it herself, and not just because she had a U.S.A.I.D. grant for a research center she runs yanked back when Mr. Trump abruptly slashed its funding.

As it turns out, you sometimes end up missing the very same meddling you once chafed against.

“The knowledge that there was a gatekeeper somewhere and someone who’d slap your wrist if you really went rogue,” she mused. “It had a certain power.”

ARTICLE

How Much Space Does $400,000 Get You?
The median national home price gets you a vastly different spread, depending where you are.
By Arnesa A. Howell
Published 2026-10-08 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/realestate/how-much-space-does-400000-get-you.html

Over the past six years, the national median home sales price has jumped over 20 percent to $400,000, according to a PropertyShark market study. Just how much space the median price gets you largely depends on — you guessed it — location.

PropertyShark analyzed the 100 largest U.S. cities to find that those in the Northeast and West offered the least space for the national median sale price. In Manhattan (New York City’s boroughs were considered individually in the report), a $400,000 budget would nab only 267 square feet, the least among all places studied. In Brooklyn one could expect 476 square feet. Of the 10 most expensive places, six were in California.

The study culled data from the U.S. census, PropertyShark sales data and other sources for its analysis, factoring in a mix of single-family homes, townhouses and condos.

“What these cities typically have in common are thriving economies, the major employment opportunities,” Laura Pop-Badiu, the author of the PropertyShark study, explained. Despite that $400,000 purchased only 393 square feet in San Francisco, Ms. Pop-Badiu said the city’s proximity to Silicon Valley attracted many professionals. Most downsize, the study found.

Comparatively, houses in the Midwest had the most floor space at the national median home price. The roomiest homes were in Detroit, where $400,000 could buy you a spacious, nearly 5,000-square-foot home. The cost: $81 a square foot.

While the national median sale price of $400,000 was the study’s point of comparison, in expensive markets, finding any home at that price is unlikely. In Manhattan, last year’s median sale price was far greater, $1.65 million, and the median home size, 1,100 square feet.

ARTICLE

Man vs. ‘Terminator’-Like Robot in a Cage. California Called It Illegal.
A tech start-up’s stunt in San Francisco tested the boundaries of combat sport safety and regulations.
By Adeel Hassan
Published 2026-10-08 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/technology/human-robot-cage-fights-california-rek.html

The 6-foot-tall, steel-framed humanoid robot, which looked like James Cameron’s original “Terminator,” entered the cage, followed by a 5-foot-5 male human in a helmet and other protective gear.

You can probably guess what happened next.

The robot, which was operated by a human pilot using a remote virtual-reality system, pummeled its fleshy opponent, Frankie LaPenna, repeatedly knocking him to the canvas and driving him into the walls of the octagonal enclosure.

Mr. LaPenna, a social media influencer, injured his hand while punching one of the metal robot frames during one of the three bouts he had with different robots. He landed a few punches, but each time he knocked a robot down, it bounced back almost instantly. The crowd of about 100 (humans, not humanoids) was thrilled.

The fight, promoted as “Human vs. Robot,” was staged on Sept. 18 in San Francisco by a tech start-up called REK, which stands for Robot Entertainment Kombat.

It caught the attention of the California State Athletic Commission, which sent the company a cease-and-desist letter. The commission, which regulates professional and amateur boxing, kickboxing and mixed martial arts, had not sanctioned the event.

REK, which bills itself as “the humanoid robot fighting league” (“Real robots, real combat”) — celebrated the letter.

“We made it boys,” its chief executive, Cix Liv, said in an online post.

The letter said that the commission must grant approval to any boxing or mixed martial arts contest, match or exhibition that involves any human in the state of California.

It is a misdemeanor, it added, to promote or participate in an unlicensed boxing or martial arts contest, match or exhibition involving any human.

Mr. Liv dismissed the regulator’s claims.

“The law clearly states that a ‘match’ is between two persons,” he said in an interview, adding that state regulators were welcome to try to argue in court that a humanoid is somehow human.

He said that his company, whose goal is to create a sport in which humanoids engage in MMA-style fighting, did not need permission from the authorities.

However, Mr. LaPenna repeatedly sought permission from REK to fight its robots, which a human operator controls similarly to how one operates a drone. Mr. LaPenna, who did not respond to a request for comment, is known for posting videos of himself getting hurt.

The event produced the most-viewed content that REK has so far shared online, but Mr. Liv said there wasn’t a plan to repeat it. Instead, the company plans to host the first fight between humanoids armed with blades on Friday night in San Francisco.

“We’re going to democratize MMA so we can essentially experience the blood sport without anyone getting hurt,” he said.

Mr. LaPenna had to sign a legal waiver that said if were killed during the fight, it would not be REK’s fault.

“Our hope was to basically get some good shots without actually hurting Frankie,” Mr. Liv said.

The athletic commission said in a statement that it was “committed to protecting the safety of the public and integrity of combat sports.”

“Unsanctioned activity puts the physical and financial well-being of all those involved at risk and such activity will not be tolerated,” it said, adding that it would consider new guidance as robot technology evolves.

Combat sports are regulated by states and tribal commissions in the United States, said Erik Magraken, the managing partner of MacIsaac & Company, a law firm specializing in combat sports regulatory issues and the publisher of the blog Combat Sports Law.

“These laws were written with no contemplation of people fighting machines, so many commissions will be ill equipped to address this novel form of fighting,” he said.

“Many athletic commissions will simply have no ability to shut down such events without amendment of their legislation or regulations,” he added.

Humanoids have been developing faster than lawmakers can keep up. In April, a humanoid robot named Lightning ran a half-marathon in Beijing in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, faster than the human world record of 56:51, which Yomif Kejelcha of Ethiopia set in August.

The Humanoid Robot Games, first held in Beijing last year, and again this summer, featured running, kickboxing and soccer. While there was plenty of running, kicking and punching, the robots also flailed around, crashed and fell over many times.

Those who know humanoid robots best highly recommend against fighting them.

“It’s very unfair to put a human in with a heavily motorized system that’s only going to dominate,” said Ken Goldberg, a professor who oversees the automation lab at the University of California, Berkeley. “There’s not nothing surprising about that.”

Dr. Goldberg boxed a smaller robot last year, for educational purposes and not in a cage. “I gave it one of my old kung fu side kicks from high school and it stumbled back and it tripped and fell,” he said. But they bounce back quickly, he added.

He said he understood the appeal of the fights that REK was staging, noting that it tapped “into some of the fear and frustration with robots that people feel.”

“I mean, they love to see the human kick the robot’s gearbox,” he said.

But the odds of that human fighter getting his gearbox kicked are much greater, Dr. Goldberg said, given that REK’s humanoid robots can weigh several hundred pounds and are made of steel.

“If you program that thing to just come swinging and punching at you, I don’t think you’ll get away from it,” he said. “It’s pretty scary.”

ARTICLE

Amex Supersizes Newark Airport Lounge Before It Even Opens
To meet skyrocketing demand, lounge operators like American Express are racing to build bigger, and the Centurion in Newark’s Terminal A will be a giant.
By Christine Chung
Published 2026-10-08 12:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/travel/amex-centurion-lounge-newark.html

American Express is going big at Newark Liberty International Airport.

The credit card issuer announced on Thursday that its Centurion Lounge at Newark — the only major New York metro airport without one of the premium Amex retreats — would occupy a 30,000-square-foot, two-floor space instead of the 18,000 square feet that Amex had originally planned.

That lounge, scheduled to open next year in Terminal A, will leapfrog Amex’s current largest offering, the 26,000-square-foot Centurion at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport.

Audrey Hendley, the president of American Express Travel, said that Newark’s opening would solidify its presence in the New York metro area’s airports.

“New York is unique because travelers move among three major airports, and Newark is an important addition to our network,” Ms. Hendley said in a statement.

The Centurion Lounge will be Newark’s first lounge operated by a credit card issuer, beating out both J.P. Morgan Chase, which operates Chase Sapphire Reserve lounges, and Capital One, which runs lounges and lounge-restaurant hybrids it calls Landings.

Newark’s Centurion Lounge will have three bars, including one that celebrates New Jersey’s Italian heritage, in addition to a coffee bar. Like other Centurions, it will also feature dishes created by notable chefs such as Kwame Onwuachi and Sarah Grueneberg.

Amex also announced a series of other expansions: a second lounge at Heathrow Airport in London, as well as renovations to existing lounges at Philadelphia International Airport and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston.

In Philadelphia, the lounge will double in size to 12,000 square feet over two stories by late next year. In Houston, the overhaul will be even more substantial: Amex plans to triple the lounge space to more than 23,000 square feet by 2028.

Amex opened its first Centurion lounge in 2013 at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas. It now has 33 Centurion locations globally, making it the credit card issuer with the most airport lounges. Chase offers Sapphire Reserve lounges at nine airports. Capital One has five lounges and two Landings locations.

In April, Amex also teased a new Centurion lounge at Boston Logan International Airport, expected to open in Terminal C in 2029, and updates at the Centurion location at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

Access to lounges is increasingly influencing the way that customers fly. In a survey of more than 1,400 travelers conducted last fall by J.D. Power, the analytics firm, nearly half of lounge customers said they planned their flights based on preferred lounge access.

To cater to this growing market, lounge operators appear to be in a race to build bigger. This week, American Airlines announced it would open its largest Admirals Club lounge, a 40,000-square-foot space at Charlotte Douglas International Airport, in North Carolina, most likely by early 2028, a spokeswoman said. Later this month, United is expected to open a 54,000-square-foot lounge at George Bush Intercontinental Airport. This will be its most spacious United Club and also the largest airline-owned lounge in North America, a United spokeswoman said.

Lounges are also expanding in response to increasing grumbling about overcrowding.

“To protect that value proposition and keep cardholders paying those annual fees,” said Sally French, a travel expert at the personal finance website NerdWallet, “lounge operators have no choice but to build bigger and bigger lounges.”

Instead, the Democrats’ dream blue wave could come from Republicans who sour on President Trump and stay home. “I don’t hear the chatter on the Republican side of ‘Trump this, Trump that.’ He wonders if Mr. Trump does, too.

ARTICLE

‘He’s Not Making Sense’: How Trump Has Alienated Voters for the G.O.P.
Signs are emerging that dispirited Republican voters may stay home in November, bringing a Democratic surge without many conversions.
By Sabrina Tavernise and Jamie Kelter Davis
Published 2026-10-08 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/us/elections/trump-voter-enthusiasm-midterms.html

If Democrats make big gains in the midterm elections in four weeks, it may not only be because their most loyal voters come out in force, or because their candidates have converted Republican voters to their cause.

Instead, the Democrats’ dream blue wave could come from Republicans who sour on President Trump and stay home. It already has a name: the red undertow.

Across the country, signs are emerging of an enthusiasm gap between Democrats and Republicans, even among those who consider themselves likely to vote. A stretch of rural southwest Michigan — long a Republican stronghold — illustrates the point, with more signs for blueberries and eggs than for political candidates. Volunteers are not showing up to door-knock. And many voters say they are tuning this election out.

“People are just more focused on everyday life,” said Lindsay Kronemeyer, 35, a conservative Christian mother of two who works in the construction industry. “I don’t hear the chatter on the Republican side of ‘Trump this, Trump that.’ He’s just not there in my head anymore.”

Jim Pasek, a retired pharmaceutical plant maintenance worker who lives in the tiny town of Gobles, Mich., was baffled by a president he has voted for twice.

“He’s not making sense,” Mr. Pasek, 80, said. “It confuses me, and then I just get disgusted and tune out.”

The idea of the red undertow was introduced last month by the political analyst Charlie Cook, who argued that the Democratic brand was still underwater, but that this election was not about a rising Democratic tide. It was about a drowning Trump brand.

In its wake, Mr. Cook wrote, an undertow will “pull many Republicans under.”

In nearly three dozen interviews in Western Michigan, a sense of fatigue was constant, and that feeling goes beyond that region.

“President Trump has been saying, ‘Vote as if I was on the ballot,’ and that’s exactly what I’m going to do — not vote,” said Brandon Tremaine, 24, a graduate student in Texas who voted for Mr. Trump in 2020. “You do not campaign on being the ticket of peace and start a war of choice that is directly hurting Americans here at home and gotten Americans killed overseas.”

Polls can be unreliable, and moods may be fleeting. Trump loyalists are also known for not taking the calls of polling outfits, and that may be overstating Democratic strengths. Disaffected Trump voters may yet rally to vote as the possibility of a Democratic victory nears, and many Americans still love Mr. Trump.

“I’ll go the length with Trump,” said Jeff Gilbert, 67, a friend of Mr. Pasek in Gobles.

The numbers aren’t drastically far apart. A New York Times/Siena University national poll from last month found that Democrats were more likely to say they were absolutely certain to vote than Republicans, 61 percent to 56 percent. While Democrats led Republicans nationally by seven percentage points among registered voters, that advantage rose to nine points among likely voters.

But in close races, a small gap could prove meaningful.

“People are tired,” Al Pscholka, a Republican and a former member of the Michigan House of Representatives, said of Mr. Trump. “The whole divider-in-chief thing, it’s gotten to the point where it’s just exhausting.”

The concern is showing in unlikely places. Representative Bill Huizenga, a Western Michigan Republican whose four House victories were all by comfortable margins, is in “the fight of his life” against a well-funded centrist Democrat from Kalamazoo named Sean McCann, said Rob Pocock, a retired Republican political consultant who has worked on campaigns in the region.

Nancy DeBoer, the local Republican state representative, also faces a serious fight against Joseph McClusky, a graduate of Hope College, a conservative Christian liberal arts college in Holland, Mich., who is openly gay.

“I would be shocked if Joseph wins, but I can’t believe he’s done as well as he has,” said Mr. Pocock, who teaches at Hope and had Mr. McClusky as a student. He said in Ottawa County, he was seeing Democratic yard signs in numbers he’d never seen before.

Western Michigan — home of Gerald Ford — may be seeing the ebb tide of the president’s MAGA movement, which had surged in this region, once known for a sober, Christian-inflected conservatism. In Ottawa County, ardent Trump supporters secured 8 of the 11 seats on the county commission after Covid. Pro-Trump forces won control of the state party, too.

Today, the MAGA wing is down to three seats in Ottawa County. They have also lost posts in Berrien and Kent counties.

“I think there’s a shift in the party back toward, we need a little bit of the establishment folks,” Ms. Kronemeyer said. “They exist for a reason.”

If anybody should be enthusiastic about the election, it is Ms. Kronemeyer. She ran for a statehouse seat in 2022. She door-knocked for Mr. Trump in 2016 and 2020. But she said that when a friend asked her recently about the races in her area, she had to admit she hadn’t been following them closely. She lives in deep-red Allegan County, where “traditionally in election years, yard signs would be peppered everywhere,” she said.

But the only signs she’d seen this year were for a judge, she said.

Ten years have passed since Mr. Trump took the country by storm, bringing a message of economic populism that appealed to millions of working-class Americans.

“He was a ball of energy,” Mr. Pasek said, sitting at breakfast in Gobles last week with his friend, Mr. Gilbert. “You could feel it. You could see it.”

Now, Mr. Pasek said, Mr. Trump seems to have lost his way. He started a war when he said he wouldn’t, sending the price of gas through the roof. And he seems to talk more about ballrooms and arches than he does about how he will bring prices back down.

“He’s losing touch with the American people,” Mr. Pasek said.

Mr. Gilbert said that he had stopped following the news closely, choosing to spend more time outside with his dog, Mabel. But he voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, and he said he stands by that choice. He said he believed Mr. Trump had a plan for Iran.

Mr. Pasek countered, “He says he has a plan, but then he doesn’t tell us what it is.”

Mr. Pasek cited gas prices: “He says it’s chump change. No, it’s not! It’s killing the people.”

He has noticed someone living in a car in a parking lot when he drives into town, he said. He worried about his granddaughter, 28, a college graduate from Michigan State University, who is working three jobs — one full-time and two part-time — but can’t find a house she can afford.

Those misgivings are being felt at the local party level. Doug Koopman, a member of the Kent County Republican Party’s executive committee, said that it had been a struggle to get the foot soldiers of the midterm elections — volunteer door-knockers and canvassers — to pick up brochures to distribute door to door, leaving bags of them sitting around the party headquarters.

“There’s very low energy on the Republican side,” he said.

In 2024, people lined up for nearly a mile in the rain in Grand Rapids to see Mr. Trump speak the night before the election. His campaign was dominant on social media, reaching younger people who’d never voted before, such as Sebastian Covey, who remembered Mr. Trump “popping” on his feeds. Mr. Covey had not voted before 2024; he did that year, for the president.

Now 24, he said his focus was elsewhere. He lives more than an hour away from his landscaping job in Hudsonville, a bustling suburb just west of Grand Rapids, because rents are cheaper, but the rising gas price has made his commute painful. He swapped his truck for a car, but a colleague he had been car-pooling with just found another job. He and his girlfriend have been looking for a rental closer to work, but so far they have not found anything they can afford.

He said he hadn’t thought about whether he would vote.

“I should care more, but it’s hard to keep up,” he said during a lunch break in a Wendy’s restaurant.

Even Republicans who are in politics say they are tired — worn out by the battles between pro-MAGA politicians and traditional Republicans. Bob Harrison, 76, a Republican county commissioner in Berrien County, where MAGA forces won control of the county G.O.P., said those forces took away the right to vote on party decisions from local elected officials like him.

Those officials “pretty much all walked away from the Berrien County Republican Party” to raise funds for their own political candidates, said Dr. Harrison, a retired community college president.

Dr. Harrison, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said the hard-core Trump supporters remained unchanged, but “they’ve lost the support of the moderates like myself, people who think and choose and maybe split their votes.”

Warren Stewart, 69, who lives in Stevensville, Mich., and works restoring old homes, said he liked to think that Mr. Trump was working to restore the country, but he is starting to have doubts.

Clients often get nervous when the project is only halfway through, he said, but he assures them that he always has a plan for bringing the home back to its original beauty. He wonders if Mr. Trump does, too.

“Does he really know what he’s doing?” Mr. Stewart said.

He would never vote for a Democrat; he feels bludgeoned by liberals online, he said. But he’s not sure he’ll vote for Republicans, either.

“I just spent $60 on $30 worth of groceries and am about to go fill up for $5 a gallon,” he said, carrying two bags of groceries to his car. “It feels like they’re stress-testing us.”

india-cockroach-janta-party.html

SUMMARY

Now, the Gen Z movement that Abhijeet Dipke birthed five months ago and called the Cockroach Janta Party has become a formidable finger in the eye of the Indian government. For Mr. Dipke — and the cockroaches — the risks are enormously high. For Mr. Dipke, fixing schools is personal.

ARTICLE

India’s Cockroach Party Leader Carries Gen Z’s Demands. They Are Many.
Abhijeet Dipke started the movement as a joke. But after ousting a minister over a dysfunctional college entrance exam system, India’s youth say they now want to save democracy.
By Somini Sengupta and Pragati K.B.
Published 2026-10-08 07:10 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/08/world/asia/india-cockroach-janta-party.html

He uncorked a generation’s anger at a broken college entrance exam system.

Now, the Gen Z movement that Abhijeet Dipke birthed five months ago and called the Cockroach Janta Party has become a formidable finger in the eye of the Indian government.

The cockroaches’ latest aim is the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner, over what they say is a politically motivated purge of 130 million voters from the election rolls.

This Saturday, in perhaps their biggest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration, they are calling on supporters to defy a police ban and stage a mass protest in New Delhi.

“For the nation, its democracy and our future, let’s all come together,” Mr. Dipke, 31, said on social media Thursday, appealing to Indians of all generations and ideologies. “Irrespective of your political inclinations, march with the youth.”

In fact, India’s youth have many more grievances: failing schools, insufficient jobs, violence against women, a lack of government accountability. Their frustrations have been boiling for years. There are so many of them — 367 million people between ages 15 and 29, the world’s largest Gen Z cohort.

Mr. Dipke says he feels intense pressure.

“It’s like someone has dropped a baby at my doorstep,” Mr. Dipke said on a recent road trip to highlight the problem with public schools in the countryside. “It actually scares me, to be very honest.”

“People have too many expectations, too many hopes,” he went on. “It’s like people are expecting me to resolve everything at once.”

Mr. Modi has not commented on the cockroach protests, though criticism has come from senior politicians of his Bharatiya Janata Party, including the chief minister of Maharashtra state, Devendra Fadnavis, who said their “fake narrative” over the voter roll revision would not succeed.

For Mr. Dipke — and the cockroaches — the risks are enormously high.

In a country where space for dissent has shrunk, they could be crushed as quickly as they appeared. The Delhi police have detained hundreds of people who defied the ban and protested in Delhi this week.

The cockroaches’ four leaders are all under the age of 32, with no political experience. Signs of friction have appeared with the main opposition party, the Indian National Congress. Its leader, Rahul Gandhi, is holding another rally across the country, in Chennai, on Saturday.

The cockroaches already have one win under their belt: the rare ouster of a government minister in connection to the entrance exams. They seem to have emboldened many more Indians to speak out against the government. Over the last week, a range of groups, from left-wing student activists to conservative regional politicians, have rallied in several cities.

“We are just frustrated by everything. Everything” said Aayushi Gaikwad, 18, who traveled three hours by train to attend a cockroach protest in Mumbai last Friday.

It was her first time at a protest. Around her, thousands of people waved Indian flags. As evening fell, Mr. Dipke led the crowd in singing the national anthem.

Ram Guha, a historian and an outspoken critic of Mr. Modi, credited the cockroach leaders for puncturing the “invincibility of the Modi government.”

“They clearly have a raw courage,” he said.

A Campaign to Fix Schools

Not long after they forced the resignation of the education minister in July, the cockroaches turned to India’s rural schools. A range of Instagram-worthy horrors awaited them at government schools. Clogged toilets. Broken water taps. Overheated tin sheds for classrooms. Rotten onions in a school kitchen. Children wading through floodwaters to reach school.

We joined Mr. Dipke as he visited a remote district in western Maharashtra state, called Nandurbar, where he had spent the first five years of his childhood before his family moved to a city.

For Mr. Dipke, fixing schools is personal.

He was born to a Dalit family, seen as low on the Hindu caste ladder. He attended private schools. But his cousins, whose parents were not as educated as his, attended rural government schools, and the contrast was obvious to him, even as a child. He sat at a desk; they sat on the floor. He drank filtered water; they sometimes had no water. He went on to Boston University for a master’s degree; they repaired cars or worked construction.

“That has been one of the most neglected things since independence. Government schools have never been given the attention they need,” he said.

At a residential girls’ school in a village called Sari, he learned there was no running water in the fourth-floor bathrooms. The girls hauled buckets of water up four flights of stairs.

At a primary school, he met the one teacher who taught a class of first through fourth graders. There was no electricity, and the girls had to fetch water for their bathroom from across a field. The boys had no toilet at all.

Vishwas Thakarey, the teacher, said he, like many teachers, had been diverted from the classroom because he had been told to work on the voter roll revision. (Teachers are often pulled away on other government duties.)

At another residential school an hour’s drive away, Mr. Dipke found a dormitory for girls made of tin walls and a tin roof. There were no beds, only thin cotton mattresses to lay out every night. Mr. Dipke compared it to “an animal shed.” “If there are no basic facilities, how can we expect a quality education?” Mr. Dipke said.

The schools in the area serve mostly Indigenous children, among India’s most neglected.

Some education advocates say that the cockroaches’ focus on school infrastructure is neither new nor especially useful to improving educational outcomes. The latest Annual Survey of Education Results, an independent assessment, found roughly 30 percent of eighth graders in rural schools struggle with second grade-level texts, and around half with basic arithmetic.

In a measure of his naïveté, and also his awareness of it, Mr. Dipke said he had not yet read the ASER reports. He said he would.

Nor was he schooled in the realities of Nandurbar. The district’s top administrator, Mittali Sethi, is. She is trying to fix the electricity system in Sari village, address its groundwater shortage, and train teachers in schools that have fallen behind.

She said she welcomed the attention on school conditions, whether it came from the cockroaches or not. “If someone has raised a problem and it’s a problem, I will fix them,” she said.

(Since Mr. Dipke’s visit, a district water engineer and a health official had visited the village, a local activist said.)

Education experts said they hoped the cockroaches would continue their schools campaign to shine a light on an issue politicians had long ignored.

“The kind of attention they’ve been able to bring to schools, no one I can think of has been able to do that for 20 years,” said Reetika Khera, an economist at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi who has researched rural schools for decades.

‘Not Scared’

Last May, Mr. Dipke saw that India’s top judge had referred to young Indians as “cockroaches.” On a lark, he came up with the idea of the Cockroach Janta Party. Its website welcomed the “lazy” and the “unemployed.”

The idea caught fire, thrusting him into the public eye after anger boiled over at the leaked exams. “We didn’t plan or strategize this movement at all,” he said.

He admits to being no expert, on education or anything else. He says he is not a veteran activist nor a skilled orator. His sister reminds him that he was so camera-shy that he refused to take selfies with her. Now everyone wants a selfie with him.

In Mumbai last week, he went, as hundreds of fans do daily, to gawk at the home of Shah Rukh Khan, a Bollywood actor who played a character Mr. Dipke has long admired — only to be stopped for a selfie by one of his own fans. More people were looking at Mr. Dipke today, the fan said, than at the actor’s house.

Mr. Dipke smiled sheepishly, looked at the house, and said, “Oh ho. I’m still a big fan of yours.” He promptly shared the video with his 5.9 million followers on Instagram.

The next day, he stood on a makeshift stage with his fellow cockroach leaders, speaking to a crowd of thousands with a copy of the Indian constitution in his hand.

“Finally someone’s asking for accountability. Finally not being scared,” said Madhur Manohar, 26, who joined the protest.

“For the longest, everybody’s had frustrations,” her friend, Surabhi Apte, 30, said. “They didn’t know how to channel it. It was only dinner conversations, where your parents were like, ‘Ignore it.’”

“This is finally us doing something,” Ms. Manohar added.
