SUMMARY

Artificial intelligence companies racing to shape how the federal government might regulate their industry amid rising safety and economic concerns are spending heavily to influence which candidates make it to Congress. A New York Times analysis of federal campaign finance data shows that the political groups aligned with the two leading A.I. developers, OpenAI and Anthropic, have quietly but decisively intervened in key 2026 races, spending on campaign advertising and outreach to voters to the tune of $55.7 million. The Times analysis of federal advertising and campaign outreach expenditures made by the four major super PACs during this cycle showed that they have spent far more money in support of Democrats — $28 million to back 21 Democrats and nearly $19 million to boost 30 Republicans — and that the candidates they backed almost always won.

ARTICLE

A.I. Groups Are Spending Millions to Influence the Midterms
See how groups aligned with Anthropic and OpenAI have funneled major money into the fight for control of Congress.
By Catie Edmondson, Matt Zdun and Daniel Wood
Published 2026-09-29 04:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/29/us/politics/ai-super-pac-money-midterm-elections.html

Artificial intelligence companies racing to shape how the federal government might regulate their industry amid rising safety and economic concerns are spending heavily to influence which candidates make it to Congress.

A New York Times analysis of federal campaign finance data shows that the political groups aligned with the two leading A.I. developers, OpenAI and Anthropic, have quietly but decisively intervened in key 2026 races, spending on campaign advertising and outreach to voters to the tune of $55.7 million.

So far, the spending has been concentrated almost entirely in the primaries. The two groups have spent $52.6 million on safe seats — those that are unlikely to change party hands but that often feature intense intraparty contests. The big A.I. players have also spent more heavily for Democrats than Republicans. They have boosted candidates who align with their agendas, helped defeat those they see as hostile to it and ingratiated themselves with front-runners who are likely to be in positions of power in the next Congress to make decisions critical to their bottom lines.

But with voters quickly souring on their industry — including demanding that lawmakers do more to regulate A.I. and halt or mitigate the proliferation of data centers — they have taken pains to obscure their involvement. With few exceptions, they have intervened without ever explicitly mentioning A.I. or data centers in the TV and digital ads they have purchased.

(The Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

The Times reviewed 95 unique ads bought by four A.I. super PACs heavily funded by the two biggest players — the OpenAI-aligned Leading the Future and the Anthropic-aligned Public First Action — each of which funnels its money through separate Republican and Democratic groups. None of the ads mentioned data centers. Only seven mentioned A.I. or an A.I. company directly.

An ad for Representative Barry Moore, Republican of Alabama, featured the phrase “CHAMPION AMERICAN INNOVATION” as he shook hands with firefighters in a garage — one of several A.I.-backed advertisements that used that phrase over images of workplaces that appeared to have nothing to do with artificial intelligence.

Another was in support of former Representative Jesse Jackson Jr., a Democrat running for an open House seat in Illinois. It was paid for by Think Big, which is aligned with OpenAI, and praised him as committed to reducing gun violence and supporting law enforcement.

And in some instances, both the Republican and Democratic groups funded by the same big A.I. player created advertisements advocating opposing sides of an issue. For example, these two spots for House candidates in Texas, one Democrat and one Republican, praise opposite positions on immigration. Both are funded by the Anthropic-aligned super PACs.

“It’s so cynical,” said Nate Blouin, a state senator in Utah who lost a Democratic primary to an opponent who had been backed by more than $1 million in A.I.-funded ads. “They’re coming into races in safe seats that they know that they’re going to be decided in the primaries, and they are spending millions of dollars on things that are unrelated to the core issue that they are pushing for.”

It is a strategy that has also been deployed this cycle by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, another major interest group whose brand has become a liability in recent years and has spent in the midterms to the tune of tens of millions of dollars while rarely mentioning its top issue.

The companies behind the spending have somewhat different policy agendas. Anthropic generally supports stricter regulation on A.I. development, while OpenAI, tends to push for fewer guardrails to allow for the acceleration of A.I. development. But they both share the same goal: promoting A.I. and electing policymakers who hold a favorable view of it.

In a statement, Anthony Rivera-Rodriguez, a spokesman for Public First Action, vehemently denied that the Anthropic-aligned group had a parallel agenda to the political group affiliated with OpenAI.

“We reject any suggestion that we have anything in common with Leading the Future, a group that exists to gut every serious attempt to regulate artificial intelligence,” he said. His organization, he added, “was founded to be the counterweight to Big Tech’s political machine,” and stands “with the people willing to fight for real rules on this technology and protect kids, workers and families from A.I. harms.”

Jesse Hunt, a spokesman for Leading the Future, said the group was “focused on building a bench of champions who understand the need for a national A.I. framework that keeps America at the forefront of innovation while putting responsible safeguards in place to protect workers, families and communities.”

The Times analysis of federal advertising and campaign outreach expenditures made by the four major super PACs during this cycle showed that they have spent far more money in support of Democrats — $28 million to back 21 Democrats and nearly $19 million to boost 30 Republicans — and that the candidates they backed almost always won.

Rewarding the A.I.-Friendly

Late last year, Representative Valerie P. Foushee, a Democrat who represents most of North Carolina’s research triangle, was staring down a formidable primary challenge.

Then, two days before Nida Allam, a younger, more progressive candidate who had challenged her in the past, announced that she was running again against Ms. Foushee, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader, named the congresswoman as co-chairwoman of the party’s new Commission on A.I. and the Innovation Economy.

Two months later, the Anthropic-aligned Jobs and Democracy PAC spent $1.6 million in support of Ms. Foushee. She won narrowly, defeating Ms. Allam by less than 1 percentage point.

“These committees and task forces — they’re basically a flag or indicator to the lobbyist industry that these are people who will have decision-making power over your industry and so you need to go spend money on their campaigns,” Ms. Allam said in a recent interview. “No one is spending that amount of money unless they’re getting something in return.”

In a statement, Ms. Foushee denied that the money had bought any favorable treatment for A.I., saying that her work on the issue “has centered on establishing guardrails, holding corporations accountable, and protecting our children, communities and jobs.”

She pointed to legislation she joined after her primary win that would tax large A.I. companies to establish a federal jobs program and direct the National Institute of Standards and Technology “to ensure proper watermarking, digital fingerprinting and metadata is required for audio and visual content generated by artificial intelligence.”

That record, Ms. Foushee said, “clearly demonstrates that I am here to put A.I. regulations in place that prioritize people over corporations and billionaires.”

Still, unlike many Democrats who have aggressively criticized the industry, Ms. Foushee, a member of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee who also sits on a bipartisan A.I. task force, had already signaled an embrace of the technology. In 2024, she led legislation that aimed to increase diversity in A.I. research and education.

(She was not the only Democrat on the party’s A.I. task force to benefit from the industry’s largess. Public First bought ads in support of Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey that advocate implementing A.I. safeguards, including one that praises him as someone who “can make sure A.I. serves us — not the other way around.”)

In Washington State, American Mission waded into the G.O.P. primary to replace Representative Dan Newhouse, who is retiring at the end of this Congress, to back Amanda McKinney. Ms. McKinney, a Yakima County commissioner, won President Trump’s endorsement this cycle, but was running against a former racecar driver who had won Mr. Trump’s endorsement in 2024 when he challenged Mr. Newhouse.

“She believes the United States must lead in artificial intelligence and advanced technologies, not surrender leadership to China or other adversaries,” her campaign website says. “Amanda opposes heavy-handed regulation that stifles innovation or drives jobs overseas.”

American Mission spent about $780,000 to support Ms. McKinney. She advanced from her primary with 35 percent of the vote.

Punishing the Skeptics

With other seats, in Utah, Illinois and New York, the PACs moved to undercut candidates who had established themselves as foes of A.I.

The most prominent example was in the primary to succeed Representative Jerrold Nadler, Democrat of New York. The race was inundated by outside spending after Alex Bores, an assemblyman, sponsored legislation seeking to regulate advanced artificial intelligence models. That set off a multimillion-dollar influx from rival A.I. interests, with Think Big, aligned with OpenAI, attacking Mr. Bores and Jobs and Democracy, aligned with Anthropic, defending him. He narrowly lost the race.

Along with Ms. Foushee’s contest in North Carolina and a primary in the district of Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz, the former chairwoman of the Democratic National Committee, the race drew the most money from the A.I. PACs this cycle.

In Utah, Think Big intervened to boost Ben McAdams, a former Democratic congressman.

It was not expected to be a highly competitive primary, and was made even less so after Punchbowl News unearthed a series of old posts in which his opponent, Mr. Blouin, joked about sexual assault and made offensive comments about women and Mormons. Mr. McAdams made no mention of A.I. on his campaign website, though he wrote an opinion essay arguing that schools “should begin treating A.I. fluency as a basic form of literacy.” He said he opposed the construction of a 40,000-acre A.I. data-center campus proposed in the district.

But Mr. Blouin, the state senator, described himself as a “leading skeptic of the push for unchecked growth of data centers,” and grew increasingly vocal about A.I. and data-center regulation as the race went on.

Think Big spent about $1.1 million on television and digital ads and text-message blasts supporting Mr. McAdams. Asked for comment, Mr. McAdams reiterated a previous statement he had made during a June debate, in which he said that “every member of Congress needs to be proactive in providing oversight of A.I. in order to protect jobs, our kids, the environment and the fabric of our communities.”

“That will require federal guardrails to make sure this technology happens carefully and transparently, with appropriate regulation, strong oversight, human accountability, and safeguards for data privacy and civil rights,” he said. “A.I. could potentially cure cancer, but it could also destroy our kids. I believe thoughtful policy can unleash the good and stop the bad.”

And in a pair of crowded Democratic primaries in the Chicago area and parts of central Illinois, Think Big spent a combined $2.6 million in support of two centrist former members of Congress — Melissa Bean and Mr. Jackson — who were both running against more progressive opponents.

Mr. Jackson was lagging in fund-raising behind both Robert Peters, a state senator, and Donna Miller, a Cook County commissioner. In the two months before the primary, his campaign raised just $72,000, compared with Ms. Miller’s $670,000 and Mr. Peters’s $224,000.

That is when Mr. Jackson leaned into talking about A.I. He cited it in an opinion column touting the benefits of the technology for family caregivers, discussed it at a local candidate forum and even used it in an ad in which A.I. simulated the voice of former Representative Bobby Rush, whose vocal cords had been damaged by cancer, offering his endorsement of Mr. Jackson.

The progressive candidate in that race, Mr. Peters, had supported a law banning A.I. mental health therapy, and legislation creating legal safeguards for artists whose work was copied or reproduced using A.I.

As Think Big began pouring money in support of Mr. Jackson into the race, Fairshake, a pro-cryptocurrency group, began running advertisements against Mr. Peters, who was backed by Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and other progressives, accusing him of being beholden to corporate interests.

“For me,” Mr. Peters said, “it was like a punishment on my legislative record.”

In the end, neither man won the primary. The victor, Ms. Miller, was not backed by either of the major A.I. players. But they may have seen her as an ally, anyway.

The A.I. section of the “Priorities” section of Ms. Miller’s campaign website is roughly seven times as long as all other issue sections, including health care and jobs.

“I’ll support responsible innovation in technology, digital assets and business development that benefits working people and local communities,” she wrote.

Backing the Front-Runners

The A.I. groups spent in support of clear front-runners in primaries all across the country, including favorites of party leaders, many of them Republican. Representative Kevin Hern of Oklahoma, who was widely expected to win the nomination to replace Markwayne Mullin in the Senate, was backed by nearly $1.3 million spent by American Mission and Defending Our Values before his victory in June.

Defending Our Values also supported Carlos De La Cruz, the brother of Representative Monica De La Cruz of Texas, who both received speaking slots at the midterms convention in Dallas. Mr. De La Cruz is favored to win his election; the nonpartisan Cook Political Report recently rated Ms. De La Cruz’s race as a “tossup.”

American Mission spent about $375,000 to support Senator Lindsey Graham for his primary campaign in South Carolina, though it was never expected to be particularly competitive. After he died, the super PAC spent nearly $1.2 million supporting his sister, Darline, in the primary and general contests.

A Vanishing Money Trail

With five weeks left until the midterms, the A.I. groups have yet to wade into many general election contests.

American Mission has doled out roughly $500,000 each on behalf of three Republican candidates for Senate who are running in less competitive races: Representative Julia Letlow in Louisiana, and Senators Darline Graham of South Carolina and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi. Think Big, the Democratic super PAC, has spent nearly $300,000 to support three House candidates — Representatives Greg Stanton of Arizona, Emilia Sykes of Ohio and Steven Horsford of Nevada — as well as roughly $50,000 to support Representative Joseph D. Morelle in New York.

The amounts could grow. But political operatives closely following their spending believe that the groups will have to shift their strategy amid the furious outpouring of anti-A.I. sentiment, and will instead move money through other means. That could include donating directly to the major political PACs associated with House Democrats or Republicans, or establishing smaller, more obscure groups to move the money through, as AIPAC has done.

Usamah Andrabi, the communications director for Justice Democrats, the ultraprogressive organization that backed many candidates whom A.I. groups spent against, said the industry’s influence was already becoming as difficult to track as that of AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups.

“There was a time where I could tell you every Israel lobby super PAC, and I cannot tell you that anymore because there’s so many pop-up PACs, there’s so many shell PACs, there’s so many pass-throughs,” Mr. Andrabi said. “And I think the same thing is happening with the A.I. lobby.”

SUMMARY

In the lead-up to the midterm elections, calls for generational change have echoed through districts across the country, as younger candidates have pushed to replace the old guard. In Massachusetts, Senator Ed Markey, 80, was diagnosed with “chronic re-election disorder” by allies of his younger primary opponent. In primary after primary, voters rejected those calls for younger leadership, voting for incumbent politicians who were notably older than their challengers, according to an analysis by The New York Times.

ARTICLE

Voters Say Congress Is Too Old. But Older Candidates Keep Winning.
In primary races across the country, incumbency trumped calls for generational change, as older members of Congress held off younger challengers.
By Lisa Lerer, Matt Zdun and Ashley Wu
Published 2026-10-04 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/10/04/us/elections/gerontocracy.html

In the lead-up to the midterm elections, calls for generational change have echoed through districts across the country, as younger candidates have pushed to replace the old guard.

In Massachusetts, Senator Ed Markey, 80, was diagnosed with “chronic re-election disorder” by allies of his younger primary opponent. “Doctors agree: Democracy suffers when politicians won’t pass the torch,” said an actor dressed as a doctor in an attack ad.

In Northern California, a spot denouncing Representative Mike Thompson, 75, compared the Capitol to a refrigerator, full of “career politicians” who “sit there year after year behind the pickles.” Thompson, the ad said, was “past his expiration date.”

And in Mississippi, an ad featured a woman identified as a retired public-school teacher wondering about the effectiveness of Representative Bennie Thompson, 78, who has been in Congress for over three decades. “Has he made things better here?” she asked. “Absolutely not.”

And yet, the gerontocracy remains alive and well in American politics. In primary after primary, voters rejected those calls for younger leadership, voting for incumbent politicians who were notably older than their challengers, according to an analysis by The New York Times.

Their wins didn’t stem from a failure by younger candidates to press the case: Campaign ads pushing for new, younger leadership ran in at least 77 House and Senate primary races, according to a Times analysis of data from AdImpact, a media tracking firm.

Instead, the results point to an unshakable reality of American politics: Incumbency remains a near-invincible force in congressional elections. With stronger name recognition and a fund-raising advantage, members of Congress typically hold onto their seats as long as they like.

Over the past four decades, the re-election rate for incumbents has rarely dipped below 80 percent. The incumbent has lost in only 78 primary races out of several thousand over the past two decades, according to a New York Times analysis of data from Ballotpedia.

Heading into November, several older incumbents are facing general election challenges from much younger candidates. In Ohio, for instance, Representative Marcy Kaptur, an 80-year-old Democrat, is in a tough race against Derek Merrin, a Republican who is 40.

Should they win in the general election, many of those older politicians will find themselves in good company in Washington. The current Congress is the oldest in modern history, with more than 135 members who will be 70 or older by the end of their term.

Octogenarians hold some of the most powerful positions in the federal government long past the point when most Americans have retired.

President Trump, now 80, became the oldest president to ever take office when he started his second term in 2025 — a title he claimed from former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., who entered the White House at age 78.

“In actuality, life begins at 80!” Mr. Trump proudly declared on social media in 2022, back when he was a spry 76 years old.

Senator Charles E. Grassley, Republican of Iowa, is third in line to the presidency at age 93 and leads the powerful Judiciary Committee. Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent who continues to hold sway in Democratic politics, is 85, one of seven octogenarians in the chamber. Senator Mitch McConnell, 84, who recently returned to the Senate after suffering a fall at his Capitol Hill home, served as party leader until the age of 82.

Like the indignities of growing older, signs of the nation’s aging political class have become increasingly difficult to ignore.

In 2023, video of Mr. McConnell, then 81, freezing for 20 seconds in front of television cameras reverberated across the internet and newscasts. Soon after, a clip surfaced of Senator Dianne Feinstein, 90, appearing confused when asked to vote in committee.

A year later, Mr. Biden ignited a firestorm after he faltered in his final presidential debate, inflaming long-simmering concerns about his fitness to serve a second term that culminated in an extraordinary wave of calls from within the Democratic Party to replace him on the ticket.

The party’s defeat — and the many months of recriminations that followed — ignited a broader reckoning over its aging leadership and a deep desire among Democratic voters for new faces.

Some members of both parties seemed to heed the call: This Congress saw a notable number of retirements, with 28 members over age 65 announcing their exit, according to a Times analysis. Their ranks included longtime party leaders like former Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, 86, and Mr. McConnell, who is not seeking re-election.

“Watching the Biden thing really said something about the necessity for generational change in the party, and I think I want to respect that,” Representative Jerrold Nadler, 79, a New York Democrat, said when he decided to step aside last year after more than three decades in the House.

Several other older members died while in office. Over the past two years, the deaths of six lawmakers scrambled races from South Carolina to Arizona. Over the summer, Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina, died of a heart issue two days after his 71st birthday — relatively young by congressional standards.

But this year, when faced with the choice between an older incumbent and a younger challenger, voters more frequently chose experience over a fresh voice.

In Massachusetts, Mr. Markey defeated Representative Seth Moulton, 47, a moderate Democrat who had campaigned on a message of generational change. The oldest senator in his state’s history, Mr. Markey arrived in Washington in 1976, entering Congress before a majority of his current constituents were born. He served nearly 20 terms in the House before being elected to the Senate in 2013.

In Republican primaries, the biggest age gap was in Texas, where Representative John Carter, 84, defeated Valentina Gomez, who was 26 on the day of the election. For Democrats, it was in Ohio, where Joyce Beatty, 76, faced off against Joe Gerard, 26. The Gen Z challengers in each of those races captured less than a quarter of the vote.

Only seven Gen Z candidates took on incumbents in primaries, and all but one came up short. The exception was in Colorado’s First Congressional District, where Melat Kiros, who was 29 on Election Day, ousted the incumbent, Diana DeGette, who was 68.

To be sure, not all older incumbents succeeded. And among the handful who lost, several were bested by far younger opponents — in races with some of the largest age gaps in recent history. In New York, where Representative Adriano Espaillat lost to Darializa Avila Chevalier in a Democratic primary, there was a 39-year gap. In Texas, where Representative Al Green lost to Christian Menefee, the age gap was 40 years.

In Connecticut, Representative John Larson, a 78-year-old Democrat who attracted attention after suffering a complex partial seizure on the House floor last year, failed in his efforts to win a 15th term.

Campaigning across his Hartford-area district, Mr. Larson, who was backed by his party’s leaders, argued that voters would lose political power if they ousted him from his post as the top Democrat on the House Social Security Subcommittee.

His opponents questioned the potency of his seniority, noting that Mr. Larson failed to advance his signature piece of Social Security legislation for more than a decade, including when Democrats controlled Congress.

“This notion that you show up and you’re going to pass something — that’s a fallacy,” Mr. Larson said in an interview, as he campaigned at a senior center over the summer. “It takes time.”

But in August, Luke Bronin, 47, the former mayor of Hartford, won the primary race by a double-digit margin.

“This is a political earthquake in Connecticut,” Mr. Bronin proclaimed at his victory night party in Hartford.

Part of the challenge facing proponents of generational change in Congress is that Americans do not agree on how old, exactly, is too old.

While polling consistently shows that broad majorities of Americans support age caps for Congress, voters disagree over when those limits should kick in.

Rahm Emanuel, a prominent Democrat who has signaled his desire to run for president in 2028, has called for a mandatory retirement age of 75 for the president, cabinet officials, members of Congress and federal judges. Other politicians, including Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida and Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, have proposed term limits — a policy that sidesteps the issue of age but would likely force the retirement of some of Congress’s oldest members.

But while other industries have mandatory retirement ages, members of Congress have shown little desire for policies that would amount to voting themselves out of a job.

Nor, it seems, have their voters.

One pilot stabbed another at the controls of an Emirati flight to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, causing it to suddenly plunge thousands of feet until passengers and the crew won a fight to regain control of the plane.

Passengers described a terrifying fall during the attack, which ended when some of them stepped into the melee and managed to subdue the aggressive pilot. “Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” he said.

Passengers on a morning flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv recounted scenes of panic and terror on Wednesday as their aircraft suddenly plunged thousands of feet while screams for help came from behind the cockpit door.

Israel and Saudi Arabia don’t have formal ties, but Israelis have occasionally landed there.

The flight to Israel that was diverted Wednesday morning after a clash in the cockpit landed safely in Saudi Arabia, a country that Israeli citizens rarely set foot in.

The two nations don’t have formal diplomatic, trade or tourism ties, though attempts to forge them have been central to U.S. regional diplomacy in recent years.

Still, their proximity has taken Israelis to Saudi Arabia under exceptional circumstances.

The 1944 Convention on International Civil Aviation, known as the Chicago Convention, laid the foundation for how global civil aviation is governed. It states that all parties to the agreement, which include Israel and Saudi Arabia, should assist aircraft in distress in their territory.

After Wednesday’s emergency landing at the Tabuk airport, a civil-military facility in northwestern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi authorities said that they would provide “necessary care” to passengers. Their statement did not mention the flight’s connection to Israel. The FlyDubai aircraft had been flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

In the past few years, at least two other passenger flights en route to Tel Aviv have made emergency landings in Saudi Arabia.

In September 2025, a flight from Dubai landed in the kingdom because of a medical emergency on board, according to a statement by the Israeli Foreign Ministry carried by Israeli news media. The plane then continued on to its destination, according to the statement, which did not say which airline operated the flight or where it landed in Saudi Arabia.

In 2023, an Air Seychelles flight from the Seychelles, an island nation in the Indian Ocean, landed in Jeddah because of a technical malfunction, according to the government-funded Seychelles News Agency. The airport said at the time that roughly 130 passengers were staying at an airport hotel.

In a statement at the time, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel thanked the Saudi authorities for their “good neighborliness” and “warm attitude” toward the Israeli passengers.

FlyDubai operates up to 10 daily flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv.

FlyDubai became the first airline offering commercial flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv in 2020 after Israel and the United Arab Emirates signed an agreement to normalize relations.

The new route meant that Israeli passengers could catch connecting flights in the Persian Gulf, rather than having to go via Europe, significantly cutting down on travel time.

FlyDubai operated the first scheduled commercial flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv in November 2020, after Israel and the Emirates signed the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords, strengthening economic, political and security relations.

A low-cost carrier, FlyDubai initially offered two daily flights from Dubai International Airport to Tel Aviv and now operates up to 10. One of those flights made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after what passengers described as a midair altercation between the pilots, which the Israeli authorities were still investigating.

The airline, which began flying in 2009, is wholly owned by Dubai through the Investment Corporation of Dubai, the government’s main investment arm, which also owns Emirates Airlines.

All of the flights between Dubai and Israel travel through Saudi airspace. On Aug. 31, 2020, an El Al jet carrying American and Israeli officials flew to Abu Dhabi along nearly the whole length of Saudi Arabia, the first time Riyadh had allowed an Israeli passenger plane to cross its skies. Two days later, Saudi Arabia said flights from any country to and from the Emirates could fly over its territory, without naming Israel. Saudi Arabia does not have diplomatic relations with Israel.

Most FlyDubai flights fly out of Dubai International Airport’s Terminal 2. Passengers bound for Tel Aviv check in from the much larger Terminal 3, which has heightened security, and can add roughly an hour to the process.

Etihad Airways, Abu Dhabi’s main carrier, added a sixth daily flight to Tel Aviv this summer, making the route its busiest weekly route worldwide.

A passenger describes the chaos of the FlyDubai flight and fears that it would crash.

“We heard screams on the plane, and when they opened the cockpit, there was a lot of blood,” she said.

“Within a few minutes, our plane completely lost control, and we felt that this was it — we were about to crash,” the younger Ms. Ohayon said, adding that she began reciting a Jewish prayer often said in times of distress.

SUMMARY

The death row inmate Christa Pike was in critical condition and receiving medical care, her lawyers said Thursday, a day after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her. The failed execution on Wednesday night was the state’s second bungled death penalty attempt this year, and Mr. Lee on Thursday said he was suspending executions — including Ms. Pike’s — to allow an independent review. Christa Pike’s botched execution is the second this year in which Tennessee has failed to execute an inmate using lethal injection drugs.

Live Updates: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
The inmate, Christa Pike, is “alive right now” after surviving an attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer said. He called on Gov. Bill Lee to reduce her sentence to life in prison.
By Billy Witz, Emily Cochrane, Jacey Fortin, Maia Spoto, Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs, Benjamin Mueller, Shaila Dewan, Rick Rojas and Yan Zhuang

Latest

Here’s the latest.

The death row inmate Christa Pike was in critical condition and receiving medical care, her lawyers said Thursday, a day after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her. They called for Gov. Bill Lee to reduce her sentence to life in prison, calling the botched attempt to end her life with two doses of pentobarbital “cruel and torturous.”

The failed execution on Wednesday night was the state’s second bungled death penalty attempt this year, and Mr. Lee on Thursday said he was suspending executions — including Ms. Pike’s — to allow an independent review.

Lawyers for Ms Pike said that did not go far enough, and urged Mr. Lee to take her off death row. Ms. Pike “has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty,” said one of her lawyers, Randy Spivey.

Mr. Lee previously denied a similar request and his office did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment. Speaking to reporters earlier Thursday, he said the failed execution “shouldn’t have happened.” He added, “We should find out what happened and make those changes necessary to do what the people of this state want done.”

The governor said it was not immediately clear who would conduct the independent review, but said that the Tennessee Department of Correction appeared to have followed its procedures.

Ms. Pike, 50, was to become the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. It was not clear why the execution attempt failed. Mr. Spivey said it had taken an hour to establish an intravenous line, and that he had counted seven needles used in her left arm alone.

In 1996, Ms. Pike was found guilty of torturing and murdering a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in an attack carried out with her boyfriend and another friend. They slashed at Ms. Slemmer with a box cutter, carved a pentagram into her chest and removed a piece of her skull.

Ms. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has long favored Ms. Pike’s execution. “Nobody remembers Colleen,” she told The New York Times last month.

Here’s what we’re covering:

In the final months of his term, Tennessee’s governor confronts another failed execution.

In the waning months of his tenure as Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee is confronting another uproar over the state’s secretive lethal injection process.

On Thursday, he stopped all remaining executions and ordered an investigation into how Christa Pike, the lone woman on the state’s death row, survived two rounds of lethal drugs being injected into her. But Mr. Lee, who is term-limited, may not be around in office to see the investigation through.

Speaking to reporters a day after the failed execution, Mr. Lee acknowledged that things might change under a new governor. The Republican nominee to replace him as the leader of the deep-red state, Marsha Blackburn, had already called for the return of the electric chair in response.

“What I think should happen, while I’m the governor, is that we should determine the steps forward,” Mr. Lee said. “We should find out what happened and make those changes necessary to do what the people of this state want done.”

Asked about Ms. Blackburn’s comments, he declined to comment. Jerri Green, the Democratic nominee for governor, said she would keep a pause on all executions if elected.

The state’s handling of executions have been a recurring problem. In 2022, during his first term, Mr. Lee paused executions after the drugs used in the lethal injection process had not been tested properly. An independent investigation was conducted, and executions resumed in 2025 under a new protocol.

Then, earlier this year, Mr. Lee granted a temporary reprieve to one death row inmate after prison and medical staff failed to find a vein to inject the lethal drugs. He did not order an investigation or call for a broader pause after that failed execution.

Asked what was different this time, Mr. Lee replied, “We need to find out what happened, and until we find out, there’ll be a stay on executions.”

Most Americans favor the death penalty, but support has declined.

A majority of Americans are in favor of the death penalty for a person convicted of murder, public polling has found, though support has decreased in recent decades.

In the 1990s, about four in five Americans supported capital punishment. But by 2025, 52 percent of Americans favored the death penalty, according to polling by Gallup.

A 2026 survey by the Pew Research Center also found that about 66 percent of Americans favored the death penalty for people convicted of murder, which was about on par with its findings in 2020.

Wide gaps exist in support along partisan lines, with Republicans overwhelmingly in favor and Democrats more split in their opinions, Pew found.

As opposition to the death penalty has risen, a number of states have stopped executions.

Today, 23 states have abolished the death penalty, with Virginia becoming the first Southern state to do so in 2021. The state’s governor, Ralph S. Northam, a Democrat, pointed to racial disparities, noting that a majority of Virginia inmates executed in the 20th century were Black.

Now, executions are mostly conducted by a handful of states. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Florida has executed 16 inmates so far this year, and Texas has executed six. Alabama, Arizona, Oklahoma and Tennessee have also carried out executions.

The Supreme Court briefly banned the death penalty in 1972 but restored it four years later. Since then, dozens of other countries have abolished capital punishment, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Gallup found in 2023 that, for the first time since it began asking the question in 2000, more Americans said they believed the death penalty was applied unfairly, rather than fairly.

America’s long history of executions includes many botched ones.

The failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee was the latest in a long string of botched executions in the United States, a history that extends almost as far back as executions themselves.

The failures have varied widely — trouble finding a vein; drugs that didn’t kill, as happened in Tennessee on Wednesday night; and gruesome scenes involving blood or flames. Ms. Pike snored and breathed for an hour before prison officials abandoned the effort to end her life with pentobarbital.

Even as the technology has evolved from ropes to firing squads to modern chemistry, the effort to spare prisoners a protracted, painful death is still far from reliable. While most executions end with the death sentence fulfilled, mistakes can be harrowing.

‘An Awful Sight’

New York carried out the United States’ first execution by electric chair in 1890 when it put William Kemmler to death at a prison in Auburn.

A front-page headline in The Buffalo Evening News said the execution “was an awful sight” and declared “the process a failure.” One doctor involved predicted, wrongly, that “there will never be another electrocution.”

The Evening News article described Mr. Kemmler as the “coolest man in the room” as he adjusted his tie and sat in the electric chair.

The current was turned on and the doctor soon announced that the man was dead. Moments later, in a panic, he asked for the current to be run again.

“This man is not dead,” the doctor cried, according to the Evening News account. “Faces grew white,” the article said.

Mr. Kemmler’s lips dripped, his chest moved, and he made a loud wheezing and groaning sound. Finally, he was again pronounced dead.

“FAR WORSE THAN HANGING,” The New York Times wrote on its front page on Aug. 7, 1890.

Flames and Smoke

One of the more horrific executions took place in 1983 in Alabama, when executioners sent three different jolts of electricity into John Evans III’s body. The first two failed to kill him, but rather sent flames flying from his leg and head.

Mr. Evans’s lawyer called the execution “a barbaric ritual” and said that his client had been “burned alive tonight by the state of Alabama.”

In 1990, a similarly disturbing execution took place in Florida, when fire and smoke emanated from the body of Jessie Tafero as he was put to death.

Unreliable Injections

The Death Penalty Information Center, a research group, says that lethal injection, introduced as a humane alternative to the chair, had the highest botch rate in executions between 1890 and 2010.

In 2018, Alabama prison officials were unable to insert an intravenous line into Doyle Hamm, who was terminally ill, and he became one of a small group to have survived an execution attempt. He died in prison of natural causes three years later.

In Oklahoma, John Grant vomited and shook for several minutes in 2021 during the state’s first execution since 2015, when it had mistakenly used the wrong drug to stop his heart.

The next year, again in Alabama, executioners tried for hours to find the veins of Joe Nathan James in 2022 as he lay in the death chamber. They eventually sliced into one of his arms in what is known as a “cutdown” in order to give him the fatal drugs, according to a private autopsy.

And in 2024, Idaho executioners tried for nearly an hour to insert an intravenous line into the arms, then hands, then legs of Thomas Creech, who was then 73. “I was thinking the whole time that this is really it,” he told The Times several months later. He remains one of eight people on Idaho’s death row.

New Method, New Problems

Alabama pioneered killing prisoners with nitrogen gas in 2024, the first new execution method in decades.

Kenneth Smith, one of three men convicted of murdering Elizabeth Dorlene Sennett, was the first prisoner killed by nitrogen gas. After the execution, the state prison commissioner, John Q. Hamm, said that “nothing was out of the ordinary from what we were expecting.”

But several witnesses told The New York Times that what they saw was disturbing.

“We were told by some people that worked" in the prison system “that he’d take two or three breaths, and he’d be out and gone,” said Mike Sennett, Ms. Sennett’s son. “That ain’t what happened. After about two or three breaths, that’s when the struggling started.”

Mr. Hamm and Mr. Sennett said they believed Mr. Smith might have tried to hold his breath to delay his death.

“With all that struggling and jerking and trying to get off that table, more or less, it’s just something I don’t ever want to see again,” Mr. Sennett said.

Witnesses reported that two other men who were later killed by nitrogen — Alan Miller in 2024 and Anthony Boyd in 2025 — shook and gasped for several minutes before they were pronounced dead. Alabama officials have maintained that the executions had followed protocol.

There are several possibilities for why the Tennessee execution failed.

The execution team went through at least seven needles trying to find a vein suitable for delivering doses of a lethal drug to Tennessee inmate Christa Pike, her lawyers said on Thursday.

Ms. Pike, who survived the botched execution on Wednesday night, was left with blistering and burning around the intravenous insertion sites that the execution team ultimately used to deliver the drug, the lawyers added.

Those details reinforced the sense among outside medical experts that Ms. Pike had survived the procedure because the drug, pentobarbital, probably poured into tissue surrounding the insertion sites instead of entering her bloodstream.

That could have prevented the drug from reaching the levels needed in her circulatory system to stop her breathing.

The drug may nonetheless have lowered her oxygen levels or weakened her circulation enough to cause permanent brain damage. Any leak of the drug into her tissue could also have caused chemical burns.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers said she was in critical condition and receiving lifesaving medical care.

Stephen Ferrell, one of her lawyers, said that while details of the execution attempt were consistent with there having been problems with the intravenous delivery, a number of other factors could have been involved.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement on Wednesday night that it “had followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general’s office.” Officials did not answer questions on Thursday about what went wrong with the administration of the drug.

Medical experts said there were signs that the two intravenous catheters, rather than directing the drug into Ms. Pike’s bloodstream, had allowed it to leak into the tissue surrounding the insertion point.

That could have been because of how or where the catheters were inserted, the fragility of Ms. Pike’s veins, or for another reason. Her lawyers said that doctors had always had difficulty finding veins during her blood draws and that Ms. Pike has a blood disorder that exacerbates that problem.

During the execution attempt, they added, Ms. Pike even tried to help the staff place the two IV lines.

“She over and over again said, ‘Please, try up on my shoulder higher, please try here, please try here,’” Randy Spivey, another of her lawyers, said. He added that Ms. Pike thanked them once staff members thought they had established the two lines.

Instances in which intravenous drugs leak into tissue under the skin are known as “IV infiltration,” and have been cited in past botched executions, including ones that caused extensive chemical burns.

Experts said that experienced doctors in a medical setting would typically be able to recognize signs of an IV infiltration as it occurred.

Members of the news media who served as witnesses to the execution attempt said that Ms. Pike at one point described a burning spot in her arm that felt as if it were going to burst and asked if that was normal.

“The pain in her arm should have been a bright red flag that the IV was infiltrating,” said Dr. Mark Heath, an assistant professor of anesthesiology at Columbia University Irving Medical Center.

Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology at the Emory University School of Medicine who said that he had previously been retained by Ms. Pike’s lawyers as a medical expert, said that such an event would have caused the type of reaction that witnesses described.

The result, he said, could have been a highly alkaline solution leaking into Ms. Pike’s arm. “Essentially, they’ve injected bleach into the tissue of her arm,” Dr. Zivot said.

He added that he was speaking on his own behalf and not for Ms. Pike’s legal team, and that he had no direct knowledge of what happened during the execution attempt.

Having examined Ms. Pike’s medical records before the execution attempt, Dr. Zivot said that she was also susceptible to an IV infiltration. Ms. Pike’s lawyers had previously argued that the procedure could be agonizing for her in part because she has small veins.

“Her venous system was small, and there could be some fragility there,” Dr. Zivot said. “You push a lot of a caustic substance into a small vein like that, under pressure, it’s going to blow.”

He said chemical properties of the lethal drug, pentobarbital, mean that it can burn tissue and skin during executions.

Pentobarbital is a barbiturate that can treat seizures; it works by depressing activity in the nervous system. It is a mainstay drug for euthanizing animals. The drug has also been used in states with legal medical aid in dying.

Its main effect is to shut down electrical activity in the brain, including neurons in the brainstem that control breathing. The body enters a coma-like state, followed by respiratory failure and cardiac arrest.

The federal government adopted single-drug pentobarbital for lethal injections during the first Trump administration.

Under President Biden, the protocol was rescinded after a review by the Justice Department in January 2025 concluded that there remained “significant uncertainty” about whether using the drug for lethal injections “causes unnecessary pain and suffering.”

President Trump’s current administration has reinstated its use, and has said it will also use firing squads.

In Ms. Pike’s case, medical experts said it was also possible that there had been something wrong with the pentobarbital itself.

The primary manufacturer of pentobarbital has restricted the drug’s use in executions, the Justice Department review noted. As a result, states have turned to chemical companies and compounding pharmacies, which are more loosely regulated.

“Is it possible that the pentobarbital itself was somehow not constituted properly?” Dr. Zivot said. “Could it have degraded? Could it have expired? All of those things are possible.”

Almost as soon as lethal injection was first adopted in the United States in the late 1970s as a more medicalized, less painful method of execution, there were prolonged or botched executions.

In part, that was because the injections were often administered by correctional workers with limited medical training. Most doctors and anesthesiologists declined to advise or participate on ethical grounds.

In 2009, the maker of one of the key drugs, sodium thiopental, stopped production in the United States. Other drug companies prohibited the use of their products for executions.

States began scrambling to obtain the drugs, turning to compounding pharmacies and resorting to legally questionable arrangements like loaning the drugs to one another and importing drugs labeled for veterinary use. At one point, the Drug Enforcement Administration even seized Georgia’s supply of lethal injection drugs.

Prisoners argued in court that lethal injection did not eliminate pain and suffering, but only masked it. “It is not the most humane, it is the most humane-looking,” said Corinna Lain, a law professor and the author of “Secrets of the Killing State: the Untold Story of Lethal Injection,” published last year.

In response to the controversies, states shrouded the process in secrecy, passing laws that kept the public from learning details such as how the drugs are obtained and what dosage is used.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers said on Thursday that they hoped records would be preserved that would allow them to learn how her execution had gone wrong. They said they had long warned in court that Ms. Pike’s medical conditions could cause problems, but that those warnings went unheeded.

Mr. Spivey, her lawyer, said that among the at least seven needles used to try to establish an IV line in Ms. Pike’s left arm alone was one that appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt.

Whatever the reason the execution failed, medical experts said, the possibility that Ms. Pike had suffered the effects of a nonfatal dose of pentobarbital for an extended period created a risk for lasting brain injury.

“She could be facing profound medical complications,” Dr. Zivot said.

Pike said she rued a grisly crime. The victim’s mother wants her dead.

Everything changed for two women when Colleen Slemmer died three decades ago.

Ms. Slemmer, 19, had been studying at a Knoxville, Tenn., education program when three classmates lured her into the woods, tortured her and killed her.

Her mother, May Martinez, had already been uneasy about her daughter traveling hundreds of miles away from Jacksonville, Fla. The loss of her daughter, she said in an interview last month, was devastating.

“I’m not the same person I used to be,” Ms. Martinez said.

Christa Pike was the only person involved in the murder who was sentenced to death. In response to questions from The New York Times, she conceded that initially, she did not feel remorse. But over years of isolation, as a result of being the lone woman on death row, she said she had grown to regret her actions and work to make amends.

“Over years of sitting in here with deep contemplation and reflection, I know and understand the life that I have taken and how much it matters, how much it means, how many effects she could have had on the world, just like the effects I could have on the world,” Ms. Pike said.

Ms. Martinez, who fund-raised the money to drive to witness the execution, said she could not fathom Ms. Pike changing. She and her husband, Raul, remained firmly in support of the execution going forward.

On Wednesday, Ms. Martinez was on the grounds of the prison waiting for the execution. She did not say anything.

Christa Pike’s failed execution echoes another in Tennessee this year.

Christa Pike’s botched execution is the second this year in which Tennessee has failed to execute an inmate using lethal injection drugs.

In May, medical staff members tried to tap into Tony Carruthers’s veins but acknowledged after several attempts that they could not find a “suitable vein” for the drugs, the Tennessee Department of Correction said. Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, then ordered that any execution of Mr. Carruthers be delayed for a year.

Mr. Carruthers was convicted in connection with three 1994 murders. His lawyer, Maria DeLiberato, later wrote in an opinion essay in The New York Times that she had witnessed her client in “agony” as the execution team tried to insert an intravenous line for over an hour.

Tennessee’s use of lethal injection had come under scrutiny for its effectiveness even before the attempted executions of Ms. Pike and Mr. Carruthers. In 2022, the state paused executions for more than two years after Governor Lee said prison officials had failed to properly test its lethal injection drugs. Inmates have sued the state over its new injection procedure.

Mr. Carruthers represented himself in a 1996 trial over the killings of Marcellos Anderson; his mother, Delois Anderson; and Frederick Taylor. All three were found buried in a Memphis cemetery.

The American Civil Liberties Union argued that Mr. Carruthers was “plainly neither competent to stand trial nor competent to defend himself.” Lawyers who tried to represent him for his trial said they endured personal attacks, which were later connected to Mr. Carruthers’s mental illness.

His case drew attention before the execution attempt because allies and lawyers argued that he had been wrongfully convicted. They said that his mental illness prevented him from understanding his legal situation and the execution.

Multiple judges denied requests for new forensic testing that allies and lawyers said could help prove Mr. Carruthers’s innocence, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied his request to stop the execution.

Critics of the death penalty seized on Mr. Carruthers’s failed execution. Laura Porter, the executive director of the U.S. Campaign to End the Death Penalty, said at the time that “Tennessee has effectively made the case against the death penalty.”

In an interview on Thursday, Ms. DeLiberato said that Mr. Carruthers was still struggling with having full feeling and mobility on one side of his body. She added that his legal team was working to have an outside doctor examine him.

“Having been in that room, knowing exactly where everyone’s standing, what it looks like, what it smells like, what it sounds like, it was a difficult evening for me,” Ms. DeLiberato said, “and I can only imagine it was difficult for Tony.”

An Idaho death row prisoner described living through a botched execution.

Thomas Creech had been imprisoned in Idaho for nearly 50 years, convicted of five murders in three states and suspected of several more, when he was wheeled into an execution chamber in February 2024. For nearly an hour, medical workers at the Idaho Maximum Security Institution struggled to insert an intravenous line to pump a deadly drug into his bloodstream before the proceedings were called off.

Starting with his arms, then his hands and finally his legs, they tried and failed to get a needle into a suitable vein. “The worst ones was when they got down to my ankles,” Mr. Creech said in an interview a few months after his botched execution. “I was thinking the whole time that this is really it. I’m dead. This is my day to die.”

Mr. Creech described what it was like to endure the repeated needle jabs, knowing that any of them — if successful — could mean he would be dead within minutes. He described fear, pain, and his commitment to keeping his focus on his wife, who was sitting just a few feet away in the witness room, behind a glass panel.

Mr. Creech, who is considered a serial killer and is one of the longest-serving death row prisoners in the country, has offered conflicting accounts about his crimes over the years. At one point, he testified that he had killed as many as 42 people, some of them on behalf of a motorcycle gang or as part of a satanic religious ritual. Later, he took back many of those supposed admissions and said he had been put up to the claims by a fame-seeking lawyer.

More recently, and in his interview with The Times, he has said that he believed he had killed seven people. He claimed that he was in the throes of drug abuse at the time and that his victims had all been involved in a gang-rape of his former wife, who later died by suicide.

On the books, though, he has been convicted of five murders, including the fatal beating of a fellow prisoner, David Jensen, in 1981, for which he was sentenced to death.

Mr. Creech described the moments before he was to be executed. He recalled looking over to his current wife through the glass, and trying to tell her that he was sorry. Then he remembered the execution team starting with his right arm and failing to find a usable vein. They moved on to his right hand, his left hand and then his ankles.

The team spent about 42 minutes trying to insert an IV line before the execution was called off, according to Mr. Creech’s lawyers.

When the execution was called off just before 11 a.m., Mr. Creech said, he had trouble believing that he had really survived.

“I thought maybe I might already be in the afterlife,” he said. “Even now, today, I stop and I have to catch myself and think, ‘Am I really dead? I was supposed to be dead on the 28th of February. Am I really dead, and this is part of the afterlife? Continued punishment for my sins that I’ve committed?’”
